title: Explosive device kills a police officer in northern Spain
summary: Spain's police say that one police officer was killed and another seriously wounded when an explosive device went off while they were responding to a shooting in the northern city of Oviedo
story: Spain's police say that one police officer was killed and another seriously wounded when an explosive device went off while they were responding to a shooting in the northern city of Oviedo

MADRID -- One Spanish police officer was killed and another was seriously wounded when an explosive device went off while they were responding to a shooting in the northern city of Oviedo, Spain’s National Police said Tuesday.
There is no indication as of yet that the explosion was terror-related, according to authorities.
Police were searching for a suspect who fled the apartment building where officers found a backpack containing the bomb after responding to a call to alert them to shots being fired.
The backpack went off while the bomb squad was trying to remove it from the building, where it was found in the stairwell, police said.
On arriving at the scene, police found that one woman had been shot by the suspect. She's being treated at a local hospital. Her life reportedly isn't in danger.
The officer who died was a member of the dog unit. The injured officer, who is hospitalized, is in the bomb squad.
Spanish government spokesperson Elma Saiz expressed the government’s condolences for the felled officer.
“I also want to send a message for the recovery of the officer who was seriously injured during the explosion,” Saiz said.
Spanish news agency EFE said that the suspect has a record of petty crime.

title: At COP31, Turkey pushes zero-waste plan to curb climate change
summary: As world leaders arrive at United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya, calling for urgent climate action, co-host Turkey also wants to halve the amount of global waste in the next decade
story: As world leaders arrive at United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya, calling for urgent climate action, co-host Turkey also wants to halve the amount of global waste in the next decade

ANTALYA, Turkey -- As world leaders gathered for United Nations climate talks in the Turkish resort town of Antalya on Wednesday, host Turkey urged countries to commit to a zero-waste initiative aimed at reducing emissions and helping get global efforts to curb climate change back on track.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan touted his country's progress on recycling, saying its rate had risen from about 13% in 2017, when the zero waste movement began, to about 40% by the end of 2025.

"Some 90 million tons of waste have been brought back into our economy,” Erdogan told the leaders' summit. “We’ll not stop here and we will continue working and making every effort until we achieve the goal of zero waste."

Turkey has outlined 10 priorities for this year’s climate talks, known as COP31, with a pledge to accelerate electrification and the zero-waste initiatives emerging as major talking points during the opening days of the conference.

Turkish first lady Emine Erdogan, who attended Wednesday's talks, has been a driving force behind the zero-waste initiative, which aims to reduce methane emissions, cut food waste and promote a circular economy in which materials are reused and recycled.

“Recovered materials can be cheaper when reliable supplies, efficient processing and nearby demand outweigh the costs of collection, sorting and transport,” said Samed Agirbas, president of the nonprofit Zero Waste Foundation and a COP31 high-level climate champion.

If implemented, energy experts say the initiatives could slow global warming and reduce the environmental footprint of renewable energy technologies, like solar panels and batteries. But there is still a risk these climate ambitions may fall flat.
Conference agreements are often nonbinding and past hosts have been criticized for failing to follow through on promises. Turkey also faces scrutiny over its own climate record.

“The Zero Waste target is a good target. It definitely needs to be supported with concrete measures and further action,” said Berk Butan, who heads the waste campaign for Greenpeace Turkey. “But fundamentally, we also need to recognize its shortcomings.”

As the second biggest cause of climate change after carbon dioxide, the reduction of methane emissions could significantly slow global warming, according to the U.N. During the first three days of the climate talks, leaders repeatedly called for urgent climate action.
The U.N. recently had to readjust a decades-old goal of limiting the rise of global temperatures because the world was blowing past previous thresholds.

While Turkey wants countries to commit to reducing methane emissions, it has not signed the Global Methane Pledge. Launched at the 2021 climate talks in Glasgow, the initiative aims to reduce methane emissions by at least 30% from 2020 levels by 2030.
Turkey is also the world’s fifth-biggest emitter of methane from solid waste, according to nonprofit emissions tracker Climate TRACE.
“Methane emissions from waste disposal are an important challenge,” said Agirbas, with the Zero Waste Foundation.

A circular economy — an economic model that generally prioritizes recycling and other regenerative approaches that create less waste— would help reduce emissions, but not every country has the resources to take such steps.
Ke Wang, an energy expert at the WRI's Polsky Center for the Global Energy Transition, said that this is “a vital strategy for cutting greenhouse gas emissions."

But recycling food waste is difficult because it decomposes quickly, making separation and processing expensive. Collecting and transporting wet, smelly food waste also requires specialized logistics and infrastructure that many countries lack.
“Waste and food loss account for almost 10% of total emissions, so we need to integrate these actions,” Adalberto Maluf, a top official in Brazil’s environment ministry, told The Associated Press.

The recycling of already-mined materials is key to reducing the reliance on mining, according to experts, which will only become more important as the world relies more on critical mineral-dependent renewable technologies.
The International Energy Agency estimates that scaling up recycling could lower the need for new mining by between 25% and 40% by 2050.

Most countries don’t recycle critical materials because it’s cheaper to mine them. The technology and infrastructure needed to recycle these materials are also concentrated in a handful of nations, like China. The European Union and the U.S. will likely only have the capacity to recycle 30% of their raw materials by 2040, according to the IEA.

“We must do a better job with our materials retrieval, reuse and recycling,” said Aimee Boulanger, executive director of the Initiative for Responsible Mining Assurance. She stressed the need to create incentives for “retrieving the materials, taking things apart, being able to reuse them again in a circular way.”
Arasu reported from Bengaluru, India, Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan and Delgado from Bangkok.

title: Portugal closes all schools and non-essential services ahead of a major Atlantic storm
summary: Portugal has closed all schools and non-essential public services as a major Atlantic storm approaches the mainland
story: Portugal has closed all schools and non-essential public services as a major Atlantic storm approaches the mainland
LISBON, Portugal -- LISBON, Portugal (AP) — Portugal closed all schools and shuttered non-essential public services on Wednesday as a major Atlantic storm headed for the country's mainland.

Streets remained largely deserted ahead of the arrival of Storm Charles after the government told people to stay at home as heavy rain and rough seas were expected to batter the Portuguese coast, with wind gusts of up to 140 kph (85 mph).
It was the first time in living memory that Portugal’s roughly 8,000 schools had canceled classes nationwide over a storm forecast.

Buses without passengers drove through the country's capital, Lisbon, where some streets flooded due to clogged drains. A national supermarket chain closed its stores, while an international technology conference in Lisbon attended by around 70,000 people called off the day's events.

In January, the country's center-right government faced harsh criticism for its weak response when Storm Kristin hit central Portugal, felling thousands of trees and causing widespread property damage that is still being repaired.

The brunt of Storm Charles was expected to hit the Atlantic coast on Wednesday afternoon and evening, coming from the southwest after it had struck the Portuguese island of Madeira on Tuesday with 130 kph (81 mph) winds.

title: Alice Huang, who reportedly had an affair with Nvidia CEO, is a Chinese banker turned tech exec
summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is reportedly involved in a scandal with Alice Huang, a former tech executive accused of being a Chinese spy
story: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is reportedly involved in a scandal with Alice Huang, a former tech executive accused of being a Chinese spy

She was building a career in Chinese finance before turning to tech with a leadership role at a data center company in Singapore. He is the high-profile CEO of Nvidia, the California-based company that makes computer chips relied upon by advanced artificial intelligence systems.
An affair between Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, who reportedly was suspected of working as a spy for Beijing, has rocked the tech and political worlds.

The Chinese businesswoman also known as Huang Le had a close relationship with Jensen Huang, according to reports over the past month by the New York Times. The newspaper also reported that top policymakers were informed in a memo that intelligence indicated she was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security, recruited to influence Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available in China.

In one widely shared photograph of the pair, Jensen Huang and people surrounding him are holding drinks in Taipei, while Alice Huang sits behind him, apparently watching him in conversation. The picture was posted in 2024 by software company NetThunder to its LinkedIn page.
It remains unclear how long the affair lasted, and when exactly the relationship might have ended. The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang for comment.
Publicly available information about Alice Huang is scant.
She was a Chinese finance executive before becoming involved in artificial intelligence, data centers and computer chips.

In 2023, she became a director at Singapore-based Megaspeed, which describes itself as an “NVIDIA cloud partner.” Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. over its alleged skirting of U.S. export restrictions and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips for Chinese users.

Megaspeed was incorporated in 2015 in Singapore with the name 7Road International, after being spun off as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer, according to corporate registration records.
Filings show that in March 2023, it renamed itself Megaspeed International, with all of the shares transferred to Huang Le Limited, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands.
That same month, Alice Huang became Megaspeed’s controlling shareholder, according to research by the C4ADS, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on global security.
But by November 2023, she was no longer listed as a director at Megaspeed, and all her shares were transferred to a Singaporean businessman, Tan Yong Pong, who also is known as James Tan.

While public records suggest Alice Huang left Megaspeed, short seller Culper Research issued a report in May this year that cited a Megaspeed employee saying Huang was “actually still our boss” and was still involved in the company’s daily operations.

Before Megaspeed, Alice Huang previously held senior positions at the Chinese firm Shanghai Hexi Investment Co. from around 2015 to 2017, according to social media posts and records from Simuwang, a Chinese private equity database.
Her roles at Hexi included deputy general manager, executive director and member of the investment committee, according to Hexi's social media posts, among possible other roles.

Hexi's founder Kang Wei, who appeared on some records alongside Alice Huang, was fined in 2018 by China's securities regulator 400,000 yuan ($60,000) over financial misconduct behaviors while Hexi was fined 17.7 million yuan ($2.7 million).
Before that, Alice Huang worked at HSBC’s Hong Kong private banking arm and at CITIC Securities, a Chinese investment bank.
HSBC and CITIC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on her employment history.
Beijing has refuted claims that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Its Foreign Ministry said this week that the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated. It is nothing but smears against China.”
With the emergence of the latest scandal, Singapore-based AI computing company Megaspeed, where Alice Huang was a senior executive, is once again under the spotlight.

Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer, was originally incorporated in 2015 before changing its name to Megaspeed International in 2023. Nvidia lists Megaspeed as a partner on its website, while Megaspeed says on its website it's “a core business partner of NVIDIA’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region.”
It was the overseas gaming arm of Shenzhen-based developer 7Road Holdings Ltd.

Late last year, Megaspeed denied accusations following reports that it was routing Nvidia chips to China, saying in a statement on its website that “there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities.”

Singapore’s government said in late October, after fresh reports that Alice Huang was accused of being a Chinese intelligence source, that authorities were investigating Megaspeed and that Singapore “does not condone businesses” circumventing or violating other countries’ export controls. However, it said, there were no investigations conducted in respect to Alice Huang.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Japanese automaker Nissan reduces red ink and vows to return to profit for the full year
summary: Japanese automaker Nissan has trimmed its losses over the first fiscal half, compared to the previous year, and reaffirmed its promise to turn profitable for the full year
story: Japanese automaker Nissan has trimmed its losses over the first fiscal half, compared to the previous year, and reaffirmed its promise to turn profitable for the full year

TOKYO -- Japanese automaker Nissan trimmed its losses over the first half of the fiscal year, compared to the previous year, and on Wednesday reaffirmed its promise to turn profitable for the full year.

Losses at Nissan Motor Co., based in the port city of Yokohama, for the April-September period totaled 39.7 billion yen ($250 million), smaller than the 221.9 billion yen red ink for the same period last year.
Nissan’s six-month sales rose 8.8% to 6.07 trillion yen, helped by a favorable exchange rate and pricing.

U.S. and Japanese markets did well as far as vehicle sales, while the situation remained challenging in China, where competition remains fierce. The unrest in the Middle East, which has raised the price of some raw materials, while blocking shipments, continues to hurt Nissan, as with other Japanese companies.

Nissan stuck to its earlier projection to return to profit for the fiscal year through March 2027, at a net profit of 20 billion yen. That marks a recovery from the last two fiscal years, when Nissan has been in the red.
“The second half offers real opportunities to make progress,” said Chief Executive Ivan Espinosa, stressing that model launches will build on the recovery “momentum, market by market.”
“The next step is to build on that foundation,” he told reporters.
Nissan’s new business plan is set to be announced in February next year.

Nissan, which makes the Rogue sport utility vehicle, Z sports car and Infiniti luxury models, is allied with Renault SA of France and Mitsubishi Motors Corp. of Japan. It also has a partnership with Japanese rival Honda Motor Co., sharing technology and some parts.
Nissan’s results were hurt by an earthquake that struck Kumamoto, southwestern Japan, earlier this year. Nissan’s plant there lost days of production, but no employee was injured.
Nissan’s stocks, which have declined over the past year, slipped 1.5% in Wednesday trading, ahead of the earnings announcement.
Yuri Kageyama is on Threads: https://www.threads.com/@yurikageyama

title: Prada’s new Milan exhibition turns a century of fashion into fresh discoveries
summary: Prada has launched a new permanent exhibition in Milan called “Pradasphere,” showcasing over a century of fashion history
story: Prada has launched a new permanent exhibition in Milan called “Pradasphere,” showcasing over a century of fashion history

MILAN -- MILAN (AP) — Iconic A-line skirts twirl overhead, silver-covered handbags gleam in a secret underground passage and a spacesuit prototype brings more than a century of fashion history into the future at Prada’s new permanent exhibition in Milan, called “Pradasphere.”

The highly visual journey through the Italian luxury brand’s evolution is connecting Prada aficionados with the fashion house’s heritage in ways that go beyond nostalgia, and already is promising a commercial payoff.
“The exhibition is a multiplier,” said Lorenzo Bertelli, Prada Group's chief group marketing officer.

Prada projects that the Pradasphere exhibition anchoring the brand's expansion in the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele shopping arcade will add 100 million euros ($111 million) in annual revenues, and Bertelli said that target could be surpassed.

Pradasphere is fully booked into the new year and Bertelli said visitors have shown a tendency to spend more after immersing themselves in the brand’s history, sometimes going back to make an additional purchase after walking through the eight Pradasphere spaces.

“We see that the customers who go through the museum have a completely different perspective of the brand and also they browse the store with completely different minds,” said Bertelli, who has been identified as the future leader of the Prada Group. The 38-year-old, whose roles include executive chairman of Versace, is the son of creative director Miuccia Prada and Prada Group chairman Patrizio Bertelli.

Longtime Prada lovers will know that Mario and Martino Prada founded Fratelli Prada in 1913 in the historic Galleria. But they may never have seen in person the luxury bags and accessories, including a pleated evening bag with a devilish head-shaped clasp, its tongue sticking out, a detail that appeared on the Spring-Summer 2024 runway.
And it may be news that the brothers designed the brand’s signature inverted triangle logo.

Miuccia Prada’s third-generation entrance into the family business is announced with trademark nylon bags that she began designing in the 1970s, embodying the Prada high-low, industrial-luxury paradox, and a chocolate brown opera coat from her first runway collection presented in 1988.

The exhibition contains many runway hits, including the 2012 Flame heels and the Formica tile prints that gave birth to Prada’s “ugly chic” reputation, while also highlighting Miuccia Prada’s and the senior Bertelli’s reach into art, architecture, film and sport.

“Curiosity and having fun is what drives my parents,” the younger Bertelli said, adding that experimentation doesn't always bring immediate financial success, “but for sure it drives the enrichment of our story, and our culture and our knowledge.”

He cited as an example investments in sports and engineering made with the formation of the Luna Rossa America’s Cup sailing team in the 1990s, which helped develop the kind of materials expertise that led Prada to collaborate with Axiom Space on a space suit, a prototype of which is displayed at the end of the exhibition.

Prada helped design the suit’s outer layer, which is engineered to withstand extreme thermal conditions, as well as the high-performance inner layer, with a focus on thermal regulation and comfort. It is intended for astronauts walking on the moon on NASA’s Artemis IV mission, targeted for 2028.
Just 20 visitors are admitted to Pradasphere by appointment each hour to explore the compact eight rooms of the exhibition, which Bertelli promises will be in constant evolution.

Prada’s presence in the Galleria now spans eight floors, encompassing the existing Marchesi 1824 pastry shop and Osservatorio Fondazione Prada contemporary art space, alongside the new exhibition, private salon and apartment.
Most visitors end their journey in a secret underground passage connecting the menswear and womenswear boutiques, the latter occupying the original Fratelli Prada premises.
The passage contains “lesser-known” chapters from the brand’s history, including a chandelier dress created for Baz Luhrmann’s “The Great Gatsby.”

“It was a great experience,” said Luca Missio, an architect from the northeastern Italian city of Udine. “I recognized the stores I’ve visited around the world, in Tokyo and New York, in the models and displays. That was lovely.”

title: How Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's extramarital affair could cause collateral damage in Washington
summary: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, is under scrutiny after revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying
story: Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, is under scrutiny after revelations of an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is suspected of spying
WASHINGTON -- Extramarital affairs are usually private matters. Jensen Huang’s has global implications.

The 63-year-old is the leading face of the artificial intelligence revolution with his black leather jackets and fluff of grey hair. He runs the company Nvidia, which produces highly coveted computer chips. That's landed him on a late-night-phone-call basis with President Donald Trump, a promoter of the industry.

But Huang was also liaising with a Chinese businesswoman who has allegedly fed intelligence — as well as advanced chips — to China. The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive at the Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed.

It's a saga of personal betrayal, corporate espionage and high-tech development, and the fallout is spreading across Washington. There are bipartisan calls for investigations on Capitol Hill. The U.S. Department of Justice has opened its own probe. Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, is conducting an internal review.

Some expect the technology to reshape human civilization by imbuing computers with the vast powers of creation and analysis, and Trump has repeated that “whoever wins AI, wins." Nvidia is the backbone of America's plans for dominating the field.
When asked about Huang's affair, Trump said this week that he had spoken to the tech executive as the scandal grew.
“I think he’ll be in good shape," Trump said, adding that "he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”
As for when the president first learned about the concerns involving Alice Huang, Trump brushed off the question.
“They could have been mentioned," he said. "Certainly it didn’t make much of an impact on me.”
With the AI race between the U.S. and China often framed as a fierce and consequential rivalry, the Justice Department has persistently warned of the espionage threat posed by Beijing.
That includes efforts to cultivate well-placed relationships in government and private industry, as well as to acquire sensitive technology such as AI chips developed in the U.S.

Last year, Megaspeed faced scrutiny from the U.S. Commerce Department over its alleged skirting of U.S. export laws and routing of a large amount of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese users. The company denied those allegations. U.S. intelligence officials eventually concluded that Alice Huang had spied for China, according to The New York Times.

The Commerce Department's probe was handed off to the Justice Department, and its National Security Division is investigating whether Megaspeed violated export control laws in an inquiry that will also include scrutiny of Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the matter who insisted on anonymity to discuss an ongoing law enforcement probe.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday, and The Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang.

Jensen Huang has apologized to his company about the affair, saying he hurt his wife and their children, but he didn’t address reports that Alice Huang was a suspected spy. Nvidia’s board said that it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, and that Huang would remain in charge while cooperating with the investigation.
Beijing has said the “Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated" and called it “nothing but smears.”
After their first dinner together at Mar-a-Lago in early 2025, Trump latched onto Huang as a tech titan positioned to deliver on the president’s own promises of an economic renaissance.

The computer chips produced by Nvidia would essentially turn data centers into factories that made raw intelligence, which could then be applied across the economy to produce cars, new pharmaceutical drugs, advanced weapons and seemingly unparalleled wealth.
Trump would regularly phone Huang to discuss this future.

“From the moment that I met him, the only thing that he’s ever talked to me about is creating more jobs, re-industrializing the United States, of protection, of national security,” Huang told AP in an interview this summer. "He knows that if America is wealthy, we have a lot of tax revenues. We can fund the military, we can fund our economy, we fund our communities, create more jobs.”

Trump saw his political fortunes — and that of the country — in Huang's Nvidia. Huang joined Trump on Air Force One for a state visit to Beijing earlier this year. Just last month, Trump awarded Huang with a National Medal of Science.
The president called him “a man whose determination laid the foundations for the explosion of super intelligence and put America at the front of the race, an amazing man, gotten to know him so well.”
Nvidia also donated $25 million to help fund the construction of Trump’s White House ballroom.
Multiple estimates suggest that more than half of the stock market gains during Trump's second term came from the growth of the AI industry and the construction of data centers.

Without that growth, consumer spending could slump, delivering another economic setback to a president who has already failed to deliver on his campaign promise of stopping inflation. Rising prices were among the reasons that voters delivered a harsh rebuke to Republicans in last week's midterm elections, returning control of Congress to the Democrats.

While Huang said his interests were in helping America succeed, he also expressed a strong view that Nvidia should be able to sell some of its less advanced chips such as the H200 to China. Nvidia long argued that the sales would help ensure that the broader AI ecosystem was tied to America, boxing out Chinese chipmakers that are developing semiconductors and systems to compete with his company.

Those arguments previously came under scrutiny, including from Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren, who wanted him to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to answer questions about his desire to loosen export restrictions.

Huang has so far refused to appear, and Democrats responded angrily when his infidelity came to light, raising concerns that a bulwark of American technology may have been compromised by the Chinese government.
Warren said in a statement Monday that Nvidia had reportedly gotten approvals to export “hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips to China, including to companies tied to China’s military.”
And Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, Warren continued, “raises important questions NVIDIA must answer about the extent to which these activities were related."

Chan reported from Hong Kong and Ng from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Associated Press journalists Wu Jia in Beijing, Didi Tang in Washington and Russ Bynum in Savannah, Georgia, contributed to this report.

title: US futures climb and Nvidia shares stabilize in a brutal week for the chipmaker
summary: U.S. futures are rising as Nvidia’s shares look to rebound and Brent crude remains below $100 a barrel
story: U.S. futures are rising as Nvidia’s shares look to rebound and Brent crude remains below $100 a barrel
U.S. futures are rising with crude still below $100 a barrel as shares of Nvidia stabilize in a brutal week for the chipmaker.
Futures for the S&P 500 gained 0.9% on Wednesday, while those for the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 0.2%. Nasdaq futures climbed 1.9%.
Nvidia was the single heaviest weight on the S&P 500 on Tuesday, but shares are up 3.7% in early trading Wednesday. They are still down almost 10% this week.

The company that is central to the artificial intelligence boom has been under pressure since the company’s board announced an investigation into its CEO, Jensen Huang, following revelations of his affair with a purported Chinese spy. President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating the affair, which Huang has acknowledged and apologized for.
Among other technology stocks, CoreWeave jumped more than 15% before the market opened after posting better-than-expected third-quarter revenue and a boost in its 2026 revenue outlook.
The U.S. bond market is closed Wednesday for Veterans Day, but the stock markets remain open.

The price of Brent crude, the international standard, rose 1.9% to $93.22 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil gained 1.2% to $87.05 per barrel. Brent remains well below $100 a barrel, with Trump saying late Monday that the war in Iran, which sent oil prices much higher, “militarily is effectively over.”
Oil prices are still about $30 higher per barrel than at this time last year.

New data on consumer inflation Tuesday upended markets and sent the 10-year Treasury yield charging above 5% again. On Friday, the U.S. releases its producer price index for October, which captures inflation before it reaches consumers. The September report showed the biggest increase since December 2022 and that data showed that rising fuel prices, particularly for diesel fuel, continue to push shipping and warehousing prices higher.

In Europe, Germany’s DAX rose 0.7% to 26,531.66 after inflation fell to 2.8% in October from a year earlier, according to the federal statistics office on Wednesday. The CAC 40 in Paris climbed 0.3% to 8,302.23. Britain’s FTSE 100 added 0.4% to 10,797.68.
Asian markets were mostly higher. China’s biggest online shopping festival, Singles Day, began Wednesday. Its sales data will offer a gauge of consumer demand in the world’s second-largest economy.
The U.S. dollar rose to 159.15 Japanese yen from 158.70 yen. The euro fell to $1.1133 from $1.1171.

title: Spain’s workers hold a general strike over housing costs ahead of a national election
summary: Millions of Spanish workers have shut down businesses and disrupted transport in a massive protest over housing costs
story: Millions of Spanish workers have shut down businesses and disrupted transport in a massive protest over housing costs

BARCELONA, Spain -- Millions of Spanish workers shut down businesses and snarled transport in a massive protest Wednesday over housing costs that the government hopes to leverage ahead of a national election later this month.
The walkout — under the slogan “Salaries. Housing. Prices.” — was the first general strike in Spain in 14 years.

In Barcelona, the country’s second-largest city, most storefronts on a main shopping boulevard were boarded up in anticipation of violence during protests later in the day. Some retail chains were open to business while public transport was at a standstill or facing long delays.
The subway opened only for the rush hour.

Carlos Ferrer, a 45-year-old customer service worker who was trying to get back home to Alicante by train from Barcelona, said sometimes only “radical measures, such as a general strike” can force a change of course.
“Authorities need to feel pressure from the citizens so they can do something," he said.

Rain pelted the capital, Madrid, as strikers marched down main streets and blocked off Gran Vía, the city’s main thoroughfare, where big brand stores remained open although some were also boarded up. Unions have called for workers to march through the city center later Wednesday, and protests are also planned in more than 50 cities and towns.
Manuel Gómez, a 19-year-old student in Madrid, welcomed the protests, which he said marked a change for the country.
“In Spain, we have a serious problem, which is that when we don’t like something, we never go out to protest,” he said.
About 5% of flights for Wednesday were canceled at airports across the country, according to the country’s airport operator, AENA.
“The strike has exceeded the labor unions’ expectations,” said Unai Sordo, secretary general of CCOO, one of the two unions calling the strike. “It has been a success in terms of turnout.”

Earlier, the two unions — CCOO and UGT — reported significant work stoppages in strategic sectors. They said the stoppages amounted to 90% in the automotive and port sectors, 85% in the meat industry, 82% in waste collection, and 75% in the energy sector.

Minor incidents were reported in the first hours of the strike. Tires were set on fire at roadblocks in Barcelona, and scuffles with police were reported near the main wholesale market on Madrid’s outskirts. Police also used pepper spray against the strikers in some places.

Many schools and universities reportedly closed or are working at minimal capacity. In Madrid, this added to an ongoing strike started by teachers nearly a month ago demanding better working conditions. In southwestern Spain, classes were suspended due to bad weather.

“It’s extremely important to remind people that we, the workers — who are also renters or who also pay mortgages — are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill,” Sandra Mora, spokesperson for the Tenants Union, told national radio, RNE.

The strike brought workers, activists, politicians and ordinary Spaniards around the same interests — accessible housing. The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, eating into household budgets and angering voters.

The anger reached a boiling point following the nationally televised eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home in Madrid last month. The subsequent death of Maricarmen, as the woman became known, caused even more indignation and solidified her as a symbol of Spaniards who feel they pay too much in rent and can’t even dream of homeownership.
Housing activists leveraged the uproar over Maricarmen's eviction to call for the general strike, and soon won the backing of the UGT and CCOO unions.

The housing activists are seeking the elimination of pricey tourist apartments, a crackdown on real estate speculation and the automatic renewals of leases as a way to protect renters. Unions demand more government intervention in the housing market and a new minimum wage agreement through talks with the business owners' association.

The nationwide protests over Maricarmen's eviction propelled Spain’s government to push through emergency measures to limit evictions and help tenants, but right-wing parties in the Parliament refused to ratify them, claiming they would provoke a flight of properties from the rental market.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez then doubled down and called an early election, hoping to earn four more years in power for his left-wing coalition. The vote is set for Nov. 29.

Then, in late October came a brutal high-speed train collision — Spain's second deadly rail disaster of the year — that killed 69 people. The aftermath of the tragedy has dominated Spanish news and created a drag on Sánchez's campaign just when he had hoped to build momentum.
The strike now offers a much-needed opportunity for Sánchez’s Socialists and other parties on the Left seeking to stay in power, analyst Oriol Bartomeus said.

“The Socialists need for the strike to be a success and for there not to be any violence so that the election campaign can swing back to being about housing,” Bartomeus, a professor of political science at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, told The Associated Press.
On Thursday, Sánchez's government will again try to have a reduced interim Parliament ratify the two housing decrees that the full lower chamber rejected last month.

Sánchez posted a long video on social media this week, lauding past social policies like the 40-hour work week and national health insurance, which were the fruit of the workers' movement and the right to strike.
“It wasn’t easy, but they changed Spain,” Sánchez said, warning that right-wing parties would bring austerity and underfunded social services if they took over.
The traditional conservative Popular Party and the far-right Vox oppose any government intervention in the housing market, other than incentivizing construction of new homes.
The two also argue that the unions are trying to help Sánchez stay in office, with months of polling showing voters leaning toward the right.
If the strike descends into violence or has a low turnout, right-wing parties, which already have joined forces to govern in some Spanish regions, could benefit, Bartomeus said.

“The Popular Party and Vox both want the strike to be a flop and to end in scenes of burning dumpsters and shattered shop windows,” Bartomeus added, so that the next morning, "they can say, ‘This is chaos and we are coming to establish order.’”
Associated Press journalists Hernán Muñoz in Barcelona, Spain, and Iain Sullivan in Madrid contributed to this report.

title: Subdued sales for Singles' Day, China's online shopping festival
summary: Early signs suggest China’s biggest annual online shopping festival is failing to persuade anxious consumers to spend more, despite discounts
story: Early signs suggest China’s biggest annual online shopping festival is failing to persuade anxious consumers to spend more, despite discounts
HONG KONG -- Early signs suggest China ’s biggest online shopping event is struggling to persuade anxious consumers to spend more, despite discounts.

The Singles’ Day festival, a major discount campaign comparable to Black Friday and Cyber Monday in the U.S., centers on Nov. 11. But it begins weeks earlier and is seen as a barometer of the broader economy.
Retail data platform Syntun said cumulative sales as of Oct. 31 totaled just over 1 trillion yuan ($154 billion), broadly in line with the same period last year.
Retailers have increased sales mainly by extending the festival. Total Singles’ Day sales in 2025 reached a record of almost 1.7 trillion yuan ($254 billion).
Consumer demand in China remains subdued, however, as a prolonged property downturn and other pressures weigh on confidence.
“Optimism over a recovery in domestic demand has faded,” said Max Zenglein, Asia Pacific senior economist at The Conference Board. “Improvements in sentiment have repeatedly proved short-lived.”

E-commerce giants such as Alibaba have turned to artificial intelligence to encourage frugal shoppers to spend more. Alibaba integrated its Qwen AI into its Taobao and Tmall platforms to help shoppers place orders and find products.

Plans offering AI tokens are also being prominently promoted during Singles’ Day for the first time. This month, a livestream by Li Jiaqi, dubbed the “Lipstick King” for his huge lipstick sales, sold plans covering roughly 2 trillion tokens within half an hour, according to Chinese media.
Singles’ Day originated as “Bachelors’ Day,” a celebration of being single. The nationwide shopping festival began in 2009 and now targets everyone.

While China’s broader economy continues to grow at a relatively robust pace, expanding 4.6% from a year earlier in January-September, much of that momentum came from a boom in exports. Retail sales of consumer goods rose just 1.1% over the same period.

China’s vast domestic market has struggled as a yearslong real estate downturn has left households feeling less wealthy. Home prices have fallen roughly 20% or more from their 2021 peak, with smaller cities and the resale market seeing steeper declines.
Although home prices appear to be stabilizing in larger cities, many homeowners remain concerned they could fall further, said Andy Rothman, founder and CEO of the advisory firm Sinology.
In the southern furniture manufacturing hub of Foshan, 24-year-old Gabby Liang said she was feeling cautious.

“I’ve been buying much less online, especially when it comes to non-essential items,” she said. “During the Singles’ Day festival last year, I bought quite a bit of skincare products. But this year I expect to buy fewer.”
Other shoppers are also reining in spending.
“I’m perhaps not as keen on pursuing famous or high-end brands as I used to be,” said Beijing resident Kong Min, referring to this year’s Singles’ Day.
Middle-class Chinese consumers have lost confidence, and many festival discounts are less generous than they once were, said Shaun Rein, managing director of China Market Research Group in Shanghai.

More shoppers are experiencing “discount fatigue,” said Yaling Jiang, founder of market research company ApertureChina. With discounts available year-round, Singles’ Day may be losing its power to boost spending, she said.

“Looking at what Singles’ Day originally was: a shopping festival where people used to expect the largest discounts of the year,” she said. “That is not true any more after it was extended to multiple platforms, then to a monthlong thing.”
Liang, who works in furniture sales, said extras such as cameras and game consoles were off her shopping list this year.
“We’re undergoing a consumption downgrade,” she said. “Even the amount that we earn has somehow been downgraded.”
Business has stalled as Chinese shoppers tighten their belts, Liang said, despite rising exports to markets such as the Middle East and Africa.
An oversupply of goods, from cars and TVs to shoes and other electronics, has intensified competition in China’s crowded domestic market, pushing manufacturers to expand overseas.

Exports overall surged 35% from a year earlier in October, driven by high-tech products such as semiconductors and electric vehicles. China is on track to surpass last year’s record trade surplus of $1.2 trillion.
Domestic demand for big-ticket items, including cars and some luxury goods, has been particularly weak.
Passenger car sales in China have fallen for most of this year, dropping almost 25% in January-September, according to industry data. The decline partly reflects cuts to government subsidies.
That contrasts sharply with a 71% jump in passenger car exports over the same period.

Luxury spending has also weakened. LVMH, whose brands include Louis Vuitton, Dior and Fendi, and Kering, which owns Gucci, Balenciaga and Saint Laurent, both reported softer demand in China in recent months.
Chinese leaders have pledged for years to accelerate growth in domestic demand. But strong exports have reduced the urgency of introducing policies to stimulate spending at home, analysts said.

“As long as China continues to make progress on its industrial and technological ambitions, policymakers have little incentive to fundamentally rebalance the economy toward household demand,” Zenglein said.
Not all retail categories are struggling. Health, lifestyle and experiences are increasingly becoming status symbols for Chinese consumers.
“It’s not a simple case of big-ticket items falling,” said Jacob Cooke, CEO of Beijing-based consultancy WPIC Marketing + Technologies. Health-related products are selling relatively well, he said.

According to WPIC data, online sales of imported fish oil rose nearly 43% from a year earlier in the 12 months through September. Sales of other supplements aimed at improving sleep or supporting joint and bone health grew between 28% and 37%.
Cooke expects some growth in this year’s Singles’ Day sales.
ApertureChina’s Jiang described this year’s defining consumer trend as “just living life,” with people moving away from grand gestures and focusing on “the bare necessities and internal fulfillment.”

Many families are holding back as youth unemployment hovers around 18% and income growth lags. Yet China’s household savings remain vast. With a population of 1.4 billion, the country has enormous spending potential, even as consumer preferences and spending patterns shift.
Zenglein, the Conference Board economist, sees growing divergence in Chinese consumption, with pockets of stronger demand amid subdued overall sentiment.
“It’s still enough to make a living, but there’s just not much extra to splurge,” said Liang, the furniture sales worker in Foshan.

title: Poultry in motion: The ubiquitous Buffalo wing, as assessed by a local who loves 'em
summary: You know the old saying: You can take the wing out of Buffalo, but you can’t take the Buffalo out of the wing
story: You know the old saying: You can take the wing out of Buffalo, but you can’t take the Buffalo out of the wing
BUFFALO, N.Y. -- You know the old saying: You can take the wing out of Buffalo, but you can't take the Buffalo out of the wing.
Ok, fine, that's not a saying. But it's true that Buffalo chicken wings are so ubiquitous that people forget where they came from — unless you're from Buffalo.

Yes, you can find them everywhere: your local pub, chains like Wing Stop or Buffalo Wild Wings, the frozen food aisle of the supermarket (sometimes — gasp! — boneless ). Then there are the offshoots: Buffalo-flavored potato chips, peanuts and pretzels. There's Buffalo ranch salad dressing, Buffalo mac-and-cheese, Buffalo casseroles.
Back in the day, though, there was only one place where you could get these fiery flavor bombs that can only be tamed with blue cheese dressing. You guessed it: Buffalo.

This former steel town tucked away in western New York near the Canadian border is home to the genre's original wing. Teressa Bellissimo came up with the recipe late one night in March 1964 while feeding her son and his hungry friends. Today, that same recipe is served up at the Anchor Bar.

But there are loads of places you can get great wings in Buffalo. On a recent family visit, I discovered Bar-Bill Tavern, where you can opt for a “suicidal wing” to be mixed in with a batch of milder wings and then guess who snagged it by watching their face melt.

At Duff's Famous Wings, you get your choice of mild, mild medium, medium light, medium, medium hot and hot, with a warning that “medium is hot” and “hot is very, very hot.” The faint of heart will go for mild, the brave will go for hot, and those who order lemon pepper wings will be judged.

Wings from Buffalo separate themselves from impostors with their deep-fried crispy outer layer drenched in vinegary hot sauce, coating the tender meat inside. You eat enough of these and the rims of your lips will burn and your skin will be stained in red.

While lots of places outside of Buffalo claim to have mastered the wing, I have yet to find one that tastes like home. And maybe that's because I associate this food with friends and family and a city that I love, the City of Good Neighbors. Contrary to popular belief, it's not just snow (although there's lots of it) and a football team that lost the Super Bowl four heartbreaking times in a row (but this year is our year — Go Bills!).
One other thing to know about Buffalo: Here, we just call them wings.

Pia Sarkar is deputy global business editor for The Associated Press. Part of a recurring series, “American Objects,” marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. For more American objects, click here. For more stories on the anniversary, click here.

title: IRS raises 2027 standard deduction and child tax credit in its annual inflation adjustments
summary: The IRS has released its annual inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year, raising the standard deduction and the child tax credit
story: The IRS has released its annual inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year, raising the standard deduction and the child tax credit

NEW YORK -- The IRS released its annual inflation adjustments for the 2027 tax year, raising the standard deduction and the child tax credit. These adjustments will apply for tax returns filed in 2028.

Many of the increases, which the IRS released on Nov. 5, are routine and rise each year based on how much prices climbed. For 2027, that increase is about 3.2%. But several of the most popular tax breaks that Republicans included in their 2025 law remain fixed and do not adjust for inflation, meaning they will be worth slightly less each year.

The standard deduction for single filers will increase to $16,600 from $16,100. For married couples filing jointly the standard deduction will rise to $33,200 from $32,200. The standard deduction for heads of household will be $24,925, up from $24,150.

For a married couple earning $100,000 who use the standard deduction, their federal income tax bill would fall to $7,504 from $7,640, according to an Associated Press calculation. A single filer earning $60,000 would see their tax bill drop to $4,952 from $5,020. Those calculations assume the household’s income stays the same. Because these are inflation adjustments, workers whose pay increases with inflation will see their tax bills stay roughly unchanged.
The maximum earned income tax credit for a worker with no children will rise to $685 from $664. For a family with two children, the maximum credit will rise to $7,552 from $7,316.

The child tax credit will rise by $100 to a maximum of $2,300 per child, and the refundable portion will rise by $100 to $1,800. The 2025 law set the credit at $2,200 and tied future increases to inflation.

Several breaks from the 2025 law are not adjusted for inflation. Workers can still deduct up to $25,000 in tip income and up to $12,500 in overtime pay, or $25,000 for joint filers. People 65 and older will be able to claim an additional $6,000 deduction. All three tax breaks are set to end after the 2028 tax year unless Congress extends them.
The estate tax exclusion, which the 2025 law made permanent at $15 million, will rise with inflation to $15.48 million.
The top income tax rate stays at 37%, and in 2027 it will apply to income above $661,375 for single filers and above $793,650 for married couples filing jointly.

title: DOJ sues Lyft alleging discrimination against riders with disabilities
summary: The federal government is accusing Lyft of discriminating against passengers with disabilities
story: The federal government is accusing Lyft of discriminating against passengers with disabilities
The Justice Department has filed a lawsuit against Lyft, accusing the company of discriminating against passengers with disabilities who seek rides on its platform.

The federal lawsuit, filed Monday, says Lyft “is aware of, but fails to prevent and remedy” several discriminatory practices against riders who need accommodations under the Americans with Disabilities Act. That includes denying rides to people who have service animals or use stowable wheelchairs and refusing to let passengers with mobility issues sit in the front seat, the suit alleges.

“Individuals with disabilities should be able to rely on rideshare services free of discrimination,” said Jesus A. Osete, acting assistant attorney general, in a statement. “We intend to uphold the ADA’s promise that people with disabilities are entitled to equal access in every part of public life, including essential transportation services.”
Lyft firmly rejected the accusations in a statement.

The lawsuit is the latest from the federal government that targets ride-hailing companies for treatment of would-be riders with disabilities. The administration filed a similar lawsuit against Uber last year, which is ongoing. Uber settled a separate suit in 2022, and Lyft settled a different one in 2020. The companies stress that their policies and in-app tools require that drivers provide ADA accommodations and remind them of the consequences of refusing to do so.

The new lawsuit against Lyft named several examples of people across the country who hailed a ride on the platform but had one — or, in some cases, several — drivers refuse to take them to their destination, including as recently as last month. Those individuals experienced delays in getting to medical appointments, cancellation fees and other issues as a result, the suit said.

Lyft policies require drivers to accommodate riders who travel with service animals or mobility devices and “drivers who violate these policies face serious consequences, including permanent deactivation,” the company said in a statement.
“We’ve cooperated with the DOJ throughout its review and remain committed to serving every rider, including riders with disabilities,” the company said.

The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The DOJ said it is seeking $53 million for individuals who have been discriminated against and have submitted complaints to Lyft or the department.

title: Paid recruits tied to banned group behind 3-day crude bomb attacks in Bangladesh, police say
summary: Unidentified individuals have exploded crude bombs and torched vehicles in Bangladesh's capital and other areas over the past three days
story: Unidentified individuals have exploded crude bombs and torched vehicles in Bangladesh's capital and other areas over the past three days

DHAKA, Bangladesh -- Dozens of crude bombs have exploded and passenger vehicles have been set on fire in Bangladesh’s capital and elsewhere over the past three days, leaving one person dead and others injured, authorities and media reports said Tuesday.
The violence coincided with reports that the ousted former prime minister, Sheikh Hasina, plans to return from exile next month, though any connection remained unclear.

Mohammad Akhtar Hossain, a police spokesman, said at least 33 people were arrested Monday in Dhaka and more arrests were made elsewhere. He said a banned group was behind the attacks but did not identify it.

As many as 15 crude bombs exploded in the central district of Manikganj, near Dhaka, early Tuesday, and a driver was killed when a parked bus was set on fire, the country's leading newspapers reported.
In Dhaka, crude bombs exploded over the three days, including at the Dhaka University campus and at the premises of a court on Tuesday, with two people injured. Several vehicles were also torched.
Hossain said seven crude bombs were recovered during search operations, and two motorcycles used in the attacks were also seized in Dhaka. He said security has been increased across the city.
The ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party accused Hasina’s followers of the violence, saying they want to destabilize the country.

Hossain, without naming any suspected perpetrators, said: “We have found that those involved in these activities are linked to an organization whose activities have been banned, or to its affiliated groups. In many cases, we have also found that some individuals were paid to carry out these acts."
Hasina has been in India since Aug. 5, 2024, when she fled the country as a student-led mass uprising ended her 15-year rule.
A special tribunal sentenced her to death in 2025 for ordering a deadly crackdown on protesters.
On Monday, Hasina requested a new passport to facilitate her return from exile.
The government has been seeking her extradition from India and has dismissed suggestions she needed new identification documents to return home.
Hasina says she wants to return to Bangladesh in December voluntarily, despite being sentenced to death.

In a letter seen by The Associated Press that was emailed to Bangladesh’s diplomatic mission in New Delhi, Hasina’s counsel urged the top diplomat to take necessary action to provide her a passport and national identity card.

The government of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman said Hasina’s email seeking the passport was a mockery. It said Hasina would be required to submit her application in person, and that an emailed request is not enough.

title: Honda reports robust results on the back of healthy motorcycle sales
summary: Honda has reported a 66% rise in net profit for the first half of its fiscal year, driven by strong motorcycle sales
story: Honda has reported a 66% rise in net profit for the first half of its fiscal year, driven by strong motorcycle sales
TOKYO -- Honda’s net profit rose 66% in the first half of its fiscal year, the Japanese automaker reported Tuesday, driven by strong motorcycle sales.

Tokyo-based Honda Motor Co. reported a profit of 516.76 billion yen ($3.3 billion) for the six months through September, up from 311.83 billion yen a year earlier. First half sales rose 13% to 12 trillion yen from 10.6 trillion yen.
The robust results came despite costs in its electric vehicle program, where it dropped some models. Honda said EV-related losses erased 484.8 billion yen from its operating profits.
But officials stressed that Honda expects battery EVs might eventually become more popular and it will remain flexible enough to switch to EV production in the future.
Honda raised its full-year operating profit forecast to 780 billion yen from 650 billion yen.
Honda attributed the more optimistic forecast to favorable exchange rates and efforts to reduce the impact of U.S. tariffs, including shifting production to the United States.
The maker of the Super Cub motorcycle and Accord sedan also announced major production investments in North America and Brazil.

Honda plans to build a new auto production plant in Ohio, increasing production capacity in North America to 1.91 million vehicles by 2029 from 1.67 million. The company expects U.S. demand to grow, especially for its hybrid models.
Honda also plans to expand production of its motorcycle business at its Manaus factory in Brazil, increasing capacity to 2.3 million motorcycles by 2029 from the current 1.6 million.

Honda marked a record for fiscal first half sales in its motorcycle division, as its models proved popular in Brazil and India. It sold 11.9 million motorcycles during the six months, up from nearly 10.8 million the previous year.
However, Honda sold 1.57 million automobiles globally in the first half of the year, down from 1.68 million.
Honda shares, which have risen over the past year, had slipped 1.6% in Tokyo trading on Tuesday before the financial results were released.

title: Russia and Ukraine hold nearly 4 hours of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi
summary: Russia, Ukraine, and the United States held three-way talks in the United Arab Emirates to address the ongoing war
story: Russia, Ukraine, and the United States held three-way talks in the United Arab Emirates to address the ongoing war

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates -- ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates (AP) — Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States opened Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, as Washington made another push to end the war that followed Moscow's all-out invasion of its neighbor nearly five years ago.

The two-day session in the UAE's capital, Abu Dhabi, is the first such meeting since February. It will focus on establishing future security guarantees for the warring countries, the White House said before the discussions. Russia sees NATO as a threat, and Ukraine wants to prevent future Russian invasions.

The first day of talks concluded after nearly four hours, the RIA Novosti news agency said. They are expected to resume Wednesday, according to the press office of the Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, who along with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff is trying to broker a settlement, said he believed there were “some good ideas how to bridge” the differences between the two sides.

But hopes of progress in ending Europe’s biggest conflict since World War II are tempered by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks early this year. The war has already killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say.
There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks come against a backdrop of new long-range strikes by both Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.
Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine’s air force said.

Meanwhile, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said that its forces shot down 155 Ukrainian drones overnight above eight Russian regions, as well as the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia illegally annexed from Ukraine in 2014.
“I don’t have overly high expectations” for the talks, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said in an interview with ZDF television on Monday night.
Kushner said in opening remarks at the talks that the goal is to “create a new framework and a new understanding building upon the different institutions and understandings of the past.”
“We take what’s worked, we try to identify what’s failed, why we’re in this position and hopefully create a new framework that leads us for decades, if not centuries, of peace,” Kushner said.
NATO commander U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who was also present, pointed to “some great progress in the past in a military-to-military dialogue in a trilateral format.”

He said that the U.S. delegation looked forward “to working with both sides as we seek to advance the progress we’ve made in the past and continue this pursuit to set the foundations for a lasting peace.”
Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service who is leading Kyiv’s delegation, thanked the U.S. for its efforts to end Russia's invasion.
“Our people are waiting to end this war. And we hope that we will achieve the lasting peace for Ukraine,” he said.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, expressed hope the meeting “will allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine.”
Umerov said that the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the U.S. envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission.
The Russian and Ukrainian governments remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from four regions of Ukraine that Moscow annexed in September 2022 but has never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.

Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won’t agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that it would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was visiting Denmark on Tuesday, rejects Putin’s demands to voluntarily cede territory. Zelenskyy also rejects any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.

Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled. Putin has spurned those suggestions.
The Russian and Ukrainian delegations include senior officials who have attended previous rounds of talks.

Russia’s chief negotiator is Medinsky, a Putin aide who has led Moscow’s team since the first direct peace talks with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022. The Russian delegation also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and deputy chief of the General Staff’s operational department Yuri Zhigarlovsky.

Besides Umerov, the Ukrainian delegation also reportedly includes Zelenskyy’s chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy, Sergiy Kyslytsya, and Davyd Arakhamia, the parliamentary faction leader of Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party.
Last week, Trump declared that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, describing it as “a big agreement” that is “going to involve more than Ukraine.”

Kushner said Monday on X that a “comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them.”
Moscow has praised the broad approach.

“We can only welcome the (U.S.) negotiators on President Donald Trump’s request proposing to put the issue of collective security on top of the agenda of the talks on a Ukrainian settlement,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.
Some in the European Union see Washington's proposals as too accommodating to Moscow.
Russia has objected to the Europeans’ involvement in the three-way talks, but said that EU representatives could join at a later stage.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

title: Wall Street mixed in early trading ahead of a new peek at inflation
summary: Premarket trading on Wall Street was mixed but relatively calm and oil prices fell again, one day after stocks rallied to recover most of their big losses from last week
story: Premarket trading on Wall Street was mixed but relatively calm and oil prices fell again, one day after stocks rallied to recover most of their big losses from last week
Early trading on Wall Street was mixed and oil prices fell again, one day after stocks rallied to recover most of the big losses from last week.
Futures for the S&P 500 rose 0.1% before the opening bell, while futures for the Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 0.3%. Nasdaq futures dipped 0.3%.

Oil prices continue to decline, with Brent crude falling below $91 per barrel, the lowest level in three months. The declines came after President Donald Trump said that the war in Iran “militarily is effectively over,” a week after American voters, angered by skyrocketing costs, handed both chambers of Congress to Democrats in midterm elections.
Brent crude, the international standard, fell 2.2%, or $2.02, to $90.55 a barrel. U.S. benchmark crude oil slid 1.8%, or $1.65, to $84.94 per barrel.

Nvidia shares were off less than 1% before the bell. Shares fell 4.3% on Monday after the AI chip company said it’s investigating after its CEO, Jensen Huang, acknowledged an intimate relationship with a business executive who, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for China.

Nvidia’s board said it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised but its inquiry would examine all available information. China has rejected the allegations.
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic filed papers with regulators Tuesday seeking a $1.3 trillion valuation ahead of its IPO, expected later this month.
Anthropic’s quarterly revenue swelled to $17 billion but it still posted a net loss for the latest three months, the artificial intelligence giant said in an updated IPO filing.
Last week, the San Francisco company behind the Claude chatbot said its quarterly revenue swelled to $17 billion though it still posted a loss for the last three-month period.
Anthropic said it has committed to spend $895.4 billion on AI computing and infrastructure like data centers, including $70 billion that’s due to be spent in the next 12 months.

Global demand for AI chips remains robust with AI chipmaker Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. reporting after the market closed that its October revenue was nearly six-fold that of a year earlier.
In Asian trading, Taiwan’s Taiex jumped 2.5%.
Japan’s benchmark Nikkei 225 closed 2.9% higher at 60,459.58.
Shares in OpenAI investor SoftBank Group jumped 13.9% ahead of the company’s earnings release. Its share price had fallen to its lowest level in a year on Monday.
SoftBank Group reported a $7 billion loss for the three months through September as worries about investments in artificial intelligence hurt the Japanese technology company’s bottom line.
Computer chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron surged 6.1% and testing equipment maker Advantest gained 4.6%.
South Korea’s Kospi climbed 4.4% to 5,239.13. Samsung Electronics gained 4.7% and SK Hynix climbed 6.7%.
In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng rose 0.6% to 24,584.81, while the Shanghai Composite index edged 0.1% higher to 3,663.72.
China’s exports in October climbed 35.2% from a year earlier, while imports grew 41.6%, according to customs data released on Tuesday.
That has put the country on track for another record for the year since the trade surplus for 2026 has already surpassed $1 trillion.
At midday in Europe, Germany’s DAX rose 1.2%, as did the CAC 40 in Paris. Britain’s FTSE 100 was up 0.5%.

Investors are waiting for the U.S. consumer price index report for October, which comes out later Tuesday. Data is expected to show inflation rose 3.9%, up from 3.7% in September, which many analysts expect will force the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate in the coming months.

title: China's trade surplus surpasses $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year, as exports surge 35%
summary: China says its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year
story: China says its trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a 2nd straight year
HONG KONG -- China’s trade surplus exceeded $1 trillion for a second straight year, according to official data released Tuesday, as pressure mounts for greater balance in trade with Beijing.

Exports in October surged 35.2% from a year earlier, the customs agency said. Exports have grown rapidly this year supported by high-tech goods like semiconductors and autos. Imports rose 41.6% year-on-year.
Between January and October, China logged a $1.04 trillion trade surplus, even as the trade surplus narrowed last month to $105.3 billion from $133.5bn in September as imports picked up pace.
That puts China on track for surpassing last year’s record $1.2 trillion trade surplus.
“We expect Chinese exports to stay strong for the rest of this year, led by electronics and autos,” said Dave Chia, an economist at Moody’s Analytics.

Overcapacity in many industries, excess domestic savings and weakened domestic demand are still forcing China to ship its goods abroad as some countries move to protect their own industries, said Alicia García-Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at French bank Natixis.
The situation is not sustainable, she said.

Businesses are feeling the pressure of ferocious competition as China’s economy has slowed, said Cinders Zhou, who sells eyewear for a manufacturer in Linhai city in eastern China’s Zhejiang province.

“It comes down to product quality, or rather the increasingly the lack of it across the industry, since there’s significant homogenization,” said Zhou, whose company makes frames and lenses sold both in and outside China. “That has forced everyone to compete on price,” she said.
Trade curbs by the European Union pose an important risk at a time of heightened U.S. trade barriers and tariffs, Chia said.
Top Chinese officials insist Beijing is not seeking to expand the trade surplus but wants more balanced global trade.

China’s exports could be vulnerable to setbacks for the artificial intelligence industry, a concern that deepened with the Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections given the public backlash against expansion of data centers.
“If the AI boom slows or turns into a correction, lower chip and electronics prices and smaller shipping volumes would hit China’s exports hard,” Chia said.

Trade is among the top issues likely to be on the agenda in planned meetings between U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders summit later this month in China’s technology hub Shenzhen.
A two-month extension of a trade truce until January has provided some relief to exporters, though it’s unclear how long that may last.

U.S. and European trade policies have added “a lot of difficulties” for Chinese businesses to expand in the markets, said Wang Xin, head of the Shenzhen Cross-Border E-Commerce Association, an industry group.

Strong exports have helped offset sluggish domestic demand in China, where the economy is forecast to meet Beijing’s official target of a 4.5% to 5% annual growth this year, slightly slower than last year’s 5% expansion.

title: Heat-trapping carbon pollution drops, but scientists cite Iran war
summary: Emissions of heat-trapping carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels decreased slightly this year due to the Iran war
story: Emissions of heat-trapping carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels decreased slightly this year due to the Iran war

Global carbon pollution dropped this year ever so slightly, but it's more because of oil shocks reverberating from the Iran war than anything the world has done to fight climate change, scientists said in a new study.

In 2026, the world emitted 42.2 billion tons (38.2 billion metric tons) of heat-trapping carbon dioxide from the burning of fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas. It’s a 0.4% decrease from last year, according to the scientists of the Global Carbon Project, which publishes its estimates in the journal Earth System Science Data Discussions.

“It’s downwards which sounds good, but this is largely driven by the war in Iran, what’s happened in the Strait of Hormuz,” said study co-author Glen Peters, a scientist at the CICERO Center for International Climate Research in Norway. “So in a way, a little bit of good news, but for the wrong reasons.”
The war in Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping artery for petroleum products, pushing up global prices of gasoline and oil.
They found oil emissions dropped nearly 2% and natural gas fell 0.3%, while coal was up 0.6%.

The international team of more than 140 scientists use data from around the world to calculate the yearly emissions figure, with estimates for the last few months of the year, and then present them at the U.N. climate negotiations in Antalya, Turkey. Peters said they are certain that this was related to the war-triggered energy shocks because of both the timing and type of fuel emission drops.

If the overall carbon dioxide emission drop were due solely to a rise in renewables and a systemic drop in fossil fuel use, oil emissions “would slowly come up to a peak and then slowly decline afterward, whereas what we see this year is oil emissions are going up and then suddenly BANG, down 2%,” Peters said.
This is the third time global carbon pollution dropped in the 21st century. The other two times were because of the global recession in 2009 and the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
In those past two crises, people hoped the recovery from the shocks would emphasize clean energy, Peters said, "but at the end of the day, we seem to go back to where we were before.”
Outside experts greeted the figures with a mix of hope and skepticism that it will last.

Niklas Höhne, co-founder of Germany’s NewClimate Institute, said “permanent shifts are happening” especially with skyrocketing switches to electric cars and trucks, especially in Asia. So he thinks the global peak of carbon emissions is near or here.

But Malte Mienshausen, a climate science and policy expert at the University of Melbourne in Australia, said oil producing nations and companies not affected by the blockage of the Strait of Hormuz reaped “tremendous windfall gains,” and it boosts their efforts to look for oil outside the Middle East. That, he said, will dampen any short-term effects of reduced carbon emissions from the war.
The 42 billion tons of carbon dioxide emitted this year comes to about 1,335 tons (1,211 metric tons) of the transparent, heat-trapping gas going into the air every second.

“We shouldn’t lose sight of the bigger picture. The world is still pumping more than a thousand (metric tons) of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere every second," Mohamed Adow, director of the environmental group Power Shift Africa, said in an email.

“It’s very abstract to think about the magnitude of stuff we throw in the atmosphere every year, but it’s a ginormous number,” Peters said. “If it was black and not transparent, the sky would be dark.”

And even though the amount of heat-trapping gases from fossil fuels dropped slightly, overall global carbon dioxide emissions went up 1%. That's because of land use changes, such as deforestation and human-caused peat fires, that increased faster than fossil fuel burning decreased, the study said.

Most of the world's biggest carbon polluting nations — China, the United States, Europe, Japan — showed about a 1% drop in emissions this year, but Peters attributed it to the oil shock. India's fossil fuel pollution went up 4.4% this year, the study found.
China's emission drop raised eyebrows and hope for some experts. Experts have been waiting for China's ever-growing emissions to start dropping.

“China is giving us real reasons to be optimistic that its emissions may have peaked," Adow said. “It’s building the world’s first major electrostate, investing at extraordinary speed and scale in solar power, wind energy, electric vehicles and the infrastructure to support them. This isn’t a temporary response to an oil crisis. It’s a fundamental transformation of China’s economy that is steadily reducing its dependence on fossil fuels.”
University of Michigan environment dean Jonathan Overpeck said, “We're not phasing out fossil fuels fast enough, but some progress is better than no progress.”
