Abu Dhabi National Oil Company vessel damaged in attack, UAE says
A vessel with Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC) Logistics and Services was damaged in an attack Tuesday afternoon, the United Arab Emirates state-run news agency (WAM) reported.
The attack reportedly occurred in the territorial waters of the UAE and "response efforts" were ongoing, according to WAM.
Iran war 'not necessarily popular,' Hegseth says

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth acknowledged that the ongoing war with Iran is "not necessarily popular" among American voters, when asked about the role the conflict played in the heavy Republican defeat in the midterm elections.

Vice President JD Vance last week publicly blamed the conflict for the historic Democratic Party victory in the midterm elections. Asked about Vance's remarks, Hegseth said he did not want to engage in "finger pointing."
Hegseth said the war was launched "for the right reasons, to ensure Iran never gets a nuclear weapon."
Paraphrasing Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Hegseth said of the war, "It's not necessarily popular, but it may have been necessary. And that's certainly how I feel. It was a necessary undertaking."
Hegseth says US can 'maintain oversight' of Iranian nuclear sites

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said during Tuesday's press conference that the U.S. can "maintain oversight" of Iranian nuclear sites and any attempts by Tehran to reconstitute its military capabilities.
"We're able to maintain oversight and visibility of those nuclear sites. And if we saw the kind of nefarious activity that required action, we would take it," Hegseth said.

Hegseth said the ongoing U.S. blockade of Iranian ports is "ironclad," suggesting that operation -- alongside the damage done to Iran's industrial base -- means Tehran's "ability to reconstitute is much less than ours."
"We know that they're going to attempt to reconstitute. We know that we are in a much stronger position," Hegseth said.
Hegseth defends US campaign in Iran, claims 'historic military victory'

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said during a Tuesday morning press conference that the U.S. had achieved "a historic military victory," over Iran, as he faced a House impeachment resolution introduced by Republican Rep. Thomas Massie.
Hegseth defended his tenure as Pentagon chief, including the ongoing U.S.-Israeli campaign against in Iran, which began in February, and last summer's 12-day U.S.-Israeli conflict with Tehran.
"More than 13,000 targets struck. Their navy sunk. Their air force grounded. Their defense industrial base gone," Hegseth said, listing military statistics from the conflict to date.

"More than 80% of their nuclear industrial base gone. Their military in ruin. The ironclad blockade unbroken. We control the Strait of Hormuz. Crazy Islamists in Tehran will never, ever have a nuclear weapon. A historic effort only made possible by a courageous commander in chief," Hegseth added, referring to President Donald Trump.
"He did not kick the can. He kicked their teeth in," Hegseth said of the president.

"We will not apologize for destroying the capabilities of a regime that chants, 'Death to America," Hegseth continued. "And if that regime makes one wrong move, as the president said, we remain locked and loaded with the full weight and lethality of Central Command."

title: House panel rebukes DOJ's handling of Epstein case
summary: The House Oversight Committee, in a report summarizing its 15-month Jeffrey Epstein probe, rebuked the Justice Department's handling of the Epstein case.
story: The GOP-led committee released a 136-page report on its 15-month investigation.

In a report summarizing the conclusions of its 15-month Jeffrey Epstein probe, the Republican-led House Oversight Committee rebuked the Justice Department's handling of the Epstein case and recommended that the department renew its investigation of Epstein's associates.

The 136-page report blamed the failures by federal prosecutors on "poor judgment" and "Epstein's pervasive and wide-reaching influence," and criticized the DOJ for failing to prevent the convicted sex offender's crimes through a controversial non-prosecution agreement in 2007 and for its recent efforts to release files about the case that included sensitive information about Epstein's victims.

"Upon review, the Committee finds that the crimes committed by Epstein after 2005 could have been prevented and justice served had it not been for the failures of investigators and federal prosecutors in South Florida and Washington, D.C," said the report on the committee's probe into the federal government's mishandling of investigations into Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

While the report applauded the release of the Epstein files, it also faulted the Justice Department for failing to comply with the requirements of the Epstein Files Transparency Act, improperly releasing sensitive information about victims, and preventing victims from full access to the files.

In response, a DOJ spokesperson said, "With all due respect, the Chairman's recommendations have already been addressed. The Attorney General has repeatedly said that the Epstein case is not closed and there is no statute of limitations on human trafficking."

"The Chairman should know that the FBI has a long-established 'process for crime victims and their representatives to access personal files' that starts by filing out form DOJ-361. The Committee notably fails to acknowledge the historical overlap between potential co-conspirators and victims, which all members who visited the reading room could see for themselves. The Department will continue following all additional investigative leads in matters relating to Jeffrey Epstein."

The House panel's report, authored by the Republican majority, also sought to vindicate President Donald Trump, who has long been embroiled in the controversy over the release of the files. The majority accused Democrats on the committee of being "obsessed with trying to implicate President Trump and insinuate that he was involved in the crimes of Epstein and Maxwell."

"Their unfounded witch hunt continued without regard for the interests of survivors, even though the facts gathered during this investigation do not suggest President Trump is implicated in any of Epstein's crimes," the report said.
Democrats on the Oversight Committee said the majority-authored report is incomplete and vowed to continue the investigation with the new Congress.

"Oversight Republicans have released a report based on an incomplete investigation and zero public hearings on Jeffrey Epstein," said Rep. Robert Garcia. "We will not allow the President and his allies to dismiss this investigation. We intend to hold real public hearings uplifting survivors and asking tough questions of the powerful men who associated with Epstein, including Donald Trump. Our work is just getting started."

The report had harsh words for several of the prominent individuals interviewed by the Committee -- including President Bill Clinton, Leslie Wexner, and Leon Black -- who said they were unaware of Epstein's crimes.
"The Committee's investigation instead tends to show that the willful ignorance of those in Epstein's orbit enabled him to continue his offenses for so many years," the report said.

The majority said the investigation showed that Epstein was able to use his "wealth, intimate connections, and social and professional prominence to conceal his crimes." The report said Epstein was able to use those connections as a facade to bolster his reputation, despite his conviction for soliciting prostitution from a minor in 2008.

"Some Epstein associates questioned by the Committee seemingly claimed in their testimonies that a man with connections to global political leaders, major philanthropists, titans of industry, billionaires, Hollywood celebrities, and even a British prince could not be a sex trafficker," the report said. "However, despite the repeated assertions of ignorance to Epstein's crimes, these same associates offered inadequate explanations for their continued close association with Epstein after his 2008 conviction for soliciting prostitution from a minor."

Epstein, a wealthy financier who owned two private islands in the Virgin Islands, served 13 months of an 18-month sentence for sex crime charges in 2007, and in 2019 was indicted on charges that he "sexually exploited and abused dozens of minor girls at his homes in Manhattan, New York, and Palm Beach, Florida" and used cash payments to recruit a "vast network of underage victims," some of whom were as young as 14 years old.
Epstein died in jail while awaiting trial on August 10, 2019, in what was ruled a suicide by the New York Medical Examiner's Office.

title: Democratic lawmakers want answers on 8-year-old Haitian boy taken into ICE custody
summary: A group of Democratic lawmakers is seeking information from the Trump administration after an 8-year-old Haitian boy was taken into government custody last week.
story: The young boy was detained by agents during an immigration check-in last week.
A group of Democratic lawmakers is seeking information from the Trump administration after an 8-year-old Haitian boy was taken into government custody last week.
In a letter to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Tuesday, six Democratic lawmakers asked what steps are being taken to reunite the child with his family.

"Video footage appears to show the use of restraints on a child who seemed to pose no threat to those around him, raising serious questions about the handling of this incident," the lawmakers wrote. "We express concerns about the basis for this action and the harm it may cause a young child who appeared for his required hearing."

The 8-year-old, who lost Temporary Protected Status earlier this year as part of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, was taken into federal custody during an immigration check-in last week, according to local advocates and school officials.
The third grader, who attends Fay Elementary School in San Diego, was detained alone after attending an Immigration and Customs Enforcement appointment with his uncle on Thursday.
Advocates and school officials previously said the boy had been living with his uncle and cousins after his father was deported to Mexico last year.
"They did not give the father the opportunity or chance to actually put in place legal guardianship for the kid," said Guerline Jozef, the executive director of the nonprofit Haitian Bridge Alliance.
A spokesperson for ICE told ABC News that agents acted under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act because the uncle could not establish legal guardianship.

"Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child's safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement," the spokesperson said.
Jozef called the detention "an excuse for [ICE] to remove the child and potentially put him in deportation proceedings."
"The effects of this action extend far beyond one child and his family," the lawmakers said in their letter.

title: House Republicans consider issuing subpoena to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
summary: Several House Republicans called for a closed-door briefing.
story: Several House Republicans called for a closed-door briefing.

The Republican chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Brian Mast, told ABC News on Tuesday that he's prepared to subpoena Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if he does not respond by Wednesday to a request from several House Republicans for a closed-door briefing on Huang's reported relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Last week, Mast as well as Rick Crawford, the chair of the House Intelligence Committee, and John Moolenaar, the chair of the House China Committee, sent Huang a letter requesting he appear for a "joint, closed-door briefing."

The focus of the briefing would be on Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage" after the tech giant on Sunday announced an investigation into its CEO following New York Times' reporting that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent, identified as Alice Huang, a top executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed.

Jensen Huang has not yet responded to the Republicans' request that he appear for a briefing. Asked by ABC News if he would consider issuing a subpoena to Huang should he not respond, Mast said "absolutely."

It's unclear how a potential subpoena of Huang would play out. House Republicans lose control of their committees in January when the chamber turns over to Democrats. The subpoena would likely expire and Democrats would need to issue a new one.
ABC News reached out to Nvidia for comment from Huang for this story.

Congressional Republicans on the Select Committee on China also sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear for a closed-door briefing Nov. 18 concerning his relationship with Alice Huang. It is not known if Huang will appear before that committee; Nvidia hasn't publicly responded to the request.

Mast said there is a "lengthy" list of things he wants to hear from the Nvidia CEO including what correspondence he had with the Chinese government. Mast added that he is "100%" worried about the national security implications of Huang's reported relationship given that he runs the world's largest computer chip manufacturer.

"They're American chips. You know. So we thank God that Jensen is an American entrepreneur. You know, it's an American tech company because they're the best chips anywhere in the globe," Mast said. "But that being said, we don't want China to access them, to use them, to produce them like that."
Nvidia's board said they have "no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised" by Huang's affair.
Huang "fully supports the review" and will cooperate with it, the Nvidia statement further said.

Several Democrats have expressed concerns about national security after the report, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries telling ABC News that there are "real concerns" that need to be addressed.

"We're going to need a full briefing, specifically as it relates to the Nvidia issue, so we can all get to the bottom of what has happened and what the implications are in terms of America's national security," Jeffries said.

On Monday, President Donald Trump said the FBI is investigating the matter. Trump said he spoke with Huang in a phone call on Monday, during which the CEO said that he "didn't know" he was involved with an alleged Chinese spy.
"He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," the president told reporters during a press briefing on Monday.
It's unclear when -- if ever -- the Trump administration alerted Nvidia that its CEO was the target of an alleged Chinese espionage plot.
The Chinese government has denied the allegations, calling them "baseless and purely slanderous smears against China."
Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment about the New York Times story on the relationship.

title: California's Prop 40 'billionaires' tax' measure is rejected, AP projects
summary: The tax was introduced in response to steep cuts to California's healthcare funding that resulted from the passage of President Donald Trump's "Big Beautiful Bill."
story: The main group opposing the tax raised $333.1 million ahead of the midterms.
Voters rejected California's so-called "billionaires' tax" ballot initiative, according to a projection from The Associated Press on Monday.
This means that the state will not levy a 5% tax on the wealth of California taxpayers and trusts with assets valued over $1 billion. This measure is known as Proposition 40.

The tax was introduced in response to steep cuts to California's healthcare funding that resulted from the passage of President Donald Trump's "Big Beautiful Bill." Yes on 40, the main group backing the measure, had said the tax would generate around $100 billion over five years. The measure would have affected roughly 200 of California's billionaires.
Building a Better California, the main group opposing the tax, raised $333.1 million since the beginning of the year. Most of that money came from billionaires.

Sergey Brin, co-founder of Google, is the organization's top donor. He gave $102 million to Building a Better California. Because of Brin, "co-founder" is the occupation that gave the most to the group overall, a total of $105.3 million. Donors who listed their occupation as "Investor/Philanthropist" gave the group $47.7 million. CEOs gave $46.6 million. People who listed their occupation as "chairman" contributed $43 million.

Naturally, many of the major donors reported being based in California. $43.9 million came from donors in San Rafael, California, a city in the San Francisco Bay Area. $40.2 million came from West Hollywood. $34.7 million came from Redwood City, another Bay Area city, and $28.4 million came from San Francisco itself.
The largest share of contributions, however, came from Sergey Brin, in Reno, Nevada.

Gov. Gavin Newsom became its most prominent opponent, arguing that the tax could be dodged by billionaires who could leave the state for another. As ABC News has reported, Newsom has shared a counterproposal: a national billionaire tax focused on loans taken against assets.
Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Ro Khanna were huge proponents of the measure, arguing that it could set the stage and be an example for a national wealth tax.
Khanna told ABC News in early October that he and Newsom are "polar opposites" on the issue. Both have openly discussed that they are weighing a presidential bid in 2028.

"He [Newsom] doesn't want to offend some of the billionaires who he wants to finance his campaigns, and that's the question: Are we going to be a party for the working class? Are we going to be beholden to our donors?" Khanna said.
Tech investors pushed back hard on the measure. Vinod Khosla warned that the state's top wealth creators would leave, and Mark Cuban told Khanna he doesn't understand business.

title: Jimmy Carter's family farm to be preserved and opened to the public
summary: The family farm where President Jimmy Carter tended peanuts, corn and sugarcane as a boy and returned throughout his life will be preserved and opened to the public
story: The family farm where President Jimmy Carter tended peanuts, corn and sugarcane as a boy and returned throughout his life will be preserved and opened to the public
The family farm where President Jimmy Carter tended peanuts, corn and sugarcane as a boy and later returned throughout his life will be preserved and opened to the public.

Preservation group The Conservation Fund said Monday that it has acquired the farm as part of a 2,458-acre (995-hectare) purchase. The farm is just outside Plains, Georgia, the 39th president's hometown. Carter spent his youth exploring the woods around the farm and returned many times as an adult to walk with his wife Rosalynn and hunt, the fund said.
Near the end of his life, Carter, who died in 2024 at 100, returned to the farm for one final fishing trip to its pond. Rosalynn Carter died in 2023.

“For our family, this land was always about more than a farm. It was home — a place my grandparents treasured. We’re grateful to The Conservation Fund and to everyone working to make sure it’s protected for generations to come,” Jason Carter, a grandson of the Carters, said in a statement.

The farm should be open to the public for hunting, fishing and outdoor recreation as soon as next year, The Conservation Fund said. The fund said it plans to transfer the land to the Georgia Department of Natural Resources the following year. The purchase price was $8.5 million, The Washington Post reported.

The family kept a stand of mature longleaf pines at the farm at Carter's request, The Conservation Fund said. One of his final decisions about the property was to replant much of it with young longleaf pines, the fund said.

The replanting effort means the property is a natural fit to expand Georgia's Lanahassee Creek Wildlife Management Area, which will grow to almost 7,000 acres (2,833 hectares), the fund said. The Plains area is also home to Jimmy Carter National Historical Park, which includes Carter's boyhood home.

“Long before Jimmy Carter protected millions of acres across America, he was a boy working the fields and roaming the woods of southwest Georgia,” said Stacy Funderburke, vice president of the central Southeast region at The Conservation Fund. “This land shaped him and his legacy, and he never stopped coming home to it. We’re honored to help ensure this land remains healthy habitat for wildlife, and we look forward to the day it is open to everyone who wants to experience it.”

title: NYC sightseeing helicopter makes emergency landing after reporting possible engine trouble
summary: A New York City sightseeing helicopter on a maintenance flight has made an emergency landing at a New Jersey cargo port after the pilot reported possible engine trouble
story: A New York City sightseeing helicopter on a maintenance flight has made an emergency landing at a New Jersey cargo port after the pilot reported possible engine trouble
BAYONNE, N.J. -- A New York City sightseeing helicopter on a maintenance flight made an emergency landing on Tuesday at a New Jersey cargo port after the pilot reported possible engine trouble.

Two people were aboard the Bell 206L-4 helicopter when it came down on a road at the Port Jersey Marine Terminal in Bayonne, across the Hudson River from Manhattan, around 8:55 a.m., the Federal Aviation Administration said.
No injuries were reported, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said. Messages seeking comment were left for the helicopter’s operator, FlyNYON.
Video of the scene shows part of the helicopter’s tail sitting on the road about 30 feet (9 meters) from the aircraft, which was manufactured in 1999, according to FAA records.

In a recording of the air traffic control audio posted on the ATC app, the pilot can be heard saying, “Mayday, mayday, mayday" and “We need to land outside of the airport.” The helicopter landed several minutes later, just outside of the container terminal, the Port Authority said.

Last year, a Bell 206L-4 sightseeing helicopter plummeted into the Hudson River, killing all 6 people on board. The National Transportation Safety Board said the remains of several geese were found on the helicopter, suggesting it may have struck several birds before crashing.

Last week, the U.S. Department of Transportation’s Office of Inspector General announced an audit of sightseeing helicopter regulations, citing “longstanding concerns regarding the industry’s safety and whether the current regulatory framework provides adequate safeguards."
Since 2008, there have been at least 58 helicopter crashes involving tourist helicopters in the U.S., including 11 that were fatal, Assistant Inspector General Marshall Jackson said.

title: An Idaho man gets 18 years in prison for an Islamic State support plot
summary: An Idaho man has been sentenced to 18 years in federal prison for attempting to support the Islamic State group
story: An Idaho man has been sentenced to 18 years in federal prison for attempting to support the Islamic State group
BOISE, Idaho -- An Idaho man has been sentenced to 18 years in federal prison for attempting to provide material support to the Islamic State group.

Alexander Scott Mercurio, 21, pleaded guilty to the federal terrorism charge last month. U.S. District Judge David C. Nye sentenced him Tuesday and said Mercurio would be placed on lifetime supervised release after completing his prison term.

Prosecutors said Mercurio had pledged his allegiance to IS and planned to attack churches in Coeur d'Alene on the group's behalf, using explosives, knives, firearms and other weapons. He was arrested by the FBI on April 6, 2024, one day before the planned attack, according to prosecutors.

Idaho U.S. Attorney John Shirts said the sentence “sends the clear message that where individuals intend to pursue acts of terrorism against the United States — whether in Coeur d'Alene, or any other community — they will be brought to justice.”

Mercurio's defense attorneys, Carter Powers Beggs and J. Stephen Roberts Jr. with the Federal Defenders of Eastern Washington and Idaho, declined to comment on the case. But in a court document, they described Mercurio as a depressed teen when he was arrested who was raised in a dysfunctional family that exposed him to white supremacist ideology at a young age.

Mercurio was dealing with family trauma and isolated from the outside world when he was befriended online by a government informant, his attorneys wrote. He had already bounced between multiple political ideologies by that time, ultimately embracing radical Islam when the COVID-19 pandemic hit in 2020, they said.

“Starting when he was just seventeen years old, Mr. Mercurio spent his days holed away in his basement bedroom, talking with his best friend about increasingly radical terrorist ideologies,” his attorneys wrote. “Together they brainstormed a plan that was as horrific as it was unlikely to succeed: a suicidal attack on local churches using his father's firearms and an untested improvised explosive/flamethrower.”
Mercurio has since renounced his extremist views, and has been assessed as a low risk of future danger, his attorneys said. They asked the judge to impose a sentence of nine years in prison.

According to court records, Mercurio created an online repository for pro-IS content and originally wanted to travel overseas to support the organization but lacked the money and resources to make the trip. Shortly before his arrest, he gave the informant an audio recording pledging his support for IS, along with a photo of himself holding a knife in front of an IS flag.

The Islamic State group, which the U.S. government designates a terror group, took control of a large swath of territory in Syria and Iraq in 2014 and declared the territory to be a caliphate. The group had been largely defeated in both countries by 2018, but still has sleeper cells that carry out deadly attacks in both countries, and IS affiliates also operate in West Africa.

title: The US to become first nation to fully shun a UN Human Rights Council review
summary: The United States is to become the first country to skip a regular review of its human rights record at the U.N.'s Human Rights Council
story: The United States is to become the first country to skip a regular review of its human rights record at the U.N.'s Human Rights Council
GENEVA -- The United States is set Tuesday to become the first country to fully shun a regular review of its human rights record at the U.N.'s top rights body since it was created two decades ago.
The Trump administration last year pulled the U.S. out of the Human Rights Council, accusing it of an anti-U.S. and anti-Israel bias, and alleging that it didn't uphold the very values it promotes.

Supporters back the council's mandate to keep tabs on human rights in all U.N. member states including the U.S., which has drawn criticism for its policies including strong-arm deportations and targeted killings of alleged drug-runners in the Caribbean and Pacific — which the administration has said are designed to protect U.S. workers and help keep the country safe.
The Geneva-based council regularly examines the rights records of all 193 U.N. member states — generally about every four to five years — as part of a process known as the universal periodic review.

The United States, under Trump, already skipped its appointment for its review a year ago. The scheduled November 2025 review was pushed back until Tuesday in hopes that the U.S. government might change its mind.
It did not.
“(W)e give no credibility to the agency,” a State Department spokesperson said in an email to The Associated Press.

“This irredeemable body makes a mockery of human rights through consistent failures to uphold its own ‘values’ as it pushes anti-American rhetoric,” the spokesperson said, alleging the council's “persistent failure to condemn the most egregious human rights violators.”
The council says the process requires participation of the country in question, and in the case of an absence of any national representatives, the review cannot go forward.

As part of such reviews, national delegations — which at times can include a dozen officials or more — make a presentation, face questions and hear recommendations from other national envoys. It's supposed to be a sweeping and constructive process, akin to holding up a mirror to governments to improve their human rights policies.
Critics of the U.S. snub warn that the walkout could encourage other countries — many of which bristle about intense scrutiny from human rights monitors — to follow suit.

Jamil Dakwar, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's human rights program, said: “The administration is saying to the world, ‘we don’t care about whether you would review us or not, we’re going to continue to violate human rights unabashed’."

"And we are saying: ‘No, enough is enough. This council should hold the United States accountable’,” he told reporters Monday in Geneva, as part of a push by civil society to raise awareness about the U.S. rights record.
He said the ACLU and allies have called on the U.N. human rights chief to respond by presenting an update on rights in the United States early next year.
Eric Tistounet, a visiting professor at the Geneva Graduate Institute who was the council's first secretary, said the U.S. walkout could affect the credibility of the council's review system.
“If the predominant global power — which has always claimed to adhere to the human rights norms — doesn’t show up and doesn’t even justify why, then you are in big trouble," he said.
