title: Enrolling in Medicare? Here's what to consider before Dec. 7.
summary: Medicare open enrollment, which runs from Oct.15 to Dec. 7, gives people a chance to change their health coverage. Here's what to know.
story: The Medicare open enrollment window has arrived, giving millions of seniors across the U.S. the chance to revisit their coverage choices. Even if you're happy with your plan, experts say it's still worth exploring your options.

Health plans change every year, meaning people could see updates to premium costs, prescription drug coverage and available providers in their network. New plans also come online, expanding the already broad list of coverage options.
"There's really no one who can't benefit from at least taking some time to take a look," Alex Cottrill, senior policy analyst with KFF's program on Medicare policy, told CBS News.

People enrolled in Medicare Advantage or a Part D prescription drug plan typically receive an "Annual Notice of Change" in September outlining any updates to their coverage, according to Medicare.gov, the government website for the program.

"Pay attention to those notices, and frankly, even if you don't receive an annual notice of change, you still want to review your current plan and make sure that it is the right one for you," said Jessica Rivkin, vice president of Reliance Medicare Advisors, an insurance agency that helps people enroll in Medicare Advantage plans.
Americans now have less than a month to make their Medicare choices, with open enrollment set to close Dec. 7. Here are some considerations as you navigate the process.
Choosing between Medicare and Medicare Advantage

One of the biggest decisions people face when enrolling in Medicare is whether to choose traditional Medicare or Medicare Advantage, a comprehensive plan in which private insurers are paid to manage your care.

By contrast, people who enroll in regular Medicare plans must separately select a Medicare Part D prescription drug plan and Medigap, private insurance people can layer on top of their plan to help defray out-of-pocket costs.
"You only have to pick one plan rather than having these modular options that you have in traditional Medicare," Cottrill said of Medicare Advantage.

A drawback of Medicare Advantage is its more stringent requirements. Some plans only allow you to visit in-network providers. If the plan does allow you to go out-of-network, you may face steeper cost-sharing rates, Cottrill said.

"That's a consideration for people who have either a preferred provider that they really want to stay with ...or people who have really complex health needs where they have to see maybe a lot of different specialists, or they need a very specialized type of care," he told CBS News.

For those leaning towards Medicare Advantage, Cottrill said it's worth double-checking that the providers you need are covered by the plan. People should also consider what it might mean for the Medigap coverage, he said.

If people enroll in Medicare Advantage and later switch back to traditional Medicare, they may face higher premiums due to their age or pre-existing conditions, compared to someone who enrolled in Medigap through a traditional Medicare plan from the outset, according to Cottrill.
Comparing plans

Cottrill said a good place to start is Plan Finder, a tool offered by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) that allows people to compare Medicare Advantage plans and Part D plans and to see whether providers are in-network.
The website, however, is just a jumping-off point. People should still conduct independent research to ensure their coverage needs are met, Cottrill said.
"If something is really crucial for somebody's care, they should reach out to the plan directly, talk to their provider directly and don't just rely on the website," he told CBS News.

For general information, people can contact 1-800-Medicare, the CMS-run helpline for Medicare information, or consult their State Health Insurance Assistance Program, which provides more tailored counseling.

Seniors may also consider working with a broker who can help sort through the different options. But they should keep in mind that these people may have a financial stake in their decision, Cottrill said.
"They're often paid on commission," he said. "That's not to say that they can't be helpful, but it's worth getting a second opinion from someone who doesn't have that financial stake."
Enrollment timeline
The plan you choose during open enrollment takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027, for the full calendar year.

While the deadline to make changes is Dec. 7, some people have some extra wiggle room. Medicare Advantage enrollees can switch to another Medicare Advantage plan from Jan. 1 through March 31 during a separate enrollment period.

"You can also choose to leave your Medicare Advantage plan and return to original Medicare during that same time frame, with the option of also enrolling in a Part D plan," said Will Kinkead, associate vice president of Reliance Medicare Advisors.
Some people also qualify for special enrollment periods if they move or lose access to their current health care coverage and need to make a change.

As people research Medicare plan options, they may find they need to chase down details from their providers or consult with an expert. So it's important not to wait until the last minute to start the enrollment process, Rivkin said.

"This can be a really complicated decision for some people, so take the time to get comfortable with the questions you have, what you need in 2027, and make sure that you're getting all of your needs covered," she told CBS News.

title: Seeking relief from chronic pain
summary: With about one in four American adults living with chronic pain, Dr. Jon LaPook examines some of the current treatments, from medications and surgery, to nerve stimulation, biofeedback and self-hypnosis.
story: Veterinarian Dr. Troy Hudnall enjoyed an active practice in Missouri. But in 2022, during an intense delivery of a calf, he felt a sharp pain, and heard a strange sound: "A snap or a pop, snap's probably the best way to describe it," he said.

Herniated discs and a pinched nerve in his neck caused numbness and severe muscle loss in Hudnall's right hand: "The first thing that I really remember is, I couldn't click my mouse on my computer. I started having trouble with instruments. Anything that required much agility in the fingers was almost gone."

Hudnall had multiple surgeries to help free up the nerves, but as sensation returned, he began experiencing severe pain … pain so bad, he says, he thought about amputating his own arm. Asked to describe how it felt, Hudnall replied, "For me, it's always been electricity. If you've ever touched an electric fence on a farm, or accidentally touched both prongs while you're plugging something in, it's that, but it's repetitive, it pulses."

That chronic pain has haunted Hudnall for three years now, forcing him to stop working. He treats it with a daily handful of pills, including opioids, and has tried red light therapy, physical therapy, electrical spine stimulation, and lidocaine injections. But despite all that, he says he experiences pain every second of every day. Rating his pain level from zero to ten, Hudnall says his "best days" rank at six to eight.
About one in four American adults lives with chronic pain, defined as pain lasting more than three months. Most are still suffering a year later.
"When you have chronic pain day in, day out, you're just inundated with this signal all the time; it's crushing you completely," said pain specialist Dr. Lara Crock.
A global problem

We followed Hudnall's care at one of the nation's top pain centers, the Washington University School of Medicine Pain Center in St. Louis, where, Crock explained, patients often end up trying many different approaches. "We throw medicines at it, we try different injections, we try different procedures," she said. "But really, we don't have a full understanding of why one person with the same injury continues to hurt while the other person heals and no longer hurts."

Treating chronic pain requires understanding the different ways a body can react to a painful stimulus. For example, when a person burns their hand, an electrical signal travels up nerves in the arm to the spine, then on to brain cells that interpret that signal as pain. In most people, once the painful stimulus stops, the sensation of pain stops. But not always.

Crock said, "The tissue that was injured before may be healed, or the injury that you had is recovered, but that signal continues to go and go." Why? "We don't know!" she said. "Your arm is totally normal, every scan, everything about your arm is completely normal, but there's an area of your brain that is affecting your hand that's damaged and causes your arm to hurt all the time."

Chronic pain is a global problem. Over the last 35 years, more than 900 journals in 86 countries have published thousands of articles about chronic pain. Approaches to treatment include using devices that stimulate the vagus nerve in the neck to lower pain in patients with rheumatoid arthritis or migraine headaches. And researchers are testing new non-opioid medications that block tiny gateways in nerve cells (called sodium channels) to keep pain signals from traveling to the brain.
Biofeedback

At Washington University, researchers are trying to lower pain by "retraining" the brain. Doctors Eric Leuthardt and Simon Haroutounian have come up with a headset, wearable at home, that uses biofeedback to train patients to increase certain brain waves that ease pain. "We have conducted a pilot in a small group of about six patients with chronic pain that was non-responsive to other treatments, like surgery, medications," said Haroutounian. "And everyone improved to some extent."

The positive assets of the device, Leuthardt said, include, "It's not a drug, it's got no pathologic side effects, it's not addictive, and in many ways, [it] empowers the patient to rehabilitate their own neural circuits for improvement."
Self-hypnosis

Still in early research stages, that headset isn't ready for patients like Troy Hudnall. But since last May, Hudnall has been trying hypnosis, in sessions conducted by pain psychologist Sarah Buday. "Clinical hypnosis is not your Las Vegas stage show; I'm not trying to make anyone cluck like a chicken or be under my control," Buday said. "The way I think of it is, I'm teaching somebody the skill of self-hypnosis. We are having them go into a very deep state of relaxation, at which point, I start to make suggestions about maybe the quality of the pain or the meaning of it, their emotions."
Several weeks ago, with the help of self-hypnosis, Hudnall endured another surgery. As for his future, he says he tries to remain positive.
And Buday is positive about Hudnall's outlook as well: "I think it's good. It's already getting better. And he is somebody that has a lot of optimism and hope."

And Lara Crock says, even if – despite all you throw at it – pain is only partially relieved, "It can be the difference from being able to get up and take your kid to school or eat breakfast or dinner with your family, versus laying in bed all day. So, that can be huge."

title: Americans wary of AI for medical care and insurance claims
summary: Most Americans have qualms about using AI in healthcare for tasks such as diagnosis and treatment, Pew Research poll finds.
story: How much artificial intelligence is too much when you visit your doctor? Although patients are generally open to healthcare professionals using AI to handle administrative and some medical tasks, they want humans wielding the stethoscope, a recent survey suggests.

A solid majority of Americans are comfortable with AI translating patient notes or scheduling appointments, either on its own or with some human oversight, according to the Pew Research Center, which polled more than 3,400 U.S. adults in June. More than half the respondents were also open to using AI to analyze medical scans and lab test results, provided a healthcare professional supervised the process.

But people draw the line when it comes to AI driving diagnoses or making insurance decisions, Pew found. Almost half of those surveyed said they don't want an AI model deciding whether to accept or reject an insurance claim, while 41% said they don't want AI making a diagnosis on its own.

Galen Stocking, associate director of science and society research at Pew Research Center, said people see value in applying AI to healthcare. Still, patients want to know when and how healthcare providers and administrative staff are using the technology.
"Overall, people say it's extremely important that their healthcare provider tell them if they are using AI," he told CBS News.

"There is a lack of clarity on the side of the public," he added, noting Pew's finding that 46% of the survey respondents said they don't know if AI has ever been used in the course of them receiving care.
Indeed, 60% of respondents said they are uncomfortable with doctors using AI for tasks such as diagnosis and treatment; only 30% are OK with that, while 10% are unsure.
"People are concerned about patient-doctor relationships and the security of their own health information," Stocking said.

More broadly, Americans are split over whether AI will improve the quality of medical care. Some 37% of respondents said AI will improve health outcomes, while a nearly equal share think the technology could reduce the quality of care.

title: Megaspeed's vacant offices raise questions about ties to Nvidia, China
summary: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's powerful AI computer chips, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.
story: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based company at the center of the Nvidia Chinese spy scandal, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.

One of Megaspeed's leaders is Alice Huang, the woman with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair, and who is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. In the past three years, Megaspeed, formerly a gaming company, has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.

And yet Megaspeed's corporate headquarters sat practically empty, according to The Straits Times, an English-language newspaper in Singapore. Questions have also been raised about its outposts in Australia and Malaysia.

Published reports in recent days revealed that the company listed a newspaper vendor as the director of its Australian subsidiary, and one of its Malaysia offices consisted of a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur. Yet another Malaysia office was tucked into a shopping mall.

Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to restricted Nvidia AI computer chips. U.S. investigators say that Alice Huang used her contacts in the industry and a series of shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export into China. Now it is being probed in both the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
President Trump said this week the FBI is also investigating romantic and business ties between Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang and Alice Huang (who are not related).

Earlier this week, Jensen Huang, who is married, apologized for the affair in a statement to Nvidia's employees. The company launched an independent investigation of the matter, and an Nvidia shareholder filed a class action lawsuit Tuesday alleging that Huang concealed a relationship with Alice Huang and misled shareholders about national security concerns raised by the relationship.
Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," its statement said.

China expert Jacqueline Deal said that Nvidia's advanced AI chips could have ended up with the Chinese military. Deal, who is an adviser to State Armor, a nonprofit that studies global security threats, told CBS News, "If allegations are true, who will be fired? Nvidia has a compliance team that may have failed utterly."

She also questioned the effectiveness of the U.S. Commerce Department, which has jurisdiction over export controls that may have been bypassed, potentially giving the Chinese military access to the world's most advanced chips.
Here's what we now know about Megaspeed:

It is a major Nvidia customer. Megaspeed and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, purchased $4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence equipment and processors over the last three years.
In 2025, Megaspeed International faced an investigation by Singapore police for alleged breaches of local laws, but no details have emerged about the probe, according to The Straits Times.
The company grew rapidly.

"Megaspeed International is a premier business partner of NVIDIA, strategically positioned in the Asia Pacific region," according to its LinkedIn profile, which claims it has between 201 and 500 employees. Three years ago it listed between two and 10 employees, according to the South China Morning Post.

Megaspeed International did not reply to a request for comment. It posted an "official statement" on its website addressing what it called "misleading information" and "incorrect insinuations" accusing it of involvement in illegal chip transfers.

"We want to be absolutely clear over the past six months our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the US Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia and NVIDIA," said the message, which also appeared on the company's LinkedIn page.
"These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities," the company said.

Megaspeed was originally incorporated in 2015 under the name 7Road International, a subsidiary of a Chinese developer of popular video games and mobile apps based in Shenzhen, China, according to corporate filings.
Huang Le Limited, a shell company in the British Virgin Islands, acquired 7Road International in March 2023. Huang Le is the Chinese name of Alice Huang.
That same month, 7Road International was renamed Megaspeed International, and Huang became its managing director. The company also launched a subsidiary called Speedmatrix.

By the end of October 2023, Huang and another Megaspeed director, Cang Yang, resigned from the company after it was bought up by a firm called Swiftdata, whose director is based in China, documents show.

But there's some indication Huang may still be affiliated with the company. Culper Research, an activist short-selling firm, published a 40-page report on Nvidia in May that cited Megaspeed employees who said Huang was still running the company.

The report also raised some concern about Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang, stating, "Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has not only vouched for Megaspeed, but seems to have quite literally walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, while maintaining an uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang, a Chinese national."
Megaspeed lists its headquarters office address on the seventh floor of the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore, a glass office tower in Singapore's central business district.

When the Straits Times and The New York Times visited the Singapore offices around the same time late last year, they found little or no staff working. The Straits Times said the door was locked, and the Times found just two people in its office on a workday.

Megaspeed has an Australian subsidiary on the 10th floor of a commercial and retail tower in the heart of Sydney's central business district. Forty other businesses are on the same floor, and space in the building can be rented for as little as $17 per day, Australia's ABC News reported. Corporate filings name Shanghai-born Kai Kang, a 29-year-old newspaper vendor, as the director, according to Australian news reports. But Kang's newsstand is in Northern Victoria, over 400 miles from Sydney. Kang's father told Australia's ABC News this week that he had never heard of Megaspeed.

title: Enrolling in Medicare? Here's what to consider before Dec. 7.
summary: Medicare open enrollment, which runs from Oct.15 to Dec. 7, gives people a chance to change their health coverage. Here's what to know.
story: The Medicare open enrollment window has arrived, giving millions of seniors across the U.S. the chance to revisit their coverage choices. Even if you're happy with your plan, experts say it's still worth exploring your options.

Health plans change every year, meaning people could see updates to premium costs, prescription drug coverage and available providers in their network. New plans also come online, expanding the already broad list of coverage options.
"There's really no one who can't benefit from at least taking some time to take a look," Alex Cottrill, senior policy analyst with KFF's program on Medicare policy, told CBS News.

People enrolled in Medicare Advantage or a Part D prescription drug plan typically receive an "Annual Notice of Change" in September outlining any updates to their coverage, according to Medicare.gov, the government website for the program.

"Pay attention to those notices, and frankly, even if you don't receive an annual notice of change, you still want to review your current plan and make sure that it is the right one for you," said Jessica Rivkin, vice president of Reliance Medicare Advisors, an insurance agency that helps people enroll in Medicare Advantage plans.
Americans now have less than a month to make their Medicare choices, with open enrollment set to close Dec. 7. Here are some considerations as you navigate the process.
Choosing between Medicare and Medicare Advantage

One of the biggest decisions people face when enrolling in Medicare is whether to choose traditional Medicare or Medicare Advantage, a comprehensive plan in which private insurers are paid to manage your care.

By contrast, people who enroll in regular Medicare plans must separately select a Medicare Part D prescription drug plan and Medigap, private insurance people can layer on top of their plan to help defray out-of-pocket costs.
"You only have to pick one plan rather than having these modular options that you have in traditional Medicare," Cottrill said of Medicare Advantage.

A drawback of Medicare Advantage is its more stringent requirements. Some plans only allow you to visit in-network providers. If the plan does allow you to go out-of-network, you may face steeper cost-sharing rates, Cottrill said.

"That's a consideration for people who have either a preferred provider that they really want to stay with ...or people who have really complex health needs where they have to see maybe a lot of different specialists, or they need a very specialized type of care," he told CBS News.

For those leaning towards Medicare Advantage, Cottrill said it's worth double-checking that the providers you need are covered by the plan. People should also consider what it might mean for the Medigap coverage, he said.

If people enroll in Medicare Advantage and later switch back to traditional Medicare, they may face higher premiums due to their age or pre-existing conditions, compared to someone who enrolled in Medigap through a traditional Medicare plan from the outset, according to Cottrill.
Comparing plans

Cottrill said a good place to start is Plan Finder, a tool offered by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) that allows people to compare Medicare Advantage plans and Part D plans and to see whether providers are in-network.
The website, however, is just a jumping-off point. People should still conduct independent research to ensure their coverage needs are met, Cottrill said.
"If something is really crucial for somebody's care, they should reach out to the plan directly, talk to their provider directly and don't just rely on the website," he told CBS News.

For general information, people can contact 1-800-Medicare, the CMS-run helpline for Medicare information, or consult their State Health Insurance Assistance Program, which provides more tailored counseling.

Seniors may also consider working with a broker who can help sort through the different options. But they should keep in mind that these people may have a financial stake in their decision, Cottrill said.
"They're often paid on commission," he said. "That's not to say that they can't be helpful, but it's worth getting a second opinion from someone who doesn't have that financial stake."
Enrollment timeline
The plan you choose during open enrollment takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027, for the full calendar year.

While the deadline to make changes is Dec. 7, some people have some extra wiggle room. Medicare Advantage enrollees can switch to another Medicare Advantage plan from Jan. 1 through March 31 during a separate enrollment period.

"You can also choose to leave your Medicare Advantage plan and return to original Medicare during that same time frame, with the option of also enrolling in a Part D plan," said Will Kinkead, associate vice president of Reliance Medicare Advisors.
Some people also qualify for special enrollment periods if they move or lose access to their current health care coverage and need to make a change.

As people research Medicare plan options, they may find they need to chase down details from their providers or consult with an expert. So it's important not to wait until the last minute to start the enrollment process, Rivkin said.

"This can be a really complicated decision for some people, so take the time to get comfortable with the questions you have, what you need in 2027, and make sure that you're getting all of your needs covered," she told CBS News.

title: Hotter-than-expected inflation raises chances of Fed rate hike
summary: Inflation rose at a monthly pace of 0.4%, hotter than economists had forecast and raising expectations that the Federal Reserve will increase interest rates in December.
story: Consumer prices rose more than economists expected in October on a monthly basis, offering little relief to Americans grappling with high living costs.
The Consumer Price Index, which tracks changes in prices over time, rose at a monthly pace of 0.4%, the Labor Department reported on Tuesday.
The Labor Department did not report a year-over-year inflation rate for October 2026 because the 2025 government shutdown left it without October 2025 consumer price data for comparison.
By the numbers
October's monthly inflation increase cooled from September, when headline inflation rose 0.6% on a monthly basis.
However, the figure was hotter than expected, with economists polled by FactSet predicting October prices would rise 0.3% month-over-month.
The October inflation data is one of the first snapshots of the economy following the midterm elections, which underscored Americans' frustration with high prices.

"Today's CPI report suggests underlying inflation remains more persistent than the Fed would like," Andrew Davis, head of investment strategy at Bryn Mawr Trust, said in an email. "While headline inflation moderated from September, core prices rose 0.3% for the third consecutive month, indicating that underlying price pressures have yet to meaningfully ease."

While inflation in recent months has largely been driven by higher energy prices, October's data shows that costs for other types of goods and products are also rising. Shelter costs, which rose 0.3% in October, accounted for more than 30% of the monthly all-items increase, the Labor Department said.
Food prices also accelerated, rising at a monthly pace of 0.5% last month after remaining flat in September, the data shows.
Energy prices
Energy costs, which have surged due to the Iran war, contributed less to the monthly rise in inflation than in past reports. Energy prices rose 0.7% in October, compared to 5.2% in September.
Gas prices have been falling for weeks as stations switch to cheaper winter blend and people pull back from summer travel.
Global oil costs, the main factor in setting prices at the pump, have also dipped amid hopes that the midterm elections could open the door to a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the war.
On Tuesday, the national average prices for gasoline sank below $4 a gallon for the first time in nearly four months, according to AAA.
Core inflation, which excludes volatile energy and food prices, rose 0.3% in October, in line with September but slightly above economists' forecasts.

Josh Hirt, senior U.S. economist for Vanguard, said in an email that elevated energy prices have led to a "longer-lasting shock pass-through" to core inflation, prompting the investment company to raise its year-end 2026 core inflation forecast to 3.2%.
What this means for interest rates
Wall Street analysts predicted that firmer inflation last month will spur the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates when it meets in December.

"This is the last look at CPI inflation the Fed will get before its December meeting, and it most likely seals the deal on a rate hike to close the year," James McCann, senior economist for investment strategy at Edward Jones, said in an email. The bigger question, he added, is whether the central bank will raise its benchmark rate by a quarter or half of a percentage point.
After the latest inflation data, CME Group's FedWatch tool showed an 85% chance the Fed would raise rates by 0.25 percentage points in December and a 15% chance of a 0.50 percentage-point hike.
The central bank stayed on the sidelines at its October meeting, although two Federal Open Market Committee members voted in favor of a rate hike.

During a conference in London on Tuesday, Christopher Waller, a member of the Fed's Board of Governors, said policymakers should consider a 0.50 percentage-point increase when the central bank meets on Dec. 8-9.
"Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take," he said.

title: What stores are open and closed for Veterans Day 2026?
summary: See which businesses are operating and the deals they are offering veterans and active military members for their service.
story: Veterans Day, observed annually on November 11, honors Americans who have served in the U.S. military. Formerly known as "Armistice Day," the holiday was celebrated nationally for the first time in 1919 at the direction of former U.S. President Woodrow Wilson. Congress officially recognized it as a federal holiday in 1926.

This year, Veterans Day falls on a Wednesday. Read on to see which businesses are operating and some of the deals they are offering veterans and active military members to thank them for their service.
What stores are open on Veterans Day?
Most major grocery chains are open, including Aldi, Food Lion, Publix, Stop & Shop, Trader Joe's, Wegmans and Whole Foods.
Walgreens confirmed that it will welcome customers on Wednesday. CVS locations will be open, although some stores and pharmacies may have reduced hours, a spokesperson said.
Other retailers are also generally open on Veterans Day, although it's a good idea to check your local retailer's hours ahead of time.
Is Costco open?
The big-box store will be open for Veterans Day, according to its holiday schedule.
Is Target open?
Target stores will be open on Wednesday during regular business hours, a company spokesperson confirmed.
Is Walmart open?
Walmart stores will operate during their regular hours on Veterans Day, according to a company spokesperson.
Are banks open or closed today?
Major banks such as Bank of America, Chase and TD Bank are closed on Wednesday, as Veterans Day is a federal holiday observed by the Federal Reserve.
Americans can still visit ATMs and check online account activity. However, the holiday may affect the time it takes to process certain transactions, Bank of America says on its website.
Is the post office open or closed on Veterans Day?
All post office locations will be closed, and mail will not be delivered on Wednesday due to the federal holiday. Mailing and retail services will resume on Thursday, Nov. 12, according to the USPS.
Is the stock market open?

The U.S. stock market will be open, with Veterans Day not among the holidays observed by the New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq. The next time markets will be closed is on Thanksgiving, which falls on Thursday, Nov. 26.
Veterans Day deals at retailers, grocery stores and restaurants

title: Nvidia's trillion-dollar bind: Can it afford to lose Jensen Huang?
summary: Other CEOs have been ousted over undisclosed relationships, but Nvidia's inquiry shines a spotlight on how closely the chipmaker's fortunes are tied to its co-founder.
story: Nvidia's board of directors faces a trillion-dollar dilemma: Can the chipmaker afford to part with its storied co-founder and CEO, now embroiled in multiple investigations into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy?

In recent years, several high-profile CEOs have been ousted after their relationships with employees and customers came under scrutiny, including former McDonald's CEO Steve Easterbrook and Kohl's CEO Ashley Buchanan. But none is so closely identified with their companies as Huang. Over more than three decades, he has led Nvidia as it grew into one of the world's most valuable companies, with many investors viewing him as equally critical to the company's success as Elon Musk is to SpaceX or Steve Jobs was to Apple.

Huang is facing serious challenges, including an independent inquiry by Nvidia's board into the affair, a shareholder lawsuit and questions from lawmakers. Heightening the stakes are allegations that Huang had a close relationship with a former female executive at an Nvidia customer who is also suspected of working with China's intelligence agency.
$450 billion drop
Nvidia shareholders have been spooked by the disclosure, with the company's shares shedding 10% of their value — or about $450 billion — in the last two trading days alone.
"It exposes how dependent the company is on this one person," Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, told CBS News.
He added, "This is like asking if something happens to Elon Musk, what happens to Tesla and SpaceX's valuations? If something happens to Jensen Huang, what happens to Nvidia's valuation?"

Yorkville Ives tech analyst Dan Ives estimated in a research note that Nvidia could lose as much as 30% of its valuation if Huang is removed from his role, while noting that for now most investors expect the executive to retain his post at the company.

"At the end of the day, there is only one Jensen, and Nvidia will dramatically change as a company if he is no longer CEO, with a major negative ripple impact across the tech industry and AI Revolution," Ives said.
"Do not proceed"

Corporate governance experts said Huang's alleged relationship with Alice Huang — a Chinese executive linked to the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia — appears to violate Nvidia's code of conduct. That policy highlights that personal relationships could create a conflict of interest for Nvidia, while Huang himself specifies in the code of conduct that the company's workers have a responsibility "to maintain high ethical standards."

Nvidia's code also instructs employees to ask themselves whether they could defend an action if it were made public on social media or known to colleagues. If not, the policy states, "do not proceed."

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment about whether Huang had violated any company rules. In a message to company employees on Sunday, Huang admitted, "I was unfaithful to my wife," and he apologized for hurting her and their two children, both of whom also work at Nvidia. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.

But Huang's conduct "is definitely a violation," said Jay Aldebert, chief growth officer at International Services, a consulting firm that advises small and midsize businesses on issues including governance. "How he handled it based on their code of conduct is where you're going to see continued issues."
Still, while Huang may have violated company rules, he may be given more leeway than other employees due to his importance to Nvidia, governance experts said.

"This is an outlier — I don't remember a case like this," Columbia's Rajgopal said. "This company is so important to the U.S. in terms of AI, especially with China and other powers. So even if there is a violation of the code of conduct, if I were the chair of the board, I would not dismiss him."

Nvidia's 11-person board includes Huang, although the other board members are considered independent, according to a company regulatory filing. They include California Institute of Technology professor John Dabiri and former Taco Bell International president Melissa Lora. All board members except Dabiri have experience in corporate governance, the filing states.
Nvidia board members should demonstrate their independence by hiring a law firm to help with the investigation, and immediately develop a succession plan for Huang, Rajgopal said.
A common issue for Nvidia and other big tech companies led by their founders is that they are often run "like a family affair," he added.
"These are effectively run like family private companies, but they are mega-cap public companies where most of the capital comes from the public," Rajgopal said. "There is a duty above and beyond."
Succession planning

Huang has said he has more than 60 direct reports in a corporate structure that keeps him at the center of decision-making at Nvidia. As various investigations ramp up, the succession plan to replace him remains unclear, heightening pressure on the board, experts said.

"The Nvidia board is between a rock and a hard spot. They have almost no good options — Jensen is Nvidia," said David Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School. "And if he has done something wrong and he needs to be removed, and they have no successors, that's a terrible outcome."

If Huang resigns or is removed by the board, speculation on possible replacements has turned to figures including Nvidia co-founder Chris Malachowsky, who is a senior technology executive at the company, and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress.
Nvidia employs more than 40,000 people worldwide, and there are "lots of other great leaders" within the company, said Bob O'Donnell, president, founder and chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research.

"I think it's important that the company starts to let some of these other folks come out as spokespeople so people feel trust, they feel good about Nvidia and their future, even without Jensen," O'Donnell said, although he said he does not think Huang will leave his post.

title: Study shows who is hit hardest by data center costs
summary: A new study found that lower-income, rural households bore a disproportionate share of the financial burdens associated with AI data centers and the energy they use.
story: With data centers cropping up around the United States, the cost of the energy infrastructure on which they rely, and who pays for it, are among the country's most debated economic and political questions. A new study finds that in 2025, the rising energy costs associated with AI data centers landed hardest on lower-income, rural households, which bore disproportionate shares of the financial burdens compared with the data centers themselves.

Authored by Cornell University researchers and published this week in the journal Nature Energy, the study analyzed growth in both energy demand and infrastructure projects along four major U.S. power grids between 2020 and 2025. It also looked at data from 4,000 existing and proposed data centers across the U.S. Its results showed that the AI boom, and the buildout of data centers used to support it, hike up energy costs in ways that place the greatest economic strain on people who benefit least from the technology.

The study found that data centers unevenly raised wholesale power prices. Those costs are determined through an open marketplace where electricity is bought and sold in bulk between power generators and utilities before reaching transmission lines, and, eventually, consumers. Power grids that were already stretched saw the greatest price increases, researchers said.

In California's southern Bay Area, data centers were estimated to raise wholesale energy prices by almost 20% last year. In Texas' Dallas-Fort Worth area, the increase in 2025 approached 17%, according to their estimates. Both regions have seen influxes of data centers in recent years. Places like New York, where data centers are less prevalent, didn't experience significant changes in wholesale energy prices, according to the study.

Higher wholesale prices had a downstream effect on energy consumers, the researchers said, as residential customers paid huge fractions of the spending on transmission built for data centers. The study found that spending across the four power grids jumped from $2 billion in 2020 to $34.2 billion in 2025, with data centers responsible for $8.25 billion of energy infrastructure costs last year. Residential users were responsible for just under $3.5 billion, but they were billed more than $16 billion while data centers were billed about $3 billion.

Researchers said that antiquated formulas used to allocate energy costs along a power grid have historically divided those costs based on previous energy consumption, rather than new growth. That means households take on much of the costs for developing new power infrastructure.

"It's kind of a chicken-and-egg problem," said Fengqi You, one of the study's authors, in a statement. "Because if you're going to build a data center, you need to expand this power infrastructure. Otherwise, there's no electricity for them to run. But before they build, they're not using energy."

Residents of rural and lower-income areas saw their bills skyrocket, and in some cases faced increases in energy costs that were 76% larger than residents of urban communities, according to the study.

The researchers said that despite the concentration of data centers near metropolitan hubs, the financial loads they trigger often seep into surrounding suburban and rural areas because of policies that govern how energy costs are shared across regions. They argued that such policies warrant review.

Researchers also pointed to what they called a "paradoxical mismatch": According to the study, states that faced the largest cost increases, like West Virginia and Ohio, also reported the lowest uses of generative AI compared with other states around the country.

The study also found instances where states saw price increases linked to AI data centers located geographically far from them, essentially paying for infrastructure "they neither contribute to nor benefit from," researchers said. Residents in New Jersey and Pennsylvania helped pay for power grid updates tied to data center growth in Virginia, for example.

"As I often emphasize, you do not have to live next to a data center to help pay for its power infrastructure," You told CBS News. "Our goal is to provide science-based evidence so policymakers, companies, and communities can make informed decisions about how to balance these benefits and costs."

Researchers suggested that data centers cut back on their energy use during their region's peak demand hours or pay states directly for the new energy demand they add to a given power grid. Since regulating data centers was a huge focus of November's midterm elections, You said his team hoped their findings could help lawmakers decide what to do next.

"This is an issue that connects directly to debates in many states and in Congress," said You. "We want to provide science-based evidence and concrete data so that all the stakeholders can better understand the picture and weigh their options."

You told CBS News that, eventually, "the key idea is that the data center sector should really pay for the power energy infrastructure upgrades they need, not the other customers, not the households, and definitely not the low-income ones." But, he added, "unfortunately, that's the situation right now."

title: 24% of Americans with a credit record are behind on their debts
summary: More U.S. households are falling into debt as they grapple with medical bills, student loans and other expenses, data show.
story: More Americans are tumbling seriously into debt as prices and the overall cost of living continue to rise.

Roughly 24% of people with a credit record are behind on medical bills, student debt, or auto or retail loans, according to a new analysis from the Urban Institute, a nonpartisan think tank. The median balance owed: $2,913. In communities of color, 30% of people are behind on payments, with a median debt in collection of $3,009.

"The increasing cost of living makes it harder for people to make payments on basic needs," Breno Braga, senior fellow in the family and financial well-being division at the Urban Institute, told CBS News.

Rising interest rates this year as the Federal Reserve tries to tame inflation are also making it harder for people to catch up. "It's a reflection of the financial life of Americans these days as we know it," Braga added.
Consumers' credit card balances have surged to a record $1.29 trillion, up nearly 70% from five years ago, according to new figures from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Years of high prices have forced Americans to deplete their savings and finance their daily expenses with debt, according to Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit debt counselor. As a result, many household budgets are at a "breaking point," he said in an email to CBS News.

Consumer prices have risen by an average of 30% since 2019, Rossman noted. Meanwhile, the share of Americans with debt in collection this year is up about one percentage point, from less than 23% in 2025, according to the Urban Institute, which based its findings on an analysis of more than 10 million credit records and U.S. Census data.
Student loans and medical bills

Roughly one in six, or almost 16%, of student loan borrowers are behind on payments, although the figure varies by geography. In Louisiana, for example, the state with the highest share of people with debt in collections, the student loan delinquency rate is roughly 22%.
Braga attributes the disparity to several factors, such as lower incomes and higher poverty rates in some parts of the country.

"People there tend to have lower credit scores, so when they get a credit card or take out an auto loan, they tend to pay higher interest rates," he said. "That makes it harder to make those payments, especially if you are low income. It makes you more likely to fall behind."
Many people also are shouldering heavy medical bills despite having health insurance, reflecting insufficient coverage and the high cost of care across the U.S.

According to the Urban Institute, 3% of Americans have medical debt in collections, with a median balance of $1,492 — a figure that reflects only unpaid hospital or other medical bills, while excluding credit card debt stemming from health care costs.

"People without health insurance are more likely to have medical debt, but having coverage does not protect you at all from having medical debt, especially not now with the high deductible plans we are seeing," Braga said.
Fifteen states have passed legislation barring health care providers from reporting medical debt to credit rating agencies, which can lessen the damage to consumers' credit records.
"It's good for patients that it's not reported to the agencies, but that doesn't mean it disappears. It just isn't reported anymore," he noted.

title: Gas prices slip below $4 a gallon for first time since July
summary: Petroleum expert Patrick De Haan predicts prices will continue to sink and reach $3.75 a gallon by Thanksgiving.
story: Gasoline prices in the U.S. are below $4 a gallon for the first time in nearly four months.
According to AAA, the national average for a gallon of gasoline was $3.98 on Tuesday, down from $4.56 a gallon earlier this year.
"We're heading in the right direction in terms of what drivers want to see," AAA spokesperson Aixa Diaz told CBS News. "They don't want to be paying more than $4 a gallon at this time of year.
Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at tracking firm GasBuddy, predicts that fuel prices will continue to ease into the Thanksgiving holidays.
Diesel costs have also fallen, with the national average now running at $6.16 a gallon, down from $6.53 in late September.
Far from normal

Although lower gas prices offer relief to motorists, prices are still historically high for this time of year, AAA's Diaz said. The record high for average U.S. prices at the pump around the Thanksgiving holiday was $3.58 a gallon in 2022, data from the motor club shows.
"We're still a ways away from even being close to normal for this time of year," Diaz said.

The average price of regular gas has jumped $1 per gallon since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Consumer prices rose at a monthly rate of 0.5% in October, new government data shows.

October's CPI data, released Tuesday, suggests high fuel costs may be spilling over into other categories, such as food, which rose at a monthly rate of 0.5% in October after remaining flat in September.
Why are prices down?

Gas prices have fallen in recent weeks as filling stations switch from summer-blend fuels to cheaper winter blends. Federal rules require gas stations to sell a summer blend, designed to guard against evaporation, from June 1 to Sept. 15. Outside that period, stations are allowed to use a winter blend, which is cheaper to produce, explaining why prices often fade in the fall.

The winter blend switch coincides with a drop in fuel demand, as people take fewer road trips and vacations later in the year. According to AAA, gas prices typically fall by around 10 to 30 cents per gallon during the winter months.
Global oil costs, the main factor affecting gas prices, have also dipped amid hopes that the midterm elections could open the door to a deal between the U.S. and Iran to end the war.
"Some optimism about what could happen over in the Middle East and along the Strait of Hormuz certainly plays a role here," Diaz said, while also acknowledging the impact of lower winter fuel costs.
On Tuesday, Brent crude, the international benchmark, was trading at around $91 per barrel.
In an interview with CBS News "60 Minutes" on Sunday, President Trump said he is "not looking" to escalate the war in Iran.
"I don't think there's any reason to," he told "60 Minutes" correspondent Ross Douthat.

The timeline for reaching a resolution, however, remains unclear. Gregory Brew, senior analyst for Iran and energy for the political risk consultancy Eurasia Group, said Monday that the prospect for a deal remains "unlikely."
"Despite ongoing mediation, neither the U.S. nor Iran has shifted its negotiating position," he said in a research note Monday.

title: California voters reject billionaire wealth tax, CBS News projects
summary: Voters in California have rejected a tax on the state's wealthiest residents, CBS News projects, following a campaign that has split traditional allies and shattered spending records for a tax-related measure in California.
story: Voters in California have rejected a tax on the state's wealthiest residents, CBS News projects, following a campaign that has split traditional allies and shattered spending records for a tax-related measure in California.

Proposition 40 would have levied a one-time 5% tax on California residents with a net worth of $1 billion, excluding real estate and certain retirement assets. Proponents of the measure said it was expected to generate $100 billion over five years, with 90% going toward healthcare programs and the other 10% for education, food assistance, and administration of the tax.
The proposal came at a time when other states and federal policymakers are debating how to tax extreme wealth and finance public services, and how Proposition 40 was viewed as a bellwether.
The vote was framed by supporters as part of a broader struggle over economic inequality and the political influence of the billionaire class.

Supporters say the state needs additional money to help offset federal healthcare cuts implemented in 2025 under H.R. 1, known as the "One Big Beautiful Bill Act," and to protect hospitals, emergency rooms, clinics and Medi-Cal services. Proponents also argue that billionaires can accumulate substantial wealth from the stock market and business valuations without paying income tax on those gains until they are realized. They also contend that those who have benefited the most from the state's robust economy should contribute more toward public services.

The measure created a divide among politicians and organizations that ordinarily align with Democratic priorities. While it was supported by the California Democratic Party and labor unions including SEIU Healthcare Workers West, the principal sponsor of the measure, it was opposed by Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Orange County Rep. Katie Porter, and major healthcare and professional organizations such as the California Medical Association and California Teachers Association.

Newsom and Porter, who have both supported higher taxes on corporations and wealthy individuals, agree with the argument that the proposal would encourage wealthy residents to leave the state and damage its long-term fiscal position by decreasing its tax revenue.

Newsom has also expressed a preference for taxing billionaires at the federal level and says a California-only wealth tax would be limited to funding healthcare and not other needs. Opponents of the measure also claim that the initiative does not provide guarantees about how the money would be allocated among providers and services.

A coalition of billionaires organized in opposition to the measure, such as Google co-founders Sergey Brin and Larry Page, venture capitalist John Doerr, PayPal and Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, venture capitalist Vinod Khosla, and Stripe CEO Patrick Collison.

Wealthy opponents contributed tens of millions of dollars to defeat Prop. 40, with most of the money going to the group Building a Better California, which has raised over $250 million in the campaign against the billionaire tax as of Oct. 28. The funding also went toward supporting two competing measures, Propositions 41 and 42, which would place limits on special taxes and could prevent the billionaire tax from taking effect if either receives more votes than Prop. 40.

A Stanford University study indicated that billionaires who have already left the state, including Brin, Page, and Thiel, have removed about $540 billion, or 30%, of California's billionaire wealth from potential taxation. The study also concluded that Prop. 40 may generate only about $30 billion instead of the $100 billion estimated by its proponents.

Other economists, including Nobel Prize winners Daron Acemoglu of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Joseph Stiglitz of Columbia University, supported the measure, saying that California has attracted more venture funding since Prop. 40 was introduced. An open letter from the economists noted that between 2019 and 2025, the California income tax paid by billionaires was "only 1.6% of their $1.4 trillion wealth gain, much less than what ordinary Californians pay on their paychecks."
One California billionaire who did support Prop. 40 is Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose estimated net worth is about $200 billion.

"I don't mind paying taxes; the more you make, the more taxes you pay, so I'm okay with that," Huang told CBS News. "I don't like tax dollars wasted. But I also support all that this country represents."

title: Nvidia, CEO Jensen Huang face shareholder suit over affair
summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing fresh turmoil after shareholders sued him and his company for allegedly misleading them over his affair with an accused Chinese spy​.
story: Tech titan Jensen Huang faced fresh turmoil on Tuesday as shareholders sued him and his company for allegedly misleading them over his affair with an accused Chinese spy.

The Rosen Law Firm said it had filed a class-action lawsuit in federal court in San Jose, California, accusing Huang and AI behemoth Nvidia of failing to disclose information to shareholders about the Nvidia CEO's links to the woman accused of funneling information to Beijing.

The New York Times reported last month that Taiwanese-born Huang developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese executive linked to Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia.
The woman isn't related to the 63-year-old CEO.
Nvidia said it launched an independent investigation of Huang.

Two law enforcement sources confirmed to CBS News on Monday that the Justice Department's National Security Division is investigating Megaspeed over potential violations of U.S. export restrictions on advanced AI chips.
Shares of the chipmaker tumbled after Nvidia's board opened an inquiry into reports that its CEO had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort," which Beijing denies.
China is in a race for tech dominance against the United States, which restricts the export to China of the most cutting-edge silicon chips.
Nvidia, a global leader in producing chips used to train and run AI models, is one of the world's most valuable companies.

The lawsuit asserted that Huang and Nvidia misled shareholders about the national security concerns raised by the affair, and that their misleading statements "artificially inflated" Nvidia's share price.

"As a result of Defendants' wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company's securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages," the lawsuit alleges.
Huang admitted in a message to Nvidia employees released on Sunday that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife.
"My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he said.
Huang is a central figure in the artificial intelligence boom and a close informal adviser to President Trump, who has repeatedly opposed regulating the industry so China doesn't gain the upper hand.

title: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang over Chinese spy concerns
summary: The board of Nvidia said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
story: Nvidia has launched an independent investigation of its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, over allegations he was the target of an intelligence effort by China.

The allegations center around a Chinese business executive named Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was an asset of China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency.
The CIA, NSA and ODNI did not immediately respond to CBS News requests for comment.

The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities were investigating Alice Huang (no relation to Jensen), a former executive of the Singapore-based Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia. The report claims Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security.

Two law enforcement sources confirmed to CBS News on Monday that the Justice Department's National Security Division is investigating Megaspeed. The investigation involves potential violations of U.S. export restrictions on advanced AI chips, the sources said.

In a message to Nvidia employees Sunday, Jensen Huang admitted, "I was unfaithful to my wife," and apologized for hurting her and their children, although he did not name the woman involved. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he wrote.

"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," Nvidia's board of directors said in a statement Sunday. "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."
The board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement said.
John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."
Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters Monday, "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear."
A company spokesperson said Jensen Huang "fully supports the review" and is committed to continuing to lead the company.
Jensen Huang said he had fallen short of his responsibilities to the company's employees, board and shareholders. He said he is "fully committed to NVIDIA" and will work to earn back their trust.

"Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation," he said in a statement. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully."
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," he added.

Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to The Times.
Asked about the report on Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he couldn't comment, saying it was an "internal corporate matter."

On Monday, President Trump called Jensen Huang a "very high-quality person," saying during a White House briefing that "the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape." Mr. Trump also said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday to see how he was doing, and that Huang "said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy."

Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has regularly surpassed Wall Street's earnings expectations in the past three years since its high-end chips emerged as AI's best building blocks. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion in August.

title: Trump admin. proposes stricter unemployment work search rules
summary: Under a proposed federal rule, Americans seeking unemployment aid would have to conduct more job searches each week.
story: The Trump administration on Monday proposed stiffer rules for Americans seeking unemployment benefits that, if adopted, would require them to conduct more weekly job searches.

The proposed Department of Labor regulations, set to be published in the Federal Register on Tuesday, would require people applying for or collecting jobless aid to complete at least five unique work searches per week. Currently, many U.S. states require two to three qualifying work searches per week, while only four states require five. Some states require only one work search activity to qualify for unemployment benefits.

The Trump administration said the change is necessary to create consistent eligibility requirements for unemployment benefits nationwide. A national minimum weekly work search standard would "improve program integrity and strengthen labor market attachment," the Labor Department said in its proposal.

"This action is necessary to reduce inconsistencies beyond those created by local labor markets in State-level requirements for individuals to actively seek work," according to the agency. "The intended effect is to hold States accountable for administering [an unemployment compensation] program that provides temporary wage replacement to eligible individuals while they are actively seeking work through a meaningful engagement with the labor market."
The public has 60 days following publication of the proposed rule to offer comment.
Costly for states and workers
Labor advocates criticized the proposed change in work search rules, saying the new threshold would be hard for unemployed people to meet and costly for states to administer.

"Not only is the proposed change devastating to claimants who may not have five search options for every week they are unemployed, but it will likely cost states hundreds of thousands of dollars," Michele Evermore, senior director of economic security and worker transitions at the National Employment Law Project, a worker advocacy group, said in a statement to CBS News. "Nearly all states will have to change their claimant intake forms, and with it, their technology — a costly fix. Many states will have to rewrite their laws to meet this rule."

Evermore also said the proposed rule would disadvantage applicants who already struggle to navigate the unemployment benefits systems. Employers "want candidates enthusiastic about their job opportunities, not ticking boxes for the work search form," she added.
More level playing field?

The Labor Department acknowledged that the policy could temporarily raise costs as states and jobless aid applicants adapt to the new work requirement, but said the change is necessary to ensure that the eligibility rules are applied consistently across the U.S.

"These inconsistencies can create confusion for individuals, lead to uneven enforcement when allowable activities are not clearly defined, and increase the likelihood that otherwise eligible individuals may fail to meet requirements simply because expectations are unclear," the Labor Department said. "Additionally, variability in how States notify individuals of work search requirements can result in individuals engaging in activities that may not support reemployment or may not satisfy the State's rules."

Various activities would satisfy the proposed requirement that people seeking jobless aid conduct at least five work searches per week, according to the Labor Department. For example, beyond contacting a prospective employer, registering with or contacting a job placement agency or union would also count as a qualified work search.

Under the proposal, states could also designate other activities as satisfying the requirement. Additionally, states could adapt the weekly job search threshold to account for local labor market conditions through a points-based system that would allow someone applying for jobless aid to accrue multiple points for a single activity.
"Under such a system, States may assign point values to qualifying work search activities and require individuals to accumulate a minimum of five points per benefit week," the Labor Department said.

title: Nvidia stock slumps amid board investigation into CEO Jensen Huang
summary: Investors are questioning whether Huang's future as Nvidia's CEO may be at risk amid allegations that he was targeted in a Chinese intelligence operation.
story: Nvidia's stock price slid on Monday amid questions about CEO Jensen Huang's future at the chipmaker, following the board of directors' investigation into allegations that China targeted him in an intelligence operation.

The investigation is raising concerns about Huang's role at the company, which he co-founded and helped build into the world's second-most valuable company, with a $4.5 trillion valuation. Nvidia is barred from selling its high-end chips, specifically designed to power artificial intelligence models, to China due to competitive concerns.
Nvidia shares sank 4.3%, or $7.97, to $178.67, shrinking the chipmaker's market valuation by about $193 billion.

The allegations center around reports that Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency. On Sunday, Nvidia's board said it is starting an "independent investigation" into the allegations, sparking questions about the CEO's future with the company.

"This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons," Dan Ives, a tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said in a research note. "The key question investors will be asking is: Will Jensen remain CEO of Nvidia?"

Ives added, "There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation, and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally."

In a statement to CBS News, an Nvidia spokesperson said that "Jensen is committed to continuing to lead Nvidia as CEO without interruption." The company didn't respond to a question about whether Huang had violated any of its corporate policies.

The company's board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised. John Rizzo, a spokesperson for Nvidia, told CBS News on Sunday, "We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the U.S. government would have notified us."

The Chinese government dismissed allegations that it targeted Nvidia's chief executive, who co-founded the company in 1993, as part of an espionage operation. "The so-called Chinese spy narrative is entirely baseless and constitutes slander and smear," Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, said in a statement.
Who is Alice Huang?
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a former executive at a Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed International, whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Many offices in Singapore were closed on Monday for a holiday. Megaspeed and the Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Succession challenges

Replacing Jensen Huang, 63, would prove challenging because he is viewed as integral to the company's success, tech analysts said on Monday. Huang also serves as the public face of Nvidia, appearing at industry events and media interviews in his trademark black leather jacket.
Huang is the company's fifth-largest shareholder, with about 3.4% of its shares, according to financial data provider FactSet.

"There is no known succession plan, and there is no leader in the company who would be the clear next step if he had to step down. In many ways, Jensen is Nvidia's Steve Jobs," said Daniel Newman, CEO of tech consulting firm Futurum, in an email.
He added, "That does not mean they cannot find a Tim Cook in the future, but it would be a massive changing of the guard, and the company has not been set up for that."
Another blow for the AI trade

The scandal puts more pressure on Nvidia shares, which have already been bruised by mounting investor concerns about the valuations of companies driving AI growth. Prior to Monday's early decline, Nvidia's shares had tumbled almost 20% over the last month amid a broader sell-off in AI stocks.

The board investigation into Huang could loom over Nvidia and raise the risk that U.S. regulators could impose additional restrictions on the company's chip exports, according to Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge.

"The key questions are whether he was aware of any espionage activities and whether any confidential or strategically sensitive information was compromised," said George Chen, a partner and chair of digital practice at The Asia Group, a Washington-based consultancy.

In recent years, Jensen Huang has lobbied federal authorities to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China, winning approval from President Trump to sell its H200 chips this year. Those chips are not Nvidia's most advanced models, but they are still considered important products for Nvidia.
Previously, Huang also lobbied Mr. Trump to be allowed to sell Nvidia's less-advanced H20 chips, which were designed to comply with U.S. export restrictions on China.

"The real potential fallout from the Jensen Huang scandal will be the U.S. government imposing dramatically more draconian restrictions on sales of sophisticated chips to China (the issue isn't the H200 but instead the fact that a large amount of higher-end Nvidia products are still making it into the hands of Chinese buyers)," Crisafulli said in a research note.

title: Google faces mounting backlash for controversial AI school policy
summary: Google puts schools in an "impossible position" by blocking students from using its search platform unless AI tools are also enabled, Senator said.
story: Google faces mounting public pressure to change a new policy that would limit U.S. students' access to the internet giant's widely used search platform unless schools also offer its artificial intelligence-based education tools.

In a letter to Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai on Monday, Sen. Edward Markey demanded that Google's corporate parent reverse the policy, which blocks search for K-12 student accounts that don't also provide access to apps such as Google Classroom.

Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat, said Google shouldn't use its dominance in the education technology market to effectively force AI on students by restricting their access to critical research tools like Google Search. Roughly 150 million students and teachers use Classroom.

"At a time when schools, parents and policymakers are working hard to implement safeguards on AI chatbots for our children, Google is recklessly forcing AI on schools and treating kids like collateral damage," Markey said in the letter. "Schools deserve the right to block student access to AI chatbots without also forfeiting access to an important educational tool."

Google maintains that its policy change gives schools more control over how they allow AI into schools. An Alphabet spokesperson also told CBS News that Google's AI features are now so tightly integrated into search that it cannot offer the latter without also enabling the AI services.

"We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach," Google vice president and general manager of education Chris Phillips wrote last week in a blog post announcing the policy change.
Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Markey's letter.

Markey said Google's decision to block search access for students who opt out of AI "places schools in an impossible position," forcing them to choose between giving students access to a potentially dangerous technology and depriving them of "a critical educational research tool."
"Although Google has a right to create and offer new educational tools, it should not use its dominant market position to force schools to adopt them," he added.

Markey is asking Alphabet if Google will commit to allowing schools to turn off AI features and chatbots in K-12 student accounts while still allowing students to access Google Search. He also requested that Google disclose any research it has conducted on the impact of its AI tools on students' mental health.
Markey has requested that Google disclose any research or testing it has conducted on the safety of its AI functions and their impact on the mental health of K-12 students.

Google's policy has drawn fire from other critics. In a statement posted on social media, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani accused the tech giant of "trying to use its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools."

title: U.S. gas prices on track to fall below $4 a gallon, experts say
summary: Fuel prices have dropped in recent weeks amid hopes that the midterm elections would increase pressure on the U.S. and Iran to reach a peace deal.
story: Motorists could soon see U.S. gasoline prices fall below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to energy experts.

Patrick De Haan, a petroleum expert at price-tracking firm GasBuddy, told CBS News that he expects the national average for gas, which the price-tracking firm put at $4.06 a gallon on Thursday, to dip below the $4 threshold by next week. He also predicted diesel could fall below $6 a gallon by Thanksgiving.
The average price was still at $4.06 early Friday, according to GasBuddy.

Gas and diesel prices have both dropped in recent weeks. The decline was partially due to market expectations that the U.S. midterm elections would underscore public dissatisfaction with the war in Iran and increase pressure on the Trump administration to strike a deal ending the conflict, De Haan said.
"Oil prices have been falling in the run-up to the election," he said. "My read is because there was optimism that after the midterms these problems would be addressed."
Other factors pushing down gas prices
Other factors are also putting downward pressure on fuel costs. Oil tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has picked up, easing constraints on global oil supply, De Haan said.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, fell below $100 on Thursday for the first time since September, trading at $97.44 by midday. West Texas Intermediate, the U.S. benchmark, was trading at $90.42 a barrel.

The recent drop in gas prices is also partly due to seasonal shifts. Prices tend to dip in the fall when Americans pull back on road trips and summer travel, De Haan noted. Filling stations are already switching to winter-blend gas, which is less costly to produce than summer-blend fuel.

Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser for Gulf Oil, predicts that the average U.S. gas price will sink below $4 within the next 10 days. The profit gas stations earn on each gallon of gas sold — currently around 75 cents per gallon — is also larger than usual.

"Historically, that is too outsized," he said in an email. "A more normal markup would be 40 cents a gallon, and that means that even if futures prices and physical markets hang around present levels, we should see lower pump prices for the foreseeable future."

The Trump administration has used various tools to ease gas prices. That includes expanding access to tax-free red-dyed diesel, opening the door to Russian diesel imports, and waiving what's known as the Jones Act, a federal statute that requires goods shipped between U.S. ports to be moved on ships that are U.S.-built, U.S.-flagged and U.S.-crewed.
