title: Matthew Farwell convicted of killing Sandra Birchmore, unborn child
summary: A jury has found former Stoughton, Massachusetts, police officer Matthew Farwell guilty of killing Sandra Birchmore and her unborn child.
story: A jury has found former Stoughton, Massachusetts, police officer Matthew Farwell guilty of killing Sandra Birchmore and her unborn child. The verdict was read in federal court in South Boston Tuesday afternoon.
Farwell was charged with killing a witness or victim and causing the death of an unborn child. He pleaded not guilty. The jury had previously said in a note on Monday that it was "in a deadlock."
There were gasps from Birchmore's family as the verdict was read aloud in court.

Farwell faces a mandatory sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole. Sentencing is scheduled for Feb. 3, 2027. The Department of Justice could have pursued the death penalty against Farwell, but decided last year it would not.

Jurors heard from 50 witnesses over four weeks of testimony. To convict Farwell on the charge of killing a witness or victim, jurors had to find find that he not only killed Birchmore, but that he did so to prevent her from reporting his crimes to federal authorities.

"Today, justice was served for Ms. Sandra Birchmore and her unborn son, both of whom died at the hands of Matthew Farwell. The evidence presented at trial was both shocking and clear," U.S. Attorney for Massachusetts Leah Foley said during a news conference, calling Farwell's actions "absolutely diabolical behavior."

Farwell and Birchmore met when she was a 13-year-old cadet in the Stoughton Police Department's youth explorers program. Prosecutors say Farwell began a sexual relationship with her when she was just 15.
"We finally got justice," family says

The 23-year-old Birchmore was found dead in her Canton apartment with a strap hanging around her neck in February 2021. Her death was initially ruled a suicide. But more than three years later, Farwell was arrested and the medical examiner changed Birchmore's manner of death to "undetermined."

Prosecutors made the case that Farwell strangled Birchmore, who was pregnant with what she believed was his child, and then staged her death to look like a suicide in order to cover up their years-long affair. The defense said Birchmore had a history of mental health problems and committed suicide because Farwell told her he was not the father and the relationship was over.
Barbara Wright, Birchmore's cousin, said she was feeling a mixture of sadness, happiness and relief.

"It's been almost six years since we lost Sandra and let's not forget her baby boy," she said outside court. "We finally got justice. We've been fighting long and hard for her. And she deserves it. She's waited a long time."
Norfolk DA responds to verdict
Norfolk District Attorney Michael Morrissey said in a statement that he hopes the verdict brings closure to Birchmore's family and friends.
Morrissey's office has faced criticism from Birchmore's loved ones for choosing not to prosecute Farwell on state charges.

"The Norfolk District Attorney's Office (NDAO) recognizes the criticism it has received for its handling of this case. However, its ability to prosecute was constrained by the finding of the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner (OCME) that the manner of death was suicide," the DA said. "The NDAO referred the case to the Attorney General's Office for further review, and at all times worked collaboratively with the federal prosecution, including funding the development of additional evidence. Beginning as early as October of 2022, in an effort to be transparent, the NDAO made public its case file and investigative materials in its possession. We respect the jury's verdict and will have no further comments."
Stoughton Police Department reaction
James O'Connor, acting police chief of the Stoughton Police Department, released a statement following the verdict.

"I am grateful for this verdict. It is the outcome Sandra, her unborn child, and her family have deserved for more than five years. The jury heard the evidence and reached a decision, and I fully support it," O'Connor said. "What happened to Sandra is a profound betrayal of the trust every police officer is sworn to uphold. Matthew Farwell used his position to harm someone the community had put in the care of this department. He no longer wears this badge, and he does not represent the men and women of the Stoughton Police Department, who serve this town with honor every day."

Chief Donna McNamara is currently on paid leave from the Stoughton Police Department as part of an investigation not related to the Farwell case. McNamara said in a statement that the verdict is not about Farwell, but instead honoring Birchmore.

"That's what today is about. Today is not just about a verdict. Today is about Sandra. Today a federal jury has confirmed what became apparent to me some time ago, that Sandra was murdered and that her murderer was a police officer who took advantage of her trust and faith in the badge and uniform," McNamara said. "There are those who wanted to forget Sandra Birchmore. But enough people would not remain silent. Enough people spoke up. Enough people asked questions. And rest assured that there are still more questions unanswered than are answered, even after today."

title: Kennedy family members join lawsuit to block Trump's arch
summary: Several members of the Kennedy family have joined the legal battle to prevent President Trump from building a large triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.
story: Several members of the Kennedy family have joined the legal battle to prevent President Trump from building a large triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery.

In court filings Tuesday, nine members of the famous family — including several children and grandchildren of Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy and Sen. Ted Kennedy — argued the 250-foot-tall arch would block the sightlines of the Kennedy family's gravesites and the "Eternal Flame" commemorating President John F. Kennedy. The three brothers — Robert F. Kennedy, Ted Kennedy and John F. Kennedy — are buried at Arlington.
The family members wrote that the project will "permanently cast a shadow over the graves of servicemen and women who made the ultimate sacrifice for this country, including the Kennedy Gravesites."

The family members are seeking to intervene as plaintiffs in a lawsuit opposing the arch from the city of Washington, D.C., and the Commonwealth of Virginia. Several Vietnam War veterans are also suing the Trump administration over the arch.

"Americans from every corner of the country visit Arlington to honor those who served and sacrificed for our nation," Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy said in a statement on the lawsuit. "A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come."
The Justice Department had no comment on the filing when reached by CBS News.

The proposed arch — slated for a traffic circle across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial in D.C. — is part of a slew of construction projects in and around the nation's capital that Mr. Trump has personally pushed for. His administration says the arch would commemorate 250 years of American independence. It sought to break ground as early as this month.

But the project has drawn stiff pushback from local officials, congressional Democrats and some veterans and others with an interest in Arlington National Cemetery. Opponents argue the Trump administration did not follow the proper legal processes to build the arch, and warn it would block the sightlines between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial.

The National Capital Planning Commission, which is stacked with Trump allies, voted to approve plans for the arch last week. But U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan quickly blocked the government from starting any "construction-related activity" for 14 days, finding the plan is likely illegal. The plaintiffs have asked the court for a longer-term injunction.
The government has argued the proposed arch does not violate the law, and says the plaintiffs don't have standing to sue over the project.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement last week: "We are confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds and look forward to seeing the completion of this magnificent Arch — a tribute to 250 years of American greatness."

It isn't the first time that members of the Kennedy family have criticized Mr. Trump's architectural overhaul of the D.C. area. Several family members have also spoken out against Mr. Trump's attempts to add his name to the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, including the niece and grandnephew of the center's namesake, Kerry Kennedy and Joe Kennedy III, both of whom are seeking to join the triumphal arch lawsuit as plaintiffs.

Kerry Kennedy's brother, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., told CBS News earlier this year he was not involved in the proposed name change for the performing arts center and did not recommend against the move.
"Of course, I understand it, but I have bigger fish to fry," he said when asked about the pushback from some of his relatives.

title: House blocks Massie's effort to impeach Hegseth
summary: GOP Rep. Thomas Massie said Monday he would not bring up another resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
story: Washington — The House on Tuesday blocked an effort led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, largely over the war with Iran.

The House voted 211 to 204 to refer the resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively killing it. Massie was the lone Republican to vote with all Democrats against it. Though Republicans have been frustrated with Hegseth's handling of the war that has stretched into its ninth month, many did not think his conduct rose to the level of impeachment.

"I wasn't surprised, but I was disappointed," Massie said after the vote. "My diagnosis of Congress is these people know what to do. They just can't bring themselves to do it, even when it would benefit them politically."

Massie, a Kentucky Republican, said Monday he would not bring up another resolution to impeach Hegseth. He is retiring in early January after losing his primary earlier this year. Democrats could still force the issue, especially when they retake control of both chambers in January.
"This is not the end of it. It's just the beginning," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a New York Democrat, said following the vote.
Massie said Tuesday he planned to force a vote on a war powers resolution.
"We're going to see all these Republicans who said, 'Oh, we lost this election because of the war,' will they still vote for it?" Massie said.

The impeachment resolution accused Hegseth of abusing his office by launching the Iran war without congressional approval, ignoring laws designed to minimize civilian casualties, directing extrajudicial killings for the Pentagon's boat strikes in the Caribbean, directing the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and retaliating against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, among other allegations.
In a news conference Tuesday morning, Hegseth denounced the impeachment effort, calling it a "farce" and "political spectacle."
"None of these are high crimes or misdemeanors," Hegseth argued. "They're partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military."
President Trump mocked the impeachment effort, saying it "miserably FAILED!"
Seven Republicans and 11 Democrats missed the vote.

Only two Cabinet secretaries in U.S. history have been impeached. Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over a corruption scandal in 1876, and Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached over his handling of the southern border in 2024. Belknap was acquitted by the Senate, while Mayorkas had his charges dismissed.

title: First snow of the season is coming to Northeast
summary: Parts of the Northeast could see their first snowfall of the season later this week, as a cold snap spreads over the eastern half of the U.S.
story: The first snowfall of the season is expected in parts of the Northeast later this week, although there is uncertainty over how much snow will fall and which parts of the region will be hit hardest.
Temperatures are also forecast to drop well below average for this time of year in that region and other parts of the eastern U.S., impacting a large swath of the country.
Cold snap to spread over eastern U.S. this week

A large dip in the jet stream will cause cold air to spread across the eastern half of the U.S. starting Wednesday through the end of the week, reaching from the Canadian border to the Gulf Coast. Temperatures are expected to drop between 20 and 25 degrees below average for this time of year.

Overnight feels-like temperatures are forecast to be near or below freezing in major cities, including Chicago and Atlanta. Daytime highs will only reach the mid-30s and 40s from Thursday through the upcoming weekend.
Snowfall potential
A separate storm system developing over the Midwest on Wednesday will strengthen and head to the Northeast before the end of the week, potentially helping usher in the first snowfall of the season.

Some of the moisture associated with the storm will fall as cold rain, which is expected in cities like Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and Washington, D.C., even though the I-95 corridor will likely see warmer temperatures this weekend.
But places at higher elevations and those in the interior Northeast, like upstate New York, New Hampshire and Vermont, could see their first snowfall.

The storm is expected to move away from land once it reaches the Mid-Atlantic region. A second, smaller storm could potentially form off of that system and impact coastal areas from the Mid-Atlantic up to New England. The path of the second, smaller storm will determine how much snow or rain may fall in those areas, and exactly which locations could be affected.

title: Why did Hegseth face an impeachment push? Inside the 8 articles
summary: The impeachment resolution focuses on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term.
story: Washington — Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky led a now-blocked push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing the Pentagon chief of a broad range of high crimes and misdemeanors stemming from his conduct in office.

The charges were laid out in a 34-page impeachment resolution spanning eight articles that Massie introduced in the lower chamber on Monday. The House voted late Tuesday to refer the resolution to a committee, effectively killing it, after no Republicans joined Massie and House Democrats.

The impeachment resolution focused on Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term: the war with Iran, boat strikes in the Caribbean, an attack on an Iranian school and the capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Hegseth called the resolution "political spectacle" in a press conference Tuesday morning.
Here's a look at what the impeachment resolution says:
Article I: Starting the Iran war without authorization
The first impeachment article accuses Hegseth of following illegal orders to begin the Iran war.

"Secretary Hegseth directed and caused United States Armed Forces to be introduced into hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran," even though Congress had not declared war or authorized an attack, Article I says.
The resolution says Hegseth acted in violation of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which allows the president to use force without congressional authorization in narrow circumstances.

"Secretary Hegseth nevertheless knowingly executed and implemented the order to commence such hostilities, employing the powers, personnel, weapons, and resources of the Department of Defense to initiate military action against another sovereign nation," the article says.
Article II: Ignoring Congress to continue the war
The second article accuses Hegseth of ignoring a resolution approved by both chambers of Congress that directed the administration to end the Iran war.

The House and Senate both approved a measure in June that ordered the administration to "remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran," the mechanism for Congress to force the executive branch to end fighting under the War Powers Resolution. Massie's impeachment article notes that this was "the first successful passage of such a legislative vehicle by both chambers of Congress" in history.

"In response, and without lawful cause or excuse, Secretary Hegseth continued to direct United States Armed Forces into hostilities with the Islamic Republic of Iran on June 26, 2026, and continues to do so," the impeachment article says.
At the time, the administration argued that "hostilities" with Iran had already ended, rendering the war powers measure inapplicable.
Article III: Ignoring the War Powers Resolution's deadline
The War Powers Resolution says the executive branch must end the use of force within 60 days if Congress has not approved the operation, with another 30-day window to safely remove troops.

Mr. Trump notified Congress of the hostilities on March 2, so the 60-day window closed on May 1. In a letter that day, the administration told Congress that "hostilities" had "terminated." Hegseth told senators: "We are in a ceasefire right now, which in our understanding means the 60-day clock pauses or stops in a ceasefire."

But the impeachment resolution says Hegseth kept directing hostilities after that deadline and beyond June 1, "the date on which even the maximum possible additional 30-day withdrawal period would have expired."

The article also says Hegseth directed U.S. forces to keep fighting "in a manner calculated not to terminate the unauthorized use of such forces and bring about their prompt removal, but rather to continue prosecuting the war to pursue additional military objectives not authorized by Congress."
Article IV: Ignoring laws meant to minimize civilian casualties

The fourth article accuses Hegseth of dismantling systems and processes at the Pentagon that Congress established to minimize civilian casualties, saying that his actions led to the deadly strike on an Iranian school in the first wave of attacks against the country in February. The Tomahawk missile strike killed roughly 170 civilians, most of them children, Iranian media has reported. The U.S. has not directly accepted responsibility for the attack.

The resolution says Hegseth oversaw "the systemic deterioration and removal of Department of Defense infrastructure that Congress had mandated by law to limit collateral damage to civilians and non-military objects during military operations." The article cites Hegseth's cuts to staff dedicated to mitigating civilian casualties, his firing of the military's top lawyers and his public comments about the "stupid rules of engagement."
Hegseth's actions laid the groundwork for the strike on the school, Massie alleges.

"By directing the Department of Defense in a manner that foreseeably dismantled the safeguards necessary to distinguish civilian objects from military objectives, Secretary Hegseth thereby effected the murder of civilians," the article says.

"The strike on the elementary school was not an isolated targeting failure divorced from the conduct of the Secretary of Defense, nor can Secretary Hegseth's conduct be dismissed as a single targeting error or isolated failure in the fog of war," the resolution says.
Article V: Carrying out "extrajudicial killings" through boat strikes

The fifth article centers on the Pentagon's campaign against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific Ocean. The resolution says the strikes have killed at least 243 people since September 2025.
Massie accuses Hegseth of using the military to target suspects of crimes.

"By subjecting persons merely suspected of criminal conduct to lethal military force without judicial process, without congressional authorization, and without establishing a lawful basis for treating such persons or vessels as military targets, Secretary Hegseth arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury, and executioner and asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die," the article says.
The article also cites the first strike of the campaign, on Sept. 2, 2025, when the military hit the same boat a second time.

"The strike destroyed and capsized the vessel. Approximately 45 minutes later, while two survivors clung to the wreckage, a secondary strike was ordered, killing both survivors," the resolution says. "In doing so, Secretary Hegseth has endangered members of our Armed Forces in future military engagements by encouraging adversaries to subject American service members to the same treatment."
Article VI: Retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly
The sixth article accuses Hegseth of "retaliating against a Member of Congress for constitutionally protected speech," specifically Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona.

In November 2025, Kelly, a retired Navy captain, appeared in a video with other lawmakers to deliver a message to members of the military and intelligence community: "Our laws are clear. You can refuse illegal orders."
Hegseth issued a letter of censure and threatened to reduce Kelly's rank, which would have cut his retirement benefits. A federal judge blocked the move.

Massie's resolution says Hegseth "weaponized the Department of Defense to chill a core function of the Legislative Branch" and "place the First Amendment rights of millions of United States veterans at risk of irreparable harm."
Article VII: The capture of Venezuela's Maduro

Article VII deals with the military operation to capture Maduro and his wife in Caracas in January 2026. It calls the raid "an act of war against a sovereign country executed under the guise of narcotics law enforcement, though in actuality intended to assert U.S. control over Venezuela's oil reserves."

The resolution says the operation involved more than 200 special operations personnel and more than 150 aircraft and drones, and killed at least 83 people. It argues Hegseth acted without a declaration of war or authorization from Congress, in violation of the War Powers Resolution.
The article cites Mr. Trump's remarks after the raid that "we're going to run the country" and that U.S. oil companies would "go in… and start making money."
Hegseth "gambled the lives of Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps personnel in order to facilitate the illegal taking of national oil," the article says.
Article VIII: Strikes on Yemen
The eighth and final article focuses on more than 1,100 U.S. strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen between March and May 2025.
The article again accuses Hegseth of using military force without congressional authorization and says the strikes led to civilian casualties.
"In less than eight weeks, there were nearly as many civilian deaths in Yemen as United States military actions had caused in that country during the preceding twenty-three years," the article says.

The article cites leaked messages from Hegseth and other top officials in a group chat on Signal that The Atlantic published last year. It argues that the conversation shows the administration knew the Houthis did not pose an imminent threat that would have required an immediate U.S. response.

title: Sanders won't back Schumer as Democratic leader
summary: Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he won't support Sen. Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader in the new Congress, becoming the most prominent progressive to oppose his candidacy to date.
story: Washington — Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders said Tuesday he won't support New York Sen. Chuck Schumer as Democratic leader when the party takes control of the Senate, becoming the most prominent progressive to oppose his candidacy to date.

Sanders made the announcement at a press conference at the Capitol, saying last week's midterm elections were "about change." Democrats will control at least 54 seats when the 120th Congress convenes in January.

"It was an election across the country, in red states and blue states, where people were looking around them and saying, 'What is going on in America, when I am struggling to put food on the table, pay for healthcare, pay for housing, and I'm worried not only that my life economically is going nowhere, everything being equal, my kid in the richest country in the history of the world is going to have the lowest standard of living than I do?' And while all of this is going on, the billionaire class has never ever had it so good," Sanders said.

He added: "I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer. But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader."
Sanders, an independent who caucuses with the Democrats, called for "a vigorous debate about the direction of the Democratic Party."
"We need to have that out in the open to show the American people that a new day has come and that their votes meant a new direction in Washington," he said.

Sanders appeared alongside Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin, who said that "whoever wants to run this caucus should come forward with a plan on how they're going to govern differently, what they're going to do in the first 100 days to put money in people's pockets, and then in particular how they're going to communicate differently."
Slotkin said she is "not actively seeking this job" but is "seeking change."
"Whoever wants my vote is going to have to show me a concrete plan that's definitively different," Slotkin said. "I'm a no until and unless I see that from anyone."

No contender has emerged to challenge Schumer's role atop the Senate Democratic caucus, but Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland has come the closest to throwing his hat in the ring. After initially saying he would not pursue the position, Van Hollen has said this week that he's exploring a potential run.
"What I've said from the very beginning is, we shouldn't have a coronation," he said on Monday. "I'm in listening mode and haven't shut the door."
At an event on Tuesday, Van Hollen said he is "in the process right now of calling my colleagues."
"I'm actively calling my colleagues because at the end of the day, this is a vote in the Democratic caucus," he said.
Democrats are expected to hold their leadership elections in early December.

title: 24% of Americans with a credit record are behind on their debts
summary: More U.S. households are falling into debt as they grapple with medical bills, student loans and other expenses, data show.
story: More Americans are tumbling seriously into debt as prices and the overall cost of living continue to rise.

Roughly 24% of people with a credit record are behind on medical bills, student debt, or auto or retail loans, according to a new analysis from the Urban Institute, a nonpartisan think tank. The median balance owed: $2,913. In communities of color, 30% of people are behind on payments, with a median debt in collection of $3,009.

"The increasing cost of living makes it harder for people to make payments on basic needs," Breno Braga, senior fellow in the family and financial well-being division at the Urban Institute, told CBS News.

Rising interest rates this year as the Federal Reserve tries to tame inflation are also making it harder for people to catch up. "It's a reflection of the financial life of Americans these days as we know it," Braga added.
Consumers' credit card balances have surged to a record $1.29 trillion, up nearly 70% from five years ago, according to new figures from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Years of high prices have forced Americans to deplete their savings and finance their daily expenses with debt, according to Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit debt counselor. As a result, many household budgets are at a "breaking point," he said in an email to CBS News.

Consumer prices have risen by an average of 30% since 2019, Rossman noted. Meanwhile, the share of Americans with debt in collection this year is up about one percentage point, from less than 23% in 2025, according to the Urban Institute, which based its findings on an analysis of more than 10 million credit records and U.S. Census data.
Student loans and medical bills

Roughly one in six, or almost 16%, of student loan borrowers are behind on payments, although the figure varies by geography. In Louisiana, for example, the state with the highest share of people with debt in collections, the student loan delinquency rate is roughly 22%.
Braga attributes the disparity to several factors, such as lower incomes and higher poverty rates in some parts of the country.

"People there tend to have lower credit scores, so when they get a credit card or take out an auto loan, they tend to pay higher interest rates," he said. "That makes it harder to make those payments, especially if you are low income. It makes you more likely to fall behind."
Many people also are shouldering heavy medical bills despite having health insurance, reflecting insufficient coverage and the high cost of care across the U.S.

According to the Urban Institute, 3% of Americans have medical debt in collections, with a median balance of $1,492 — a figure that reflects only unpaid hospital or other medical bills, while excluding credit card debt stemming from health care costs.

"People without health insurance are more likely to have medical debt, but having coverage does not protect you at all from having medical debt, especially not now with the high deductible plans we are seeing," Braga said.
Fifteen states have passed legislation barring health care providers from reporting medical debt to credit rating agencies, which can lessen the damage to consumers' credit records.
"It's good for patients that it's not reported to the agencies, but that doesn't mean it disappears. It just isn't reported anymore," he noted.

title: Massie introduces Hegseth impeachment articles, teeing up vote
summary: Rep. Thomas Massie on Monday introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war against Iran without congressional authorization.
story: Washington — Rep. Thomas Massie on Monday introduced articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing him of waging war against Iran without congressional authorization and abusing the powers of his office.

The impeachment effort could attract more bipartisan support, since members of both parties are frustrated with Hegseth's handling of the war with Iran and Republicans are reeling from their defeats in the midterm elections. Lawmakers returned to Capitol Hill on Monday to reconvene for the final weeks of the GOP-controlled Congress, and Massie's move will force leaders to bring the impeachment resolution up for a vote within two legislative days.

Even before the midterm elections highlighted voters' concerns about the war in Iran and its impact on the cost of living, the push to impeach Hegseth was underway in Congress. Massie, a Kentucky Republican who has broken with the administration on a number of fronts over the past year, originally introduced impeachment articles against the defense secretary in September. House GOP leaders recessed the chamber early, pushing off a vote on the issue until November.
Massie introduced updated impeachment articles on the House floor on Monday, restarting a two-day clock for GOP leaders to schedule a vote.

The Kentucky Republican accused Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanours in a 34-page impeachment resolution with eight articles. Three charges accuse him of abusing the powers of the Department of Defense by waging war against Iran without congressional authorization.

Massie also alleged that in the conflict, Hegseth ignored laws that minimize civilian casualties, citing the strike on an Iranian school earlier this year. Another impeachment article points to the Pentagon's boat strikes in the Caribbean, while one cites the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. Another centers on free speech and the Pentagon's scrutiny of Sen. Mark Kelly after he was among a group of lawmakers who released a video calling on service members to "refuse illegal orders."

Massie argued that Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law."
"Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office, and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust, or profit under the United States," Massie wrote.

Massie urged the GOP-controlled Senate to take up the resolution if it passes the House, noting that the articles will survive into the next Congress, when the upper chamber has a Democratic majority.

"If the Senate doesn't deal with this before the end of this Senate, they're turning it over to a Democrat Senate who can then have the trials and deal with it," Massie said at a news conference Monday afternoon.
Massie argued he was being "polite" with the impeachment effort and that "when the Democrats get in charge, they are going to be very vicious."

"What is an impeachment? An impeachment is just firing somebody, really. You don't go to prison. You don't go to jail. You don't pay a fine," he said. "But the Democrats are going to have hearings. They won't have just eight articles of impeachment. … The Democrats are going to bring people in here who have served under him and with him, give them protection."
Hegseth has criticized the effort by Massie, who's leaving Congress after losing his primary earlier this year.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said in a video posted on X last week. "You see, their policies don't work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."
Hegseth told reporters Monday, "we're not worried about that." He said he planned to hold a news conference on the impeachment effort Tuesday morning.

Whether other Republicans support the effort remains to be seen. But some GOP members appeared more open to the prospect, and more eager to criticize the defense secretary, after the brutal losses for their party in the midterms.
Rep. James Comer, a Kentucky Republican who leads the House Oversight Committee, said on News Nation that "there's a lot of questions about Hegseth."

"We have no idea what the strategy is moving forward in Iran. No one's happy about Iran," Comer said. "I think the Republican voters are more upset about what's going on in Iran than the Democrat voters."

GOP Rep. French Hill of Arkansas indicated that he's still considering whether to support the effort, saying on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sunday that he wants to hear the debate on the issue "to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War."
"If you don't think he's done a good job conducting his job, that doesn't mean per se that he's committed an impeachable offense," Hill said.
Retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of the administration on some issues, said he's "wrestling" with whether to support the impeachment resolution.
He said Hegseth's handling of a number of topics "bothers me" and "I feel like he deserves a little bit of his own treatment, but that's not the right way to handle impeachment."
"I don't think he's been a good secretary, but do you impeach a guy for that? It has to be a high crime or misdemeanor," Bacon told reporters Monday at the Capitol.
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, said Monday that impeaching Hegseth amid hostilities abroad "would be a terrible, terrible look."

Democrats are widely expected to support the impeachment effort. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week" on Sunday that he's a "hard yes" on the impeachment effort. But with a narrow GOP majority, Republican votes will be needed.

Massie said in a post on X on Monday that he's seen some of his colleagues say "Hegseth has been effective and they agree with the war, so they'll vote not to impeach." But he said "that's not the question."
"The question is whether he committed impeachable acts," Massie said. "And the answer is yes, eight times."

Hegseth would be the third Cabinet secretary in history to be impeached. Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached in 1876 over corruption allegations. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached by the GOP-controlled House in 2024 over the Biden administration's handling of the southern border. Belknap was acquitted by the Senate. Mayorkas had his charges dismissed.

title: NASA is recruiting new astronauts. Here are the qualifications.
summary: The space agency is recruiting its next class of astronauts as the U.S. plans a new mission to the moon. Here's the kind of person NASA is looking for.
story: NASA is recruiting its next class of astronauts, inviting U.S. citizens to apply before midnight ET on Dec. 3 for the chance to "live and work" on the moon.

The space agency's application portal states there are "few vacancies" for the role, which pays $164,395 annually and requires recruits to relocate to Houston, where they'll work at the Johnson Space Center.

While the job is open to all citizens, applicants must meet certain educational criteria and possess specialized experience. In other words, not just any Tom, Dick or Harriet will qualify for the job.

The next group of astronauts is being selected as the U.S. plans to build a moon base and send crewed missions to the lunar surface. NASA's Artemis II mission recently sent a crew of four astronauts around the moon in April, setting a record for the farthest distance humans have ever traveled from our planet.

"The people we select could walk on the moon, live and work at the moon base, and help pioneer the systems and operations that will ultimately carry crews to Mars," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said in a statement. "Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork and courage."
Here are the qualifications NASA is looking for in an astronaut.
Educational background
NASA's job application portal states that applicants must fit into one of the following four educational profiles:

A master's degree in a qualifying field of engineering, biological science, physical science, computer science or mathematics.Two academic years of qualifying doctoral coursework in one of those fields. A qualifying medical degree, such as an MD, physician assistant or nurse practitioner. Completion of a recognized test pilot school by July 2027.
A master's degree in a qualifying field of engineering, biological science, physical science, computer science or mathematics.
Two academic years of qualifying doctoral coursework in one of those fields.
A qualifying medical degree, such as an MD, physician assistant or nurse practitioner.
Completion of a recognized test pilot school by July 2027.
Specialized experience

Applicants must also select a discipline they best qualify for based on their work experience, with NASA requiring three years of professional experience after completing their degree program or pilot training.

Pilots: Must meet one of three thresholds: 750 hours as lead pilot of a high-performance jet; 1,500 hours in other fixed-wing aircraft, with 750 in command; or 1,000 hours in rotary-wing aircraft, with 300 in command. Initial flight training and drone hours are excluded.Flight test: Requires test pilot school completion or enrollment, with completion by July 2027, as well as three years of related flight test experience.Medical: At least three years of professional experience after earning a medical degree. NASA said that residencies count toward the experience.Biological and medical science: At least three years of related experience.Physical science: Three years of related work experience.Engineering: Three years of related work experience.Operations: Three years of related work experience in "high-consequence environments that require real-time decision-making and intensive teamwork, where errors carry irreversible and physical risk to personnel, missions or vehicles," NASA said.

Pilots: Must meet one of three thresholds: 750 hours as lead pilot of a high-performance jet; 1,500 hours in other fixed-wing aircraft, with 750 in command; or 1,000 hours in rotary-wing aircraft, with 300 in command. Initial flight training and drone hours are excluded.
Flight test: Requires test pilot school completion or enrollment, with completion by July 2027, as well as three years of related flight test experience.
Medical: At least three years of professional experience after earning a medical degree. NASA said that residencies count toward the experience.
Biological and medical science: At least three years of related experience.
Physical science: Three years of related work experience.
Engineering: Three years of related work experience.

Operations: Three years of related work experience in "high-consequence environments that require real-time decision-making and intensive teamwork, where errors carry irreversible and physical risk to personnel, missions or vehicles," NASA said.
Other requirements
Applicants must also pass a series of clearances, including medical and psychiatric exams; vision that can be corrected to 20/20 in each eye; and a background check and drug screening.

Aspiring astronauts must be able "to perform moderate to arduous physical activities, including heavy lifting, crouching, crawling and exposure to inclement weather" and "be willing to work in dangerous, life-threatening situations and live/work in remote, isolated, small or confined spaces for prolonged periods." Applicants also have to pass a swimming test.
On top of that, applicants must "be willing to deploy to space for 12 months or longer, accepting extreme isolation, austere living conditions and separation from loved ones."

title: Thomas Markle Sr., Meghan's father, arrested in Florida
summary: It was reported in October that Meghan's estranged father, Thomas Markle, was under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse materials.
story: Thomas Markle Sr., the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was arrested Friday in Florida in connection with allegations he possessed child sex abuse material in storage units in California, the Justice Department announced.
The announcement came after three sources familiar with the matter confirmed the arrest to CBS News.

The Justice Department said Markle was arrested for allegedly keeping child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades.

"These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law," Bill Essayli, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said in a statement.

Markle, who made his first court appearance in federal court in Tampa on Friday, entered the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing black pants and a black T-shirt with an illustration of a cat drinking a tropical drink.

Markle was advised that this hearing was related to the items found in two storage units in California. Prosecutors said they have not made a determination on whether he stays in Florida or is transferred to California, where the charges originated.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Thomas Wilson ordered Markle released on personal recognizance and ordered him to submit to home detention and electronic monitoring. Markle is also not permitted to travel outside the Middle District of Florida and the Central District of California.
No plea was taken. Markle's arraignment date in the Central District of California is not yet scheduled, but likely won't happen for at least several weeks.
The Daily Mail, a British tabloid newspaper, first reported Markle's arrest.
Allegations in Philippines lead to U.S. and Mexican investigations

Last month, it was reported that Markle was under investigation by authorities in the Philippines for alleged possession of child sexual abuse material. Markle has denied the claims against him, calling them "sick lies."
"I have never downloaded anything like that in my life," he was quoted as telling the Daily Mail.

A spokesperson for the Philippine National Police told CBS News in a statement that they launched an investigation after Markle's personal items were turned over to law enforcement by his son, Thomas Markle Jr.
Markle Jr. told the Sun tabloid last month that he reported the images to police in the Philippines and contacted the FBI.
"I have supported, cared for him and helped him for years — but that stops now," Markle Jr. told The Sun. "I won't speak to my father ever again unless I'm called to give evidence against him."
The Daily Mail reported last week that it alerted the FBI of a cache of child porn found inside a storage unit Markle Sr. had rented near his former home in Rosarito, Mexico.
In a statement on Friday, the Baja California State Attorney General's Office in Mexico confirmed to CBS News that a search was conducted on Oct. 29 after a report via the 911 emergency line.

"During the operation, three old magazines and VHS tapes containing child pornography were discovered," the office said in its statement. "The evidence and the associated case files were referred to the Attorney General's Office (FGR), which will handle the follow-up to the case."
DOJ's claims against Markle Sr.

According to an affidavit in the complaint filed in federal court, the investigation in the Philippines led law enforcement to investigate two storage units registered to Markle Sr. in the Los Angeles area that he had rented since 2008, with the most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay.

Inside the units, agents with the FBI seized 78 items, including slides, film negatives and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse materials. In one of the units, agents found at least 18 images that appear to constitute child pornography.
Two of the images found allegedly show an adult man — whom a witness identified as Markle Sr. — with a nude prepubescent girl, the affidavit said.

A third image allegedly shows a nude prepubescent girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines. Other photos allegedly show Markle Sr. with children in various stages of undress, the affidavit said.

"Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement, adding: "This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide."
If convicted, Markle Sr. would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.
Meghan distanced herself because of allegations years ago

After the reports of the investigation were made public, Meghan, who recently moved back to Britain with her husband Prince Harry and their children, said in a statement sent to CBS News that she had been aware of the allegations against him since 2018 and that the allegations were shared with U.K. authorities at the time.
She said it was based on that information that she and Harry decided to cut her father off from contact with their children.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them," she said.

Meghan also confronted her father last year about the child sexual abuse allegations leveled against him, according to CBS News partner BBC News. Video that the British tabloid the Daily Mail says it obtained exclusively shows Markle accepting a letter sent by his daughter in his hospital room in the U.S. in December 2025.
According to the BBC, in that letter, Meghan wrote that she and authorities "knew he had abused young girls," adding that he would never meet her and Harry's children Archie and Lilibet.
Meghan will not be commenting on the arrest at this time, sources say.

title: Megaspeed's vacant offices raise questions about ties to Nvidia, China
summary: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's powerful AI computer chips, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.
story: The unusual global footprint of Megaspeed International, the Singapore-based company at the center of the Nvidia Chinese spy scandal, is fueling questions about whether it's a front for the Chinese government.

One of Megaspeed's leaders is Alice Huang, the woman with whom Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair, and who is suspected by U.S. intelligence of being an asset of China's Ministry of State Security. In the past three years, Megaspeed, formerly a gaming company, has been one of Nvidia's biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5 billion in AI chips and advanced hardware, The New York Times first reported.

And yet Megaspeed's corporate headquarters sat practically empty, according to The Straits Times, an English-language newspaper in Singapore. Questions have also been raised about its outposts in Australia and Malaysia.

Published reports in recent days revealed that the company listed a newspaper vendor as the director of its Australian subsidiary, and one of its Malaysia offices consisted of a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur. Yet another Malaysia office was tucked into a shopping mall.

Megaspeed began as an offshoot of a China-based gaming firm and grew into a juggernaut by gaining access to restricted Nvidia AI computer chips. U.S. investigators say that Alice Huang used her contacts in the industry and a series of shell companies to gain access to 240,000 chips banned for export into China. Now it is being probed in both the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
President Trump said this week the FBI is also investigating romantic and business ties between Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang and Alice Huang (who are not related).

Earlier this week, Jensen Huang, who is married, apologized for the affair in a statement to Nvidia's employees. The company launched an independent investigation of the matter, and an Nvidia shareholder filed a class action lawsuit Tuesday alleging that Huang concealed a relationship with Alice Huang and misled shareholders about national security concerns raised by the relationship.
Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," its statement said.

China expert Jacqueline Deal said that Nvidia's advanced AI chips could have ended up with the Chinese military. Deal, who is an adviser to State Armor, a nonprofit that studies global security threats, told CBS News, "If allegations are true, who will be fired? Nvidia has a compliance team that may have failed utterly."

She also questioned the effectiveness of the U.S. Commerce Department, which has jurisdiction over export controls that may have been bypassed, potentially giving the Chinese military access to the world's most advanced chips.
Here's what we now know about Megaspeed:

It is a major Nvidia customer. Megaspeed and its Malaysian affiliate, Speedmatrix, purchased $4.8 billion of Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence equipment and processors over the last three years.
In 2025, Megaspeed International faced an investigation by Singapore police for alleged breaches of local laws, but no details have emerged about the probe, according to The Straits Times.
The company grew rapidly.

"Megaspeed International is a premier business partner of NVIDIA, strategically positioned in the Asia Pacific region," according to its LinkedIn profile, which claims it has between 201 and 500 employees. Three years ago it listed between two and 10 employees, according to the South China Morning Post.

Megaspeed International did not reply to a request for comment. It posted an "official statement" on its website addressing what it called "misleading information" and "incorrect insinuations" accusing it of involvement in illegal chip transfers.

"We want to be absolutely clear over the past six months our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the US Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia and NVIDIA," said the message, which also appeared on the company's LinkedIn page.
"These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities," the company said.

Megaspeed was originally incorporated in 2015 under the name 7Road International, a subsidiary of a Chinese developer of popular video games and mobile apps based in Shenzhen, China, according to corporate filings.
Huang Le Limited, a shell company in the British Virgin Islands, acquired 7Road International in March 2023. Huang Le is the Chinese name of Alice Huang.
That same month, 7Road International was renamed Megaspeed International, and Huang became its managing director. The company also launched a subsidiary called Speedmatrix.

By the end of October 2023, Huang and another Megaspeed director, Cang Yang, resigned from the company after it was bought up by a firm called Swiftdata, whose director is based in China, documents show.

But there's some indication Huang may still be affiliated with the company. Culper Research, an activist short-selling firm, published a 40-page report on Nvidia in May that cited Megaspeed employees who said Huang was still running the company.

The report also raised some concern about Jensen Huang's relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang, stating, "Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has not only vouched for Megaspeed, but seems to have quite literally walked alongside Megaspeed at every step, while maintaining an uncomfortably close relationship with Megaspeed's Alice Huang, a Chinese national."
Megaspeed lists its headquarters office address on the seventh floor of the Ocean Financial Centre in Singapore, a glass office tower in Singapore's central business district.

When the Straits Times and The New York Times visited the Singapore offices around the same time late last year, they found little or no staff working. The Straits Times said the door was locked, and the Times found just two people in its office on a workday.

Megaspeed has an Australian subsidiary on the 10th floor of a commercial and retail tower in the heart of Sydney's central business district. Forty other businesses are on the same floor, and space in the building can be rented for as little as $17 per day, Australia's ABC News reported. Corporate filings name Shanghai-born Kai Kang, a 29-year-old newspaper vendor, as the director, according to Australian news reports. But Kang's newsstand is in Northern Victoria, over 400 miles from Sydney. Kang's father told Australia's ABC News this week that he had never heard of Megaspeed.

title: Thousands of schools in Europe get hoax bomb threats
summary: Less than a week after more than 20 European flights got fake bomb threats, hundreds of schools in Italy, the U.K. and Ireland were hit by similar hoaxes.
story: Rome and London — Thousands of schools across Europe received apparently hoax bomb threats Wednesday, prompting mass evacuations in Italy. The threatening messages were sent to at least 6,300 schools in Italy alone, as well as hundreds in Ireland and across the U.K.

There have been no reports so far of explosives or suspicious devices found at any of the schools, but investigations were continuing. The threats came less than a week after more than 20 European commercial flights got fake bomb threats, forcing many to divert.

While authorities have not assigned any blame yet for the bomb hoaxes, they are fueling growing concern about the impact of wider hybrid warfare tactics that officials and security experts say Iran and Russia are using to target Europe amid the ongoing wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.

Schools in Rome, Milan, Naples, Palermo, Bologna and several other cities were affected, with lessons suspended and precautionary evacuations ordered. Police, bomb disposal specialists and the Postal Police conducted inspections and were investigating the origin of the messages.

Italian news outlets published an email they said was received by the schools across the country on Wednesday claiming to be from "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan," a Russian misogynistic extremist group that was banned by authorities in Moscow several years ago.
CBS News confirmed last week that a message attributed to the same name and same group was sent to airport authorities in Rome, threatening two of the flights affected by the mass hoaxes on Nov. 5.
"We have come to annihilate you," read the email published by Italian media on Wednesday. "I have just left a powerful explosive device with a remote detonator inside a plastic bag in your building."
The email also contained threats to Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
Meloni said there was no "concrete danger" behind the threats, and called it part of "a strategy aimed at causing alarm and concern."

She called a meeting for later Wednesday with Italian intelligence officials and cybersecurity experts, to discuss the potential connection with recent threats against airlines, and the identification of those responsible.

This is the third wave of bomb threats against Italian schools in a month, following messages received on Oct. 19 and then Nov. 2, when approximately 280 schools got threatening messages, according to Italian media.
Hundreds of schools in Ireland and across the United Kingdom also received threatening emails Wednesday.

Ireland's national police, the Garda, said in a statement that it was "aware of a generic communication that has been sent to a number of educational establishments" but it added that the threat had been deemed "not credible" and that the force was "not advising any educational establishment to evacuate."
Police in Northern Ireland said emails threatening schools there appeared to have originated outside the United Kingdom.

In addition to the threats to airliners last week, the school threats also come amid international investigations into cyberattacks targeting grocery store refrigeration units in both Europe and the U.S., blood banks in France, and wider "hybrid warfare" sabotage and disruption efforts attributed by Western authorities largely to Russia and Iran.

The New York Times and Reuters reported, meanwhile, that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had relocated from his home in Washington, D.C. to a military base following an Iranian threat to his life.
Hybrid warfare targeting "people, businesses, communities"

In October, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, said security threats facing the U.K. and Europe were evolving, with malicious actors attacking not only things owned and controlled by governments, but also "aiming at people, businesses, communities."

"Russia remains aggressor number one," McCallum said, accusing its military and intelligence services of "once again escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," and adding that Moscow was "being careful to stay below the NATO Article 5 threshold" with its actions, which would trigger the alliance's collective defense principle.

Iran, he said, had made a "major shift" in its efforts to attack the U.K., including going after harder targets such as military bases and "using criminal proxies to try to intimidate oppositionists, Iranian media organizations, and Israeli sites" across Europe.
Experts told CBS News earlier this year that Russia and Iran were stepping up efforts to recruit sometimes-unwitting criminals to carry out sabotage attacks, often for small payouts.
McCallum noted "a wave of arson and sabotage incidents targeting Jewish communities in the U.K. and other European nations," but said Iran was also targeting "harder targets, like military sites."

Many of the attacks on soft targets have been claimed by a group called Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), or the Islamic Movement of the Companions of the Right, which U.K. authorities have sanctioned and said is tied directly to the elite Quds Force of Iran's Revolutionary Guards, which Britain considers a terrorist organization.

A CBS News investigation in March found the group appeared to have links to Iran, and a member said it would "keep threatening U.S. and Israeli interests worldwide until we've avenged every child in Gaza, Iran, Lebanon, and the resistance nations … We urge people to stay away from Zionist and American interests and individuals to keep themselves safe."

title: Bessent relocates from home to military base after Iran threats
summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a U.S. military base.
story: Washington — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a military base following a series of Iranian threats against his life.

"The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran's economy," a Treasury Department spokesperson said.

The decision comes as Bessent has spearheaded a U.S. push to cripple Iran's economy, vowing an "economic onslaught" against Tehran through a web of sanctions. The New York Times first reported Bessent's relocation.
A source familiar with the situation pointed to a Wall Street Journal story as the impetus for the move.

"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety," the person told CBS News.
CBS News has also reached out to the White House for comment.
U.S. national intelligence chief Jay Clayton warned last month that Iran has "substantially increased" its efforts to target Americans in the Middle East and beyond.

Those efforts include beefing up the targeting of current and former U.S. officials such as Bessent, the Times reported. Iranian plotting against U.S. officials has reached a "more advanced stage," according to the anonymous sources cited in the Times.

Clayton's warning, contained in an unclassified memo that was sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and obtained by CBS News, came as the State Department adjusted staffing at diplomatic posts across the Middle East, and the U.S. military pared back its footprint in the region, amid concerns about direct threats from Iran and threats from the Iranian-backed Houthi movement in Yemen.
The U.S. military has also removed some aircraft from two British bases in recent weeks following reported threats from Iran.

Diplomatic efforts to end the war are gathering steam, with Rubio saying on Tuesday that he saw no need to resume major combat operations against Iran because economic sanctions and other restrictions were working so effectively.

title: Cartel boss helped Olympian traffic drugs, evade capture, U.S. says
summary: A cartel boss bribed Mexican public officials to help Olympian Ryan Wedding avoid capture while running a multinational drug trafficking organization, the Department of Justice said.
story: A cartel boss shot to death by police in Mexico last week helped Olympian Ryan Wedding traffic drugs and avoid the authorities before his arrest in January 2026, the U.S. Department of Justice said on Tuesday.

In an indictment unsealed Tuesday, federal prosecutors alleged that Edgar Aaron Vazquez Alvarado, or "El General," trafficked cocaine for Wedding's criminal enterprise and provided the organization with "near-daily, rotating code words" that were used for safe passage through law enforcement checkpoints. Vasquez, 42, also allegedly paid Mexican public officials to slow down criminal investigations, tamper with evidence and dismiss criminal charges.
Vasquez also helped Wedding personally avoid U.S. law enforcement for two years, the Justice Department said.

The founder of Mexico City's El Cártel Nuevo Imperio, Vasquez was shot and killed by Mexican security forces attempting to serve an arrest warrant in Naucalpan, Mexico, according to Mexico's Security Minister Omar García Harfuch. Harfuch said Vasquez fired on security forces and was responsible for the 2024 death of Milton Morales, a Mexico City police chief.

The U.S. Justice Department also announced a six-count federal indictment against Roberto Gomez, a U.S. citizen and gang member living in Mexico. Federal prosecutors allege that Gomez has spent the past decade as a drug supplier to international criminal organizations, including Wedding's.

Gomez primarily transported cocaine, methamphetamine and fentanyl from Central America to Mexico with planes and maritime vessels, then used land-based methods to bring those substances into the U.S. and Canada, prosecutors say. His efforts allegedly included attempting to broker the sale of 1,000 pounds of methamphetamine between a supplier and Wedding. The sale would have been worth about $550,000, the Justice Department said.

From 2024 to 2026, Gomez, 51, also allegedly helped Wedding avoid apprehension by U.S. authorities. The department said that Gomez's connections with cartels, including the powerful Sinaloa Cartel, and relationships with "individuals who had access to law-enforcement sensitive information from Mexican and U.S. agencies" allowed him to obtain information about law enforcement operations.
If convicted on all charges, Gomez would face a mandatory minimum sentence of 10 years in federal prison and a maximum sentence of life in prison.

The United States has made dozens of arrests while investigating Wedding's international drug trafficking network. Wedding allegedly ran the network as part of the Sinaloa Cartel and orchestrated several killings.
A Mexican judge was arrested last week and charged with taking bribes to free an accused drug trafficker linked to Wedding.
FBI Director Kash Patel has referred to the former Olympian as "a modern-day 'El Chapo." Wedding was placed on the FBI's Top Ten Most Wanted List before his arrest.

Wedding faces 17 felony charges, including those related to drug trafficking and murder, across two indictments. He has pleaded not guilty. The Justice Department said that he will remain in U.S. custody without bond.

title: U.S. soldier accused of spying linked to Russia arrested in the U.K.
summary: A U.S. official told CBS News the suspect is a senior officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters for NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.
story: A U.S. Army soldier has been arrested in the U.K. on suspicion that he engaged in espionage linked to Russia, British and U.S. authorities announced Tuesday.

The 41-year-old suspect was not identified, but a U.S. official told CBS News he is a senior officer based at Imjin Barracks, home to the headquarters of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. He was arrested Tuesday near Gloucester, about 100 miles west of London.

The soldier is suspected of violations under Section 1 and Section 3 of the U.K.'s National Security Act of 2023 — obtaining or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service, respectively. The London Metropolitan Police said the suspected activity relates to Russia and that the force was carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire — the county where the base is located — related to the investigation.
The suspect was in custody in a London police station as of Tuesday, according to Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command.

"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing force, said in a statement. "This activity demonstrates the strength of our UK and US law enforcement and national security partnerships, and I commend the work of all the teams involved. We will work together to take robust action against those we suspect of any criminal activity that could undermine our national security."

FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement that "this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners."
Speaking to reporters Wednesday in Moscow, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russia had "nothing to do with" the detention of the U.S. soldier.

In an annual threat update last month, Sir Ken McCallum, the head of Britain's MI5 spy agency, accused Russia of "escalating their attempts at hybrid warfare," calling them "aggressor number one" when it comes to threats against the United Kingdom.

The arrest came as the U.S., Russia and Ukraine began a new round of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, the first such talks aimed at ending the war between Russia and Ukraine in about nine months. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the discussions "constructive and quite substantive," although it seems none of the participants expect any immediate breakthroughs, with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov rejecting European demands for an immediate ceasefire.

U.K. police said the arrest was not related to "any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations," meaning it appears to be unrelated to the recent suspected plot at RAF Fairford, which officials have said is linked to Iran. The U.S. military last month removed its bombers from that base after a security incident that led to the arrests of five British men and one U.K.-Iranian national in late September. There are U.S. troops stationed at RAF Fairford, a British Royal Air Force base.

On Tuesday, the U.S. Justice Department announced that three people it accuses of being Iran-backed operatives were charged with plotting a terrorist attack at RAF Fairford. One of the suspects is in custody in New York. However, the other two are not in custody at this time, two sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

title: 4 grizzly bears killed mom and daughter in Canada, DNA confirms
summary: DNA tests linked four bears to the deaths of Jenny Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed, officials said. All four bears were killed to protect the public.
story: Four grizzly bears captured in western Canada were responsible for killing a mother and her adult daughter this month in what investigators believe was a rare predatory attack, wildlife officials said Tuesday.

DNA tests conclusively linked a female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the deaths of Jenny Balcarras, 48, and her 20-year-old daughter, Selah Reed, the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said. All four bears were killed to protect the public.
"Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behavior, which I can tell you is very rare," Inspector Jeff Tyre told an online briefing.
"That is to say, we don't know how it started, but we know how it ended."
The women's remains were found about 150 meters (490 feet) apart near a trail outside Bella Coola, a remote community about 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) north of Vancouver.

Family members raised the alarm after Reed missed a routine Saturday night call with her sister. Searchers found her mother's remains first, then discovered Reed's remains in a bear cache, where bears store food.

Tyre said the bears were not involved in a separate grizzly attack last November on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers in the same area. Eleven people were injured, including two critically.
The latest killings have shaken the Nuxalk Nation community, which is still recovering from last year's attack. Local authorities imposed a voluntary curfew, and police escorted children to school.
"This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack," said Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner, the Nuxalk Nation's elected chief councilor.
He said community support services would remain available as long as needed.
Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks cannot be rehabilitated or relocated because they pose an extreme risk to public safety.

"This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community. We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure," Tyre said.
Other bear attacks in British Columbia

There are between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears estimated to live in British Columbia, according to the province's Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks. The species is classified as vulnerable. Conflicts between grizzly bears and humans are considered "relatively rare," the ministry said, unless the animals are startled or protecting their cubs or food. Still, there have been a number of grizzly bear attacks in the province in recent years.

In October 2025, a grizzly bear injured two hikers in British Columbia's McGregor Mountain area, northeast of Prince George. One of the hikers was transported to the hospital in critical condition and died a few weeks later due to complications from the injuries. The grizzly bear was later found dead, according to the B.C. Conservation Officer Service.

A man suffered "significant injuries," including broken bones and lacerations, after being attacked by a grizzly bear while hunting in British Columbia's Elkford region in May 2024. He was able to shoot the bear to defend himself. The animal was later found dead. The man was flown to an area hospital for treatment.

A 21-year-old woman was seriously injured by a grizzly bear near Tumbler Ridge in British Columbia in July 2023. Authorities described the incident as a "defensive attack." The victim was transported via helicopter to an area hospital.

title: Judge denies motion to dismiss Trump's defamation case against BBC
summary: A U.S. federal judge has denied a motion to dismiss President Trump's defamation case against the BBC, allowing the case to proceed.
story: A U.S. federal judge denied a motion on Tuesday to dismiss President Trump's defamation case against the BBC, allowing the case to proceed.

In December 2025, Mr. Trump filed a $10 billion lawsuit against the British Broadcasting Corporation, the U.K.'s public broadcaster, over a documentary that featured edited parts of the speech he delivered on Jan. 6, 2021, as his supporters massed around the U.S. Capitol in what would become an assault on the heart of the government.

In the lawsuit, filed in the Southern District of Florida, attorneys for Mr. Trump accuse the BBC of publishing a "false, defamatory, deceptive, disparaging, inflammatory and malicious depiction" of him in an episode of the network's "Panorama" program, which aired a week before the 2024 election.

The case alleges the BBC "intentionally and maliciously sought to fully mislead its viewers" by "splicing together" two clips of the same speech Mr. Trump gave to supporters before the riots began. The president's legal team claims the two clips were 55 minutes apart and the edit omitted "his statement calling for peace."
On Tuesday, Judge Jeffrey Kuntz denied the BBC's motion to dismiss the defamation case, effectively allowing it to proceed.
"Whether President Trump can prove these claims and establish he sustained damages at summary judgment or trial is left for another day," Kuntz wrote in his decision.
Mr. Trump hailed the decision as "A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth," in a post on his Truth Social platform.
A spokesperson for the BBC, quoted by the network's news division, said: "We are surprised by this decision but respect the Court's authority and note the case will now proceed to the next stage."
"We remain confident in our position and will continue to respond through the proper legal process," the spokesperson added.

On Oct. 22, a federal judge in Miami said Mr. Trump must sit for a deposition with BBC lawyers by Dec. 11, warning that if he did not, he could face penalties, including possible dismissal of the lawsuit, unless the period for the president and the network to collect information in the case is extended.

Mr. Trump had been due to sit for a deposition in October, but his lawyers told the BBC in late September that he would no longer be available to answer questions, "due to other matters of national importance."
The president has said he will be available for the deposition in the second or third week of January, according to the BBC.
In November 2025, the BBC issued an apology to the president over the editing of his speech as featured in the documentary.

"BBC Chair Samir Shah has separately sent a personal letter to the White House making clear to President Trump that he and the Corporation are sorry for the edit of the President's speech on 6 January 2021, which featured in the programme," the BBC Press Office said in its statement at the time.
"While the BBC sincerely regrets the manner in which the video clip was edited, we strongly disagree there is a basis for a defamation claim," the press office added.
