title: Hegseth labels impeachment push a policy dispute, but do lawmakers' allegations rise to high crimes?
summary: Pete Hegseth calls eight impeachment articles mere "policy disagreements" as Rep. Thomas Massie alleges war powers violations and unlawful strikes.
story: Fox News’ Jonathan Turley and Kerri Urbahn assess articles of impeachment filed in the House against War Secretary Pete Hegseth. Jennifer Griffin reports the latest, with additional analysis from former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo.

War Secretary Pete Hegseth pushed back against an impeachment effort Tuesday, accusing lawmakers of trying to turn disagreements over President Donald Trump's military policies into impeachable offenses.
Congress is preparing to vote on eight articles alleging the Pentagon chief violated federal law and abused his authority.

"One disgruntled congressman wants to shred it over policy disagreements. That's what it is: policy disagreements, not high crimes, not misdemeanors, not treason, not bribery, not the kinds of offenses the founders intended when they wrote the impeachment clause," Hegseth said at a Pentagon press conference Tuesday morning.
"The proper remedy for a policy disagreement, it's legislation, it's debate, it's the next presidential election," he added.

But the impeachment resolution introduced Monday by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., goes beyond objections to the administration's military strategy. It alleges that Hegseth violated congressional war powers, authorized unlawful military operations and retaliated against a sitting senator for exercising his constitutional rights.
HEGSETH RIPS IMPEACHMENT PUSH FROM OUTGOING REPUBLICAN AS 'FARCE,' 'STUNT'

ARLINGTON, VIRGINIA - NOVEMBER 10: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth takes questions from reporters during a news conference at the Pentagon on November 10, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-TX) introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, saying he violated the Constitution by waging war in Iran without congressional authorization and other charges. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

The clash puts the limits of impeachment at the center of a growing fight over Trump's national security agenda, testing whether lawmakers can make a constitutional case for removing Hegseth or are just using impeachment to challenge military and policy decisions they oppose.

Massie's eight articles center on several of the Trump administration's most controversial national security decisions, with three accusing Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution during the war against Iran.

The outgoing Kentucky Republican alleges that Hegseth initiated hostilities without congressional authorization, continued military operations after Congress directed their termination and disregarded statutory deadlines requiring the withdrawal of U.S. forces.

Other articles accuse Hegseth of failing to comply with laws intended to minimize civilian casualties, including in connection with a strike on an Iranian school, and conducting unlawful maritime strikes against suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean.
7 REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO REIN IN IRAN WAR POWERS

The resolution also alleges that Hegseth retaliated against Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., over a video urging service members to refuse unlawful orders, and unlawfully directed military operations in Yemen and the capture of former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., speaks on impeaching U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth outside the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 9, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Massie has rejected the suggestion that the impeachment effort is simply a referendum on Hegseth's job performance or the administration's military policies.
"The question is whether he committed impeachable acts," Massie wrote on X Monday. "And the answer is yes, eight times."
Constitutional law scholar Jonathan Turley largely agreed that the impeachment effort was on shaky ground, arguing that six of Massie's eight articles should be dismissed outright.
"In my view, six of the eight articles should be nonstarters, including the Iranian articles," Turley wrote on X Tuesday.

Turley acknowledged that Congress has a legitimate constitutional interest in asserting its war powers, but argued that Massie was attempting to use impeachment to settle a longstanding dispute over presidential authority. Presidents of both parties, including Bill Clinton, Barack Obama and Joe Biden, have claimed broad authority to launch military operations without congressional approval, he noted.
"Massie is not going to 'litigate' the matter through impeachments," Turley wrote, arguing that Trump was exercising authority long claimed by his predecessors.
GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth testifies before the Senate Armed Services Committee, on Capitol Hill, in Washington, Thursday, April 30, 2026. (Cliff Owen/AP Photo)
Vice President JD Vance, however, argued Tuesday that lawmakers were using impeachment as a substitute for exercising their legislative powers.
"Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes? The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not," Vance wrote on X.
"Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements. Rather than use them, they're going to try to impeach Pete Hegseth," he continued.

Vance suggested the effort was driven less by the war with Iran than by opposition to Hegseth's broader changes at the Pentagon, including shifting U.S. forces away from Europe and Ukraine and reorganizing the military's senior leadership.
TRUMP’S PENTAGON SHAKE-UP REVIVES A PRESIDENTIAL POWER PLAY WITH A LONG HISTORY

ARLINGTON, VIRGINIA - NOVEMBER 10: U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks during a news conference at the Pentagon on November 10, 2026 in Arlington, Virginia. U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie (R-TX) introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, saying he violated the Constitution by waging war in Iran without congressional authorization and other charges. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
"This isn't about Iran, this is about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon," Vance wrote.
DRAMATIC FOOTAGE SHOWS ALLEGED NARCO BOAT ERUPT IN FIREBALL DURING US MILITARY STRIKE
Turley dismissed the article of impeachment concerning Maduro's capture, pointing to court precedent involving the U.S. seizure of former Panamanian leader Manuel Noriega.

But Turley drew a distinction between those disputes over executive authority and two allegations he considered more serious: the maritime strikes against suspected drug traffickers and Hegseth's treatment of Sen. Mark Kelly.
"The 'double tap' allegation would be a war crime, if true," Turley wrote, noting that Trump and Hegseth have denied issuing such orders.

The effort to punish Kelly over a video urging troops to refuse unlawful orders also raised serious questions about a sitting senator's free speech rights and potential undue command influence, Turley argued.
Still, he stopped short of concluding that either allegation met the constitutional threshold for impeachment, saying more evidence was needed.
DEMOCRATS RALLY BEHIND GOP LAWMAKER'S HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT PUSH, SIGNAL MORE TO COME IN JANUARY
"I will be looking for the underlying evidence on those two articles," he wrote, describing both as potentially problematic but difficult to establish as "high crimes and misdemeanors."

The Constitution authorizes impeachment for treason, bribery or other high crimes and misdemeanors, a standard that does not require proof of a criminal offense. Congress has historically treated serious abuses of official power as potential grounds for impeachment, though the precise boundaries remain contested.

That distinction complicates the argument that the allegations can be dismissed simply because they involve military policy. Lawmakers can disagree with a defense secretary's decisions without those disagreements constituting impeachable misconduct, but allegations that an official knowingly violated the law or abused the powers of his office present a different constitutional question.
Hegseth, meanwhile, has maintained that the operations cited in the resolution were lawful and directed by the president.
"I stand behind every one of these operations. I was proud to execute them, and I would do it again tomorrow," Hegseth said Tuesday.

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth gives a State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Quantico, Va., on Sept. 30, 2026. Secretary Hegseth delivered his address to junior officers, enlisted leaders, and special guests including Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey. (Getty Images)
President Trump also rallied behind his defense secretary following the press conference, praising his performance and attacking Massie, who lost his Republican primary earlier this year.

"In just under two years, Secretary Hegseth has worked side-by-side with President Trump to restore American power on the world stage, build the strongest military in generations, and instill a warrior ethos at the Pentagon. President Trump and Secretary Hegseth have taken bold, necessary action to deny the Iranian regime the ability to develop a nuclear weapon, bring narco-terrorist Nicolás Maduro to American justice, and defend our homeland from dangerous terrorists and cartels – saving American lives," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital.

"This spectacle only proves what we’ve known all along: Thomas Massie and the Democrats are far more interested in playing political games than working to improve the lives of the American people," Wales added.
Trump Cabinet officials rallied behind Hegseth, with Collins, Burgum, Rollins, Mullin and Turner posting messages of support on social media. Rubio and Blanche also defended Hegseth publicly.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Rubio said he carried out Trump’s orders "quite effectively" and Blanche rejected claims that he had done anything illegal or wrong.

The House is expected to vote Tuesday evening on whether to advance Massie's impeachment resolution. Impeachment would require a simple majority in the House, but removing Hegseth from office would require conviction by a two-thirds majority in the Senate.
The vote will test whether lawmakers view the allegations as grounds for impeachment or a dispute better addressed through Congress's legislative and oversight powers.

title: Florida AG subpoenas DSA over potential illegal funding from Cuba and China
summary: James Uthmeier says a subpoena targets the Democratic Socialists of America over possible foreign donations tied to Cuba and China delegations.
story: The AG’s office is examining whether the Democratic Socialists of America took contributions from ‘foreign sources of concern.’ (Credit: @AGJamesUthmeier).

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Tuesday that his office issued an investigative subpoena to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) to investigate whether the organization accepted contributions from "foreign sources of concern," including entities in Cuba and China.

"Our laws prohibit accepting contributions from foreign sources of concern," Uthmeier said in a video statement. "We will not allow foreign adversaries to influence Florida through the backdoor of non-private fundraising."

The subpoena demands documents related to recent DSA delegations to China and Cuba, where organization members met with Cuban government officials, to determine if the DSA violated Florida's Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act, according to Uthmeier.
DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA ACTIVISTS SIGNED PLEDGE TO SUPPORT, DEFEND 'CHINESE SOCIALISM'

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier issued a subpoena to the Democratic Socialists of America to determine whether the organization accepted donations from "foreign sources of concern," including entities in Cuba and China. (Getty Images)
Uthmeier did not detail specific criminal allegations or name individuals accused of violating state law.
The DSA has repeatedly praised the Cuban regime and routinely advocates for lifting American sanctions and ending the U.S. embargo against Havana.
RNC WARNS DEMOCRATS FACE 'POLITICAL SUICIDE' AFTER DSA PRAISES FIDEL CASTRO, DEMANDS RUBIO'S PROSECUTION

The organization has sent multiple delegations to Cuba in recent years. During a 2023 trip, DSA members met privately with Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel and sought to establish formal communication channels with government ministries, according to a State Department report released in July.
The legal action comes shortly after several DSA-backed candidates won races across federal, state, and local levels in last week's elections.

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier issued a subpoena to the Democratic Socialists of America to determine whether the organization accepted donations from "foreign sources of concern," including entities in Cuba and China. (Amy Beth Bennett/Getty Images; Yamil Lage/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to the DSA for comment.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Senate GOP rebellion fizzles as Thune keeps power despite historic midterm massacre
summary: John Thune secured another term as Senate GOP leader despite Ron Johnson and Rick Scott pushing to delay elections after midterm losses.
story: Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., isn’t ready to back John Thune for another term as Senate GOP leader. He and other Republicans want specifics on how Thune, or another contender, would get work done as Democrats prepare to take control.

There was neither an exodus nor a mass housecleaning in the Senate GOP leadership, despite frustration and rumblings of discontent among some lawmakers reeling from last week’s devastating midterm losses.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., secured another term as the top Republican behind the closed doors of the Old Senate Chamber, where lawmakers charted their course for their few remaining weeks in power and beyond.
Thune, along with the bulk of his leadership team, which now includes Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, were swiftly elected after a group of Republicans failed to delay the leadership elections.
It wasn't without a fight, though, with conversations behind closed doors dragging on for over seven hours.
GOP SENATOR WITHHOLDS SUPPORT FOR THUNE AS LEADERSHIP SHOWDOWN LOOMS
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., talks with reporters in the Capitol Visitor Center on Nov. 9, 2026. (CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)
Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., led the charge to delay, and didn't stick around after his attempts to do so failed on a 31 to 15 vote in the Old Senate Chamber to proceed with the scheduled election.

Johnson and others wanted to have a deep conversation about what had happened during the midterm elections, and a roadmap on what Republican leadership candidates could accomplish with the little time they had left in power.
SENATE GOP REBELS MOVE TO DELAY LEADERSHIP VOTE, DEMAND RECKONING AFTER MIDTERM DISASTER
But there was no opposition to any of the lawmakers running for leadership.

"This has never been anything against John Thune," Johnson said. "I think he has been very unfairly attacked, you know, by our base, and I don't agree with that. What I didn't agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position."
On Monday, Thune was adamant that he’d still run but was unsure of the outcome.
"That's the hope," Thune said when asked if he had the Senate GOP’s support. "You never know right until they vote."
Before the vote, Johnson and a handful of others believed there should be a shakeup in leadership, but didn’t offer an alternative to Thune.
"After the stunning defeat, you just can't continue on business as usual," Johnson said. "I mean, that kind of defeat demands change."
When asked if he’d be interested in running, Johnson said, "That’s part of the problem. Would you want it?"

"I think there's a number of people with talent," Johnson said. "Again, I'm not — at a minimum, we need to see out of our leadership team what's the strategy moving forward, and you can't come off of a defeat like that and just ram through elections and oh yeah, ‘let's just elect that leadership team by acclamation.’"

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., had previously run for leader twice and most recently against Thune. But the lawmaker, who joined Johnson’s crusade for change, declined to throw his hat into the arena again.
"I think we have to acknowledge the voters are not happy," Scott said. "We have to start listening to voters."
CONGRESS RETURNS TO BRUTAL LAME-DUCK STRETCH WITH SHUTDOWN DEADLINE, LEADERSHIP RACES: 'CLOSET IS FULL OF S—'

Sen. Ron Johnson speaks during a hearing of the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee in the Dirksen Senate Office Building on Feb. 12, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Scott wanted ironclad promises on the GOP’s to-do list, including ramming through judicial nominees, government funding "without a massive omnibus," a stock trade ban, permitting reform, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, taking another crack at the SAVE America Act and balancing the budget — possibly through budget reconciliation.

Johnson and Scott were joined by Sens. Ted Budd, R-N.C., Mike Lee, R-Utah, John Kennedy, R-La., Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Dave McCormick, R-Pa., in a push to delay the elections that was not met, and the would-be coup faded as the secret ballots were cast.

Still, there were others outside that cohort who weren’t happy with last week and believed that there should be deeper soul-searching on what Republicans did over the last two years that led to a historic night for Senate Democrats.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., contended that much of what the GOP listed as accomplishments over their time in power is what worked against them.
"And, you know, you have the kind of record that this Congress has had, I think we better have a pretty tough family conversation about what it is we're doing," Hawley said.

"When you cut Medicaid, but you fund data centers, when you cut rural hospital funding, but you fund Planned Parenthood, when you let the cost of healthcare for working people go through the roof, but you can't do anything for them on other issues of affordability, from fertilizer to gas," he continued. "Yeah you know what? The public doesn’t like that very much."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Democrats accused of 'No Kings' hypocrisy over push to change voter-approved trans sports measures
summary: Colorado's Philip Weiser and Rep. Pramila Jayapal face "No Kings" hypocrisy claims after signaling efforts to overturn transgender sports ballot measures.
story: The ‘Outnumbered’ panel discusses Democratic efforts to overturn voter-approved protections for girls’ sports, including measures in Washington and Colorado. They also examine divisions within the Republican Party as Reps. Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan compete for House leadership following the midterm elections.

Voters in two Democratic strongholds approved restrictions on transgender participation in girls' sports last week, delivering rare Republican victories amid a blue wave. But Democratic officials are already discussing ways to change the measures, drawing accusations of hypocrisy from Republicans who point to their support for the "No Kings" movement.

Colorado Gov.-elect Philip Weiser, who also criticized a separate ballot measure restricting gender-related surgeries for minors, and Rep. Pramila Jayapal , D-Wash., both raised objections to the measures approved in their respective states.

At his first post-election news conference, he suggested Colorado's Democratic-controlled legislature could revisit the voter-approved measures, saying that it is "statutory … and a natural and I believe appropriate role for the legislature to say ‘what are the adjustments that need to be added."
PRO-TRANS ACTIVISTS HOLD RALLY AGAINST WASHINGTON STATE BALLOT INITIATIVE TO PROTECT GIRLS SPORTS

Colorado voters approved ballot measures increasing penalties for fentanyl-related offenses, restricting transgender athletes from competing in sports designated for the opposite biological sex and prohibiting gender-related surgeries for minors. The measures passed even as Democrats swept into power across the state.

"I don’t believe it would be acceptable to Colorado to have every student athlete to have to go through full-body examinations or other invasions of privacy," Weiser added of the sports-related referendum, according to the Denver Post.
COLORADO MOM WHO SAID DAUGHTER WAS SECRETLY TRANSITIONED HELPS LEAD EFFORT TO BAN BOYS IN GIRLS' SPORTS
Colorado Gov.-elect Philip Weiser, pictured July 22, 2025, suggested changes to voter-approved ballot measures following the November 2026 election. (Hyoung Chang/The Denver Post via Getty Images)
Weiser did not respond to a request for comment.
Republicans in suburban Denver criticized the governor-elect, dubbing him "King Phil I" and characterizing his response as "know[ing] better than Colorado voters in a healthy democracy."

"But before the ink on the ballots is even dry, Governor-elect Phil Weiser is already signaling that the vote of the people is merely a ‘suggestion’. With Coloradans approving ballot measures to crack down on fentanyl and protect youth sports and children, Weiser walked up to the podium on Wednesday and essentially declared that the will of the majority needs to pass his personal vibe check first," the Adams County Republican Party said in a statement.
Republicans characterized Weiser’s position as "you voted for it, but I don’t like it…"

"No Kings," the Adams Republicans added, invoking the protest movement that Weiser has supported through participation in "No Kings" protests. The movement's demonstrations have criticized President Donald Trump over what organizers characterize as authoritarian conduct.
The Colorado House Republican caucus echoed the sentiment, adding in a statement: "If the Democrats truly believe there should be ‘No Kings’ in America, it is time they take their own advice."
'NO KINGS' FOOT SOLDIERS IGNORE ORGANIZERS' WARNING, GO ALL IN FOR DEMOCRATS
Meanwhile, in Washington State, Jayapal condemned a similar measure approved by voters.

Initiative 638 prohibits students defined as "biologically male" from competing in girls' K-12 school sports and requires students seeking to participate on girls' teams to provide verification of their biological sex from a health care provider. The measure passed with approximately 56% support in the reliably Democratic state.
Following the election results, multiple local news outlets reported that Jayapal pledged to "take our state back" after voters approved the initiative.

"We're going to start planning for how we overturn these bad initiatives and how we go back to loving everyone with gender inclusivity the way we have for decades," she said, according to several reports.
Jayapal did not respond to a request for comment.
Critics also pointed to Jayapal's past support for "No Kings" protests, accusing her of contradicting her own rhetoric about respecting the will of voters.

One critic highlighted a November 2025 social media post in which Jayapal wrote: "We have democracy for a reason. America doesn’t belong to kings it belongs to the people and we're going to keep it that way."
"Rep. Jayapal, this you?" they asked.
Jayapal also faced previous criticism over her support for the "No Kings" movement after praising remarks by Britain's King Charles III during his visit to the United States.

Washington Democratic Party Chair Shasti Conrad signaled support for a legal challenge, calling the ballot measure "unconstitutional on its face" and indicating the party would "support [for] organizations planning to challenge it in court."
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., speaks during a House Budget Committee hearing on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C., on April 15, 2026. Jayapal criticized a Washington state ballot measure restricting transgender participation in girls' sports following the November election. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Under Washington's Constitution, lawmakers cannot repeal a voter-approved initiative during its first two years but can amend it with a two-thirds vote in each legislative chamber. After two years, the legislature can amend or repeal the measure with a simple majority.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The controversy leaves Democrats in both states confronting a similar political dilemma: whether to preserve the restrictions voters approved or pursue changes through the legislative and judicial processes available to them.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

title: Top Dem cries ‘weaponization’ as comments warning young people not to join Trump admin land her in hot water
summary: Dem Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., cries "weaponization" after Trump ordered the Justice Department to investigate her remarks warning young Republicans about joining his administration.
story: Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich, says her lawyer asked the Justice Department what it plans to do after President Trump called for an investigation into her comments about young Republicans.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., is accusing President Donald Trump of escalating a coordinated "weaponization" campaign against her after he ordered the Justice Department to examine remarks she made warning young Republicans they could face "a ton of problems" if they joined his administration.

In a Truth Social post over the weekend, President Trump accused Democrats of political weaponization and singled out Slotkin for "go[ing] after all young people that believe in Republican values" in her October remarks. "By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!" Trump wrote.

In a video response posted Monday, Slotkin defended her remarks, saying she was referring to people who might be asked to violate the law or misuse taxpayer dollars and citing her First Amendment rights.

"A couple weeks ago, I talked about how anyone who is violating the law or misusing taxpayer dollars should be held accountable, and if there's young people who are thinking of joining people who are doing that, they should think twice," Slotkin said. "If you're not violating the law — no problem."
DEMS PIVOT FROM 'AFFORDABILITY' PITCH TO DHS PROBE THREATS AFTER MIDTERM WINS

Trump faced criticism after posting online about Democrats allegedly urging the military to refuse orders, later clarifying he was not making threats. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images; Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Slotkin said Trump began targeting her after her October remarks, first by "name-checking" her from the Oval Office before he "really ramped up his coordinated play" following Democrats’ midterm election gains. She also pointed to Attorney General Todd Blanche's Sunday television appearances discussing possible investigations. Slotkin said her attorney sent the Justice Department a letter Monday asking, "What are you going to do?"

The Justice Department has not confirmed whether it has opened an investigation into Slotkin. During an interview Sunday on CNN’s "State of the Union," Blanche declined to identify a specific crime when asked whether Democrats’ rhetoric could constitute one, saying, "It depends on what’s said. So, yes, it could be."
A DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital that Slotkin’s comments should be evaluated under the facts and law but did not confirm an investigation.
OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE AT CENTER OF TRUMP'S ANTI-WEAPONIZATION FUND CASE HIT WITH MISCONDUCT CLAIM

"Senator Slotkin said publicly that the prospect of future investigations should deter young people from joining this administration," the spokesperson said in a statement. "The Department believes public service should not be met with threats of retribution, and this Department is committed to ending the weaponization of government. We follow the facts and the law."
U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche speaks during a news conference at the Robert F. Kennedy Department of Justice building on April 7, 2026. (Getty Images)

Slotkin's original remarks also prompted a congressional ethics complaint. Michael Bicksel, a University of Chicago student who first publicized her comments, filed the complaint with the Senate Select Committee on Ethics on Oct. 22.

Bicksel argued that Slotkin had proposed using congressional investigations and potential prosecutions to deter young people from joining a Republican administration, asking the committee to determine whether her comments amounted to "improper conduct which may reflect upon the Senate."
Fox News Digital reached out to Slotkin for comment but did not hear back in time for publication.
"It's a coordinated, manufactured response," Slotkin previously said about the backlash to her remarks concerning young Trump supporters. "They want to intimidate you to be quiet."

Attendees of a Turning Point USA event pass through a protest as they leave the event, which featured U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance in Athens, Georgia, U.S. April 14, 2026. (Elijah Nouvelage/Reuters)

Slotkin made the remarks Oct. 13 during a University of Chicago discussion about how Democrats could exercise congressional power if they regained control of Congress. Fox News Digital previously reported that Slotkin advocated pursuing "signature cases" against people who enabled Trump rather than focusing exclusively on the president. She also argued that the prospect of legal trouble could deter young Republicans from joining his administration.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The latest dispute follows an earlier Justice Department investigation involving Slotkin and five other Democratic lawmakers who posted a video reminding military personnel and intelligence officials that they were not required to follow unlawful orders. A federal grand jury declined to indict the lawmakers.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

In a letter to Blanche made public Monday, Slotkin's attorney, Preet Bharara, argued that her remarks were protected by the First Amendment and the Constitution's speech or debate clause. Bharara demanded that Blanche publicly confirm the Justice Department would not investigate the senator.

"Just like last time, Senator Slotkin will not be deterred," Bharara wrote. "She will continue to call out corruption by this administration and to exercise her First Amendment rights to speak out against the President’s many abuses of power."
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Shanghai-based tycoon Neville Roy Singham's 'Squad,' Bernie Sanders donations resurface
summary: FEC records show Neville Roy Singham and CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans have donated a combined $47,000 to Bernie Sanders, Pramila Jayapal and more.
story: Fox News Digital's Asra Nomani spoke with Jodie Evans during a New York City protest that took place while Israeli Prime Minister Bibi Netanyahu delivered remarks at the United Nations General Assembly.

A Shanghai-based tycoon known for pushing Chinese Communist Party talking points, whose activist network is flooding Capitol Hill this week, has directly funded some of the most powerful progressives in Congress, including members of "The Squad."

Federal Election Commission records show that Neville Roy Singham and his wife, CodePink co-founder Jodie Evans, have given more than a combined $47,000 to Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Reps. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and Chuy García, D-Ill.

Omar's campaign took $4,200 from the couple from 2019 to 2023, according to FEC records. Singham gave her campaign $2,700 in March 2019, just weeks after she took office, and Evans gave $1,500 in two contributions in November and December 2023. None of it has been refunded.
HOUSE PANEL TO PROBE FOREIGN ‘TROJAN HORSES’ AS SINGHAM SCRUTINY WIDENS

Federal Election Commission filings show Singham and his wife, Jodie Evans, directly contributed to a number of Democratic members of Congress. (Jim Vondruska/Getty Images; Dave Kotinsky/Getty Images; Valerie Plesch/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Sanders' campaigns have taken in at least $6,800 from the couple, according to FEC records, most of it for his presidential bids. Singham gave $2,700 to Sanders' 2016 presidential campaign. Evans gave the 2016 campaign $2,800, of which it refunded $200, and at least $252 to his 2020 campaign in 2019. She also gave $1,250 to his Senate campaign committee, Friends of Bernie Sanders, in 2011.

García's campaign took in $1,000 from Singham in August 2018, according to FEC records. He was running for his first term in Congress at the time, after winning the Democratic primary for Illinois' 4th Congressional District, Singham's home city of Chicago. The campaign has not refunded the contribution.

Jayapal has received more from the couple than any other member of Congress, a net $35,700 from 2016 to 2022, according to FEC records. Singham gave her campaign $17,800 and none of it was refunded. Evans gave $22,900, and the campaign refunded $5,000 of it in three payments between 2020 and 2023, leaving $17,900. Most of the couple's money came in 2019 and 2021, including back-to-back maximum contributions from Singham in both years.
Rep. Ilhan Omar eats lunch in Karmel Mall of Somalia in Minneapolis. Minn.. Friday, October 23, 2026. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)
Under Federal Election Commission rules, a campaign has 10 days to decide whether to deposit a check or return it.
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's, D-NY, campaign returned a $500 contribution from Evans through ActBlue on the day it arrived, Aug. 4, 2018, during her first run for Congress.
Fox News Digital reached out to the offices of Sanders, Jayapal, García and Ocasio-Cortez and Omar's office for comment but did not receive responses.
DHS, WAR DEPT JOIN PROBE INTO SINGHAM NETWORK ALLEGEDLY SOWING DISCORD IN US

After his wedding to Evans in 2017 and the sale of ThoughtWorks, the technology company he founded, Singham directed $285 million to nonprofits and media organizations, according to a Fox News Digital investigation. The People’s Forum received $22.4 million from Singham, while CodePink received $1.33 million. BreakThrough BT Media Inc., which operates BreakThrough News, received $1.098 million, according to tax filings. Singham and his wife, who are both American citizens, now live in Shanghai, China.

Organizations within the Singham network regularly participate in staged anti-ICE, anti-capitalist, anti-data centers and anti-Israel protests – many of which garner national and social media coverage.
FROM AUSTIN TO NEW YORK, PRO-CHINA NETWORK FUELS WEEK OF ANTI-US PROTESTS AS XI MEETS TRUMP
Last month, Evans and CodePink co-founder Medea Benjamin embarked on a China propaganda tour across the communist country.

The trip, according to an event promotion link for sign-up on the CodePink website, was 12 days and 11 nights in Shanghai, Chongqing, Zunyi, Loushanguan, Maotai Village and Guiyang with the cost of attendance between $3,000 and $4,000 depending on the total number of participants. The CodePink website said attendees will be "greeted by local Shanghai comrades," and a tour with Benjamin and Code Pink co-founder Jodie Evans is included.
Jodie Evans and Neville Roy Singham are pictured together. (Getty Images)

"Explore China’s revolutionary history, while marveling at high-tech infrastructure and modern socialist development," the event description reads. "Highlights include Red Memorials, Historical Re-Enactments and Museums, Socialist Infrastructure, and Rural Revitalization."

title: Peltola widens narrow Alaska Senate lead over Sullivan as counting continues
summary: Mary Peltola's lead over Dan Sullivan grew to 2,517 votes after Monday's ballot drop, but tens of thousands of absentee ballots remain uncounted.
story: The Alaska Senate race remains undecided with Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola are separated by fewer than 700 votes. Finn and Dunleavy discuss the impact of same-name candidate Dan J. Sullivan, who received thousands of votes, as the closely watched race remains unresolved.

Alaska's still too-close-to-call Senate race is expected to deliver another batch of ballot results Tuesday night after Monday's latest ballot drop expanded Democratic nominee Mary Peltola's lead over incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan to 2,517 first-choice votes.

Still current as of Tuesday midday ET, Peltola stands at 48.6% (106,321 votes) to Sullivan’s 47.5% (103,804) in the ranked-choice voting system that will kick in if neither candidate gets across the 50% threshold.

The controversial race, punctuated by the "Decoy Dan" scheme exposed by The New York Times, has Republican Gerald Heikes at 2.2% (4,865) and independent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. at 1.7% (3,651 votes). Roughly 75–76% of the expected vote is in, with tens of thousands of early, absentee and questioned ballots still to be counted.
ALASKA SENATE FIGHT HEATS UP AS SULLIVAN MOVES TO BLOCK PELTOLA LAWSUIT OVER REJECTED ABSENTEE BALLOT RECORDS

"After every vote is counted, it is clear that Mary Peltola will be elected Alaska’s next United States Senator," Peltola campaign manager Cheryl Bruce wrote in a statement Tuesday morning after that previous tranche of votes.

"Mary won today’s votes by a margin of 68-30, reflecting major support in key areas from Anchorage and Chevak. This overwhelming margin further strengthens Mary’s path to victory, and Mary is looking forward to continuing her relentless fight to lower costs and put Alaska first in the United States Senate after all votes are counted."
Monday's drop added nearly 5,000 ballots and marked a shift from the razor-thin, 637-vote Peltola edge that had held for days after Election Day.

The incumbent Sullivan and President Donald Trump have both suggested if Peltola does not get to 50% of the vote and ranked-choice voting (RCV) goes to rounds two or three that the Republican would absorb secondary voting strength in the system.
DOJ FACES ‘HEAVY LIFT’ IN ALASKA ELECTION APPEAL AS SEPARATE CRIMINAL PROBE CONTINUES

Under Alaska’s system, if no candidate reaches a majority of first-choice votes, the lowest finisher is eliminated and ballots transfer according to voters’ rankings until one candidate surpasses 50%. Right now, that would be the other Dan Sullivan, which might help Peltola break 50%.
The Official RCV tabulation is scheduled for Nov. 18 after the overseas absentee deadline.

The slow pace matches the timeline Gov. Mike Dunleavy described in an interview Sunday. He called the state’s process "very confusing" and "a slow system," pointing to significant ballot dumps expected Friday, Nov. 13, and Wednesday, Nov. 18.

Dunleavy has also continued an investigation into the "Decoy Dan" candidacy of Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., which some Republicans allege was intended to siphon votes from the incumbent; the governor has said the Division of Elections and the Department of Justice are reviewing related questions.
TRUMP ADMIN PUTS ALLEGED 'DECOY DAN' CONSPIRATORS ON NOTICE IN ALASKA ELECTION SPOILER PROBE

Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, is facing a larger gap behind Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola in the most recent ballot drop Monday night. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images; Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"We're still in the process of bringing in votes and counting votes," Dunleavy said Sunday. "And we are in the midst of investigations as to determine if there was any wrongdoing, especially anything that might resemble perjury or, you know, a misrepresentation of individual's intent on how they wanted their candidacy to be placed on the ballot."
Other statewide races remain fluid on the same ballot count:
MURKOWSKI SNUBS TRUMP-BACKED ALASKA CANDIDATE, ENDORSES DEMOCRAT FOR GOVERNOR

Nick Begich, R-Alaska, holds a clear first-choice edge at 49.19% in the U.S. House race.Ballot Measure 2, which would repeal open primaries and ranked-choice voting, trails with roughly 52.3% voting "no" against repeal to keep the system in place for future elections.

title: Instagram's AI may catch teens lying about their age
summary: Meta's AI age-estimation technology now scans Instagram accounts worldwide, placing millions of teens into stricter safety settings automatically.
story: Bipartisan state coalition secures a historic agreement as Meta agrees to a landmark $16B+ social media addiction settlement. Claudia Cowan reports on the sweeping safety changes mandated the federal court. The social media giant must implement strict daily time limits, overnight blocks and robust age verification tools for teen users on Instagram and Facebook.

My own niece has told me for years that she and her friends could get around age restrictions on Facebook and Instagram when they were younger. They knew how easy it was to make themselves appear older online. And I suspect plenty of parents have heard similar stories. So when I heard that Meta was expanding its AI technology to identify teens who lie about their age, my first thought was, it's about time.

On November 9, Meta announced a worldwide expansion of its AI age-estimation technology. The system looks for accounts that may belong to teenagers, even when someone has entered an adult birthday. Meta says the expansion will place millions more young users into Instagram's built-in Teen Account protections.

The move comes as lawsuits and growing public pressure push Meta to take greater responsibility for protecting young users. After years of concerns about children getting around social media age restrictions, this could be one of the company's most significant attempts yet to address the problem. But how does Instagram's AI figure out someone's age? And can parents trust it to get things right?

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. FRANCE BECOMES FIRST EU NATION TO BAN SOCIAL MEDIA FOR CHILDREN UNDER 15
Meta is expanding AI age checks on Instagram to identify teens who may have entered an adult birthday to bypass safety restrictions. (Javier Zayaz/iStock)
How Instagram AI age checks work

For years, entering a birthday was one of the easiest ways to tell Instagram how old you were. The problem was that the app had to rely heavily on what someone told it. Now Meta is using artificial intelligence to look for clues that suggest an account belongs to someone under 18. Instead of relying solely on the birthday listed on a profile, the company's age-estimation technology analyzes account activity and other signals to estimate whether someone may be a teenager.

Meta has previously explained that its age-detection technology can look for clues such as birthday celebrations, references to school grades and information shared in posts or comments. The company has also described separate technology that analyzes photos and videos to help identify accounts belonging to children under 13. According to the company, that technology examines general visual clues without using facial recognition or identifying specific people.

The important thing to understand is that these systems estimate age. They don't establish someone's exact birthday. If Instagram's AI determines that an account likely belongs to someone between 13 and 17, the company can automatically apply Teen Account protections. That means a teenager who entered an adult birthday could suddenly find their account operating under stricter safety settings.
What happens when Instagram identifies a teen?

Instagram's Teen Accounts have been around since 2024. However, those protections depend on the platform correctly identifying younger users. The new worldwide expansion is designed to close that gap. When Meta identifies an account that likely belongs to a teenager, it can apply safeguards that include:

Stronger privacy: Teen Accounts generally start with private settings that restrict who can see posts and interact with an account.Messaging restrictions: Instagram limits direct messages to people a teen follows or already has a connection with.Content filtering: The platform reduces exposure to sensitive material and places teens into age-appropriate content settings.Limits on unwanted interactions: Instagram restricts who can tag or mention teens and filters potentially offensive comments.Time management tools: Teen Accounts include usage reminders and overnight notification restrictions, with additional limits available through parental supervision.
Stronger privacy: Teen Accounts generally start with private settings that restrict who can see posts and interact with an account.
Messaging restrictions: Instagram limits direct messages to people a teen follows or already has a connection with.
Content filtering: The platform reduces exposure to sensitive material and places teens into age-appropriate content settings.
Limits on unwanted interactions: Instagram restricts who can tag or mention teens and filters potentially offensive comments.
Time management tools: Teen Accounts include usage reminders and overnight notification restrictions, with additional limits available through parental supervision.

Teens under 16 generally need parental permission to make built-in safety settings less restrictive. Instagram has also introduced 13+ content settings inspired by PG-13 movie ratings. Those filters are designed to reduce the amount of mature material younger users encounter.

We previously covered how Instagram's PG-13 restrictions give parents more control over what teens see. Of course, no content filter catches everything. And these protections can only help if Instagram correctly identifies the accounts that need them.
ROBLOX SHARES AI CHILD-SAFETY TOOLS PARENTS SHOULD KNOW
Instagram's Teen Account protections include stricter privacy settings and controls over who can interact with younger people on the platform. (Getty Images)
Instagram's AI age checks are going worldwide

Meta began testing AI technology to identify teens using adult birthdays in the United States in April 2025. The company later expanded the system to additional countries, including Australia, Canada and the United Kingdom. In May 2026, Meta announced further expansion into the European Union and Brazil. Now the technology is going global.

According to Meta, millions more teens will receive additional safety protections, even if they originally claimed to be adults. The company is also expanding age-detection technology on Facebook, with a similar rollout planned for Threads later in 2026.

Meanwhile, Meta says it has started using Apple's age-range signal in Australia. With the right permissions, Apple's system can share someone's age range with participating apps. That gives Meta another way to check whether someone meets an app's age requirements. The big question is whether all this technology will finally make it harder for kids to get around the rules.
Why Meta is finally getting serious about teen safety

The timing of this announcement is worth paying attention to. For years, parents and child safety advocates have raised concerns about social media platforms and their effects on young users. Meanwhile, Meta has faced lawsuits alleging that its platforms contribute to harmful experiences for children and teenagers. Meta reportedly reached settlements worth up to approximately $18 billion with nearly every U.S. state and territory in August 2026. The agreements address lawsuits brought by attorneys general over alleged harm to teens. Under those agreements, Meta committed to strengthening how it identifies teenagers and children younger than 13.

The settlement also includes stronger controls for teens in participating U.S. jurisdictions, including a default two-hour daily limit across Facebook and Instagram that requires parental permission to disable. Additional provisions address nighttime access and parental oversight. Those commitments are separate from the new worldwide AI expansion, although they reflect the broader pressure Meta faces.

And there's an important point here. Meta has known for years that younger users sometimes enter false birthdays. The challenge has been figuring out how to identify them reliably. The company has introduced safety features over time. But public criticism and legal action have increased the pressure to show that those features actually work. Meta's latest announcement suggests the company is putting more resources behind age detection. The results will determine whether this becomes a meaningful turning point. We reached out to Meta for comment on its expanded AI age checks, but did not hear back before our deadline.
Could Instagram's AI get someone's age wrong?

That's another concern worth examining. AI can make mistakes, particularly when it tries to draw conclusions from someone's online activity. An adult might regularly post photos of younger relatives. Someone could also share old school pictures or birthday celebrations from years ago. That doesn't mean one post will automatically convince Instagram that an adult is a teenager. Meta uses multiple signals when making age estimates. However, mistakes remain possible.

Meta says people who are incorrectly placed into Teen Account settings can take steps to verify their age and restore the appropriate settings. Depending on the situation, Instagram may require proof of age through identification or an age-estimation service. And there's another side to the problem. The technology could miss teenagers who successfully make their accounts appear to belong to adults.

That's why parents should still review their children's account settings rather than assuming Instagram has correctly identified their age. Meta's November 9 announcement did not provide a new accuracy figure for the worldwide expansion. I'd like to see more information about how often the system gets these decisions right and how quickly people can correct mistakes.
CHRIS HANSEN URGES PARENTS TO TEACH CHILDREN ABOUT ONLINE PREDATORS BEFORE ALLOWING INTERNET ACCESS
Meta's AI age-estimation technology will not predict an exact birthday, but it will determine whether a user is likely within the teenage age range. (Getty Images)
What parents can expect from Meta

Starting in November 2026, Meta says parents in the United States will begin seeing an informational video in their Instagram feeds. The video will explain how Meta identifies teenagers and places them into age-appropriate protections. It will also link to guidance from internet safety advocate Larry Magid, president and CEO of ConnectSafely.

The guidance explains Meta's approach to identifying younger users and how parents can help ensure their children's ages are accurate. Parents worldwide can also access age-assurance resources through Meta's Family Center. For families, this creates an opportunity to have a conversation about why social media platforms ask for someone's age in the first place.
Tips to help keep your teen safer on Instagram
Even with stronger AI protections, I wouldn't leave everything up to Instagram. There are several practical steps parents can take right now.

Ask your teen to open Instagram and go to their profile. Tap the menu, open Accounts Center, then look for Personal details and Birthday. Make sure the birthday is accurate. Instagram may require verification if someone attempts to change an account's age from under 18 to an adult age.

Open Instagram's settings and look for the account privacy controls. Check whether the account is private and review who can follow your teen. Also review who can send messages. You may find that some protections are already enabled through Teen Accounts.

Instagram's Family Center gives parents additional tools for managing a teen's experience. Parental supervision requires both the parent and teen to agree to the connection. Once connected, parents can review available safety controls and manage certain account restrictions.

Instagram offers daily usage reminders and additional restrictions for teens. Parents can also use supervision settings to manage screen time. On an iPhone, open Settings, then Screen Time to review available app limits. For Android devices, Google Family Link offers parental controls and device management options.

Instagram's 13+ content setting is designed to limit material that may be inappropriate for teenagers. Parents can review these protections and choose stricter settings where available. Remember that filters may still miss content, so it's worth asking your teen what regularly appears in their feed.

This may be the most useful step. Ask your teen whether they have ever felt tempted to enter an older birthday to unlock features or avoid restrictions. Explain that providing the correct age helps Instagram apply protections intended for younger users. And make sure they know they can talk to you if they encounter something uncomfortable online.
Kurt's key takeaways

It's about time. My own niece told me years ago how easily she and her friends could get around the age restrictions on Facebook and Instagram. And I remember wondering why these platforms weren't doing more about it. Now, with lawsuits mounting and public pressure growing, Meta is finally taking a bigger step to address the problem. I'm glad to see it, but I want to know how well this AI actually works. Will it catch teens who lie about their age? And what happens when it gets someone's age wrong? Parents have been asking for better protections for years. It's time for Meta to show that these changes are making kids safer online.

Do you think Meta would be taking these steps without years of public pressure and lawsuits, or has the company finally realized it needs to do more to protect children online? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Health insurance scams to watch for during open enrollment
summary: The FTC sent warning letters to 25 companies over misleading health insurance ads as open enrollment brings a surge of deceptive offers online.
story: CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz discusses his efforts to crack down on health and senior care fraud on ‘Hannity.’

If you've been shopping for health insurance lately, you've probably noticed the ads popping up everywhere. Some promise surprisingly low monthly payments. Others claim you'll qualify for generous benefits or even receive cash rewards for signing up. And with open enrollment underway, those offers can be awfully tempting. But here's what worries me. You could enroll in what looks like a great health insurance plan, only to discover that it barely covers your medical bills when you actually need care.

The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is now warning about misleading health insurance advertising, including plans that promise comprehensive coverage but deliver far less. Some offers promote medical discount programs rather than traditional insurance. Others may come from scammers impersonating government agencies or familiar insurance companies. With Americans reviewing their coverage for 2027, knowing how to recognize health insurance scams could save you from a very expensive mistake.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
TRUMP ADMIN CRACKS DOWN ON ESTIMATED $10 BILLION IN OBAMACARE FRAUD, BOOTS MILLIONS FROM ROLLS
Before signing up for health insurance, make sure you understand exactly what your plan covers so you don't face unexpected medical bills. (Nansan Houn/Getty Images)
FTC warns 25 companies about misleading health insurance ads

Recently, the FTC announced it was sending warning letters to 25 companies that market healthcare plans or generate sales leads for insurance-related products. The agency identified several advertising practices that could violate federal law. These include misrepresenting a plan's benefits, hiding important costs or falsely suggesting that a limited-benefit product provides comprehensive medical coverage. The FTC also raised concerns about advertisements promising free offers, cash rewards or rebates that people may never receive.

Now, there's an important detail here. The FTC says the warning letters do not accuse any of the 25 companies of wrongdoing. Instead, the agency is reminding businesses about advertising laws and warning that it continues to monitor the market. Officials also indicated that additional letters could follow.

Still, the timing deserves attention. Open enrollment brings a surge of legitimate advertising from insurance providers. Unfortunately, it also gives dishonest marketers and scammers another opportunity to reach people looking for affordable healthcare.
How fake health insurance ads can fool you

Let's say you're searching online for a more affordable health insurance plan. You type a few words into Google and see a sponsored result offering excellent coverage at a price that seems almost impossible to beat. The website looks professional. It might display a familiar logo or suggest a connection to a government program. You click through and enter your phone number to learn more. Before long, someone calls with an offer. They tell you that you qualify for special coverage and encourage you to sign up immediately. You may even hear that the deal expires today.

Here's where things can get tricky. The website might belong to a lead-generation business collecting information for insurance sellers. Lead generation itself is a legitimate practice, but misleading advertisements can send people toward products they never intended to buy. The FTC warns that scammers sometimes purchase search advertisements that imitate official websites. Some use addresses resembling HealthCare.gov or Medicare.gov. Others copy recognizable branding to create the appearance of legitimacy.

We've seen similar tactics with financial scams. CyberGuy previously reported on criminals buying Google ads to steal bank logins. In those cases, sponsored search results directed people to convincing fake banking websites. The same underlying trick can work with health insurance. When an advertisement appears near the top of your search results, it's easy to assume the company behind it has already been checked out. But a paid placement offers no guarantee that the seller or its claims are trustworthy.
The cheap health insurance plan that could cost you thousands

One of the FTC's biggest concerns involves products that look like comprehensive health insurance but offer limited protection. For example, some advertisements promote medical discount programs. You pay a fee and receive access to discounts from participating healthcare providers. While legitimate discount programs exist, they don't provide the same financial protection as comprehensive insurance.

Other products, such as fixed indemnity plans, may pay a predetermined amount when you receive certain medical services. Depending on the policy, that payment could fall far short of your actual bill. Think about what happens if you suddenly need emergency surgery. You might expect your insurance to help cover the expense. Instead, you discover that your plan pays only a limited benefit, leaving you responsible for a substantial portion of the charges.

That possibility makes understanding your coverage so important. Plans sold through the official Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace must cover essential health benefits, including emergency services and hospitalization. They also provide coverage for preexisting conditions. However, deductibles and other out-of-pocket costs can still apply.

You can review those protections directly through HealthCare.gov's explanation of Marketplace benefits at healthcare.gov/coverage/what-marketplace-plans-cover. Before purchasing any plan, ask exactly what type of coverage you're getting. A low monthly premium means very little if the policy leaves you exposed to major medical expenses.
HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS
Scammers use misleading online ads and fake health insurance websites to trick people into sharing personal information or purchasing inadequate coverage. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Why health insurance robocalls should raise suspicion

Have you ever answered your phone and heard a recorded message claiming you've been approved for an affordable health insurance plan? Maybe the recording tells you that you qualify for special benefits. It might even suggest that you're running out of time to claim them. Be skeptical.

The FTC's October 29 consumer warning specifically highlights illegal prerecorded telemarketing calls promoting health insurance. Unsolicited recorded insurance sales calls deserve particular caution. They may come from scammers or businesses using questionable marketing practices.

And don't assume a familiar name on your caller ID proves anything. Scammers can manipulate caller ID information to make calls appear to come from legitimate organizations. If you receive an unexpected insurance sales call, hang up. Then contact the insurer through a phone number you've independently verified.
Tips to protect yourself from health insurance scams
You don't need to become an insurance expert to avoid misleading offers. However, a few simple precautions can help you make a more informed decision before committing to a plan.

The safest starting point for comparing ACA Marketplace coverage is HealthCare.gov. You can also call the Marketplace directly at 1-800-318-2596. If your state operates its own Marketplace, the federal website can direct you there. Avoid starting your search through an unfamiliar advertisement or a link someone sends you unexpectedly. Typing the official website address into your browser gives you greater control over where your information goes.

A sponsored result means an advertiser paid for placement. It doesn't mean the government has approved the company or verified every claim in the advertisement. Check the website address before entering personal information. Watch for misspelled domains or websites that imitate official government branding. If something looks suspicious, close the page and navigate directly to the organization you're trying to reach.

Before enrolling, request the plan's Summary of Benefits and Coverage (SBC) when applicable. This document explains important costs and coverage details in a standardized format. Pay particular attention to deductibles and out-of-pocket limits. Check whether your doctors participate in the plan's network. Also, make sure the policy covers the medications or treatments you need. You can learn more about these documents through HealthCare.gov's Summary of Benefits and Coverage guide at healthcare.gov/health-care-law-protections/summary-of-benefits-and-coverage/.

The FTC specifically warns about misleading offers that promise cash rewards or other incentives for enrolling in healthcare plans. Now, legitimate Marketplace financial assistance does exist. Depending on your eligibility, premium tax credits can reduce what you pay for coverage. However, that assistance follows established eligibility rules. If someone promises guaranteed cash simply for signing up or refuses to explain the terms, take a closer look before providing personal information.

If you're considering a plan sold outside the official Marketplace, contact your state's insurance department. Ask whether the company and agent are properly licensed and whether the product provides the coverage being advertised. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners provides resources to help you find your state insurance regulator. Also, be cautious about anyone pressuring you to enroll immediately. Legitimate insurers should provide the information you need to review a policy before purchasing it.
FAKE SOCIAL SECURITY STATEMENT EMAIL HIDES A SCAM
Reviewing health insurance benefits and costs carefully during open enrollment can help you avoid misleading offers and expensive surprises. (iStock)

Health insurance applications can require sensitive information. That makes fake enrollment websites particularly dangerous. Never provide your Social Security number or banking details to someone who contacts you unexpectedly unless you've independently verified their identity and the reason they need the information. If you're unsure about an offer, contact the insurance company directly. You can also find trained Marketplace enrollment assistance through HealthCare.gov's official help page at healthcare.gov/find-assistance/.

Scammers may use fake health insurance websites, phishing emails or text messages to trick you into clicking malicious links. Strong antivirus software can help detect dangerous websites and block malware that could steal your passwords or personal information. Some security tools can also warn you about suspicious links before you open them. While antivirus protection can't tell you whether an insurance policy provides legitimate coverage, it adds another layer of protection when you're shopping online. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com.

Health insurance scams can expose some of your most sensitive information, including your Social Security number and financial details. An identity theft protection service can monitor for signs that criminals are misusing your information and alert you to suspicious activity. Some services also provide assistance if your identity is stolen. Keep in mind that these services can't prevent every type of fraud. If you've already shared sensitive information with a scammer, visit IdentityTheft.gov to learn what steps to take. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com.

If you create an account to compare or manage health insurance coverage, protect it with a strong, unique password. A password manager can help you create and store passwords without reusing them across multiple websites. Also, enable two-factor authentication (2FA) whenever it's available. That extra security step can make it harder for someone to access your account if your password gets stolen.
Important health insurance enrollment dates for 2027

If you're reviewing health insurance for next year, knowing the enrollment deadlines can also protect you from misleading sales pitches. According to the current HealthCare.gov enrollment calendar, federal Marketplace open enrollment for 2027 coverage began November 1, 2026, and ends January 15, 2027. However, there's another important deadline. To have your Marketplace coverage begin January 1, 2027, you generally need to enroll by December 15, 2026, and pay your first premium. Enrollments completed from December 16 through January 15 generally begin February 1, provided the first premium is paid.

Some state-operated Marketplaces may have different dates, so check your state's official website. Medicare operates on a separate schedule. Its annual open enrollment period runs from October 15 through December 7, 2026, for coverage changes taking effect January 1, 2027. If you're comparing Medicare plans, visit Medicare.gov or call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227). Knowing these dates makes it easier to question someone who calls with a supposedly urgent deadline that doesn't match the official schedule.
What to do if you've already responded to a suspicious insurance offer

Maybe you've already clicked an advertisement or spoken with someone about a plan that now seems questionable. Perhaps you've even paid an enrollment fee. The first thing I recommend is verifying whether you actually have insurance coverage. Contact the insurance company directly using its official phone number. Ask for confirmation of your policy and request written information explaining your benefits.

If you shared financial information with a suspicious seller, contact your bank or credit card company. Explain what happened and ask about protecting your account or disputing unauthorized charges. And if you provided sensitive identifying information to someone you suspect was a scammer, visit IdentityTheft.gov for guidance on protecting yourself.

You can also report misleading health insurance advertisements and illegal robocalls to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. The sooner you investigate a suspicious transaction or possible identity theft, the more options you may have to limit the damage.
Kurt's key takeaways

What concerns me most about these health insurance offers is how easily someone could believe they're protected when they're actually facing an enormous financial risk. Think about it. You pay your monthly bill, receive something that looks like an insurance card and assume you're covered. Then a medical emergency happens, and suddenly you discover your plan has serious limitations. That's a frightening position to be in, especially when medical expenses can add up so quickly. I also think this FTC warning says something important about how we shop online. We've become accustomed to seeing sponsored results at the top of our searches. But the company willing to pay for that placement may have little to do with the organization we're actually trying to reach. When it comes to health insurance, I would always start with the official Marketplace or a company I've independently verified. And before signing anything, I want to know exactly what happens if I end up in the emergency room. That's the question that can reveal whether a seemingly affordable plan will actually protect you.

title: Is AI deciding who's dangerous in Michigan prisons?
summary: Michigan's new prison scoring system claims 30% better violence prediction, but Recidiviz says it doesn't actually use AI to classify inmates.
story: Incarcerated men participate in employment counseling at a Michigan prison, where security classifications can affect access to job training and educational opportunities. (Michigan Department of Corrections)

What if a computer-generated score could influence whether someone lives in a low-security prison dorm or a tightly controlled cell? Michigan is preparing to test new technology that could affect exactly that.

State officials say the system could improve predictions of future prison violence by approximately 30%. That's a big claim, especially when the safety of correctional officers and incarcerated people could depend on getting those assessments right.

But there's something important missing from early reports about Michigan prison AI. Despite headlines suggesting artificial intelligence will determine how dangerous someone might be, the nonprofit developing the software says AI plays no role in calculating security scores.

Instead, the technology follows predetermined rules, and corrections staff make the final decisions. So, how does the system work? And can Michigan really predict prison violence more accurately without putting too much trust in a computer-generated score?
FEDERAL INMATES MAY SOON GET TABLETS WITH MESSAGING CAPABILITIES AS BUREAU OF PRISONS MAKES MODERNIZATION PUSH
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
