title: Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production after sales slump
summary: Tesla Cybertruck production is winding down at Gigafactory Texas to make room for Cybercab robotaxi manufacturing, but key questions remain for owners.
story: Elon Musk takes aim at Waymo over animal collisions and touts a Tesla robotaxi update to detect pets at night during a Tesla Owners of Silicon Valley livestream. Credit: Tesla Owners of Silicon Valley

You have to give Tesla credit for one thing. The Cybertruck certainly got people talking. With its sharp angles and stainless steel body, it looked unlike anything else pulling into a supermarket parking lot. Some people loved it. Others couldn't understand why anyone would want one. Either way, you couldn't miss it. Now, the truck that Elon Musk once promoted as the future of pickup trucks appears to be heading toward an early retirement.

On November 6, 2026, Musk announced plans to wind down Tesla Cybertruck production at its Texas factory around the middle of 2027. The reason? Tesla wants to make more Cybercabs, its self-driving taxis. For a vehicle that arrived with enormous expectations, that's quite a turnaround. And if you already own a Cybertruck, you may be wondering what this means for your investment.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
TESLA ROADSTER FLIES, FLIPS AND HITS 60 MPH IN A FLASH
Tesla's Cybertruck made a bold entrance with its stainless steel body and angular design, but disappointing sales are now threatening its future. (Reginald Mathalone/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Why Tesla Cybertruck production is winding down

Musk made the announcement in a post on X, explaining that Tesla plans to use more of its Texas factory for Cybercab production. The move signals a major change in direction for a company that once expected the Cybertruck to become a significant part of its vehicle lineup. However, there's an important detail worth pointing out. Musk specifically discussed winding down production at Gigafactory Texas. Tesla has not confirmed whether it will move Cybertruck manufacturing elsewhere or discontinue the vehicle entirely. Texas is currently the only known Tesla factory equipped to manufacture its specialized stainless steel body components.

Still, the announcement raises an obvious question. Why would Tesla scale back one of its most recognizable vehicles so soon after introducing it? The sales numbers offer a pretty convincing explanation.
We reached out to Tesla for clarification on its Cybertruck production plans and what they mean for current owners, but did not hear back before our publication deadline.
Cybertruck sales never lived up to the hype

When Tesla unveiled the Cybertruck in November 2019, enthusiasm seemed enormous. Musk reported approximately 250,000 reservations within five days. At one point, he suggested demand could support annual sales of 250,000 vehicles. There was plenty of excitement. But those early reservations required relatively small refundable deposits, and many never became actual vehicle purchases. According to Kelley Blue Book estimates, Tesla reportedly sold 38,965 Cybertrucks in the United States during 2024. That number dropped to just 20,237 in 2025, a decline of 48%. Things didn't improve much in 2026. Kelley Blue Book data indicates that Tesla sold 11,586 Cybertrucks during the first nine months of the year, down 28% compared with the same period in 2025.

Those figures tell a very different story from the excitement surrounding the original launch. And then there's the price. Tesla originally promised a single-motor Cybertruck starting at $39,900 when it unveiled the truck in 2019. That model never reached customers at the advertised price. On November 5, 2026, Tesla raised Cybertruck prices again. The Dual-Motor AWD version climbed to $82,490, although Tesla paused new orders for that model. That left the Premium AWD as the least expensive version available to order, starting at $92,490 before additional fees. Of course, the Cybertruck offers impressive technology, including powerful electric motors and the ability to supply electricity to external equipment. But at those prices, buyers have plenty of other vehicles to consider.
ELON MUSK REVEALS PRICE OF TESLA'S CYBERCAB
Tesla plans to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas by mid-2027 as Elon Musk shifts the company's focus toward self-driving vehicles. (Getty Images)
Cybertruck recalls added to its problems

Sales were only part of the Cybertruck's difficult journey. The vehicle also developed a reputation for recalls and manufacturing concerns. According to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, Tesla has issued 11 Cybertruck recalls since customer deliveries began in late 2023. Some involved software problems that Tesla could fix remotely. Others required owners to have their vehicles physically repaired. One of the most concerning recalls came in April 2024, when Tesla recalled 3,878 Cybertrucks because an accelerator pedal pad could come loose. In certain circumstances, the pad could become trapped by interior trim and leave the accelerator pressed down, increasing the risk of a crash. Then, in March 2025, Tesla recalled 46,096 Cybertrucks because a stainless steel exterior trim panel could detach while driving. That created a potential hazard for other motorists.

The problems continued in 2026. An April recall affected 173 Cybertrucks equipped with certain 18-inch steel wheels. Tesla warned that cracks could develop around brake rotor stud holes, potentially allowing a wheel stud to separate from the hub. That could increase the risk of losing vehicle control. Importantly, Tesla reported no known crashes, injuries or fatalities related to that particular defect when it issued the recall. To be fair, these recalls varied significantly in severity and the number of vehicles affected. A recall alone doesn't establish that every Cybertruck has a safety problem. However, repeated headlines about repairs hardly helped a vehicle already struggling to attract buyers. And remember the famous Cybertruck unveiling? During the 2019 demonstration, two windows cracked when Tesla attempted to demonstrate the strength of the glass. That moment went viral before the first customer ever drove one home.
Tesla is betting its future on Cybercab

Tesla is making room for a car you may never actually drive. It's called Cybercab, and Musk believes these two-seat, self-driving taxis could become a huge part of Tesla's future. There's no steering wheel or traditional pedals. You get in, tell it where you want to go and let the technology do the driving. At least, that's the idea.

Tesla began carrying paying Cybercab passengers in Austin, Texas, in September 2026. We've already covered some of the restrictions Tesla has placed on younger passengers. And while the technology sounds promising, there are still some important questions about safety. Federal regulators are examining how Tesla certified that Cybercab meets vehicle safety standards. That review has yet to establish any safety violations, but Tesla still has questions to answer.

What I find especially interesting is how much Musk is willing to bet on this technology. He's scaling back a pickup truck people waited years to buy so Tesla can build more vehicles that drive themselves. That's a pretty big gamble, especially when self-driving technology still has plenty to prove. And I wonder how many people are actually ready to climb into a car with no steering wheel and trust it to get them home safely.
TESLA TO WIND DOWN CYBERTRUCK PRODUCTION AT TEXAS FACTORY NEXT YEAR TO MAKE ROOM FOR CYBERCAB
Tesla is betting on its driverless two-seater, scaling back production of the Cybertruck to increase its output of Cybercabs. (Photo by Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu via Getty Images)
What this means to you

If you already own a Cybertruck, there's no reason to panic or rush out and sell it because of this announcement. Tesla has not announced that existing owners will lose warranty coverage or access to service. Tesla currently lists a basic vehicle warranty of four years or 50,000 miles for new Cybertrucks, whichever comes first. Its battery and drive unit warranty runs eight years or 150,000 miles, subject to the applicable terms. You can review the details on Tesla's official warranty page. However, the long-term availability of replacement parts deserves attention, especially given the truck's specialized body panels. Tesla has not provided a detailed public explanation of how its production plans will affect future parts supplies.

If you're thinking about buying a Cybertruck, consider how long you intend to keep it. Ask Tesla about service support and any outstanding recalls before making a purchase. You can check whether a specific vehicle has an open safety recall by entering its VIN at NHTSA's recall website. Resale value is another consideration. Limited production sometimes makes a vehicle more desirable to collectors. However, weaker demand can push prices in the opposite direction. Nobody can say with certainty where Cybertruck values will go. And if you're shopping for any expensive new vehicle, the Cybertruck offers a useful reminder. Exciting technology can attract attention, but long-term ownership costs deserve just as much consideration.
Kurt's key takeaways

Here's what gets me about the Cybertruck. Tesla spent years building up excitement around this vehicle. People put down deposits, waited for deliveries and ended up paying a lot more than the original advertised price. Now, roughly three years after the first trucks reached customers, Tesla is preparing to move on. I understand why Musk is excited about Cybercab. The idea of getting into a car and having it drive you home is pretty remarkable. But if I owned a Cybertruck, I'd want some reassurance that Tesla will continue supporting it for years to come. These owners spent serious money believing in Tesla's vision. I think they deserve some straight answers about what happens next.

title: Is someone already using your identity? Check these 8 places
summary: Identity theft can hide in phone accounts, medical records and utility bills long before it shows on a credit report. Eight places to check now.
story: Kurt 'CyberGuy' Knutsson joins 'Fox & Friends First' to discuss the threat of rogue artificial intelligence agents targeting bank accounts.
When people think about identity theft, they often start with a credit report or bank statement.

Those are important places to look, but they are not the only ones. Someone using your identity may be trying to open a phone line, start utility service, use medical benefits or create a payment plan that never appears on your usual accounts.

The warning signs of identity theft can be easy to miss, especially when fraudulent activity happens outside your primary financial accounts. You do not need to investigate every record today. Start with these eight places, focusing first on accounts that could cause the most damage.
SOMEONE COULD HAVE OPENED AN ACCOUNT IN YOUR NAME. CHECK NOW
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

Identity theft can go undetected when criminals use stolen personal information to open phone accounts, obtain medical care or sign up for utility services. (Bildquelle/ullstein bild via Getty Images)
1. Bank accounts, credit cards and payment apps

Review checking, savings, credit card, investment, retirement and payment-app activity for transactions you do not recognize. Look beyond purchases. A new external bank connection, authorized user, payment method, mailing address or phone number can also signal an unauthorized account change. Turn on transaction and security alerts wherever your financial institution offers them. If you find an unfamiliar transaction, contact the institution through its official website or the number on your statement. Do not use a number from a suspicious text or email.
2. Credit reports and new inquiries

Check all three major credit reports for accounts, hard inquiries, collections, addresses or employers you do not recognize. A fraudulent credit card, personal loan or retail-financing account may appear here even when your checking account looks normal. Use AnnualCreditReport.com to access your reports. You can currently request free online credit reports from Equifax, Experian and TransUnion once a week. An unfamiliar entry does not automatically mean fraud. Some lenders operate under different business names. Verify questionable information with the company before disputing it.
Pro tip: Consider freezing your credit with all three bureaus. Credit freezes are free, do not affect your credit score and can make it harder for someone to open new credit accounts in your name.
3. Buy now, pay later and retail accounts

Buy now, pay later services and store-financing accounts can be easy to overlook because they may not feel like traditional credit cards. Check services you have used for unfamiliar orders, payment plans, saved addresses or account-opening messages. Some buy now, pay later loans may not appear on your traditional credit reports.

Reporting practices vary by provider and loan type. Search your inbox for purchase confirmations, shipping notices and payment reminders you did not expect. Open the retailer's official app or type its web address yourself rather than clicking a link in an unexpected message.
4. Phone and mobile carrier accounts

Your phone number can provide access to other accounts because it may receive verification codes and password-reset messages. Review your carrier account for unfamiliar devices, lines, eSIMs, upgrades, address changes or changes to your account PIN. A sudden loss of cellular service can be an early warning sign of a SIM swap, although outages and equipment problems can have other explanations. Contact your carrier through an official channel if the change is unexpected.
Pro tip: Ask your carrier about account PINs, port-out protection and SIM-swap security features. These safeguards may help prevent someone from transferring your number without authorization.
5. Utilities and household services

Review electric, gas, water, internet and other household service accounts. Someone using your name or personal information may try to start service, change an account or leave an unpaid balance behind. Utility fraud may not appear on your credit report immediately. A bill, welcome email, service appointment or shutoff notice for an account you did not request is worth investigating.

You can also request a report from the National Consumer Telecom & Utilities Exchange (NCTUE). This specialty reporting service collects information from participating phone, pay-TV and utility companies.

You are entitled to one free NCTUE report every 12 months upon request. It may reveal accounts or service requests missing from your traditional credit reports, although it does not cover every provider. If you find an unfamiliar account, note the date, address and service details. Then contact the company and ask which information was used to open or change the account.
6. Medical and insurance records

Look for explanations of benefits, medical bills, prescription notices or insurance communications related to care you did not receive. Medical identity theft can create an unexpected bill, but it can also place incorrect information in your medical record. For example, someone may use your insurance information to obtain treatment, leaving behind records that could affect future care or insurance claims.

If something looks unfamiliar, contact the provider or insurer directly and ask for the records connected to the claim. Do not ignore a small bill simply because the amount seems insignificant. The inaccurate medical information may be a bigger concern.
7. Government, tax and employment records

Watch for notices from the IRS, Social Security Administration or a state benefits agency that do not match your situation. Examples include income reported by an unfamiliar employer, a tax return you did not file or unemployment benefits claimed in your name.

You can review tax information through your IRS online account. You can also check your earnings history through your "my Social Security" account. If you notice unfamiliar earnings, contact the Social Security Administration about correcting your record.

Pro tip: Consider requesting an IRS Identity Protection PIN. This free, six-digit number helps prevent someone else from filing a federal tax return using your Social Security number. You can learn more at IRS.gov.

Always use official government websites to review or report suspicious activity. If an unexpected message claims to come from an agency, do not follow its links. Find the agency's website independently.
8. Email, social accounts and recovery settings

Your email and social accounts may not show a financial loss, but they can reveal whether someone is trying to take over your digital identity. Review recent sign-ins, sent messages, forwarding rules, recovery addresses, trusted devices and connected apps.

Email deserves special attention because someone with access to your inbox may be able to reset passwords for other accounts. If you see unfamiliar access, change your password from a trusted device, sign out unfamiliar sessions and enable stronger multifactor authentication. Where available, use an authenticator app, passkey or security key rather than relying only on text-message verification codes.
IDENTITY RESTORATION: WHAT TO DO AFTER IDENTITY THEFT
A clean credit report does not rule out identity theft. Checking eight types of accounts and records can help uncover suspicious activity. (Peter Dazeley/Getty Images)
How to check without making it a full-time job
Spread the review across four short sessions:

Session 1: Check email, banking and phone account settings.Session 2: Review credit reports and buy now, pay later accounts.Session 3: Examine utilities, phone-service records and medical claims.Session 4: Review government records, tax information and employment history.
Session 1: Check email, banking and phone account settings.
Session 2: Review credit reports and buy now, pay later accounts.
Session 3: Examine utilities, phone-service records and medical claims.
Session 4: Review government records, tax information and employment history.

If nothing looks unusual, record the date of your review. The goal is to recognize unfamiliar activity, not question every legitimate bill. However, do not wait for a scheduled review if you receive a suspicious account alert or discover a potentially fraudulent transaction. Investigate those warnings immediately.
How to tell whether an alert deserves attention

An unfamiliar message does not always mean identity theft. A lender may use a business name you do not recognize, a family member may have used a shared device or a service provider may have changed its billing name. Look for related warning signs. A new account combined with an unfamiliar address, phone change or collection notice deserves immediate attention.

Even a single unauthorized transaction or account opening warrants investigation. When you are unsure, compare the record with your own statements and contact the company to explain the mismatch. Do not confirm sensitive personal details to an unexpected caller. Contact the company yourself using a verified number.
What to save when you find something unusual

Keep the original bill, email or letter, but do not click links inside an unexpected message. Write down the date, company name, account or service involved and the first sign that something was wrong. If you call, record the department, case number and follow-up date. For credit issues, save relevant copies of all three reports.

For phone, bank or email issues, keep account change notices and screenshots. Store these records securely so you can refer to them when speaking with the company, a credit bureau or an identity theft recovery specialist.
If the account is old or the name looks unfamiliar

Do not assume an unfamiliar record is fraudulent simply because you do not recognize the company name. A lender, utility provider or collection agency may use a parent company name. Contact the organization using verified contact information.

Ask for the date the account was opened, the address associated with it and the steps required to confirm whether it belongs to you. If the company confirms the account is fraudulent, ask for a fraud case number and written instructions. Then add the issue to your records and check whether related activity appears elsewhere.
How identity monitoring can help protect against identity theft

Checking your accounts regularly is a smart first step, but identity theft can happen between reviews. Identity monitoring tools can help by watching for certain changes involving your personal information and alerting you when something suspicious appears.

Some services monitor credit activity, financial accounts, personal information found in data breaches and certain types of account openings. Depending on the service, you may receive alerts about unfamiliar credit inquiries, changes to your personal information or possible misuse of your identity.
Not all identity monitoring services offer the same protection. Before signing up, consider these features:

Credit monitoring: Alerts you to certain changes to your credit reports, including new accounts and inquiries.Financial account alerts: Helps identify unusual transactions or changes to connected financial accounts.Personal information monitoring: Looks for certain exposures of your personal information, including data found in known breaches.Identity restoration assistance: Some services provide specialists who can help you navigate the recovery process after identity theft.Reimbursement coverage: Certain paid plans offer coverage for eligible identity theft expenses or stolen funds, subject to limits and exclusions.
Credit monitoring: Alerts you to certain changes to your credit reports, including new accounts and inquiries.
Financial account alerts: Helps identify unusual transactions or changes to connected financial accounts.
Personal information monitoring: Looks for certain exposures of your personal information, including data found in known breaches.
Identity restoration assistance: Some services provide specialists who can help you navigate the recovery process after identity theft.
Reimbursement coverage: Certain paid plans offer coverage for eligible identity theft expenses or stolen funds, subject to limits and exclusions.

One advantage of using an identity monitoring service is having someone keeping watch for suspicious activity even when you are not actively checking your accounts. Depending on the provider and plan, these services can monitor multiple sources of information and send alerts when something needs your attention. Some also provide dedicated restoration specialists who can help guide you through the recovery process if your identity is stolen.

A paid identity monitoring service may be worth considering if you want more comprehensive monitoring and additional support when problems arise. Look for a plan that covers the types of activity most relevant to you and offers timely alerts. While no service can catch every form of identity theft, combining professional monitoring with your existing account security settings can give you an additional layer of protection. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com
What to do if you find something unfamiliar

Contact the company: Use its official website or a verified number and ask for its fraud department.Verify the activity: Ask which account, order, claim or service is connected to your information.Secure your accounts: Change compromised or reused passwords, update security settings and ask the company to close or freeze fraudulent accounts.Protect your credit: Consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. You can also place a free fraud alert by contacting one bureau, which must notify the other two.Report identity theft: Visit IdentityTheft.gov when appropriate to file a report and receive a personalized recovery plan.Keep documentation: Store confirmation numbers, names, relevant correspondence and follow-up dates in one secure place.
Contact the company: Use its official website or a verified number and ask for its fraud department.
Verify the activity: Ask which account, order, claim or service is connected to your information.
Secure your accounts: Change compromised or reused passwords, update security settings and ask the company to close or freeze fraudulent accounts.
Protect your credit: Consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. You can also place a free fraud alert by contacting one bureau, which must notify the other two.
Report identity theft: Visit IdentityTheft.gov when appropriate to file a report and receive a personalized recovery plan.
Keep documentation: Store confirmation numbers, names, relevant correspondence and follow-up dates in one secure place.

Pro tip: Start with the four highest-impact places: If you only have a few minutes, check your email, bank accounts, phone account and credit reports first. Those areas can help reveal whether someone is trying to access your information, move money, receive verification codes or open new credit. A clean credit report does not rule out identity theft, so return to the other four places when you have time.
YOUR BANK MAY STOP TEXTING YOU SIX-DIGIT CODES

Fraudulent payment plans, unfamiliar phone lines and unexpected medical bills could signal identity theft that traditional credit monitoring misses. (Celine Frohnapfel/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I think one of the biggest mistakes people make with identity theft is assuming that a clean credit report means they're in the clear. Someone could be using your information to open a phone line, get medical care or run up a utility bill, and you might not find out until much later. I'd start by checking your email, bank accounts and wireless carrier settings. Then pull your free credit reports and take a closer look at places you might normally overlook.

I'm also a big believer in freezing your credit before there's a problem. It's free, and you can temporarily lift the freeze when you need to apply for credit. Identity monitoring can provide another layer of protection, but no service can monitor everything. That's why it's important to keep an eye on your accounts, too. The sooner you spot an unfamiliar account or transaction, the sooner you can start limiting the damage.

title: Chainsaw robot looks terrifying but has a real job
summary: JR East's towering ZIZAI ZX-3 chainsaw robot tackles dangerous branch-cutting along Japan's Koumi Line while a trained operator controls it remotely.
story: Theologian Jonathan Morris discusses spirituality in artificial intelligence after developers consult religious scholars on moral AI.

If you saw a humanoid robot holding a chainsaw next to train tracks, you'd probably do a double take. I know I would. But that's exactly what's happening in Japan, where a towering chainsaw robot is cutting back branches that could interfere with passing trains. It's a little intimidating to watch, especially when you see how high this machine can reach. Still, there's a pretty good reason railway crews are putting it to work.

Japan's JR East railway company is using the chainsaw robot to handle dangerous maintenance jobs that would normally require workers to operate heavy cutting equipment high above the ground. The robot does the physical work while a person controls its movements from a safer location.
I find that reassuring, especially when a chainsaw is involved. So, how does this unusual machine actually work, and could it change the way dangerous maintenance jobs get done?
HUMANOID ROBOTS PERFORM LIVE SURGERY IN WORLD FIRST
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover five ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay and downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
A humanoid robot equipped with a chainsaw trims overgrown branches along a railway line in Japan, allowing maintenance crews to work from a safer distance. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How the chainsaw robot clears railway tracks

The robot has been put to work along JR East's Koumi Line in central Japan, where overgrown branches can create problems for passing trains. What's interesting is how the machine actually handles the cutting. One mechanical arm grips a branch while the other operates the chainsaw.

The robot's upper body extends from a boom mounted on a specialized maintenance vehicle, allowing it to reach high above the tracks. That means workers can tackle branches that would normally require someone to operate cutting equipment at height.

The robot even has a name, ZIZAI ZX-3. Japanese manufacturer Nippon Signal announced its delivery to JR East earlier this year. The machine began full-scale maintenance work along the Koumi Line in October. And this technology already has some experience behind it.

JR West started using a related robotic system in July 2024. What's especially appealing about this approach is that the machine takes on the dangerous physical work while a trained operator stays at a safer distance.
Who's actually controlling this chainsaw robot?

Now, before you start worrying about robots running around with chainsaws, the ZX-3 is actually controlled by a person. A trained operator guides the robot remotely, deciding where to position its arms and when to start cutting. That's important because working near railway tracks requires careful attention. One wrong move could damage equipment or put someone in danger. So, while the robot handles the heavy lifting, a human still makes the decisions.

Nippon Signal designed the ZX-3 to make it easier for workers to control the robot's movements. Right now, its main job is cutting back trees and branches that grow too close to railway lines. However, the company hopes to give it additional tools so it can handle other maintenance work in the future.

And here's what I find interesting. Workers still need the skills to do the job, but now they can operate the equipment from a safer location. That's a pretty big change when you're talking about working high above train tracks with a chainsaw.
Why railway companies are turning to robots

Keeping train tracks clear takes more work than you might realize. Branches can grow close enough to interfere with passing trains, and cutting them back sometimes means sending workers high above the tracks with heavy equipment. That brings some serious safety risks, especially when crews are working near electrical infrastructure. Japan is also dealing with a shortage of skilled workers, so JR East is looking for ways to make these jobs safer and less physically demanding.

That's where the chainsaw robot comes in. It can reach areas that would be difficult or dangerous for workers to access while the operator stays at a safer distance. JR East is also changing when some of this work gets done. Since 2022, the company has been moving certain maintenance jobs along the Koumi Line into daytime hours instead of having crews work overnight.

That sometimes means temporarily canceling trains, which I'm sure passengers aren't thrilled about. But it also gives workers better conditions and more manageable schedules. And when you combine that with a robot that can handle dangerous cutting work, you can see why JR East is investing in this technology.
NEW AI BRAIN LETS ROBOTS MOVE LIKE HUMANS
Japan's JR East railway company is deploying a remotely operated chainsaw robot to clear vegetation near train tracks and reduce risks for maintenance workers. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Could AI eventually control a robot with a chainsaw?

Now this is where I start having a few more questions. JR East has been investing in artificial intelligence and robotics across its railway operations. The company is exploring ways to use AI for equipment inspections and other maintenance activities. Its broader technology plans include robots that can help inspect infrastructure. That raises an interesting possibility. Could a future version of this chainsaw robot identify an overgrown branch and cut it without someone guiding every movement?

It's certainly a direction robotics developers could explore. AI-powered image analysis could help identify vegetation that threatens railway operations. More advanced systems might eventually assist with some of the decisions an operator makes today. But there's an important difference between what might be possible and what JR East has actually announced.

The ZX-3 currently relies on human control, and JR East has not announced a timeline for making its chainsaw operation fully autonomous. Personally, I think that's worth emphasizing. Giving a robot greater independence sounds impressive until you consider what happens if it misidentifies an object or someone enters its working area. We recently covered how humanoid robots are getting new workplace safety systems. Those safeguards will become even more important as machines take on jobs involving powerful tools.
What this means to you

You may never see this particular chainsaw robot working near your local train station. However, the technology behind it could eventually change how infrastructure gets maintained closer to home. If you ride commuter trains, you already know how frustrating delays can be. Overgrown vegetation can contribute to service disruptions, and railway companies spend considerable time keeping tracks clear. Equipment that helps crews perform those jobs safely and efficiently could eventually benefit passengers. There are potential applications beyond railways, too.

Utility companies regularly need to trim vegetation around power lines. Construction crews also handle dangerous work in areas that are difficult to reach. Remotely operated machines could help reduce some of those risks.

Of course, there's another side to this. As robots become more capable, companies will need workers who know how to operate and maintain them. That could create opportunities for new skills while changing the way traditional maintenance jobs are performed. A

nd while robots can reduce certain dangers, they bring their own safety concerns. A machine handling a chainsaw still needs reliable controls and proper oversight. For now, the ZX-3 shows how robotics can help people perform hazardous work without placing them directly in the path of danger.
ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM
The ZIZAI ZX-3 robot uses one mechanical arm to grip branches and another to operate a chainsaw while a human operator controls its movements. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Kurt's key takeaways

I've seen plenty of humanoid robots doing backflips and showing off what they can do. But there's something different about watching one actually earn its keep. Seeing this robot handle a chainsaw high above the tracks makes me think about the risks workers face doing that job themselves. And if it can help keep railway workers out of dangerous situations, I am all for it. What I especially like is that there's still a person making the decisions. The operator brings the experience while the machine takes on the physically demanding work.

That seems like a sensible way to introduce robotics into jobs where mistakes can have serious consequences. What I'll be watching is how quickly companies push these machines toward greater independence. AI is advancing, and I suspect we'll see more robots taking on jobs that once seemed impossible to automate. But when the tool in a robot's hand is a chainsaw, I want to know someone is paying very close attention.
Would you trust a fully autonomous robot to operate a chainsaw near the trains you ride? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Homeland Security data leak exposes 41K workers
summary: A massive DHS data leak exposed records of over 41,000 employees, revealing links to undercover ICE operations, Palantir tools and AI platforms.
story: The Department of Homeland Security is investigating a massive data leak reportedly exposing the personal information of roughly 40,000 employees, including thousands of ICE and Border Patrol personnel and several undercover agents.

You might think an employee directory sounds pretty harmless. After all, most workplaces keep lists of names and phone numbers so people can reach one another. But what happens when that information belongs to thousands of federal agents, including people connected to undercover investigations?

A massive Homeland Security data leak has exposed records involving more than 41,000 employees and contractors. The information includes contact details, office locations and internal access groups tied to sensitive government operations. Some records even point to surveillance programs and artificial intelligence tools used within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Now, federal officials are scrambling to contain the fallout as concerns grow over the safety of agents and their families. And there's a bigger cybersecurity lesson here that applies well beyond Washington.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
DHS INVESTIGATES MASSIVE DATA BREACH EXPOSING 40,000 EMPLOYEES, INCLUDING ICE AND BORDER PATROL AGENTS

A massive Homeland Security data leak exposed records involving more than 41,000 employees and contractors, including personnel connected to undercover ICE operations. (Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
What the Homeland Security data leak exposed

On Oct. 28, the nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets published a collection of DHS records under the name Icepick. The information reportedly came from a group calling itself the Department of Peace, which claims it obtained access to internal government systems. The records reportedly cover DHS and seven of its component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

The files contain employee names, agency email addresses and workplace locations. They also include phone numbers, some identified as cell phone numbers, along with supervisors and internal access-group memberships. However, it has not been established that employees' private home addresses were included. CBP accounts for more than half the records, while roughly 10,000 involve ICE. Another 6,200 are tied to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. The records were last updated on Aug. 19, so some assignments may have changed. That's an enormous amount of organizational information to have floating around publicly. And the deeper researchers looked, the more sensitive the findings became.
Undercover ICE operations appear in leaked records

One of the most alarming findings involves internal groups associated with undercover investigations. WIRED identified 39 Homeland Security Investigations employees connected to access groups referencing certified undercover operations. Other groups reference communications interception programs and surveillance technology. The files also reveal reporting relationships that could help someone understand how different parts of DHS work together.

That raises a difficult security concern. People conducting undercover investigations depend on keeping certain relationships and assignments confidential. Revealing those connections could create risks for ongoing operations. Still, membership in an internal access group does not automatically confirm that every person listed was working undercover. The leaked records offer clues about sensitive assignments, but they don't establish every individual's operational role. Former acting ICE director John Sandweg called the exposure a "nightmare scenario". He warned that revealing agents' identities could put people in danger and interfere with criminal investigations.
Why Palantir and Grok appear in the DHS leak

Here's another part of this story that caught my attention. The leaked records reveal internal access groups referencing technology used for investigations and government operations. Some groups mention Palantir's Falcon investigative platform, which helps investigators analyze information. Others reference surveillance-related software, including tools used to examine phone records.

Then there's artificial intelligence. WIRED found groups mentioning OpenAI's ChatGPT, Google's Gemini and Microsoft's Copilot. One group labeled "Grok.com" included eight DHS technology officials. That doesn't prove these employees actively used the services or that the technology companies experienced breaches. The group names can reflect access permissions rather than actual activity. Even so, the information offers outsiders a closer look at the technologies DHS personnel may have access to. For an agency responsible for national security, those internal details can be valuable to people looking for weaknesses.
FBI SAYS SOURCE OF ITS JOBS PORTAL BREACH STILL UNKNOWN AS HACKERS ALLEGE EMPLOYEE DATA COMPROMISED
Leaked DHS records reveal internal access groups tied to surveillance technology and AI tools, including Palantir and Grok. (iStock; Victor J. Blue/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
How did hackers get access to Homeland Security records?

The group claiming responsibility says it accessed the information through DHS's Okta sign-in system. Okta provides identity and access-management technology that organizations use to control employee logins. However, Okta says it has no evidence that its own systems or data were compromised. That leaves the actual entry point unresolved.

DHS has acknowledged a potential breach and says it is investigating. The department has not publicly confirmed how the information was obtained. It's also important to understand what has been established so far. The reporting centers on personnel information and access-group details. It has not confirmed that employee passwords, intercepted communications or investigative case files were included. Until investigators explain what happened, there's no reliable basis for blaming a specific vulnerability or software provider.

We reached out to the Department of Homeland Security and Okta for additional comment. A DHS spokesperson provided the following statement: "DHS is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected. We will update the public when more information is available." Okta had not responded to our request for additional comment by our deadline.
DHS tries to remove leaked employee information

As the records spread online, DHS moved to limit access. On Oct. 29, a company reportedly authorized to seek content removals on behalf of ICE contacted Icelandic hosting provider FlokiNET. The request warned that the database exposed more than 40,000 identifiable individuals to potential harassment and physical harm. However, the hosting company declined to remove the material, saying the records contained workplace contact information rather than private home contact details.

The database briefly became inaccessible before appearing again elsewhere. Then, on Oct. 30, SITE Intelligence Group had reportedly identified threatening online rhetoric following the release. Some social media users reportedly threatened immigration officers and their families. Those reports raise additional concerns about what happens after sensitive personnel information becomes searchable. Even if the original files disappear, copies may already exist elsewhere.
Why this data leak should concern people outside government

You might be wondering why a federal employee database should concern someone who works in an office, owns a small business or has nothing to do with immigration enforcement. Think about how a convincing scam works. Someone contacts you claiming to be from your company's IT department. They know your supervisor's name and your work email address. They even mention an internal system you're familiar with. Suddenly, that unexpected message sounds a lot more believable.

That's the danger when attackers combine workplace records with information they find elsewhere online. They can use those details to create personalized phishing messages or impersonate trusted colleagues. We've seen related concerns before. In our reporting on the FBI hack claim involving sensitive personnel data, we examined how employee information could expose individuals and their families to additional risks. And that's what concerns me about this latest incident. Even information that seems routine can become dangerous when someone connects it to other records.
Security experts warn that exposed employee information could fuel targeted phishing attacks, impersonation scams and threats against federal workers and their families. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Tips to protect yourself from workplace data leaks
You may have no control over how your employer stores its records. However, there are ways to reduce the amount of personal information available about you and make targeted scams harder to pull off.

If someone contacts you claiming to be from your employer's IT department, don't assume they're legitimate because they know your name or job title. Contact your IT department using a phone number or communication channel you already trust. Avoid clicking links in unexpected password-reset emails, especially when the message creates urgency. A convincing message can still lead to a fake login page designed to steal your credentials.

Your primary email account deserves special attention because criminals may use it to reset passwords for other services. Use a strong, unique password for every important account and consider a reputable password manager to create and store them. Turn on multifactor authentication or passkeys wherever available. Also review your recovery email addresses and phone numbers to make sure nobody has changed them without your permission.

Once criminals have detailed information about you, they may send phishing messages containing malicious links or infected attachments. Strong antivirus software can provide an additional layer of protection by helping detect malicious downloads, known phishing websites and malware before they cause damage. Keep your operating system and security software updated so you receive the latest protections. Antivirus software cannot remove your information from a leaked database. However, it can help protect your devices against attacks that may follow an exposure. No security tool catches every threat, so continue checking unexpected messages carefully. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Here's something I strongly recommend considering. Data brokers collect personal information from public records and online sources. That information can include your home address, personal phone number and details about relatives. When someone already has your workplace information, finding additional personal details may make harassment or impersonation attempts easier. A reputable data removal service can help remove your personal information from participating data broker and people-search websites. Services such as Incogni automate removal requests and continue checking for information that reappears. You can also contact individual data brokers yourself, although that takes more time and ongoing follow-up. Keep in mind that these services cannot guarantee removal from every website or erase the original DHS leak. For more information, see our guide on how to remove your personal information from the web and keep it from coming back. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Search your own name and see what appears. You may discover old professional profiles, forgotten social media accounts or websites showing personal contact details. Check the privacy settings on your social media accounts and limit how much information strangers can see about your family. Be especially careful about publicly revealing your home location or daily routine if you work in a sensitive position. If you discover unwanted personal information online, contact the website or platform and request removal where possible.

The reported DHS records center on workplace information. So far, there has been no confirmation that Social Security numbers or financial account details were included. Still, exposed contact information can help criminals build more convincing scams. Monitor your important accounts for unfamiliar activity and pay attention to suspicious password-reset messages. If you discover that sensitive identity information has been compromised elsewhere, consider freezing your credit with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. Identity monitoring services may also help flag certain signs of fraud. However, they cannot prevent every type of identity theft or guarantee that your information will stay private. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

If someone uses your workplace information to impersonate a colleague or threaten you, document what happened. Save relevant emails, screenshots and messages, then report the incident to your employer's security team. If you receive threats of violence, contact law enforcement. You can also report suspected internet crime through the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov/. If you're an employee whose information may be involved in a breach, ask your employer whether you were affected and what protective steps it recommends. Don't rely on unsolicited callers claiming they can verify your exposure.
Kurt's key takeaways

What strikes me about this Homeland Security leak is how much damage a collection of workplace records could potentially cause. We're talking about information that many organizations use every day to help employees do their jobs. Yet in the wrong hands, those same details can help identify people involved in sensitive operations or make targeted scams much more convincing. I also believe there's an important conversation to be had about government transparency. Americans have a right to question how federal agencies operate and how officers are held accountable. But I worry about the consequences when information tied to undercover personnel becomes publicly searchable, especially now that threats against employees and their families have been reported. For me, the biggest unanswered question is how DHS allowed this information to become exposed in the first place. The department needs to explain what happened and how it plans to prevent another incident. In the meantime, there's a lesson here for all of us. Pay attention to how much personal information is available about you online. You may never be able to remove everything, but reducing your exposure can make it harder for someone to target you.

Do you believe exposing the identities of federal agents is justified in the name of government transparency, even when it could put undercover operations and employees' families at risk? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Your old Android phone could become a walking robot
summary: UCLA's PhoneBot turns old Android phones into the brain of a two-legged humanoid robot that walks, follows people and stands up after falling.
story: UCLA researchers developed PhoneBot, a small humanoid robot that uses an Android smartphone as its brain to walk on two legs. (Ruochen Hou et al./UCLA RoMeLa)

Got an old Android phone collecting dust in a drawer? You might want to hang on to it. Researchers at UCLA have figured out how to turn an aging smartphone into the brain of a small walking robot. It's called PhoneBot, and it can walk on two legs, follow people and even get back up after falling face down.

The most surprising part? The researchers estimate the robot's hardware costs about $400, excluding the phone. So, that forgotten smartphone could have a pretty interesting second life. Here's how the researchers pulled it off and what it would take to build one yourself.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
GOOGLE TURNS OLD PHONES INTO CLOUD SERVERS
How UCLA turned an old Android phone into a walking robot

PhoneBot comes from UCLA's Robotics and Mechanisms Laboratory, also known as RoMeLa. The team built a miniature humanoid robot that stands about 19 inches tall and weighs roughly four pounds, including the smartphone attached to its body.

Instead of developing an expensive custom computer, researchers used technology already inside an Android phone. The robot has 13 motorized joints, with six in each leg and another that lets its upper body rotate. That extra movement allows the smartphone's camera to turn toward someone while the robot's feet stay planted.
A box filled with electronic waste and broken devices. (Getty Images)
The researchers’ goal is to make humanoid robotics more affordable for schools and research teams that cannot spend thousands of dollars on specialized machines.
Your old Android phone becomes the robot's brain

Think about everything your smartphone already does. It can recognize objects through its camera and detect movement using built-in sensors. It also has enough processing power to run sophisticated software. PhoneBot puts those capabilities to work. An Android app uses the phone's motion sensors to help the robot maintain its balance. Meanwhile, the camera helps it recognize and track people. The phone also runs an artificial intelligence-powered walking controller that tells the robot how to move. Those instructions travel over Wi-Fi to a small computer inside the robot, which communicates with the motors. The smartphone has no physical electrical connection to the robot's hardware. That design makes it easier to swap phones without rewiring the machine. Researchers trained PhoneBot's walking system in computer simulations before testing it on the actual robot. They also developed a way to improve how evenly it uses both legs. As a result, PhoneBot can walk on flat surfaces and stand up from a face-down position. For something powered largely by an old smartphone, that's quite an accomplishment.
Even a nearly 10-year-old Android phone can work

Here's something I found especially interesting. UCLA didn't need the latest expensive smartphone to make PhoneBot work. In fact, the researchers successfully tested its core functions on four different Android devices, including an Honor 9 released back in 2017. The other models included a Samsung Galaxy A16 5G and two Motorola Moto G phones from 2024 and 2025.

Researchers purchased the three prepaid models for roughly $50 to $90 each. Those were the prices reported during testing, rather than guaranteed prices today. All four phones handled the essential functions, including movement control and camera-based recognition. However, the older Honor 9 could not run one of the robot's mapping features because the required Google services were unavailable on that device in the United States. That means you cannot assume every Android phone will work. Still, the tests suggest you may not need an expensive new phone to run a capable little robot.
A WHEELED ROBOT MAY BEAT HUMANOIDS INTO YOUR HOME
UCLA's PhoneBot demonstrates its ability to walk, track a person using its smartphone camera and stand back up after falling face down. (Ruochen Hou et al./UCLA RoMeLa)
Can PhoneBot follow you around?

Yes, at least within the limits of what UCLA has demonstrated. PhoneBot can use its smartphone camera to identify a person and adjust its movement to follow them. It can also rotate its upper body to keep someone in view. The robot supports conversational interaction, too.

However, there's an important limitation. Its current system uses a separate laptop to process speech and generate AI responses. The smartphone records your voice and plays the response through its speaker. Before you start thinking about having PhoneBot clean your house, there's something else you should know. It doesn't have arms. That means it cannot pick up your laundry or carry groceries.

Researchers also trained its walking system on flat ground, so navigating stairs and uneven surfaces remains a challenge. For now, PhoneBot is best viewed as an experimental platform. UCLA has demonstrated what it can do under research conditions, but it hasn't established that the robot can independently navigate a typical home.
Could you build a walking robot with your own Android phone?

If you're comfortable with electronics and robotics, PhoneBot could become a pretty interesting project. UCLA has developed it as an open-source research platform and published hardware designs and building resources. The official PhoneBot website at phonebot.dev/ provides information about the robot's design, components and assembly process. The published hardware materials are available for noncommercial use under a Creative Commons license.

There's an important distinction, though, between having the hardware plans and being able to build a fully working robot. The project website provides hardware designs and assembly resources but does not clearly offer a download for the complete Android app and trained walking software. Although UCLA describes PhoneBot as an open-source platform, anyone hoping to reproduce its capabilities should first confirm that the necessary software is available.

And there's another consideration: the $400 price tag. It's an approximate hardware cost, and it doesn't include the smartphone. Depending on what equipment you already have, you may also need access to a 3D printer and tools for assembly. Shipping and other expenses could push the total higher. You'll also need the technical skills to put everything together and configure the software. So, don't expect to download an app and watch your old phone suddenly sprout legs. There's real engineering involved.
Why PhoneBot could make walking robots more affordable

Humanoid robots are getting a lot of attention, but building one remains expensive. Some small research models cost several thousand dollars. More advanced systems can cost considerably more. PhoneBot takes advantage of hardware that millions of people already own. By letting a smartphone handle much of the sensing and computing, researchers can avoid buying some specialized components. That helps bring the overall cost down.

The approach could also make robotics more accessible to students. Instead of requiring a large research budget, a smaller team could experiment with a relatively inexpensive walking machine. They could test new software or explore ways to improve movement without building every electronic component from scratch.

The UCLA team already has ideas for what comes next. Researchers want to improve PhoneBot's ability to handle uneven terrain and eventually give it lightweight arms. They're also exploring ways to run more conversational AI directly on the smartphone, which could reduce the need for a separate computer. Those improvements are still future goals. Even so, PhoneBot offers a promising starting point for building more affordable humanoid robots.
PhoneBot combines a smartphone with 13 motorized joints to create a walking robot that costs approximately $400 in hardware, excluding the phone. (Ruochen Hou et al./UCLA RoMeLa)
What this means to you

You probably won't see PhoneBot on store shelves anytime soon. But this research shows how much useful technology may still be inside a smartphone you've stopped using. A phone that feels outdated for daily use could still handle surprisingly demanding tasks.

If you're interested in robotics, PhoneBot could eventually offer a more affordable way to experiment with walking machines. Meanwhile, for families with kids who love technology, an accessible version of this project could make for a fascinating hands-on learning experience.

And if you've been thinking about getting rid of your old Android phone, this research offers another reason to consider what it might still be capable of. Of course, building a robot won't be for everyone. You can also sell, donate or recycle your old phone. Before you do, check out our article on securely getting rid of your old cell phone to make sure your personal information doesn't go along with it.
Kurt's key takeaways

I love the idea that a smartphone sitting forgotten in a drawer could become the brain of a walking robot. We've gotten so used to replacing our phones every few years that we sometimes overlook how powerful these devices still are. What UCLA has done with PhoneBot makes me wonder how many other uses we're missing. Now, let's be realistic. This little guy isn't ready to take over household chores, and putting one together requires some serious know-how. But the price is what caught my attention. When researchers can build a walking robot with roughly $400 in additional hardware, it opens the door to possibilities that once seemed out of reach. I'd love to see someone turn this into an affordable kit that families could build together. That could be a great way to get kids excited about engineering.
Would you spend a few hundred dollars to turn your old Android phone into a walking robot? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fake Amazon invoice scam uses $988 iPad order as bait
summary: A fake Amazon invoice charging $988.18 for an iPad lists the same customer support phone number three times to steer panicked victims into calling.
story: A fake Amazon invoice scam uses a realistic $988 iPad receipt to trick victims into calling a fraudulent customer support number. (Getty Images)

You open your email and see an invoice from Amazon. It says you bought a new iPad for nearly $1,000. The order has supposedly shipped, and your payment has already gone through. There's even a customer support number to call if something looks wrong. Your first reaction might be to grab your phone and stop the charge. That's exactly what makes this fake Amazon invoice scam so dangerous. It uses a realistic-looking receipt and an expensive purchase to make you worry about your money. Then it offers what appears to be an easy solution. Matt, who lives in California, recently sent us one of these suspicious emails. He wanted to help others recognize the warning signs before someone falls for the same trick. After examining the message, we found several clues worth sharing.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
DO NOT CLICK FAKE 'ACCOUNT RECOVERY' AMAZON EMAIL
A fake Amazon invoice sent to a California man claims he purchased an iPad for $988.18 and repeatedly urges him to call a suspicious customer support number. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
A fake Amazon invoice that looks surprisingly convincing

Matt received the email on Oct. 28. Its subject line addressed him by name and claimed his order had already left the facility. Inside was a professionally formatted invoice featuring Amazon's familiar logo. The invoice listed an Apple iPad Air 11-inch (M4) with 256GB of storage and cellular connectivity. It showed a price of $973.19. Below that was an additional $14.99 charge labeled "Amazon Protect+ (Auto-Renew)." The grand total came to $988.18.

The document also included an invoice number, shipping details and a delivery date. It even displayed Amazon's corporate address in Seattle. All those details helped create the appearance of a legitimate transaction. However, the email also included a phone number for canceling or modifying the order. That number appeared prominently near the top, again in the payment instructions and once more at the bottom. That's where the real concern begins. The message appears designed to make someone call before checking whether the purchase actually happened.
Red flags in this fake Amazon invoice scam
Let's look at the warning signs hiding in Matt's email. Some are obvious once you notice them. Others are more subtle and help explain why these scams can fool people.

This is the biggest giveaway. The email claimed to come from someone named Jack Campos. However, the actual sender address used Outlook.com with a different personal name embedded in the address. It had no apparent connection to Amazon. Amazon says its legitimate customer emails come from Amazon domains, including amazon.com. A personal Outlook account claiming to send an official Amazon invoice deserves immediate suspicion. Scammers can write almost anything in the sender's display name. That's why I always recommend checking the actual email address before trusting a message.

The invoice displayed the same customer support number in three separate locations. It appeared inside a shaded banner, within the payment instructions and again near the bottom. That's a significant warning sign because the email steers the recipient toward making a phone call. Rather than directing Matt to verify the purchase through his Amazon account, it emphasizes contacting the number printed on the invoice. That number should be treated as unverified and potentially controlled by scammers. We have not independently established who operates it. Amazon warns that fraudulent order confirmations often encourage customers to contact supposed support representatives. Those calls can turn into attempts to obtain payment information or gain access to an account.

Look at the amount: $988.18. That's enough money to get almost anyone's attention. If you saw that charge for a product you didn't buy, you'd probably want to fix it immediately. Scammers understand that reaction. They often choose expensive electronics because the potential financial loss feels serious. The detailed iPad description makes the transaction appear more believable. However, the amount on an email invoice proves nothing about your actual bank account. Until you verify the charge independently, treat it as an unsupported claim.

Here's a detail I find especially revealing. The subject line claims the order has already left the facility. Yet the invoice says cancellations are accepted only before dispatch. So which is it? Has the package already shipped, or can the customer still cancel it? The conflicting language creates confusion while encouraging the recipient to seek help quickly. A concerned shopper may decide to call the listed number rather than spend time figuring out the inconsistency.

The email addresses Matt by name in the subject line. However, the billing section identifies the customer as "Amazon Account Holder." The invoice also lacks a clear, personalized billing and shipping address. Instead, it provides broad fulfillment details and an estimated delivery date. Generic customer information alone doesn't prove fraud. Still, it raises questions when an email claims to document a completed purchase worth nearly $1,000. If the order were genuine, Matt should be able to locate its actual details inside his Amazon account.

The invoice uses terms such as "Standard Account Allocation" and "active ledger." It also claims the authorization has been verified and automated order fulfillment is underway. Those phrases may sound official, but they provide little useful information about how the payment occurred. The email never gives Matt a reliable way to verify the transaction through his account. Scammers sometimes use corporate-sounding language to make a document seem authoritative. Don't assume unfamiliar financial terminology means the message came from a legitimate company.

Alongside the iPad, the invoice lists "Amazon Protect+ (Auto-Renew)" for $14.99. An unexpected recurring charge can create another reason for someone to contact support. Even if they aren't immediately concerned about the iPad, they might worry about paying for a subscription they never requested. The label alone doesn't establish whether the service exists or whether Matt was actually charged. However, any unfamiliar subscription on an unexpected invoice deserves verification through the company's official website.

The document features an invoice identifier beginning with "AMZ" followed by additional letters and numbers. It looks technical enough to seem convincing. However, scammers can generate invoice numbers as easily as they can copy a company logo. An unfamiliar invoice identifier should never replace independent verification. Check Amazon's Your Orders section for a matching purchase instead.

The invoice shows October 28, 2026, as both the order date and estimated delivery date. It also claims that fulfillment has already moved forward. Same-day delivery can happen with legitimate Amazon orders, so that detail alone doesn't establish fraud. Still, the message offers no independently verifiable tracking information. It relies on its own claims about shipment and delivery. The document also lists zero estimated sales tax on the nearly $1,000 transaction. That may have a legitimate explanation depending on the circumstances. However, it adds another detail worth comparing with a real order record.

Here's one of the more interesting details. The invoice includes the Amazon logo and lists Amazon.com Services LLC at 410 Terry Avenue North in Seattle, Washington. That address corresponds to an actual Amazon corporate location. This helps explain why the invoice can look credible. Scammers don't have to invent every detail. They can copy real company information and place it inside a fraudulent document. A legitimate address on a receipt doesn't authenticate the sender. The same goes for company logos and polished formatting.
IDENTITY THIEVES DON’T NEED YOUR PASSWORD ANYMORE; HERE ARE 6 NEW ACCOUNT TAKEOVER THREATS
Scammers use fake purchase invoices to create panic over unexpected charges, hoping recipients will reveal sensitive financial information. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What happens if you call the number on a fake Amazon invoice?

The likely goal of this type of scam is to move you from an email conversation to a phone call. Once someone calls, a person posing as customer support may offer to cancel the purchase or reverse the charge. To complete that supposed refund, they might request payment details or account verification information. Some scammers also ask victims to install remote-access software. They may claim the installation is necessary to resolve a billing problem. In reality, that software could give a stranger access to the person's computer.

Amazon specifically warns that its representatives will never ask you to share a one-time password over the phone. The company also cautions customers against providing financial details or granting unexpected remote access. These are documented tactics in Amazon impersonation scams. We haven't established what would happen if someone called the particular number in Matt's email. The most important point is that receiving a fake invoice does not mean you've actually been charged.

"Scammers that attempt to impersonate Amazon put consumers at risk," an Amazon spokesperson told CyberGuy. "We will continue to invest in protecting consumers and educating the public on scam avoidance. We encourage consumers to report suspected scams to us so that we can protect their accounts and refer bad actors to law enforcement to help keep consumers safe. Please visit our help pages to find additional information on how to identify scams and report them at amazon.com/ReportAScam."
What to do when a fake Amazon invoice arrives

If an unexpected Amazon invoice lands in your inbox, don't rush to cancel the order or call the number provided. A few simple checks can help you determine whether the purchase is real. And if you've already contacted the supposed support team, there are steps you can take to protect your information.

Open the official Amazon app or type Amazon.com into your browser. Select Your Orders and look for the alleged purchase. Avoid using links or phone numbers in the suspicious email. Going directly to your account helps you determine whether the order actually exists.

Sign in to your Amazon account and look for Your Messages or Message Center under your account options. Amazon says authentic customer emails appear there. When a suspicious message doesn't appear, that's another reason to question its legitimacy.

Expand the sender details instead of trusting the name displayed in your inbox. Scammers can make an email appear to come from Amazon while sending it through a personal account. Be especially suspicious of unfamiliar domains or addresses that have no connection to the company.

A fake customer support number can connect you directly to a scammer. Instead, find customer service through Amazon's official app or website. Remember, the person who sent the questionable invoice also supplied that phone number.

Amazon now lets U.S. customers use Alexa for Shopping on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app to check suspicious emails, texts and phone calls. Simply ask, "Is this email from Amazon?" and provide details about the message. The tool checks the information against Amazon's records to determine whether the communication came from the company. If it can't verify the message, it will let you know. You can also forward suspicious emails to verify@amazon.com for verification.

Never share your Amazon password or one-time security codes with someone who contacts you unexpectedly. Consider setting up a passkey or enabling two-step verification for additional protection. These safeguards can make unauthorized account access more difficult, even when someone obtains your password.

Strong antivirus protection can help detect malicious links, unsafe websites and harmful downloads that scammers may use to steal information. Choose reputable security software with real-time protection and keep it updated. While antivirus software cannot prevent someone from being tricked over the phone, it adds protection against other threats that often accompany scams. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Review your bank and credit card transactions through their official apps or websites. Look for unfamiliar purchases or charges that don't match your records. Contact your financial institution immediately if you discover unauthorized activity. You can also enable transaction alerts to help catch suspicious charges sooner.

Scammers may use personal information found on data broker websites to make fraudulent emails more convincing. A personal data removal service can help remove your name, address, phone number and other details from covered people-search sites. Although these services cannot prevent every scam email, reducing your online exposure can make it harder for criminals to research and target you.
