Identity theft protection services can help monitor certain types of suspicious activity involving your personal information. Depending on the plan, you may receive alerts about unfamiliar credit activity or signs of identity misuse. Some services also offer professional restoration assistance if your identity becomes compromised. These protections can provide valuable support when criminals obtain sensitive information, although no service can detect every type of fraud. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

Visit Amazon's official scam reporting page to report the message. You can also report attempted fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/. Amazon recommends that people without an Amazon account forward suspicious communications as an attachment to reportascam@amazon.com. Reporting these attempts helps companies and authorities identify fraudulent activity.
For additional protection, we've also covered how Amazon alerts customers about impersonation scams and the precautions the company recommends.
Calling the customer support number on a fake Amazon invoice could connect you directly to a scammer posing as a legitimate representative. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What to do if you already called the fake support number
Already called the number on a suspicious Amazon invoice? Your next steps depend on what information you shared and whether you gave anyone access to your device. Here's how to protect yourself.

End the call and stop communicating. Hang up immediately and avoid responding to follow-up calls or messages. Even without sharing sensitive information, check your Amazon account directly to verify any claimed purchases or charges.Change your Amazon password . Shared your password with the caller? Sign in through Amazon's official website or app and change it immediately. Review your account for unfamiliar activity. Also, update any other accounts that use the same password.Contact your bank or credit card company. Anyone who provided payment information should contact their financial institution immediately. Explain what happened and ask about replacing the card or disputing unauthorized transactions.Remove any suspicious remote-access software. Scammers may convince victims to install software that gives them control of a computer. Disconnect the affected device from the internet and get professional help checking for unauthorized access. Use a separate, trusted device to change important passwords.Take steps to protect your identity. Shared personal information such as your Social Security number? Visit IdentityTheft.gov for guidance on protecting your identity and recovering from potential fraud.Monitor your accounts for suspicious activity. Watch for unfamiliar purchases, password reset requests or unexpected account changes. Enable transaction alerts through your bank and turn on two-step verification wherever available.

End the call and stop communicating. Hang up immediately and avoid responding to follow-up calls or messages. Even without sharing sensitive information, check your Amazon account directly to verify any claimed purchases or charges.

Change your Amazon password . Shared your password with the caller? Sign in through Amazon's official website or app and change it immediately. Review your account for unfamiliar activity. Also, update any other accounts that use the same password.

Contact your bank or credit card company. Anyone who provided payment information should contact their financial institution immediately. Explain what happened and ask about replacing the card or disputing unauthorized transactions.

Remove any suspicious remote-access software. Scammers may convince victims to install software that gives them control of a computer. Disconnect the affected device from the internet and get professional help checking for unauthorized access. Use a separate, trusted device to change important passwords.

Take steps to protect your identity. Shared personal information such as your Social Security number? Visit IdentityTheft.gov for guidance on protecting your identity and recovering from potential fraud.

Monitor your accounts for suspicious activity. Watch for unfamiliar purchases, password reset requests or unexpected account changes. Enable transaction alerts through your bank and turn on two-step verification wherever available.

The sooner you act, the better your chances of preventing additional damage. Even a short conversation with a scammer deserves attention if you shared personal information or allowed access to your device.
Kurt's key takeaways

I appreciate Matt taking the time to share this email with us. It's a good reminder of how much effort scammers put into making fraudulent communications look credible. What caught my attention was the combination of a detailed invoice and that repeatedly displayed phone number. The message creates concern about a large purchase, then conveniently offers a way to fix it. That's where people can get pulled into a scam before they realize what's happening. And here's something worth remembering: You don't have to spot every strange detail on an invoice to protect yourself. You only need to recognize that an unexpected charge deserves independent verification. The lesson I take from Matt's experience is simple. Don't let a scary email decide whom you call or how quickly you act. Check your account through an official channel before you give anyone access to your money or personal information. I'm glad Matt reached out because sharing these examples gives more people a chance to recognize the warning signs.

title: Why are people attacking food delivery robots?
summary: A handful of food delivery robots from Uber Eats and other platforms have gotten kicked and knocked over in Philadelphia and Los Angeles.
story: An Avride delivery robot covered in graffiti travels along a Philadelphia sidewalk as frustration with AI-powered delivery machines grows. (Aluminum-001/Wikimedia Commons/CC BY 4.0)

There's something pretty strange happening on American sidewalks. People are picking fights with food delivery robots. Yes, those little four-wheeled machines that roll around carrying somebody's meal are getting kicked and knocked over. Some people are even filming themselves doing it.

Now, I can understand being curious about a robot delivering your dinner. After all, watching a small machine navigate city streets with a bag of burgers inside is pretty impressive. But apparently, some people have had enough of these rolling delivery machines. And when you look at what's happening, you start to see just how frustrated some Americans have become with artificial intelligence showing up in their neighborhoods.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.
Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
DOORDASH GETS FAA APPROVAL FOR ITS OWN DELIVERY DRONES
Food delivery robots are getting beaten up

In Philadelphia, an Uber Eats delivery robot found itself on the receiving end of two kicks in late March 2026. The second kick reportedly knocked it over near a parking garage. The people involved eventually put it back on its wheels, but the encounter became another example of people taking out their frustrations on delivery technology. And Philadelphia is hardly alone. Similar attacks have surfaced in Los Angeles and other cities. Videos circulating online show robots being tipped over or deliberately kicked. Some encounters have attracted enormous attention, turning attacks on delivery robots into viral entertainment.

Think about that for a second. These machines generally move at walking speed. Some even have friendly-looking digital eyes that make them look like little cartoon characters. Yet somehow, they've become targets for people who seem determined to teach them a lesson. Here's what I find particularly strange. A robot can't argue with someone who attacks it. It certainly can't defend itself the way a person might. So what is it about these little machines that makes some people so angry?
Why are some people angry at delivery robots?

I suspect some of this anger has very little to do with the robots themselves. For many people, artificial intelligence represents a pretty unsettling change, especially when it comes to their jobs. We've already seen AI take on tasks that people once handled. Now we're watching robots roll down sidewalks doing work that someone used to get paid for. And unlike software running quietly in the background, these machines are right there in front of us.

Consider someone who earns money delivering meals for Uber Eats. Every order completed by a robot could potentially mean one less opportunity for a human delivery worker. Companies say automation can make deliveries more efficient. But what happens to the people who rely on that income as these fleets get bigger?

That concern recently led to a confrontation in Philadelphia. On Oct. 14, police arrested 78-year-old retired University of Pennsylvania professor Carolyn Marvin after she deliberately blocked an Uber Eats delivery robot. Marvin said she was protesting companies replacing human delivery workers with machines. We covered her arrest, and one detail really caught my attention. Pennsylvania law requires delivery robots to yield to pedestrians in pedestrian areas. Marvin's arrest followed her refusal to comply with police instructions, and her case raises questions about how people can legally protest these machines.
An autonomous food delivery robot passes a man pushing a stroller in downtown Los Angeles on May 1, 2026. (Reuters)

I can understand why someone would be frustrated watching technology potentially replace jobs. That doesn't give anyone a free pass to damage property, of course. Still, companies should recognize that they're introducing these machines into neighborhoods where people may already feel anxious about automation.
MAJORITY OF YOUNG ADULTS SAY THEY ARE 'MORE CONCERNED THAN EXCITED' ABOUT AI: PEW RESEARCH
Sometimes the delivery robots create their own problems

Of course, not every complaint about delivery robots comes from someone worried about losing a job. Sometimes the robots themselves cause a headache. Remember the robot traffic jam in Chicago? In September 2026, video showed at least a dozen Coco delivery robots clustered together on a sidewalk near Lincoln Park. Instead of delivering food, they appeared to be stuck trying to get around one another. Coco told CyberGuy that a deployment error caused several robots to reroute at the same time. The company said it fixed the problem within minutes and added safeguards to prevent it from happening again. Now, I have to admit, watching a bunch of robots get tangled up in their own traffic jam is pretty funny. But consider someone using a wheelchair who needs to get through that sidewalk. Suddenly, the situation becomes a lot more serious.

And there have been other problems. In May 2026, a delivery robot reportedly entered a crosswalk against a traffic signal and was struck by a truck. Even more surprising, the damaged robot kept moving afterward. I give these companies credit for developing machines that can navigate busy streets. But if a robot can't reliably handle a crosswalk or stay out of someone's way, it's reasonable to question whether it's ready for crowded city sidewalks.
Are delivery robots becoming a target for people's anger at AI?

Here's another part of this story that I find fascinating. For most of us, artificial intelligence lives inside a computer or smartphone. You might use it to answer a question or help write an email. But there's usually nothing physical standing in front of you. A delivery robot changes that. Suddenly, AI is rolling past your apartment building. It's waiting at the same crosswalk you use every morning. And if you're already frustrated about artificial intelligence taking over more parts of daily life, that little machine becomes an easy target.

Social media can make things worse. Someone records an outrageous encounter with a robot, posts it online and suddenly thousands of people are watching. That attention may encourage others to do something similar. But here's an important reality check. These viral videos can make it seem like robots are getting attacked everywhere. The available numbers suggest otherwise.

In April 2026, Serve Robotics CEO Ali Kashani told Semafor that mistreatment occurred on fewer than 1% of approximately 100,000 trips. That's the company's experience, so it doesn't tell us what's happening across the entire industry. Still, it's worth keeping in perspective. Most of these little machines appear to be making their deliveries without anybody trying to knock them over.
Delivery robots are becoming big business

Whatever people think about these robots, the companies behind them are moving ahead. Serve Robotics reported that it had deployed 2,000 robots by the end of 2025. The company works with delivery platforms including Uber Eats and DoorDash. Other companies, including Coco and Avride, are also pursuing expansion.

If you haven't encountered one yet, here's how they generally work. The robots use cameras and sensors to navigate sidewalks while avoiding obstacles. Customers track their delivery through an app and unlock the robot's compartment when their food arrives. We've previously explained how Uber Eats delivery robots work, and I can certainly see the appeal. A small robot handling a short delivery could mean one less car making a trip through a crowded neighborhood. And if your lunch arrives quickly, you're probably not going to complain about who, or what, brought it.

Of course, there's a big difference between getting a robot to deliver lunch and making money doing it. Serve reported approximately $2.7 million in revenue for 2025 while recording substantial losses. That tells you companies are spending a lot to get these robots on the streets, with no guarantee they'll turn a profit anytime soon. The potential savings are certainly appealing. Robots can handle short deliveries without paying a human courier for each trip. However, the machines still need maintenance, and people have to step in when something goes wrong. So while the technology looks promising, the big question is whether delivering food by robot will eventually pay off.
A fleet of Serve Robotics delivery robots sits inside a truck in Miami as companies push to bring more autonomous deliveries to American cities. (Phillip Pessar/Wikimedia Commons/CC BY 4.0)
Cities are setting new rules for delivery robots

As more delivery robots roll into neighborhoods, city officials are starting to ask some tough questions. Where should these machines be allowed to operate, and who gets to decide? In September 2026, Glendale, California, approved a one-year pilot program allowing up to two delivery robot operators. The city also adopted an ordinance requiring companies to have operating agreements before deploying these machines on public streets and sidewalks. Los Angeles is taking a closer look, too. In November 2025, the City Council approved a motion calling for a review of existing delivery robot regulations. Officials want to better understand how these machines affect pedestrian access and whether current rules do enough to protect people using sidewalks.

Then there's the privacy question. Most delivery robots use cameras to see where they're going. But what happens to the information they collect as they travel through neighborhoods? And how much of that information do companies keep? Those are questions I'd want answered. On the positive side, some companies are finding ways to use this technology to help pedestrians. Coco Robotics partnered with BlindSquare, an accessibility app, to share information about sidewalk obstacles. The goal is to help people with visual impairments navigate their surroundings more safely. I like that idea. If these robots can help people get around more safely, that's a real benefit. But before companies start talking about making sidewalks better for everyone, they need to make sure their own robots aren't getting in the way.
What should you do if a delivery robot gets in your way?

As more delivery robots appear in cities, there's a good chance you'll eventually encounter one. Most of the time, you'll probably just walk past it and continue on your way. But what if one stops right in front of you or blocks a sidewalk? My advice is to give it a little space and avoid trying to move it yourself. If the robot creates a genuine accessibility or safety problem, look for the company's name on the machine. You can usually report the issue directly to the operator.

Some cities also let people report sidewalk obstructions through their local 311 services. If you can safely take a photo, document where the robot is and when the problem happened. That information may help the company identify the machine and investigate. And please, resist the temptation to give it a kick. Deliberately damaging someone else's property can lead to criminal charges, even when that property happens to have wheels and digital eyes. Reporting the problem is a much better way to get someone's attention.
Kurt's key takeaways

I have to give these delivery robots some credit. It's pretty impressive that a little machine can make its way through a busy city and show up with your dinner. I can absolutely see the appeal, especially if it means faster deliveries and fewer cars on crowded streets. But I also get why some people aren't thrilled about sharing their sidewalks with robots. Nobody wants to see jobs disappear, and I certainly wouldn't be happy if a robot blocked my way while I was walking down the street. These are legitimate concerns that companies need to take seriously.

What bothers me is that we're seeing more of these robots before we've really figured out how they should operate around people. Who's responsible when one causes an accident? What happens when it blocks a wheelchair ramp? I think companies should have clear answers before sending thousands more onto our sidewalks. And while I understand the frustration with AI taking over more jobs, kicking a robot that's trying to deliver somebody's pizza seems like a pretty ridiculous way to protest. I'm all for technology that makes life easier. But the people living in these neighborhoods should have a say in how it's used. After all, they're the ones who have to share the sidewalk.

CHESTER, N.J. — A neighbor confirmed investigators removed what appeared to be a headboard, hamper and possible comforter or quilt from the property where Brooke Hanlon, 35, was found stabbed to death earlier this year.

Fox News Digital was on the scene outside the home on Pottersville Road in Chester, New Jersey, last week and witnessed investigators carrying scads of those items wrapped in brown paper and marked with evidence tape out of the Hanlon home.

Hanlon, a psychotherapist and mother, was found fatally stabbed in the home on June 6. Her husband, James "Conor" Hanlon, had called 911 from the home after his wife was found stabbed there. No arrests have been made.

title: Florida Learjet crash 911 callers report hearing ‘bomb’ as plane carrying young family plunges near busy road
summary: Panicked 911 callers described a bomb-like explosion after the Learjet 60 crashed in Greenacres, Florida, according to audio obtained by Fox News Digital.
story: Panicked 911 callers described an explosion and smoke after a Learjet 60 crashed in Greenacres, Florida, on Nov. 1, killing all nine people on board, according to audio obtained by Fox News Digital.

Panicked 911 callers struggled to make sense of what they'd just witnessed after a Learjet went down in Florida, with one telling dispatchers a "bomb" had gone off, according to audio obtained by Fox News Digital.

The Learjet 60 departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport at approximately 10:37 a.m. Nov. 1, headed for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. Shortly before 1 p.m., the aircraft went down in Palm Beach County, killing all nine people on board.
Moments after the jet slammed down just off a busy road, witnesses could be heard telling 911 operators they were trying to piece together what they'd just seen.
PRIVATE JET WITH 9 PEOPLE ON BOARD CRASHES JUST MILES FROM MAR-A-LAGO
Investigators work at the scene of a plane crash in Greenacres, Fla., on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)
"There was an explosion," one caller said. "I think an airplane or rocket, something fell from the sky. We felt our house shake, and then we heard an explosion when we ran outside."
The caller compared the scene to a "bomb explosion," saying her power cut out for a few seconds before coming back on.
Stepping outside to look, the female caller said she saw sparks and smoke, telling the operator, "it was black, it was dark, like it was burning."
The calls came in at around 12:51 p.m., just after the plane crashed.

story: NYPD are investigating a knifepoint rape of a 39-year-old woman that happened in Central Park over the weekend. (Credit: @NYCMayorsOffice/YouTube)

Dereck Rivera-Deleon, 30, was taken into custody during an operation involving the NYPD, U.S. Marshals Service and Miami Beach police at a fast-food restaurant in the 1100 block of Washington Avenue.
"The NYPD will stop at nothing to get dangerous criminals off our streets," police said on X.

Dereck Rivera-Deleon was taken into custody on Tuesday while he was working at Burger King in Miami for allegedly raping a woman in Central Park on Oct. 24. (Miami Beach Police)

title: Former West Point cadet sued over alleged drugging, forced abortion of ex-girlfriend: 'Horrifying'
summary: A former West Point cadet drugged his girlfriend and forced abortion pills into her mouth and vagina, according to a lawsuit filed by the victim.
story: Alliance Defending Freedom attorney Erin Hawley says the alleged assault by former West Point cadet Caleb Suh, who pleaded guilty after drugging his pregnant ex-girlfriend and administering abortion pills without her consent, was "horrifying."

A former West Point cadet who pleaded guilty to drugging his then-girlfriend and administering abortion pills without her consent, causing a miscarriage, is facing a civil lawsuit that seeks unspecified damages.

Caleb Suh pleaded guilty in June to assault resulting in substantial bodily injury to a dating partner in connection with the March 2022 incident involving the woman, who was also a cadet at the U.S. Military Academy at the time.

Suh studied at two Ivy League universities since the incident, including one where he began attending classes after his guilty plea. He graduated from Cornell University this year and was enrolled as a graduate student at Columbia University when the woman filed a lawsuit Oct. 28.

The woman wanted to have the baby, but Suh did not want her to keep the child. Suh told the judge that he used the woman's identity to set up an online pharmacy account, ordered abortion drugs through the mail, obtained Xanax from a friend to use as a sedative and tricked his girlfriend into drinking what he claimed was a prenatal protein shake. When she fell asleep, Suh inserted the abortion pills into her mouth and vagina.
PRO-LIFE LEADER SOUNDS ALARM AFTER DOCTOR GETS 6 MONTHS FOR FORCING ABORTION PILLS ON GIRLFRIEND
Caleb Suh pleaded guilty this summer to the March 2022 assault on the woman, who was also a cadet. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)
Erin Hawley, a lawyer with the pro-life legal group Alliance Defending Freedom who played a key role in helping overturn Roe v. Wade, said the woman was put in an "absolutely horrific situation."

"She was expecting a child she very much wanted, was drugged and assaulted," Hawley, who is not representing the woman, told Fox News Digital. "The horrifying assault ended up causing the death of her very much wanted child — something no woman should ever have to endure. It has obviously caused a lot of harm and trauma, in addition to the loss of the baby she very much wanted."
"She was drugged and assaulted with abortion pills, even though Mr. Suh knew she very much wanted that child. I expect that he will be prosecuted to the full extent of the law," she added.
Suh is still awaiting sentencing.
Suh left the woman alone and incapacitated and ignored her attempts to reach him once she woke up and noticed that she was bleeding, according to the lawsuit. She was then hospitalized.

As the woman was receiving medical attention, Suh returned to the online pharmacy's website and posted questions about whether doctors could detect the medication he administered, according to the lawsuit.
"She’s suffered a life-changing event that she is still dealing with and will be dealing with for the rest of her life," her lawyer, Russell Kornblith, told The Associated Press last week.
"We hope that by our client coming forward with this lawsuit, it will, at least, ensure that this never happens to anyone else," Kornblith said.
INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM
Caleb Suh graduated from Cornell University this year and was a graduate student at Columbia University when the woman filed a lawsuit late last month. (TW Farlow/Getty Images)
Fox News Digital reached out to Suh's attorney for comment.
During a court hearing in June, Suh said that he was "deeply and immeasurably sorry for my actions and the pain that I have caused."
Suh's sentencing has been postponed until Jan. 21, 2027, at his attorney's request, allowing him to finish the semester at Columbia. Prosecutors did not oppose the delay for Suh's sentencing.
He has also been taking a three-month life skills course for people facing federal charges, his attorney said in a letter to the court.

Suh transferred to Cornell during the 2023-2024 school year. The university said in a statement last week that he answered "no" on an application when asked if he had been found responsible for a disciplinary violation at any previous institution.

The university said West Point noted that he was in good academic standing and was eligible to return. He had been involved in health and medicine at Cornell and wanted to become a physician, according to the university's website.

In September, Suh started a master's program at Columbia University's Mailman School of Public Health, his lawyer wrote to the judge in his federal case. A person familiar with the matter told The Associated Press that Mailman applicants are not asked about their criminal records but are questioned about whether they have ever been disciplined for student conduct violations or poor academic performance.
Suh’s application never made any mention of past disciplinary proceedings, the person told the outlet.

As the woman was receiving medical attention, Caleb Suh returned to the online pharmacy's website and posted questions about whether doctors could detect the medication he administered. (Soumyabrata Roy/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

"Regardless of one’s position on abortion, it is not good medicine to allow an abortion drug to be shipped across the country to a dorm room or a home without a woman ever having talked to a doctor," Hawley said.

"The defendant in this case impersonated his girlfriend, had those drugs shipped and then assaulted her with them. That would never have happened if the FDA had done its job in 2023. Hopefully, when the courts do their job and reinstate that safeguard, it won’t continue to happen," she continued, referring to Alliance Defending Freedom's lawsuit challenging the Food and Drug Administration's 2023 decision to remove the in-person dispensing requirement for mifepristone, after the agency had already stopped enforcing the requirement in 2021.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

However, the assault occurred in March 2022, before the FDA's 2023 decision. The agency had already announced in April 2021 that it would temporarily stop enforcing the in-person dispensing requirement during the COVID-19 public health emergency. In December 2021, the FDA announced plans to permanently remove the requirement, a change formally implemented in January 2023.
The FDA has said its decision to remove the requirement followed a review of available evidence. Other restrictions, including prescriber certification requirements, remained in place.
Hawley added that the case at West Point would never have happened if that requirement had been in place.
"Horrific incidents like that throughout the country would never have happened if that basic safeguard had been in place," she said.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: IRGC operative lands on FBI’s Most Wanted Terrorists list over alleged plot to kill former Trump advisor
summary: Shahram Poursafi allegedly sought to pay $300,000 to have John Bolton killed in a plot authorities linked to retaliation for Qasem Soleimani’s death.
story: Former Trump Deputy National Security Advisor Victoria Coates discusses Iran's 'appalling' behavior, including 'Kill Trump' banners.
The FBI on Tuesday placed a member of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) on its Most Wanted Terrorists list for allegedly soliciting the murders of two former U.S. government officials.

Shahram Poursafi is accused of hiring individuals to kill the officials between October 2021 and April 2022, according to the FBI’s Washington Field Office. Court documents detail an alleged plot targeting former National Security Advisor John Bolton.

The assassination plot was believed to have been initiated in retaliation for the January 2020 killing of IRGC commander Qasem Soleimani, who led a unit of the Qods Force, one of the IRGC's five divisions responsible for developing and carrying out lethal plotting operations.
Poursafi allegedly worked on behalf of the division and sought to pay individuals in the U.S. $300,000 to carry out the assassination.
US OFFERS $20M FOR IRANIAN IN PLOT TARGETING TRUMP’S EX-NATIONAL SECURITY ADVISER JOHN BOLTON
Shahram Poursafi (right) allegedly sought to pay $300,000 to have former National Security Advisor John Bolton killed. (Alex Kent/Getty Images/File; FBI)

Separately, the FBI released wanted posters seeking information on three alleged IRGC officials from the same Qods Force unit. The individuals were identified as Mohammad Reza Ansari, Abolfazl Alizadeh and Mohammad Hossein Shamoradizadeh.
Ansari is an alleged deputy who has supported IRGC operations in Syria. He also allegedly planned and attempted to assassinate two former U.S. government officials with the Poursafi’s support.
Alizadeh and Shamoradizadeh are both alleged battalion commanders who have participated in lethal plotting operations.
IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS
Shahram Poursafi is accused of hiring individuals to kill U.S. officials between October 2021 and April 2022. (FBI )

According to a 2022 Justice Department complaint announcing the charges against Poursafi, Poursafi initially plotted the assassination by asking a U.S. resident he had previously met online to take photographs of Bolton, claiming the images were for a book he was writing.

Poursafi later offered another U.S. contact up to $300,000 to "eliminate" the former national security advisor. Poursafi also told the contact he had an additional "job" for which he would pay $1 million.
BOLTON CALLS IRAN ASSASSINATION PLOT AN 'ACT OF WAR,' CALLS ON BIDEN ADMIN TO 'TERMINATE' NUCLEAR TALKS
Ansari is a deputy within the IRGC Qods Force unit who has supported operations in Syria, according to the FBI.  (FBI)
The plot ultimately fell through as the contact was a confidential human source working with the FBI, often considered civilian informants.

Poursafi was charged with using communication or travel networks across state lines to carry out a paid assassination. He was also accused of supplying resources or assistance for an international murder plot, according to a Justice Department complaint.
Alizadeh and Shamoradizadeh, who are both battalion commanders in the IRGC, allegedly participated in lethal plotting, according to the FBI.  (FBI)

title: Iran-backed terror suspects plotted attack on US troops using vans packed with fuel, DOJ says
summary: A Justice Department indictment alleges three Iran-backed suspects used fuel-laden vans to target RAF Fairford, a British base housing U.S. troops.
story: British prosecutors charged two men under the National Security Act after an incident at RAF Fairford, a key U.S. bomber base in England. Police believe one suspect was assisting Iran. Approximately a dozen U.S. B-1 bombers were previously withdrawn from the base after the incident.

Three suspected Iran-backed terrorists plotted an attack on a British air base housing American troops using vans carrying barrels of fuel, according to a federal indictment unsealed Tuesday by the Justice Department (DOJ).

The eight-count superseding indictment charges Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri and Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani with terrorism-related offenses tied to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Kata'ib Hizballah.
Prosecutors say the suspects targeted RAF Fairford in England, where U.S. military aircraft and personnel were stationed.
"Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American service members will be prosecuted by the United States government," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a news release.
IRAN UNDER SCRUTINY AFTER PLOT FOILED NEAR UK BASE USED BY US MILITARY
A 2024 photo released by the Justice Department shows Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi in a conference room with weapons and a map of the United States. (Department of Justice)
According to the indictment, Al-Hassani directed associates in the United Kingdom to conduct surveillance of RAF Fairford in August, paying one individual to record video of the base's perimeter.

The suspects' associates later obtained three vans and barrels of fuel, researched chemical accelerants and purchased metal objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel, prosecutors said. They also disguised the vans with commercial decals to resemble vehicles belonging to fuel delivery and swimming pool supply businesses.

On Sept. 26, Al-Hassani allegedly directed associates to drive the three vans toward the base. At least two encountered a security roadblock and were unable to proceed. British authorities recovered all three vehicles and arrested their occupants the following morning.
UK POLICE ARREST 'EXPLOSIVE' SUSPECTS NEAR US AIRBASE, KEY TO IRAN WAR

Prosecutors allege Al-Saadi helped coordinate the operation while imprisoned in New York awaiting trial on separate terrorism charges, using telephone calls with family members in Iraq to relay coded messages to his co-conspirators.
During a Sept. 24 call, Al-Saadi allegedly asked about Al-Hassani and instructed relatives to "give him [al-Hassani] money so we can do it."

The alleged plot followed a series of attacks across Europe in March and April that prosecutors say the defendants helped organize on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network. Those attacks targeted synagogues, Jewish organizations, ambulances and an Israeli embassy, and included the stabbing of two Jewish men in London.

Al-Saadi, a dual Iranian Iraqi national, was arrested abroad in May and transferred to U.S. custody. Prosecutors previously accused him of helping direct approximately 18 attacks in Europe and attempting to coordinate an attack on a Manhattan synagogue.
Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood Al-Saadi, circled in red, and Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani, circled in green, appear in a video prosecutors say shows them directing an attack in Europe. (Department of Justice)

The three defendants face charges, including conspiracy to provide material support to foreign terrorist organizations, financing terrorism and conspiracy to bomb a place of public use. Some charges carry a maximum sentence of life in prison.

Investigators say he staged the scene to make her death appear to be a suicide.
The U.S. Attorney for Massachusetts confirmed Farwell, 41, was found guilty on Tuesday of murdering Birchmore, 23, and causing the death of her unborn child. He will be sentenced on Feb. 3.
Jurors began deliberating Friday after hearing more than three weeks of testimony in the federal murder trial.

However, instead of mentoring, Farwell used his position of power to prey on Sandra, a vulnerable child who was only 12 years old when she entered the explorer program."

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: Lindsay Clancy judge denies double jeopardy motion and explains jury notes after deadlock
summary: Judge William Sullivan denied Lindsay Clancy's double jeopardy motion, ruling there was manifest necessity for the mistrial in her murder case.
story: Attorney Randolph Rice says prosecutors can use lessons from the first trial to refine their case. He also explains why he believes Judge William Sullivan’s order rejected Clancy’s double-jeopardy argument.

The Massachusetts judge overseeing the murder case against Lindsay Clancy has denied her motion to dismiss the case on double jeopardy claims, clearing the way for a retrial in the strangling deaths of her three young children that some experts believe could have a better chance at a guilty verdict.

"Because the Court concludes that there was a manifest necessity for a mistrial based on the jury’s deadlock, a retrial on the murder indictments does not violate Clancy’s right not to be placed in double jeopardy," Judge William Sullivan wrote in a 17-page order and memorandum made public Monday.

Clancy's 26-day trial ended with a deadlocked jury on Sept. 4, with jurors later saying publicly that 11 of them accepted her insanity defense and one wanted to find her guilty of first-degree murder for what the holdout called the "methodical" slayings of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months.
LINDSAY CLANCY DEFENSE FILES MOTION TO DISMISS UNDER DOUBLE JEOPARDY GROUNDS, WITH FOCUS ON HOLDOUT JUROR

Judge William Sullivan indicates he was going to declare a mistrial before changing course and giving Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney one hour to appeal, as the jury in the case has indicated that they are unable to reach a verdict on Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger via AP, Pool)
Had the motion been granted, Clancy would not face a potential second trial, said Randolph Rice, a trial attorney and former prosecutor who is not connected to the case.
Now, he says, the order gives prosecutors a chance to address what went wrong with their case in the first trial.
"I think there's real possibility that DA [Tim] Cruz says, 'We're going back to trial ... and we have learned from our mistakes,'" Rice said.
Among the lessons learned, Rice said, may be that Plymouth County prosecutors did not show jurors enough empathy when presenting their case after 11 of the 12 jurors voted against them.
What a second trial may look like remains unclear as prosecutors have so far declined to publicly commit to bringing the same or different charges.

Lindsay Clancy looks at jurors as Judge Sullivan asks them to start deliberations for a sixth day during her murder trial on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in Plymouth, Mass. (Pool Photo by Greg Derr/The Patriot Ledger)
Deliberations began on Aug. 27. On Sept. 1, they sent the first of several notes explaining their deadlocked situation.
"After many hours of deliberation, we are unable to come to a unanimous verdict," that first note said, according to Sullivan, who instructed them to keep trying.

They sent a similar note on Sept. 2, and Sullivan, without objection from lawyers on either side, read them what's known as a Tuey-Rodriguez charge — an instruction given to hung jurors encouraging them to reexamine their views with an open mind while reminding jurors they should not abandon honestly held beliefs to reach their verdict.
On Sept. 3, Sullivan received another note reading, "A member of the jury is unable to follow the instructions regarding reasonable doubt. How should we proceed?"
ATTORNEY FOR LONE HOLDOUT JUROR IN LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL PUSHES BACK ON CLAIMS OF REFUSING THE LAW
Michael P. Desronvil, the juror whose refusal to join the other 11 led to a mistrial in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial. (Fugitive TV)

In his order, Sullivan wrote that he was skeptical of the allegation that the holdout was "genuinely" unable to follow instructions regarding reasonable doubt and decided to hold a "limited inquiry" into each juror's ability to follow the law.

Prosecutors had opposed voir dire, and the defense asked for the holdout to be replaced with an alternate. The defense then asked for the judge to ask the foreperson to expand on what she meant in her latest note, and prosecutors objected, arguing that a question like that would improperly intrude into the deliberation process. Sullivan agreed with the commonwealth and asked each juror, "Are you able to follow my instructions on the law that were given to you earlier in the trial?"
LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT JUROR WON'T HAVE TO TURN OVER PHONE OR FACE INQUIRY, JUDGE SAYS
District Attorney Timothy Cruz leaves Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., on Thursday, September, 3, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)
Each juror answered "affirmatively and credibly," Sullivan wrote.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Prosecutors and the defense agreed that the court should also reinstruct the jury, as a whole, about reasonable doubt, and Sullivan did so. Afterward, however, Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, again asked for the holdout to be replaced with an alternate, and Sullivan denied his motion.
LINDSAY CLANCY'S PUSH TO PROBE HOLDOUT JUROR HITS SNAG BEFORE PIVOTAL RETRIAL HEARING
Later on Sept. 3, the foreperson sent another note, directly accusing the holdout of ignoring reasonable doubts about the case, according to Sullivan.
LINDSAY CLANCY HOLDOUT PRAISED AS 'AMERICAN HERO' BY LAWYER WHO SAYS HE REPRESENTS HIM
Callan, left, Dawson and Cora Clancy. The three children were killed at their Duxbury, Massachusetts, home in January 2023. (Lindsay Marie Clancy/Facebook)
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
"[Juror Doe] has made statements acknowledging doubt but refuses to apply it to the verdict as the law states," she wrote. "This is why we cannot come to a unanimous decision."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Jurors were sent home for the day. Before deliberations resumed on Sept. 4, Sullivan and counsel on both sides discussed the latest note. Sullivan gave jurors another instruction on reasonable doubt and following the law and told them that future notes should not identify anyone's vote based on their juror number. Two hours later, with no movement in the deliberation room, Sullivan said he planned to declare a mistrial, over Reddington's objection.
SEND US A TIP
He granted a one-hour stay as the defense appealed to the state's Supreme Judicial Court. A single justice summarily denied the defense’s emergency request, then Sullivan declared a mistrial.
LINDSAY CLANCY LAWYER SAYS HE PLANS NEW MOTION TO DISMISS AFTER JURORS SPEAK OUT ON MISTRIAL: REPORT

Clancy's defense later filed a motion to dismiss on double jeopardy grounds, arguing that there was no "manifest necessity" for the court to declare a mistrial and that as a result, a new trial would violate Clancy's Fifth Amendment rights.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Clancy contends that there was no manifest necessity for a mistrial because the Court failed to consider the alternative of inquiring into the meaning of the foreperson's notes and questioning Juror Doe to determine whether there was good cause to discharge Juror Doe," Sullivan wrote.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
That's the motion he denied Monday.

title: Tennessee warns executions could grind to a halt if Christa Pike's lawyers see a single drug label: court docs
summary: Tennessee officials warn that exposing their pentobarbital supplier could halt all future executions after Christa Pike survived two lethal doses.
story: Anesthesiologist Dr. Joel Zivot joins Bill Hemmer to discuss the legal fallout after a judge ordered Tennessee officials to preserve evidence from the botched execution of Christa Pike. Zivot, who advised Pike's attorneys, explains the complications surrounding the lethal injection drugs used in the state's attempt. Pike remains on death row following the failed execution attempt.

Tennessee officials are urging a judge to keep their lethal injection drug supplier secret, warning in court documents that executions could come to a halt if the vendor is exposed to retaliation after Christa Pike's botched execution.

Pike had been set for execution on Sept. 30 after the Supreme Court vacated a last-minute stay. She was convicted of the murder of 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville and received a death sentence.

She stood to become the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than two centuries, yet she survived after two administered doses of the lethal injection drug pentobarbital did not result in her death.

In a motion filed in the Davidson County Chancery Court on Friday, a Tennessee Department of Correction employee said that providers of the chemical used in the execution attempt have grown skittish. title: 'SNL' writer’s sister vanished — now her boyfriend and rival face charges in deadly love triangle
summary: "Saturday Night Live" writer Jimmy Fowlie's sister Christina Downer faced alleged stalking and blackmail before her disappearance and presumed death.
story: Christina Downer's boyfriend Delorean Bijon Brandon faces murder charges months after court records revealed alleged stalking, threats, and domestic violence involving both suspects.

Months before a "Saturday Night Live" writer's sister disappeared, court records showed a pattern of alleged stalking, threats, and domestic violence involving two suspects now charged with her death and disappearance.

Last month, Los Angeles County prosecutors charged Christina Downer’s boyfriend, Delorean Bijon Brandon, 41, with first-degree murder. Brandon’s former girlfriend, Kaylee Nicole Markowski, 34, is facing two felony counts of being an accessory after the fact.
Investigators believe Brandon killed Downer, 38, on or around Sept. 19, 2025. Her remains have not been located.
Christina Lynn Downer, the missing sister of "Saturday Night Live" writer Jimmy Fowlie, was last seen in Los Angeles' Koreatown neighborhood in September 2025. (LAPD)

Before Downer disappeared, she and Brandon sought separate restraining orders against Markowski, accusing her, in part, of stalking and blackmail, court records showed. Both cases were dismissed after Downer and Brandon failed to appear in court, according to court documents obtained by Los Angeles Magazine.
'SNL' WRITER'S MISSING SISTER CASE LEADS HOMICIDE DETECTIVES TO JOSHUA TREE MONTHS AFTER FAMILY'S MURDER CLAIM
Downer’s disappearance and presumed death
Authorities learned of Downer’s disappearance in December 2025, when her ex-husband reported her missing, saying he had not heard from her in months.
Downer’s brother, "Saturday Night Live" writer Jimmy Fowlie, began posting public pleas on Instagram that same month, asking for information about his sister’s whereabouts.
Brandon, who shared an apartment with Downer in Koreatown, told police that she had moved out months prior, leaving her belongings behind, including her car and beloved miniature pinscher named Rex.
TEACHER FOUND DEAD WITH THROAT SLIT; DETECTIVES SCRUTINIZE HUSBAND’S SHIFTING STORY
The LAPD’s Robbery-Homicide Division took over the investigation after Downer’s cellphone washed ashore at Santa Monica Beach.
Investigators believe Brandon and Markowski used Downer’s phone to send messages, fabricating a story that she voluntarily disappeared, according to court documents.
HORSE FARM OWNER GETS LIFE IN PRISON FOR BOYFRIEND'S MURDER AFTER CLAIMING SELF-DEFENSE

"The individual(s) in possession of her phone used it to hide the fact she was gone, to ask for money, and to create a false narrative that she was going ‘off the grid,’" Fowlie wrote on Instagram in April.

"I am sharing this because I believe that whoever is responsible is hoping to erase her in every way possible. I want to amplify her story in the only way I know how. And express that she was a beautiful person who matters in this world, especially to me."
Jimmy Fowlie attends the premiere of Netflix's "Roommates" at The Egyptian Theatre Hollywood on April 13, 2026, in Los Angeles, California. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)
Fowlie did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Restraining orders, prior domestic violence allegations
In a September 2024 restraining order petition obtained by the Los Angeles Times, Downer accused Markowski of terrorizing her since December 2023.

Markowski harassed Downer by threatening to break into her home, beat her up and by calling her racial slurs, court documents stated. She also allegedly stole Downer’s cat and a storage device containing intimate videos, which she allegedly used to blackmail Downer.
"She calls us n-----, threatens to beat me up, stole my spare key and copied it, threatens to break into my home," Downer claimed in her request.
'HOW I MET YOUR MOTHER' ACTOR NICK PASQUAL CONVICTED OF ATTEMPTED MURDER FOR STABBING EX-GIRLFRIEND

In July 2025, Brandon filed a domestic violence restraining order request against Markowski, alleging she harassed him, targeted his vehicle and attempted to interfere with Downer’s job, according to ABC7’s court records review.
Judges dismissed both cases after Downer and Brandon failed to appear in court.

In September 2025, Brandon sought another protective order against Markowski, accusing her of hitting and kicking him when he tried to leave. He said she also threatened to shoot him in the head for having a relationship with Downer.
A Los Angeles County Superior Court judge rejected the request and set a Sept. 23, 2025, hearing.

Alyce LaViolette, a licensed marriage and family therapist and domestic violence specialist not affiliated with the case, explained that courts usually examine specific details of each allegation rather than the number of complaints filed before deciding if a case proceeds. Court backlogs and limited domestic violence training can make it more difficult to assess a full abuse history, she said.
On Sept. 18, 2025, however, Brandon withdrew the request. Investigators believe Downer died within a day of Brandon withdrawing the request.
Christina Downer disappeared and is believed to have been killed. (Instagram/jimmyfowlie)
Previous accusations

The latest criminal complaint detailed allegations of domestic violence carried out by Brandon against a different woman. Brandon allegedly used scissors during one of the assaults, according to documents obtained by Los Angeles Magazine.
He is now charged with two felony counts of injuring a cohabitant in connection with the alleged 2022 assaults.

In a separate April 2022 court case, a woman filed a civil harassment restraining order petition against Markowski in Los Angeles County Superior Court. The judge dismissed the case in June 2022 for "lack of prosecution."

Markowski’s attorney, Arvand Naderi, also declined to comment on a pending case.
Risling said Brandon is being represented by the Alternate Public Defender’s Office. The office was not immediately available for comment.

title: Quiet serial killers may hide in plain sight as DNA unmasks dead 1970s Pennsylvania strangler, expert says
summary: James Richard Clark Sr. left DNA at both 1970s crime scenes, but advanced cybergenetics testing has only recently linked him to the two killings.
story: Dr. Kris Mohandie, a former FBI behavioral analysis consultant and LAPD psychologist, discussed why serial killers often have more victims than they are linked to after DNA tied a dead Pennsylvania man to two 1970s killings.
Quiet serial killers may be hiding in plain sight, an expert warns, after new DNA technology helped unmask a Pennsylvania man authorities say killed at least two women in the 1970s.
At a Thursday news conference, Pennsylvania State Police identified James Richard Clark Sr. as the man who sexually assaulted and strangled Brenda Ritter, 18, and Susan Rush, 21, in the 1970s.

Rush vanished on Nov. 24, 1976, after leaving a shopping mall, according to the City of Washington Police Department. She was supposed to meet her family at church but never arrived. Her brother spotted her car along a street the next morning, Thanksgiving Day, and her body was discovered in the trunk.
TED BUNDY LINKED TO ANOTHER DECADES-OLD HOMICIDE NEARLY 40 YEARS AFTER HIS EXECUTION
Pennsylvania State Police identified James Richard Clark Sr., who died in 2023, as the man who killed Brenda Ritter and Susan Rush in the 1970s. (Pennsylvania State Police)
Ritter disappeared from her boyfriend's house in 1977, police said. Her body was later found on a hillside, and authorities determined she had been sexually assaulted and strangled.
The suspect, Clark Sr., died at 66 on July 17, 2023, of natural causes.
DNA BREAKTHROUGH LEADS TO ARREST IN GRISLY 33-YEAR-OLD COLD CASE INVESTIGATORS NEVER GAVE UP ON

In late 2008, evidence from Ritter's killing was sent to the state police crime lab, which produced an unknown male DNA profile. The DNA was put into an FBI database, CODIS, which was searched weekly with no match. In May 2025, testing at Cybergenetics' laboratory showed the same man was responsible for the deaths of both women.

Clark left DNA at both crime scenes, according to police, and advances in testing at several labs, including Identifinders International, helped investigators zero in on him before more testing sealed the match.

Brenda Ritter, 18, disappeared from her boyfriend's house in 1977 and was later found sexually assaulted and strangled on a hillside, police said. (Pennsylvania State Police)
Police said Clark would have been 20 at the time of Ritter's homicide and 19 when Rush was killed.

Pennsylvania State Police Cpl. James Petrosky said he thinks there may be more victims.
SEND US A TIP
"I believe that once you're a serial killer, you're always a serial killer. I believe there could potentially be more victims out there," Petrosky said.

Dr. Kris Mohandie, a former LAPD psychologist and FBI behavioral analysis consultant, told Fox News Digital it's "normal" for the number of known victims to fall short of a serial killer's true toll, and that new technology is often what closes the gap.
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"I think it's normal and normative that the number of known cases is always less than what has been detected," Mohandie said. "These kind of guys often have more victims out there than they've been known to be connected to. The reality is that there are usually more crimes attributable to serial offenders than they're ever held to account for."

Susan Rush, 21, vanished after leaving a shopping mall on Nov. 24, 1976, and her body was found the next morning in the trunk of her car, police said. (Pennsylvania State Police)
Mohandie said it's not unusual for a serial killer to go quiet for years, either because they sense investigators closing in or because their lives get busy with things like raising a family.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"There are a lot of cases where they do go dormant, what we call a cooling-off period, and that can be because they realize it's too hot for them to continue to offend, that they'll get caught, so it's a strategy to avoid being captured. It may mean that they've had a close call with being captured, and it spooked them, so they'll go quiet for a while because of that," he said.

title: NTSB recovers cockpit voice recorder from Learjet crash site in Florida
summary: The NTSB recovered the cockpit voice recorder from the Learjet 60 crash site near Greenacres, Florida, as investigators probe the cause of the incident.
story: Retired Navy fighter pilot Matthew 'Whiz' Buckley discusses the aircraft's damaged tail components, rapid descent and encounter with severe weather, as investigators work to determine what caused the deadly Florida Learjet crash.

The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) announced on Monday that it has recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) of the Learjet 60 that crashed last week near Greenacres, Florida, killing all nine people on board.
"NTSB investigators have recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) of the Learjet 60 that crashed on Nov. 1 near Greenacres, Florida," the NTSB said on X.
The CVR was found at the location of the initial impact​, according to the NTSB.
The NTSB said the CVR is being evaluated in the board's Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C.
TIMELINE OF LEARJET CRASH THAT KILLED AUSTIN FAMILY TRACES FINAL MINUTES FROM TAKEOFF TO FLORIDA PLUNGE
NTSB investigators recovered the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) of the Learjet 60 that crashed in Florida. (NTSB)
The excavation work at the impact site has been completed.
This comes after investigators said on Friday that they recovered part of an engine from the Learjet.
Crews started excavating the site on Wednesday after utility workers had drained water and cleared other hazards, the NTSB said.
Once investigators began digging, they found a part of one engine, the board said.
Earlier last week, investigators recovered the left tail elevator, which controls the jet's pitch, in three separate pieces. One of them was found nearly four miles from where the Learjet 60 crashed.
FLORIDA PLANE CRASH VICTIMS IDENTIFIED AFTER 9 PEOPLE KILLED IN FIERY WRECK
The cockpit voice recorder was found at the location of initial impact and is being evaluated in the NTSB Vehicle Recorders Laboratory in Washington, D.C. (NTSB)
"Even small pieces of the wreckage may contain important evidence that could help investigators determine what happened," the agency wrote last week on X.

The Learjet 60 left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport around 10:37 a.m. on Sunday, bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. The aircraft plunged into the ground in Palm Beach County shortly before 1 p.m., killing everyone aboard.

Austin tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, 45, was killed in the crash alongside his wife, Helen Sharp, 40, their children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, the children's nanny, Anita Maria Cetina, and couple Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr.
Heavy rain and thunderstorms were reported across South Florida when the Learjet crashed. Investigators said the weather will be a major focus of their probe.
Investigators work at the scene of a plane crash in Greenacres, Florida, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

At about 41,000 feet, an air traffic controller told the flight crew that moderate precipitation was roughly five miles away and said they could move either left or right, stressing that the turn toward Freeport in the Bahamas "looks pretty bad."

The crew was then instructed to fly to a waypoint near Naples, Florida. The crew made a deviation toward Palm Beach County and reported that weather conditions were deteriorating. The crew told air traffic control that there was icing and turbulence, asking the controller if there was a "better ride" ahead.
Fox News' Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

title: South Carolina dad left sleeping 6-year-old in line for Pokémon cards at Target: police
summary: A South Carolina father allegedly left his 6-year-old asleep outside a Target overnight to hold his place in line for a Pokémon card release.
story: Matt Finn reports on the surge in Pokémon card thefts across California and beyond. In San Francisco, police arrested juvenile suspects involved in a pepper spray robbery using high-tech tools. A separate incident in Brentwood, CA saw masked bandits steal thousands worth of cards in under a minute, prompting the owner to boost security.

A South Carolina man was arrested after allegedly leaving his 6-year-old daughter asleep outside a Target store overnight so she could hold his place in line for a new Pokémon trading card release, police said.
Charleston Police Department officers arrested 35-year-old John-Michael Dooley on Nov. 6 after responding to a Target location around 2:30 a.m. on reports of an unattended child.
Upon arrival, officers learned the young girl had originally been waiting in line with her father alongside a crowd of customers gathered overnight for the release of a new Pokémon trading card set.

John-Michael Dooley, 35, left his 6-year-old daughter outside to wait in line overnight for him in anticipation of the release of a new Pokémon trading card set, police said. (Charleston Police Department/Getty Images)
Sometime after 1 a.m., Dooley gave his daughter a pillow and blanket, leaving her asleep in line before walking away, according to police.
"After approximately an hour passed without his return, concerned customers contacted police," the department said in a news release.
FBI INVESTIGATING SUSPECTED HOMICIDE ABOARD POPULAR CRUISE SHIP AFTER SUDDEN RETURN

Witnesses identified Dooley when he returned to the store, and officers took him into custody. During questioning by investigators, Dooley admitted to leaving his daughter to hold his spot in line while he went home.

A competitor holds a deck showing a Determinazione Lylia card while playing the Pokémon Trading Card Game at the Pokémon Europe International Championships at ExCeL London on Feb. 13, 2026, in London, England. (John Keeble/Getty)

Authorities did not clarify whether Dooley planned to purchase the cards for himself or his daughter. The release coincided with the rollout of the latest Pokémon trading card expansion set: Mega Evolution—Delta Reign.

The massive Japanese media franchise, centered on fictional creatures, remains exceptionally popular among both children and adult collectors. While standard booster packs retail for around $5, rare cards can command thousands on the secondary market.
Police confirmed the child was unharmed. She was placed into the custody of the South Carolina Department of Social Services.

title: Next Generation OPIR GEO: Building America’s gateway to the future of space-based missile warning and tracking
summary: As missile threats grow faster and more maneuverable, detecting and tracking them presents new challenges. Explore how Lockheed Martin’s Next Gen OPIR GEO is designed to improve infrared sensing and support timely military decision-making.
story: Next Gen OPIR GEO (Lockheed Martin)

America is advancing next-generation overhead persistent infrared capabilities to strengthen space-based missile warning and tracking for the Joint Force. Next Gen OPIR GEO is designed to provide timely warning and tracking information against evolving missile threats, supporting force protection, informed decision-making, and efforts to save lives. Building on the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) heritage, the program is designed to improve sensing, tracking, resiliency, and data processing in support of unified combat.

Missile threats have evolved in speed, complexity, and maneuverability over the last decade. As these threats proliferate, our military requires resilient capabilities to support timely missile warning and tracking. Next Gen OPIR GEO builds on existing space-based missile warning capabilities to address those evolving requirements.

Lockheed Martin is developing the system in partnership with the U.S. Space Force, subcontractors, and supply-chain partners. The effort combines scientific, engineering, systems-integration, and program-management expertise to support current and future missile warning and tracking needs.
A Bridge from Today to Tomorrow

The defense technology company is developing Next Gen OPIR GEO, building on the SBIRS foundation to advance space-based missile warning and tracking capabilities.  The system is designed to improve the detection, tracking and characterization of increasingly complex missile threats, including threats with challenging signatures, high speeds, and maneuvering flight profiles.

"For more than a decade, SBIRS has provided reliable space-based early missile warning capability," said Jim Sprunck, OPIR portfolio director at Lockheed Martin. "Next Gen OPIR GEO builds on that strong foundation and brings enhanced capabilities intended to support advanced missile warning and tracking for our nation."

Hypersonic glide vehicles can travel at high speeds and maneuver in flight, making them more challenging to detect and track.  Next Gen OPIR GEO is designed to operate in geosynchronous orbit and provide persistent missile warning and tracking coverage supporting timely awareness and decision-making.

Improved tracking requires advanced sensors with enhanced sensitivity and persistent coverage to support detection and tracking of challenging targets. Mission testing has demonstrated significant improvements over SBIRS in approved performance areas.
A Resilient Next-Generation Architecture

Next Gen OPIR GEO is being developed with modern infrared payloads designed to improve detection of launches and tracking of dim or maneuvering targets. The system also incorporates resiliency features intended to support mission continuity in contested space environments.
The space element is integrated with a next-generation ground architecture designed to process larger amounts of sensor data and provide timely decision-making for warfighters.

"Our engineers have built advanced analysis and modeling tools that simulate every phase of the mission from launch through on-orbit detection," Sprunk said. "We are leveraging decades of SBIRS experience and representative mission scenarios to inform development and integration. This work provides confidence that Next Gen OPIR GEO is positioned to meet and exceed established performance requirements, supporting enhanced missile warning and tracking operations."

Built on Lockheed Martin’s LM 2100 Combat Bus™, Next Gen OPIR GEO is designed to incorporate cyber-resilient systems, improved communications, resiliency features, enhanced spacecraft power, and improved propulsion and electronic subsystems. The system is designed to use onboard data processing to support mission continuity during communication disruptions.
The Unique Engineering Mindset
Lockheed Martin engineers and technical personnel support development of the Next Gen OPIR GEO program from early design through manufacturing and testing of the mission-ready satellite.

The team uses next generation digital-engineering methods to develop and integrate the U.S. Space Force’s next-generation missile warning and tracking capability. Engineering teams developed payload, ground systems, and spacecraft capability improvements, then validated these designs through early development demonstrations, and space-to-ground integration tests using digital simulations under representative mission conditions.

"We’ve built a collaborative environment that extends far beyond Lockheed Martin’s walls," said Theresa Ito, Next Generation OPIR GEO Principal Systems Engineer. "We are bringing together technical expertise across the program, the U.S. Space Force, subcontractors, and supply-chain partners to address complex development and integration challenges."
Developing the Workforce Behind Next Gen OPIR GEO

Next Gen OPIR GEO is more than a hardware upgrade; it brings together experienced SBIRS personnel and a new generation of engineers to develop next-generation missile warning and tracking capability for combined forces.

"Many members of the team bring years of SBIRS experience, but since Next Gen OPIR GEO began, we’ve welcomed new engineers with fresh perspectives," Ito said. "Their technical expertise and commitment complement the experience of the broader team and support the program’s mission."

SBIRS will continue to provide established early missile warning capability for traditional ballistic-missile threats. Next Gen OPIR GEO will build on the SBIRS foundation, building the gateway to the future of space-based missile warning and tracking.

title: California police probe 'suspicious circumstances' after nearly 20 hospitalized following half-marathon
summary: Santa Barbara Police Department is probing suspicious circumstances after 19 half-marathon runners sought emergency care for unusual symptoms.
story: Police in Santa Barbara, Calif., are investigating "suspicious circumstances" after nearly 20 runners were hospitalized with unusual symptoms following a half-marathon, though organizers believe the illnesses were heat related.

title: Inside Holocaust memorial in heart of Arab world as founder reveals what changed everything
summary: Inside Dubai's Crossroads of Civilizations Museum, founder Ahmed Obaid Al Mansoori reveals how a temporary Holocaust tribute became a permanent gallery.
story: Reporting from Dubai, Fox News Digital visits one of the Arab world's first permanent Holocaust exhibitions and speaks with its founder.

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — In a historic house near Dubai Creek, a small gallery commemorating the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust stands alongside collections exploring Islamic civilization, Emirati heritage and the history of Palestine and the Holy Land.

The Holocaust exhibition at the privately owned Crossroads of Civilizations Museum is among the first permanent displays of its kind in the Arab world. Opened in May 2021, less than a year after the UAE normalized relations with Israel through the Abraham Accords, it has become a symbol of the Emirates' approach to religious coexistence.

During a recent visit to the museum, Fox News Digital saw displays documenting Nazi persecution, including a life-size image of the boy from the famous Warsaw Ghetto photograph, his hands raised in surrender.
The gallery also tells the stories of Muslims who rescued Jews during the Holocaust, including Egyptian physician Mohammed Helmy, who sheltered Jews from Nazi persecution in Berlin.
US-BACKED ISRAEL-MOROCCO DEAL DEEPENS ABRAHAM ACCORDS AMID GROWING REGIONAL THREATS

An image of a young Jewish boy with his hands raised as armed German soldiers round up civilians in the Warsaw Ghetto in 1943, displayed at the Holocaust gallery of the Crossroads of Civilizations Museum in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. The photograph has become one of the most recognizable images of the Holocaust. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
But the story behind the exhibition is as personal as the objects it preserves.

In an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital, museum founder Ahmed Obaid Al Mansoori, a former member of the UAE's Federal National Council, explained that his passion for collecting historical artifacts began in childhood, when he inherited family manuscripts and objects from his grandparents.
DOMINICAN REPUBLIC JOINS GLOBAL FIGHT AGAINST ANTISEMITISM WITH LANDMARK MOVE

A sign marking the Multifaith Gallery at the Crossroads of Civilizations Museum in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, where exhibits explore the shared history and heritage of different religious communities. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)

He began collecting systematically in 1989, eventually establishing a private museum in his home in 2006. Dubai authorities later provided a historic building to accommodate his growing collection, which opened to the public in 2014.
The Holocaust gallery came much later.
9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD'

Ahmed Obaid Al Mansoori (right), founder of Dubai's Crossroads of Civilizations Museum, pictured with a rabbi. Al Mansoori established one of the Arab world's first permanent Holocaust memorial exhibitions, promoting interfaith understanding and coexistence. (Fox News Digital)

Al Mansoori said two experiences inspired him. The first was a visit to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum in Washington during the 1990s, where he was deeply moved by the message that the Holocaust was a tragedy with lessons for all humanity.

The second was a conversation with an American Jewish acquaintance who expressed fear about rising antisemitism in the United States. Initially, he dismissed her concerns. But after encountering antisemitic imagery circulating during a period of unrest in the U.S., he reconsidered. "I realized I was wrong," he said.
He turned to Jewish friends and colleagues to organize a Holocaust remembrance event in Dubai in 2021.
CHRISTIAN LEADERS HOLD EMERGENCY SUMMIT IN JERUSALEM TO CONFRONT GLOBAL RISE IN ANTISEMITISM

A shofar, a traditional Jewish ceremonial horn, on display at the Crossroads of Civilizations Museum in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. The instrument is sounded during Jewish religious observances, including Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
"The beauty about this Holocaust gallery was built by Arabs, by Jews, and by Christians," he told Fox News Digital, describing the international team that helped create the exhibition.
What began as a commemorative initiative became something much larger.

At the opening, Al Mansoori said, he was struck by the positive response from visitors, including residents of the UAE and people from elsewhere in the region. He also encountered criticism, but concluded that the gallery should become a permanent part of the museum.
"I thought it was very beautiful, very important. And it must stay," he recalled.
The exhibition formally opened on May 26, 2021, attended by the Israeli and German ambassadors to the UAE, according to The National's coverage at the time.
TRUMP CALLS ON ARAB NATIONS TO SIGN ABRAHAM ACCORDS

An ancient manuscript on display at the Crossroads of Civilizations Museum in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. The museum's collections highlight the region's rich cultural and religious heritage. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
Yet Al Mansoori's vision extends beyond Holocaust remembrance.
In another section of the museum, historical maps of Palestine appear alongside Jewish manuscripts, photographs and documents illustrating the region's overlapping histories.

"You have the maps from the Israeli perspective. You have the map from the Palestinian perspective," he said, explaining why he deliberately brings different historical narratives into the same space.
He recalled a visit by rabbis in August 2020, when Muslim, Jewish and Christian guests prayed alongside one another at the museum, each according to their own traditions.
For Al Mansoori, the purpose is not to erase religious or political differences, but to make it possible for people to respect one another despite them.
"It's how to learn to be comfortable being yourself next to others. And others must be also comfortable to be next to you," he said.

A timeline of World War II and historical documents detailing the Holocaust are displayed at the Crossroads of Civilizations Museum in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. The exhibition commemorates the six million Jews murdered by Nazi Germany and its collaborators. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)

As war and political tensions continue to divide the Middle East, Al Mansoori believes the museum offers a different way to confront the region's painful history: not by avoiding it, but by allowing visitors to encounter histories and experiences beyond their own.

title: US evacuates 13 military aircraft from second UK base as new Iran threat raises alarm

story: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday after the G7 Foreign Ministers' meeting in Paris, that "bad things are happening to the Iranian economy and it's unfortunate."
The U.S. Air Force abruptly relocated more than a dozen aircraft from RAF Mildenhall in eastern England amid an emerging security threat, U.S. officials confirmed Tuesday.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the move, citing sources who said the threat originated in Iran.

As U.S. officials assessed the threat's nature and urgency, commanders raised the base's security level to Force Protection Condition Charlie, the military's second-highest alert level, indicating a likely terrorist threat against personnel or facilities.
IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS
U.S. Air Force KC-135, used for in-flight refueling, takes off from RAF Mildenhall Airbase. (AP Photo/Max Nash, File)
Flight-tracking data and open-source analysts with the Military Air Tracking Alliance identified 13 U.S. aircraft leaving the base late Monday, the Associated Press said.
Nine Boeing KC-135 Stratotankers were moved to airfields in Scotland, Germany and Spain.
Three CV-22B Ospreys were relocated to nearby RAF Lakenheath, which has hardened aircraft shelters.
A U.S. official told The Associated Press the moves were precautionary, noting that some aircraft were on rotational deployments while others were permanently stationed in the United Kingdom.

The move marks the second major relocation of U.S. military aircraft from Britain in less than two months.
In early October, the Air Force pulled heavy bombers from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire after British counterterrorism police stopped three suspicious vans headed toward the base Sept. 27.
Two men have since been charged under the United Kingdom's National Security Act.
Separately, the Justice Department unsealed indictments against three Iranian-backed operatives on Tuesday accused of involvement in coordinated terrorist plots across Europe, including RAF Fairford.

The main gate of RAF Fairford is pictured on September 27, 2026 in Fairford, United Kingdom. RAF Mildenhall is home to the 100th Air Refueling Wing, the only permanently based U.S. tanker wing in Europe.
Its KC-135 Stratotankers support allied aerial refueling and long-range strike missions across the region.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday that Washington routinely repositions military forces.
"We are constantly repositioning forces around the world for a variety of reasons," Rubio told reporters when asked about the evacuation.

title: American girl, 7, killed during Mexican cartel operation; mother blames police helicopter: report
