title: Oil-rich UAE makes massive AI bet as Sam Altman unveils ambitious plan to transform energy industry
summary: OpenAI's Sam Altman named energy as his biggest challenge at ADIPEC 2026, where Abu Dhabi unveiled ambitious AI partnerships with ADNOC and G42.
story: Fox news digital visits At the ADIPEC energy conference in Abu Dhabi, where OpenAI CEO Sam Altman joined UAE officials to unveil a major partnership aimed at transforming the energy industry.

ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — At the opening of the world's largest energy conference in Abu Dhabi, artificial intelligence took center stage alongside oil and gas as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman joined senior UAE officials for the announcement of a major partnership aimed at bringing advanced AI into the energy industry.

The opening ceremony of ADIPEC 2026, attended by Fox News Digital, brought together senior government officials and energy industry leaders at a time when the war involving Iran and disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz have placed extraordinary pressure on global energy supplies.

But amid discussions about oil production, shipping routes and energy security, Dr. Sultan Al Jaber, the UAE’s minister of industry and advanced technology and chief executive of state-owned energy giant ADNOC, delivered a different challenge to the technology industry.
OIL SQUEEZE TIGHTENS AS IRAN-BACKED ATTACKS CRIPPLE HORMUZ ESCAPE ROUTES

From left to right, Mark Chen, chief research officer at OpenAI; Sam Altman, CEO at OpenAI; Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi; Ahmed Al Kuttab, chairman at the Department of Government Enablement – Abu Dhabi (DGE) announce the Machine-Readable Government initiative in Abu Dhabi. (Abu Dhabi Media Office)

"From the moment ChatGPT was born, the world has asked what energy can do for AI. And now, together, we will find out what AI can do for energy," Al Jaber told the audience, introducing a partnership between ADNOC, OpenAI and Abu Dhabi-based technology company G42.

The announcement marked a significant step in the UAE’s ambition to become a global center for artificial intelligence, using its energy resources, financial strength and growing partnerships with American technology companies to help shape the industry’s future.
Yet the question of what AI can actually deliver for the energy industry goes beyond the technology announcements.
THE AI REVOLUTION WILL GO WHEREVER THERE'S ELECTRICITY — AND CHINA KNOWS IT

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman speaks at the opening ceremony of ADIPEC 2026 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Nov. 2, 2026, as ADNOC, OpenAI and G42 announced a major partnership to bring artificial intelligence into the energy industry. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)

Speaking exclusively to Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the conference, Dr. Angela Wilkinson, secretary general and CEO of the World Energy Council, said the most encouraging element of the presentations by Altman and Al Jaber was their focus on the role of people.
"That it isn’t about AI taking decisions for humanity, it’s about AI enabling people to make better decisions," Wilkinson said.
Wilkinson argued that the growing relationship between energy and AI should be understood not simply as a way to automate industrial processes, but as an opportunity to expand human capabilities.
"I think what really cheered me up most is the recognition that it’s a people-centric conversation on both sides of the equation," she said.
ONE OF AMERICA'S OLDEST MANUFACTURERS SAYS AI IS CREATING JOBS — NOT REPLACING THEM

Dr. Angela Wilkinson, secretary general and CEO of the World Energy Council, speaks with Fox News Digital at ADIPEC 2026 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, about the future of global energy markets, the growing role of artificial intelligence and the need for greater resilience amid regional instability. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)

Amos Hochstein, a managing partner at TWG Global and a former senior adviser to President Joe Biden, welcomed the potential benefits of the new OpenAI-UAE partnership but warned that the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence must be balanced against its financial and societal costs.

Speaking to Fox News Digital at ADIPEC, Hochstein said, "The energy sector is going to be one of the big beneficiaries of AI coming into the sector." But he cautioned that the U.S. must remain a leader in advanced AI while ensuring Americans are not left paying the price for its expansion, calling on the Trump administration to work more closely with industry and other sectors of society to maximize the benefits and minimize the risks.
The ADNOC partnership is intended to connect advanced AI systems across the company’s operations, from oilfield development and reservoir management to refining, logistics and commercial trading.

According to ADNOC, one of the initial applications will bring together decades of information from thousands of oil wells, multiple reservoirs and hundreds of facilities, with the goal of completing complex development plans in hours rather than months.

The company says the technology could improve operational efficiency, lower costs and help energy producers respond more quickly to changing market conditions. Those projected improvements have not yet been independently demonstrated.
For the UAE, the initiative represents something larger than a single agreement.
AI ISN’T JUST A PROBLEM, IT’S A SOLUTION. SOME PEOPLE ARE ALREADY MAKING THE MOST OF IT
Unmanned AI-led vessels on display at the 2026 ADIPEC conference on Nov. 2, 2026. (Efrat Lachter/ Fox News Digital)

The country is already a partner in the planned Stargate UAE project, a major computing infrastructure initiative involving American technology companies. The project is part of Abu Dhabi’s broader effort to establish itself as an international AI hub.

In a separate interview with Fox News Digital in Dubai, Mohammed Baharoon, director general of the research center B’huth, described the country’s technological ambitions as an evolution from exporting barrels of oil to exporting digital computing capacity.

Baharoon said the rise of AI could produce an economic transformation comparable to previous industrial revolutions, creating new industries and opportunities even as existing professions are disrupted.
But he cautioned that governments are struggling to keep pace with the technology’s development.
"We will need to bring in the concepts of regulation at the point of development, not after the development has happened," Baharoon told Fox News Digital.
He argued that governments and technology companies need to begin addressing potential dangers while systems are being created, rather than waiting until they have already entered widespread use.
THE BIGGEST THREAT IN AMERICA'S RACE WITH CHINA ISN'T BEIJING, TECH EXECUTIVE WARNS

Attendees gather at ADIPEC 2026, one of the world's largest energy conferences, held in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, Nov. 2–5, 2026, as industry leaders discuss global energy security, technological innovation and the growing role of artificial intelligence. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
The question of human control was also central to Altman’s remarks at ADIPEC.
During a panel, Altman argued that AI should remain a tool serving people rather than replacing human decision-making.
The OpenAI chief also acknowledged a fundamental challenge facing his own industry: the enormous amount of energy required to power increasingly capable AI systems.
Asked to identify his biggest challenge, Altman answered with a single word: "Energy."
The exchange illustrated the complicated relationship between two industries that are becoming increasingly dependent on each other.

AI companies need vast quantities of electricity to operate data centers, while energy producers are increasingly looking to AI to improve efficiency, optimize production and identify vulnerabilities before they disrupt supplies.
AI BOOM: DEMAND FOR DATA CENTERS DRIVES INNOVATION BY ENERGY, TECH INDUSTRIES TO PRODUCE NEW POWER SOURCES
Racks of graphics processing units (GPUs) with a closed-loop liquid cooling system are seen inside an operational Microsoft data center. (Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP/Getty Images)

The stakes are particularly high in the Gulf, where the war involving Iran and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have forced energy producers to reconsider how they protect infrastructure and ensure supplies reach international markets.

In his opening address, Al Jaber warned that nearly a billion barrels had been drawn from global oil inventories since the disruption of Hormuz, illustrating how quickly geopolitical instability can affect global energy supplies.

The ADNOC chief presented artificial intelligence as one element of a broader effort to strengthen operational resilience, arguing that companies must develop systems capable of anticipating problems rather than simply responding after disruptions occur.
ONE OF THE WORLD'S HOTTEST INDUSTRIES IS SPARKING A BLUE-COLLAR JOBS BOOM

The exhibition floor at ADIPEC 2026 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, where global energy companies showcased new technologies and innovations amid growing concerns over energy security and regional instability. (Efrat Lachter/Fox News Digital)
Altman, meanwhile, praised the UAE’s commitment to adopting AI across government and industry, describing it as the world’s most forward-looking country in embracing the technology.
For Abu Dhabi, the emerging partnership between its traditional energy industry and the world’s leading AI companies offers an opportunity to extend its economic influence beyond oil exports.
But whether these investments ultimately deliver the promised improvements in productivity, energy security and technological innovation remains to be seen.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
AI data center. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

As the discussions at ADIPEC demonstrated, the question is no longer simply how much energy the AI revolution will require, but whether artificial intelligence can help solve some of the very energy challenges its growth is creating.

title: Melania Trump hails Oleshky ceasefire as potential ‘spark’ for progress amid Ukraine-Russia war
summary: Melania Trump called the Oleshky ceasefire "a spark in a world of darkness" as Russian and Ukrainian envoys praised the deal at a rare White House event.
story: The 'Outnumbered' panel discusses Melania Trump's diplomatic efforts, including brokering a temporary limited ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.

First lady Melania Trump and envoys from both Russia and Ukraine spoke from the White House on Thursday, hailing the ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Oleshky region as a potential "spark" for peace that lasts beyond a temporary regional ceasefire.

"We have chosen humanity over war," the first lady said in a White House trilateral news conference with the two warring countries. "Undeniably, the lives of innocent people must transcend the division of war. I hope Oleshky inspires greater peace. Every significant transformation begins with a small spark."
"Together, we can create something more enduring than a temporary ceasefire," she added, calling Oleshky "a spark in a world of darkness capable of illuminating the best in humanity."
INSIDE MELANIA TRUMP'S SECRET DIPLOMATIC ROLE IN THE RUSSIA-UKRAINE CEASEFIRE DEAL

Trump said she became aware of a humanitarian crisis in the region in September and directed her representative, Marc Beckman, to engage with Russia and Ukraine on her behalf. She said both countries agreed to work with her as an "exclusive intermediary" to establish a ceasefire in Oleshky and the surrounding Kherson region, deliver humanitarian aid and create a safe evacuation route for civilians.
Her remarks were followed by comments from Russian special envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who said Russian President Vladimir Putin appreciated President Donald Trump’s efforts to stop the fighting.
US WILL MEDIATE UPCOMING UKRAINE-RUSSIA TALKS IN ABU DHABI, WITKOFF SAYS

Leader of the Servant of the People political party of Ukraine, David Arakhamia, sitting side by side with Russia's presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev was a unique image at first lady Melania Trump's remarks on the ceasefire in Oleshky at the White House in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 5, 2026. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)

"President Putin also appreciates President Trump's peacemaking effort and his team working on a peace plan to resolve Ukrainian crisis," Dmitriev said in a rare moment of a Russian diplomat speaking at the White House. "President Trump has asked President Putin to support a number of initiatives on exchanging of prisoners, on releasing U.S. prisoners on humanitarian efforts. And President Putin supported those ideas and those initiatives."

"And it's very important that cooperation between Russia and Ukraine and Russia in the United States matters not only for our two nations, but for the entire world," he continued. "Let us continue making great humanitarian contributions. We can together, let us build a future of peace, partnership and prosperity for the benefit of our families, our children and future generations."
RUSSIA RELEASES AMERICAN TEACHER IMPRISONED ON UKRAINE MERCENARY CHARGES AFTER TRUMP PRESSED PUTIN

First lady Melania Trump, left, and civilians being evacuated from Oleshky, Ukraine, in October 2022 during the early days of the Russia-Ukraine war. (Umit Bektas/Reuters; Alexander Ermochenko/Reuters)
"Dear Melania, you saved and touched so many lives," he concluded.
David Arakhamia, the leader of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's political party, called Melania Trump's ceasefire the 'biggest de-escalation since 2022," when the war began.
UKRAINE'S ZELENSKYY OPEN TO FREEZING FRONT LINES IN CEASEFIRE WITH RUSSIA

"Madam first lady, I would like to thank you: You did an amazing job," he said. "I think when everything started with you and your team, we had about 5% of people who believed in success, and 95% of skeptics who said it wasn’t going to work. Now, after it happened, it’s switched completely: 95% of the people believe that we can do things like that, and 5% are still skeptical."
Peace is now a matter of when, not if, he added.
KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE
Signature page from Oleshky ceasefire agreement. (Provided to Fox News Digital)

Getting fearful Ukrainians out of the Russian-controlled city is an important step toward deciding how peace will be made and determining the long-term fate of the occupied territory of southern Ukraine.

"On the first day, people in the area did not believe it was happening," Arakhamia said. "They stayed in their homes, waiting to see if the clock was ticking backward. The next day, they started walking around their homes. The day after that, they came to see their broken homes and find their belongings.

"This is really emotional to watch and supervise, to understand what we are doing," he added. "I think we are creating momentum where both sides are learning the little mechanics of how to keep the peace when the peace comes.
"I would also like to sincerely thank you, from my heart, for doing this."

Dmitriev attended the event and met with U.S. officials, sources told Reuters. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, also attended the event.

title: Protests erupt across France after left-wing groups call for mobilization
summary: An estimated 270,000 people joined nationwide strikes and protests across France on Thursday, putting pressure on President Emmanuel Macron's government.
story: Fox News foreign correspondent Jeff Paul reports on nationwide protests in France, where up to 700,000 demonstrators are expected and 70,000 police officers have been deployed. The U.S. embassy is warning Americans about possible danger in traveling.
France deployed 70,000 police officers Thursday as tens of thousands of people took to the streets for nationwide strikes and protests after left-wing groups called for a mobilization.
In Paris, the Eiffel Tower was closed; in Lyon, French riot police fired tear gas and charged a group of protesters; and near Toulouse, a high school was set on fire, according to Reuters.
"We need to turn up in big numbers on the streets today," the news agency quoted the head of the left-wing CGT union Sophie Binet as saying.
The demonstrations come after France was rocked by violent protests in October, which outgoing French President Emmanuel Macron blamed on "ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic."
FRANCE'S MACRON BLAMES PROTESTS ON 'ULTRA-LEFT GROUPS WHOSE AIM IS TO BRING DOWN THE REPUBLIC'

A car burns as demonstrators look on during a nationwide day of strikes and protests over wages, the cost of living and public services, called by French labor unions and joined by high school and university students calling for better education conditions, in Lyon, France, on Nov. 5, 2026. (Reuters)
An official close to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said that by early Thursday, around 270,000 people had joined the union action in 180 rallies outside the capital.
About a third of France’s high schools were closed or unable to operate, some because of student blockades and others because teachers were on strike, The Associated Press reported.
Toby Harris, an Australian tourist who was visiting Paris on Thursday, told Fox News Digital that "I feel like it's probably a good thing that there's like political action in the city.
"So if things have to be closed, because people want to make a point, then I'm sort of all for it," she added.

Ashley Bradshaw, a tourist from Utah, said outside the Eiffel Tower that "we were going to go tour the opera today and because of the strike, we couldn't access that which was a bummer, but we're happy that we get to just be here in Paris."

French high school students, officials and protesters face off with French riot police as they block a street with garbage bins during high school blockades ahead of a demonstration in Paris on Nov. 5, 2026. (Reuters)
Nuñez said the 70,000 police officers being deployed are backed by armored vehicles, drones and helicopters.
Authorities in the western region of Brittany also said "masked individuals" tried to block roads in Rennes, while some committed "serious acts of violence," including throwing steel balls at police.
AMERICANS WARNED OF VIOLENT PROTESTS AS MAJOR TOURIST DESTINATION FACES SHUTDOWN THREAT
Protesters carry a banner and Communist flags during a nationwide day of strikes and protests in Lyon, France, on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Reuters)
France’s main unions warned that the country is on the brink of recession and that layoff plans are multiplying.
"Fuel, food products, rent, gas, electricity... everything’s going up except wages and pensions," they said in a joint statement, according to The Associated Press.
Riot police detain a protester during a protest in Lyon, France, on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Laurent Cipriani/AP)

The U.S. Embassy had issued an urgent security alert for Americans in France ahead of the demonstrations, warning travelers to brace for severe disruptions, sudden curfews and the potential for violence.
The rallies come as the campaign to succeed Macron as president next May heats up, with political parties seeking to capitalize on the movement.
A member of the French gendarmerie shoots a tear gas canister during a demonstration in Nantes, France, on Nov. 5, 2026. (Reuters)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term, while far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is the favorite to win, the AP reported.
Fox News Digital's Kelly McGreal and The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Multiple flights in Europe diverted because of bomb threats
summary: At least 11 planes from cities, including Dublin, Madrid, and Warsaw, were diverted or grounded over bomb threats that have been determined to be unfounded.
story: Fox News foreign correspondent Jeff Paul reports on a series of bomb threats forcing multiple commercial flights to divert or make emergency landings across Europe. Paul details incidents involving Aer Lingus, Finnair and Wizz Air flights alongside previous security warnings that government authorities classified as hoaxes.
Multiple planes across Europe were diverted and forced to make emergency landings Thursday because of bomb threats that have turned out to be unfounded.
At least 11 planes, originating from cities including Copenhagen, Dublin, Helsinki, Madrid, Milan and Warsaw, have been affected. The source of the threats was not immediately clear.
These incidents came after several flights in Europe received similar warnings on Tuesday that the U.K. government described as "malicious hoax threats."

"Upon receiving a threat regarding the placement of an improvised explosive device on board 4 aircraft heading to Prague, we are preparing with colleagues from Prague Airport for their landing. We assess the relevance of the threats as low," Czech Police wrote on X, before adding that inspections of the planes yielded "negative results."
The threats come at a time when European officials have been blaming Russia and Iran for "hybrid attacks" and acts of sabotage, which both Moscow and Tehran deny, Reuters reported.
RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT

A Ryanair plane sits at Sofia Airport after flights from Copenhagen and Madrid landed there, according to the Bulgarian interior minister, as bomb threats forced unplanned landings across Europe on Nov. 5, 2026. (Reuters)

Earlier, a flight from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a military air base in western France because of a bomb threat, according to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s office. That flight landed safely at the base in Evreux in Normandy, with all 151 passengers and six crew members disembarking, the office said.
A LOT Polish Airlines flight from Warsaw to Brussels landed at its destination, where inspections found no hazardous or suspicious items, the airline said.
A Wizz Air flight from Milan to Bucharest landed safely in Bucharest following a bomb threat, according to airport spokesperson Teo Postelnicu.
FRENCH SUPERMARKETS FACE MILLIONS IN LOSSES AFTER CYBERATTACK HITS REFRIGERATORS NATIONWIDE

A police officer and a sniffer dog inspect a Ryanair airplane and its baggage after Ryanair's operations center reported a bomb threat received during a flight from Manchester to Murcia, according to Guardia Civil, in Murcia, Spain, on Nov. 3, 2026. (Reuters)
Finnair said that Flight 1761 from Helsinki to Rome was targeted by a bomb threat, but nothing was found after it landed in the Italian capital.
Three Ryanair flights bound for Sofia, Bulgaria, had to make emergency landings because of bomb threats on board.

A Finnair aircraft sits on the tarmac at Fiumicino Airport in Fiumicino, near Rome, Italy, on Nov. 5, 2026, after a Finnair flight from Helsinki was escorted to its scheduled landing by Italian Air Force jets following bomb threats that forced airliners to make unplanned landings across Europe. (Reuters)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Two of the flights — one from Copenhagen, Denmark, and the other from Madrid — landed safely at Sofia’s Vasil Levski Airport, airport officials told reporters. The third Sofia-bound flight, from London’s Stansted Airport to Sofia, had been diverted and landed safely at the airport in Plovdiv, Bulgaria’s second-largest city, Plovdiv Airport CEO Krassimir Peshev said.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: US Marine dies in training incident at Japan military base, officials say
summary: A U.S. Marine with the 3rd Marine Division died during a training exercise at Camp Schwab in Okinawa, and the incident remains under investigation.
story: A U.S. Marine died following a training incident on a military base in Okinawa, Japan. (Yuichi YAMAZAKI / AFP via Getty Images)
A U.S. Marine died Tuesday after an incident during training at Camp Schwab in Okinawa, Japan, military officials said.
The incident happened in Okinawa, on a Marine Corps base near the northeastern coast of Okinawa Prefecture.
The Marine, who was identified as Lance Cpl. Devin J. Hernandez, 25, of Maryland, was with the 3rd Marine Division.
ALLEGED KILLING BY MARINE PROMPTS US MILITARY TO RESTRICT OFF-BASE LIBERTY IN OKINAWA

"It is with heavy hearts that 3rd Marine Division announces the death of a Marine following a training incident at Camp Schwab, Okinawa, Japan, on Nov. 3, 2026," the 3rd Marine Division said in a press release. "We express our deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of our Marine."

Hernandez was participating in fast-rope training at Camp Schwab when he sustained injuries during the training, the 3rd Marine Division said in a later statement to Fox News Digital. He was transported to a hospital and later succumbed to his injuries.
The Marine's death remains under investigation. (Getty Images)

"A Marine currently assigned to 3rd Marine Division was involved in a fast rope training incident at Camp Schwab on Nov. 3, 2026. The Marine was later declared deceased at the U.S. Naval Hospital, Camp Foster. The Marines and Sailors of 3rd Marine Division are deeply saddened by this loss," 1st Lt. Hannah Ladd said in a statement to Fox News Digital.
The Marine's death remains under investigation, the 3rd Marine Division said.

"The Marines and Sailors of 3rd Marine Division mourn the loss of one of our own. We extend our deepest condolences to Lance Cpl. Hernandez’s family, friends, and fellow Marines. Our focus remains on supporting them while we fully investigate the circumstances of this tragic incident," Maj. Gen. Kyle Ellison, commanding general of the 3rd Marine Division, said in a statement.
The 3rd Marine Division told Fox News Digital that there were no other injuries to service members.
MARINE MISSING FROM USS ANCHORAGE NOW FOCUS OF RECOVERY MISSION OFF CALIFORNIA COAST
The Marine was identified as Lance Cpl. Devin J. Hernandez, 25, of Maryland. (Yuichi YAMAZAKI / AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Roughly 50,000 U.S. troops are stationed in Japan, with most based on Okinawa. The island remained under U.S. control from the end of World War II until 1972.

Currently, nearly 80,000 Americans live on Okinawa, including about 30,000 active-duty service members from all four military branches, with the Marine Corps accounting for the largest presence there.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Behind the data: How NBC News tracked the decline in childhood vaccinations
summary: How an NBC News data investigation tracked vaccination and school exemption rates across thousands of counties in the U.S.
story: Editor’s note: This 2026 NBC News data investigation is an update of The Vaccine Divide, which was originally published in September 2025. The methodology for both projects is similar. The new data was collected from June to October 2026.
For Subscribers

For “The Vaccine Divide,” NBC News gathered massive amounts of data from state governments and archives of public records. With the help of infectious disease researchers at Stanford University, NBC News filed scores of requests for documents, including materials obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, and wrestled different types of data into a standardized format to map and compare rates across thousands of counties.
Methodology

NBC News built a database of childhood vaccination and exemption information using data provided by state governments, primarily health agencies. The data combines public information available for some states and data provided directly to NBC News.
The data covers kindergartner vaccinations for each academic year.
For Subscribers
After collection, the data was collated, and exemption rates were calculated in order to be analyzed. The analysis focuses on four facets of the data:
Medical exemptions: Exemptions granted when students have medical conditions that could make vaccination harmful.
Nonmedical exemptions: Exemptions for students who opt out of required vaccinations because of personal beliefs or religious convictions.

MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccinations: For states where data is subdivided by number of doses, MMR vaccination is counted by the second dose. Some states track measles, mumps and rubella immunization separately; in those states, measles was used to represent MMR rates.
Up-to-date vaccinations: Students are considered “up to date” with their vaccinations if they have received the full vaccination series required for enrollment in their schools.
With a hodgepodge of formats, jurisdictions and collection practices across states, the task required extensive work to ensure that possible inconsistencies in the data were managed.

Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.All data was checked for accuracy.
Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.
Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.
All data was checked for accuracy.

This analysis of childhood MMR vaccination rates focused on states that provided MMR figures for the 2025-26 school year. Accompanying the analysis were several variant analyses, which confirmed that the results were robust. The variant analyses all yielded similar results, mostly within 1 percentage point. We also examined the scale of MMR vaccination rate decline across counties, with almost 4 in 10 counties declining by over 5 percentage points since 2019 and about 1 in 8 declining by that amount since 2024. Fewer than 2% of counties declined by 0.1 percentage points or less since 2019.

Many states collect and report their data differently. Some use health districts instead of counties. Some states provided over a decade of data; others provided only two years’ worth. Some states redacted certain data because of privacy concerns.

Not all states have recent data. Florida did not provide data on kindergarten exemptions after the 2021-22 school year. Montana stopped collecting vaccine and exemption data after 2019, first because of Covid and thereafter because of the passage of a state bill (HB 334) in 2021 that struck down the mandate for the state to collect data on immunizations.Certain states (such as Arizona and Minnesota) do not collect overall “up-to-date” figures representing the percentage of kindergartners who are compliant with all required vaccines. Others (such as Florida, New Hampshire and South Carolina) provided only “up-to-date” numbers. In other states — Mississippi, New Hampshire and South Carolina — data was provided only for years K-12, rather than specifically kindergartners. West Virginia also falls into this category for its exemption data. Some states — Illinois and New York — do not collect data at grade level, so data is for elementary schools as a whole (up to K-8 for Illinois, and New York was based on headcounts, with elementary schools defined as having less than 3% enrollment above grades K-6), rather than kindergartners specifically. Hawaii also fell into this category (up to pre-K-5), as its school-level data was more consistent than its kindergarten-specific data.Other states did not provide data on a county level. Alaska and Nebraska provided data for other jurisdictions. Delaware and Rhode Island were unable to provide data at the county level; state-level figures were used instead. Indiana was unable to provide county-level exemption data. West Virginia was unable to provide county-level immunization data, but igt was able to provide exemption data per county, starting in January 2025.Some states (such as Michigan) collect data by calendar year, rather than school year.Wyoming did not consistently report data among kindergartners, so the most consistent reported value was used, instead: one-dose MMR among 19- to 35-month-olds. Accordingly, exemptions among children younger than 5 were used to correspond with this age group.Alaska was unable to provide regional exemption data for privacy reasons because of small sample sizes.

Not all states have recent data. Florida did not provide data on kindergarten exemptions after the 2021-22 school year. Montana stopped collecting vaccine and exemption data after 2019, first because of Covid and thereafter because of the passage of a state bill (HB 334) in 2021 that struck down the mandate for the state to collect data on immunizations.

Certain states (such as Arizona and Minnesota) do not collect overall “up-to-date” figures representing the percentage of kindergartners who are compliant with all required vaccines. Others (such as Florida, New Hampshire and South Carolina) provided only “up-to-date” numbers.

In other states — Mississippi, New Hampshire and South Carolina — data was provided only for years K-12, rather than specifically kindergartners. West Virginia also falls into this category for its exemption data. Some states — Illinois and New York — do not collect data at grade level, so data is for elementary schools as a whole (up to K-8 for Illinois, and New York was based on headcounts, with elementary schools defined as having less than 3% enrollment above grades K-6), rather than kindergartners specifically. Hawaii also fell into this category (up to pre-K-5), as its school-level data was more consistent than its kindergarten-specific data.

Other states did not provide data on a county level. Alaska and Nebraska provided data for other jurisdictions. Delaware and Rhode Island were unable to provide data at the county level; state-level figures were used instead. Indiana was unable to provide county-level exemption data. West Virginia was unable to provide county-level immunization data, but igt was able to provide exemption data per county, starting in January 2025.
Some states (such as Michigan) collect data by calendar year, rather than school year.

Wyoming did not consistently report data among kindergartners, so the most consistent reported value was used, instead: one-dose MMR among 19- to 35-month-olds. Accordingly, exemptions among children younger than 5 were used to correspond with this age group.
Alaska was unable to provide regional exemption data for privacy reasons because of small sample sizes.

title: GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar wins re-election in Florida after clashing with Trump
summary: NBC News projects that Salazar defeated her Democratic opponent in a heavily Hispanic, Miami-based district that Trump carried by 15 points in 2024.
story: GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has won re-election in her Miami-based congressional district, NBC News projects, after having clashed with President Donald Trump over his immigration agenda.

A recount that was completed Tuesday, one week after Election Day, showed that Salazar was narrowly ahead of her Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, by roughly 1,000 votes. In 2024, Salazar won re-election by nearly 20 percentage points.

Salazar drew national attention in September when she released an ad criticizing Trump’s aggressive deportation policy. She said that many Hispanics felt “betrayed” by the crackdown and that the administration’s tactics had “gone too far,” with many deportations targeting individuals without criminal records.

Trump carried Salazar’s district, which is heavily Hispanic, by 15 points in the 2024 presidential election. He responded to the ad by amplifying social media posts that labeled Salazar a “backstabber” and called for her to be replaced as the district’s GOP candidate.

Rodriguez, a former local news anchor, tried to capitalize on the rift. He said Salazar had become “so politically toxic that now even Daddy Trump appears to be distancing himself from his problem child.”
But Trump never officially rescinded his initial endorsement of Salazar.

The close election spurred a legal battle after Rodriguez sued Miami-Dade’s election supervisor, Alina García, last week, alleging that she was biased in favor of Salazar and should recuse herself from the recount. Rodriguez claimed that García’s son-in-law was representing Salazar in the recount, which he said raised concerns about impartiality. Rodriguez also cited an interview in which García told The Miami Herald, “Maria Elvira is the winner, with or without a recount.”

A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit Monday, saying the allegations Rodriguez laid out were not adequate grounds to remove García from carrying out her duties, while adding that García’s remarks had been “perhaps unwise.”

With one of the largest concentrations of immigrants in the U.S., Miami has been on the front lines of Trump’s deportation campaign, with more than 130,000 pending removal cases — the most of any county in the country. Salazar’s district has been heavily affected, as it spans multiple working-class, largely Hispanic enclaves, though it also encompasses some of the wealthiest ZIP codes in the nation.
Notably, the district is also home to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who previously represented Florida as a U.S. senator.
In 2024, Trump became the first Republican presidential candidate to carry Miami-Dade County in 36 years. Florida’s 27th District is now set to be home to Trump’s presidential library.

Salazar was first elected to the seat in 2020, when she defeated former Health Secretary and former University of Miami President Donna Shalala in a major upset. The victory foreshadowed the Miami area’s rightward shift in the years that followed.

title: U.S. charges 3 men with plotting multiple terror attacks, including on British air base
summary: One of the men helped direct the planned attack against the air base while he was in a U.S. prison, according to a Justice Department indictment.
story: Three men, including one already jailed in the U.S., were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S., as well as a planned assault on a British air base used by the U.S. Air Force.

Charges against Mohammad Al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali Al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in federal court in New York City.
Only Al-Saadi — an alleged pro-Iranian terrorist who is believed to have plotted attacks across Europe, Canada and the U.S., as first reported by NBC News — is in custody.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that Al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.

“As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said McDonald, whose office is handling the case.
“The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real,” he added in the statement.

The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight Sept. 27 on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.

The Justice Department indictment alleges that Al-Hassani paid associates to carry out surveillance of RAF Fairford in August and paid several people to move forward with the plot in September “by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel.”
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The group even made custom decals to give the vans the appearance that they were used by a fuel company and a swimming pool supply business, authorities say.
Al-Hassani is alleged to have then tasked the people to go to the base with the fuel when U.K. law enforcement took the men into custody.

Al-Saadi was helping direct the RAF Fairford plot while he was in a U.S. prison, according to the indictment. He made video and phone calls to his family members in Iraq, who are alleged to have passed coded messages to Al-Hassani and Mohajeri.
In a July call with his sister, Al-Saadi asked, “What are we doing about all our old work?” — a reference to terrorist activity — according to investigators.
His sister replied, “It isn’t cancelled,” investigators said.
In June, Al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran.

But the indictment alleges that the three men conspired to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata’ib Hizballah.

The european terrorist Attacks “were carried out in the name of a purportedly new terrorist group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (“HAYI”), which is actually a front for Kata’ib Hizballah,” the release said.
The U.S. government has designated Kata’ib Hizballah and the Revolutionary Guards as foreign terrorist organizations.

title: Antonio Sabàto Jr. and Virginia Madsen’s son arrested after fatal hit-and-run in Alaska
summary: The son of Oscar-nominated actress Virginia Madsen and soap star Antonio Sabàto Jr.
story: The son of Oscar-nominated actress Virginia Madsen and soap star Antonio Sabàto Jr. was arrested in connection with a fatal hit-and-run in Alaska, police said Tuesday.
Jack Antonio Sabàto, 32, was booked into the Anchorage Correctional Complex on suspicion of leaving the scene of a deadly accident and failing to assist, jail records show.

The crash happened a little before 5:48 a.m. local time Monday  when officers and medics came to the aid of an “unresponsive adult male” at the intersection of Airport Heights Drive and Debarr Road, according to an Anchorage police statement.
Carl Simmonds, a 42-year-old pedestrian, “had been struck by a vehicle, which then fled the scene,” police added. Simmonds was pronounced dead at the scene.
Later in the day, police identified the younger Sabàto as the driver who was allegedly behind the wheel of Chevrolet Tahoe, officials said.
On the screen, the elder Sabàto, 54, is best known for his work on “General Hospital” from 1992 to 1995 and “Melrose Place” in 1995.
In recent years, he has become an outspoken supporter of President Donald Trump — a political stance the actor claims has damaged his career in Hollywood.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
He addressed the Republican National Convention in 2016 on the same night as fellow Hollywood conservative Scott Baio.
“That’s (Trump) the only choice, there is no one else,” Sabàto told MSNBC from the convention floor. “I think Trump should just win it now and we can just move on and get our country back on track.”
The actor ran for Congress in 2018, losing in a safe Democratic district.
Madsen is best known for her work in the 2004 movie “Sideways” which garnered her a best supporting actress Oscar nomination.

title: Stanley Zabar, co-owner of iconic NYC gourmet food shop, dies at 94
summary: Stanley Zabar, co-owner of the famed New York City gourmet food shop, has died.
story: Stanley Zabar, co-owner of the famed New York City gourmet food shop, has died.
He was 94.
Zabar’s announced his death in a post on its Instagram on Tuesday, calling Stanley Zabar “a quiet force behind our family business.”
According to the post, Zabar worked alongside his brother, Saul Zabar, “to build upon and carry forward the vision of their parents, Louis and Lillian Zabar.”
Louis and Lillian Zabar opened the eatery on Manhattan’s Upper West Side in 1934.
The cause of death was not announced, but The New York Times reported that Zabar died from cancer, citing his daughter Dr. Sondra Zabar.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
According to the Instagram post, Zabar worked behind the scenes at the world-renowned shop, and his “legal and financial acumen was vital in shaping Zabar’s into a beloved New York City institution.”

According to the Times, Zabar handled the business side of the store but often appeared to greet customers. Saul Zabar, on the other hand, oversaw the store’s operations, taste-testing its famous smoked fish and coffee. A third partner, Murray Klein, did the store’s marketing, it reported.

Zabar and his wife, Judith Zabar, were also philanthropists, the store said in the post. The couple “dedicated their time and resources to the arts, education and culinary training,” it said, adding that they supported Hunter College, the New York Public Library, Symphony Space, NYU Langone Health and the Careers through Culinary Arts Program.

title: Pro-Palestinian protesters pelt objects at Biden outside Irish university
summary: Three men have been arrested after protesters pelted objects at  former President Joe Biden during protests outside a university in Dublin, police in Ireland said.
story: Three men have been arrested after protesters pelted objects at  former President Joe Biden outside a university in Dublin, police in Ireland said Wednesday.

Videos showed protesters, some waving Palestinian flags, chanting “Blood on your hands” and scuffling with police officers outside Trinity College Dublin on Tuesday, as he attended a ceremony honoring his son Hunter Biden, alongside former first lady Jill Biden. White liquid, believed to be milk, could also be seen flying through the air toward the group.

Hunter Biden was being honored by its traditional Hist debating society, which dates back to 1770. Previous recipients of the gold medal for outstanding contribution to public discourse include Irish musician Bob Geldof, South African Bishop Desmond Tutu, WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange and the late Sen. Ted Kennedy.

During his acceptance speech, Hunter Biden discussed his addictions, family life and being in the public eye. “We are living in an age of bullies,” he said, adding that he had learned this from “my own scars.”
Shortly after the ceremony, a “protest took place in Trinity’s Front Square,” Catherine O’Mahony, a spokesperson for the college, said in a statement to NBC News on Wednesday.

She said “the protest escalated while the Bidens were leaving,” and Irish police, known as the Gardaí, arrived at the scene. “The Biden family left without incident. The protest dispersed soon after,” she added.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Police said in a statement Wednesday that three adult males were arrested “in relation to a public order incident” at Trinity College Dublin. One man in his 50s “has since been charged and is due to appear before Court. The two other males have been released without charge.” The statement did not say what the man had been charged with.
Representatives for the elder Biden did not immediately reply to a request for comment about the incident.
Ireland has long had a historical solidarity with the Palestinian cause, with pro-Palestinian flags, murals and graffiti a common sight around the country.

Many in the country compare the current situation in Gaza and the occupied West Bank with Ireland’s experience of British colonial rule and struggle for self-determination. Ireland was also the recent venue for American rapper Macklemore’s sold-out “Free Palestine Tour,” which opened in Dublin last month.
The Bidens, who have Irish heritage, also met with Ireland’s Taoiseach, or prime minister, Micheál Martin.
“We reflected on his strong Irish roots and previous visits, appreciating his lifelong support for Ireland,” Martin said in a post on X, of his meeting with the former president.
During a 2023 visit to the country while he was president, Biden told the Irish parliament in an emotional address that he was “home.”

Biden’s great-great-grandfather Owen Finnegan left the Irish county of Louth for the United States in 1849, and he also has relatives from another side of his family in County Mayo, on Ireland’s west coast.
Earlier this week, Biden, 83, signaled he was scaling back public tours to promote his upcoming memoir “Promise Me, America,” as he continues his treatment for cancer.
“Some days are better than others,” Biden wrote Sunday in a lengthy post on X. “It hasn’t stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down.”

Biden announced that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer months after he left office in January 2025 and has since undertaken courses of radiation therapy and hormone treatment.
He said his doctors were “encouraged by how I’ve responded to treatment” and thanked the public for their prayers and well-wishes.

title: Man United coach faces exit as fans vent fury at U.S. owners after worst start in 40 years
summary: Michael Carrick is set to be relieved of his duties soon after one of the world’s biggest clubs has totaled only 8 points through 10 matches.
story: Manchester United is in 18th place as the Premier League heads into a two-week international break. The start — Manchester United’s worst since 1986 — is unthinkable for one of the world’s richest and most popular clubs. Just last season, it finished third behind Arsenal and Manchester City and showed signs of competing for a title in the near future.
Now it’s in disarray. Much of the blame has been placed on manager Michael Carrick, who is expected to be relieved of his duties as soon as this week.

The most glaring issues are defensive, as United has conceded 19 goals in the Premier League. That’s the same number as newly promoted side Coventry City, whose squad costs about one-third as much as United’s. Injuries and lack of roster depth have forced the team to shuffle different combinations of players from game to game. Fans have bemoaned the club’s decision not to sign any new defenders over the summer.

Critics have also pointed to one of the simplest parts of the game — running. Per Gradient Sports data, Manchester United is 19th out of 20 in the league in both distance covered and average maximum speed. Statistics like those never tell the full story, but covering ground is essential to winning back the ball effectively.
The situation has gotten so bad that even star midfielder Bruno Fernandes called out his team after a 4-1 loss at Como in Italy last month in the UEFA Champions League.

“It’s not the first time we started on the wrong foot and they scored very early,” said Fernandes, who was benched the next game for his comments. “Not much pressure on the ball, not really many good movements without the ball, not many things going our way.”

But while Carrick has received criticism, many fans don’t appear ready to completely turn on their manager, continuing to sing his name after recent defeats. After all, Carrick was a beloved player for Manchester United who manned the proverbial engine room in midfield during the late 2000s — one of the most successful stretches in club history.

The supporters’ anxiety appears to be caused more by the players and ownership. During the draw with Villa, fans chanted “You’re not fit to wear the shirt” at the 11 men on the field. Last week against AS Roma, fans released thousands of green and gold balloons — the colors the club wore at its founding in 1878 before it rebranded to red in 1902 — in protest of the Glazer family, which owns a majority interest in the club.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

The balloons were back at the Aston Villa game Sunday. Fans also unfurled signs that read “We don’t want a new stadium, we want new owners,” and “Your funeral, not ours. Sell up.” The escalating protests come just a week after Gary Neville, a former United player and one of the most prominent pundits in the sport, called for the Glazers to sell their stake.
Recent comments by co-owner Avram Glazer added fuel to the fire that the family doesn’t care about winning as long as its asset remains profitable.

Last week, an anonymous source from a September Deutsche Bank investment conference told The Athletic that Glazer said Manchester United can be commercially powerful without success on the field. The report said Glazer compared his club to American franchises like the New York Yankees or the Dallas Cowboys, who have not won a Super Bowl for 30 years and counting.
Regardless of the on-field success, you can’t deny that the Glazers have overseen massive investment in the team.

title: Kennedy family members seek to block construction of Trump’s arch
summary: Nine family members seek to join a lawsuit against the arch, arguing it would cast a shadow over the site where some of their notable relatives are buried.
story: Nine members of the Kennedy family asked a federal judge in Washington on Tuesday for permission to join the legal battle against President Donald Trump’s planned “triumphal” arch, arguing the structure would cast a shadow over some of their relatives’ graves.

The Kennedys said the arch’s planned location in the nation’s capital would also obstruct the clear sight line from the John F. Kennedy Eternal Flame memorial across the Arlington Memorial Bridge to the Lincoln Memorial, which the family called “an essential element” of the design.

The high-profile request once again pits one of the most storied families in American history against Trump. The two sides have also sparred over Trump’s attempt to remake the Kennedy Center. Trump closed the arts institution after a judge blocked him from adding his name to the building.
The Kennedys asking to join the suit include seven of Robert F. Kennedy’s living children — all except Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

In a statement, Rory Kennedy and Maxwell Kennedy said the request was about “protecting sacred spaces,” adding that they believed Trump had “violated the laws and procedures established by Congress to protect this most sacred national memorial.”

“A towering arch casting shadows across the graves of our father, mother, and uncles, as well as the graves of so many who have served our country, would also cast a shadow over our democratic principles, undermining the safeguards established by our elected representatives to protect this hallowed ground for generations to come,” the statement said.

The District of Columbia and Virginia, as well as Vietnam War veteran and former U.S. ambassador Michael Lemmon, had sued over the project. The Kennedys asked to join both suits, arguing they have a “direct, immediate stake in this matter and claims that share common questions of law.”

The arch is set to be built on Memorial Circle, between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial in Washington. It is designed to stand at 250 feet tall, more than twice the height of the Lincoln Memorial.
A federal judge blocked construction on the project last week, shortly after a planning board with a majority of Trump-aligned members voted to approve it.
Kennedy family members buried at Arlington include President John F. Kennedy, first lady Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, Attorney General Robert F. Kennedy and Sen. Ted Kennedy.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
The Kennedys asking to join the suit argue they have “a unique interest” in the property.

“As members of the Kennedy family, intervenors have a particular interest in protecting the Kennedy Gravesites, ensuring that these Gravesites remain unimpeded as a solemn and sacred memorial to the legacy of the Kennedy family,” they wrote.
White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in response to the suit that the administration is “confident we will be fully vindicated as this litigation proceeds.”

“It is unfortunate to see that some members of the Kennedy family have joined the litigation against the Arch as the project is intended to honor our heroes who rest in Arlington Cemetery,” Ingle said in a statement. “The judiciary should not be abused to politicize a structure designed to unite our nation.”

title: Antonio Sabàto Jr. and Virginia Madsen’s son arrested after fatal hit-and-run in Alaska
summary: The son of Oscar-nominated actress Virginia Madsen and soap star Antonio Sabàto Jr.
story: The son of Oscar-nominated actress Virginia Madsen and soap star Antonio Sabàto Jr. was arrested in connection with a fatal hit-and-run in Alaska, police said Tuesday.
Jack Antonio Sabàto, 32, was booked into the Anchorage Correctional Complex on suspicion of leaving the scene of a deadly accident and failing to assist, jail records show.

The crash happened a little before 5:48 a.m. local time Monday  when officers and medics came to the aid of an “unresponsive adult male” at the intersection of Airport Heights Drive and Debarr Road, according to an Anchorage police statement.
Carl Simmonds, a 42-year-old pedestrian, “had been struck by a vehicle, which then fled the scene,” police added. Simmonds was pronounced dead at the scene.
Later in the day, police identified the younger Sabàto as the driver who was allegedly behind the wheel of Chevrolet Tahoe, officials said.
On the screen, the elder Sabàto, 54, is best known for his work on “General Hospital” from 1992 to 1995 and “Melrose Place” in 1995.
In recent years, he has become an outspoken supporter of President Donald Trump — a political stance the actor claims has damaged his career in Hollywood.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
He addressed the Republican National Convention in 2016 on the same night as fellow Hollywood conservative Scott Baio.
“That’s (Trump) the only choice, there is no one else,” Sabàto told MSNBC from the convention floor. “I think Trump should just win it now and we can just move on and get our country back on track.”
The actor ran for Congress in 2018, losing in a safe Democratic district.
Madsen is best known for her work in the 2004 movie “Sideways” which garnered her a best supporting actress Oscar nomination.

title: Stanley Zabar, co-owner of iconic NYC gourmet food shop, dies at 94
summary: Stanley Zabar, co-owner of the famed New York City gourmet food shop, has died.
story: Stanley Zabar, co-owner of the famed New York City gourmet food shop, has died.
He was 94.
Zabar’s announced his death in a post on its Instagram on Tuesday, calling Stanley Zabar “a quiet force behind our family business.”
According to the post, Zabar worked alongside his brother, Saul Zabar, “to build upon and carry forward the vision of their parents, Louis and Lillian Zabar.”
Louis and Lillian Zabar opened the eatery on Manhattan’s Upper West Side in 1934.
The cause of death was not announced, but The New York Times reported that Zabar died from cancer, citing his daughter Dr. Sondra Zabar.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers
According to the Instagram post, Zabar worked behind the scenes at the world-renowned shop, and his “legal and financial acumen was vital in shaping Zabar’s into a beloved New York City institution.”

According to the Times, Zabar handled the business side of the store but often appeared to greet customers. Saul Zabar, on the other hand, oversaw the store’s operations, taste-testing its famous smoked fish and coffee. A third partner, Murray Klein, did the store’s marketing, it reported.

Zabar and his wife, Judith Zabar, were also philanthropists, the store said in the post. The couple “dedicated their time and resources to the arts, education and culinary training,” it said, adding that they supported Hunter College, the New York Public Library, Symphony Space, NYU Langone Health and the Careers through Culinary Arts Program.

title: Woman apologizes for making racist gestures outside Ole Miss students’ apartment
summary: The University of Mississippi is investigating the incident after a video caught two women mimicking apes outside three Black students’ front door.
story: One of the two young women seen on a viral video making racist gestures outside the apartment of three Black Ole Miss students apologized for her actions.

Alaina Kunes, 18, said in a statement Tuesday that she did not know the people who lived in the apartment and was “unaware of their race” until the Ring doorbell camera video that captured the moment Friday gained national attention.

The video shows Kunes and two other women walking by the front door of the off-campus apartment where the three Black Ole Miss students live. Kunes is seen beating her chest. She and a second woman, who has not been identified and has not commented on the incident, make ape noises. A third woman in the video just walks by without stopping at the door.
“To the women I offended and to the Ole Miss community, I sincerely apologize,” Kunes said in her statement. “I recognize my actions were insensitive, inappropriate, and deeply harmful.”
Kunes said she apologized to the women who live in the apartment directly. “I pray they will forgive me,” she said.

“I can never truly understand the pain I have caused them and it was never my intention. These girls deserve to feel seen and understood and what I did is not a reflection of who I am trying to become,” Kunes said.
The University of Mississippi launched an investigation into the incident, Shawnboda Mead, the school’s vice chancellor for student affairs, said in an email sent to the campus Sunday.
In it, Mead described the viral video as “showing University of Mississippi students engaging in racist gestures directed toward other students.”
Kunes has since withdrawn from the university, a source close to the 18-year-old told NBC News. It’s unclear what the enrollment status is of the other women in the video.
The University of Mississippi did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday.
For Subscribers
For Subscribers

Tasha Bolton, the mother of one of the three Black Ole Miss students, wrote about the incident in a Facebook post Saturday. Bolton said her daughter is a freshman at the university and lives in the off-campus apartment with two Black roommates. She described the women filmed on the doorbell camera as her daughter’s upstairs neighbors.

“This is absolutely disgusting and unacceptable. College is supposed to be a place where young adults can learn, grow, and feel safe,” Bolton said about the video in her post. “We want answers. Specifically, what steps will be taken to address this behavior and ensure accountability?”
Kunes said she intends to fully cooperate with the university’s investigation.

“I would have never intentionally made those noises or gestures toward a person of color,” she said in her statement apologizing for the incident. “I understand the seriousness of this situation and remain committed to taking responsibility and learning from this embarrassing ordeal.”
Kunes also requested privacy for herself and her family and alleged that they have been harassed over the past several days and received death threats.

The American Civil Liberties Union of Mississippi is also looking into complaints it has received about the incident, Candi Richardson, the organization’s director of communications and community engagement, said Monday.

title: See How TODAY Covered Prince Charles and Princess Diana’s Wedding in 1981
summary: TODAY covered the wedding of Prince Charles and Princess Diana in 1981. We look back on the day.
story: As TODAY marks its 75th anniversary, the TODAY Archive is revisiting legendary interviews, stories that moved us and other iconic moments from our 75 years on the air. These are the segments that shaped TODAY and created a lasting legacy. Today, we look back at the wedding of Prince Charles and Princess Diana on July 29, 1981.
The term “fairy tale wedding” looked like it came to life when Prince Charles and Lady Diana Spencer got married on July 29, 1981 at St. Paul’s Cathedral in London, England.
It was one of the most high profile weddings of the 20th century, completely capturing the public’s attention. The broadcast was watched by 750 million people in 74 countries, according to the BBC.
TODAY Had a ‘Splendid Morning’ From the UK
Tom Brokaw and Jane Pauley were on hand in the U.K. to report on the royal wedding. The two anchors sat at a desk decked out in the  Union Flag.

“Good morning everyone and welcome to the NBC News coverage  of the royal wedding,” Brokaw said at the top of the show. “By now, we should not have to tell you it is the royal wedding of his Royal Highness, the Prince of Wales, to Lady Diana Spencer, who in just a few hours will become the Princess of Wales.”
As he introduced himself and Pauley, she called it “a splendid morning.”
A View of Queen Elizabeth II, Prince Philip and Guests
Before the soon-to-be-husband and wife made their grand appearance, TODAY showed Queen Elizabeth II and husband Prince Philip with their traditional escorts, waving to people from their carriage.
Viewers then saw the bride and groom making their grand appearances in their respective carriages.
“Here comes the bride,” said Pauley.
Other noteworthy guests included Nancy Reagan and Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.
Diana’s Grand and Elegant Entrance
Viewers got to see Diana in an ivory taffeta gown adorned with sequins and 10,000 pearls. It also had a 25-foot train that was longer than any other worn before her by a British royal bride.

“Why, she’s floating,” Pauley said as the bride emerged from her carriage to enter St. Paul’s Cathedral. “The dress does appear to float up the steps and I had underestimated the length of a 25-foot train.”
A Slight Mistake In the Ceremony
The ceremony did feature one flub, though. During the vows, Diana referred to Charles as “Philip Charles Arthur George” rather than Charles Philip Arthur George.
“Well, he does have a lot of names and she got them slightly out of sequence,” Brokaw said, reading off the correct order of the groom’s names. “Nervousness is to be expected.”
Procession Back to Buckingham Palace and Balcony Appearance
After their wedding ceremony, they rode back to Buckingham Palace together.
“The curtains are open, that’s the signal,” Pauley said as the newlyweds made their way to the balcony.

Princess Diana would go on to reflect on her wedding in the 2017 National Geographic documentary, “Diana: In Her Own Words,” which used audio from a series of interviews she gave for her biography, “Diana: Her True Story.”

“I remember being so in love with my husband that I couldn’t take my eyes off him. I just absolutely thought I was the luckiest girl in the world and you know, he was going to look after me,” she said.
However, Princess Diana would go on to call the wedding “the worst day of my life” in the documentary, also expressing doubts about the marriage after the engagement.

The two welcomed their first child, William, in 1982, followed by Harry in 1984. The couple ultimately separated in 1992 before they officially divorced in 1996. Princess Diana would die in a car accident in 1997.
